title: Frederick Douglass Day - Rainy Forecast For Saturday Moves Some Events Indoors
content:
Frederick Douglass Day - Rainy Forecast For Saturday Moves Some Events Indoors

 September 21, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1277
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Due to a rainy weather forecast for Saturday, organizers for Frederick Douglass Day are modifying some parts of the event and relocating others.This year is the first year that the Frederick Douglass Honor Society has faced unfavorable weather for the annual event, said Debbi Dodson, the society's event planner and marketing chair.The Frederick Douglass Parade, which was scheduled to kick off at 10 a.m., will be canceled. The planned outdoor marketplace, which would have featured food and retail vendors and notfor-profit organizations, also will be canceled.Locations for the day's other outdoor activities have been changed.The welcome ceremony, originally scheduled to begin at 10:30 a.m. at the Talbot County Courthouse, will be moved to the Talbot County Free Library's meeting room at the same time.All Children's Village activities, which kick off at 11 a.m., will be held indoors at the Talbot County Free Library's children's areas.Performances at the Frederick Douglass Entertainment Stage will still begin at noon, but they will be held at the Avalon Theatre.All other Frederick Douglass Day activities follow the event's original schedule and will be held in the original locations.Despite the less than ideal forecast, gratitude is plentiful.Dodson said the Frederick Douglass Honor Society is "overwhelmed" by the generosity from the Avalon Theatre and the Talbot County Free Library in opening space for the event's activities and keeping the day going.The Frederick Douglass Honor Society joined with the Town of Easton, the Talbot County Free Library, and Talbot County to celebrate the life and legacy of Frederick Douglass on Saturday.Frederick Douglass Day, the Honor Society's hallmark event, features Frederick Douglass artifacts (courtesy of the National Park Service), lecture, book signings, a children's village, and the Frederick Douglass Geocaching Trail. All Frederick Douglass Day activities are free and open to the public.Frederick Douglass once said "It is always a fact of some importance to know where a man is born, if, indeed, it be important to know anything about him." Born in Talbot County in 1818, Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey was the son of Harriet Bailey, an enslaved field worker, and an unknown white man.Like most enslaved children, he was separated from his mother at birth and raised by his maternal grandmother, Betsy Bailey, until the age of 7. Enslaved for 20 years in Baltimore and on Talbot County farms, he fled north in 1838 and changed his name to Frederick Douglass.His brilliance, eloquence, and courage, quickly brought him to the forefront of the abolitionist movement."In listening to him", wrote a contemporary, "your whole soul is fired, every nerve strung „Ÿ every faculty you possess ready to perform at a moment's bidding." At the age of 27, Frederick Douglass authored his first autobiography, "Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave," written by Himself.It became not only a best seller but an important influence on the abolition movement and the nation at large.Toward the end of 1854 and during the first few months of 1855, Douglass worked on his ultimate declaration, "My Bondage and My Freedom." A more mature writer now, he delved deeper into the meaning of his life's story. Today the work is seen as his masterpiece, one that holds a place of prominence in American literature.Frederick Douglass changed the way people regard democracy and slavery.He strongly believed that all humans, regardless of race or gender, are created equal.He said, "In the struggle for justice, the only reward is the opportunity to be in the struggle. You can't expect that you're going to have it tomorrow. You just have to keep working on it." Douglass's message holds true today; he remains a man for all generations.Jeff McGuiness, a photographer, writer, and resident of St. Michaels, will sign copies of his beautiful 250-page, large format book, "Bear Me Into Freedom: The Talbot County of Frederick Douglass" at Vintage Books & Fine Arts, 4 N Washington Street, from 10 a.m. until 1 p.m.The Frederick Douglass Day Welcome Ceremony begins at 10:30 a.m. in the library meeting room and features guest speakers Childlene Brooks, vice President of the Frederick Douglass Honor Society; the Rev. Keith Beckett, pastor of St. Johns United Methodist Church; Mayor Megan Cook, the Town of Easton; Dana Newman, director of the Talbot County Free Library; Sharon Pepukayi, superintendent of Talbot County Public Schools; Devon Beck, facilitator of Equity, Diversity and Inclusion at Talbot County Public Schools, and Annie Mewborn, assistant principal at Easton Elementary School.Music will be provided by the Easton High and Middle School Bands, and Hip Hop Artist Baba Bomani. Other participants include BAAM (Building African American Minds) and Easton High School's NJROTC. Autumn Redman, an Easton High School senior, will serve as mistress of ceremonies.The Frederick Douglass Day Children's Village is always a hit with children and parents alike. It will be held in the children's area of the library.There will be free Frederick Douglass coloring books, hands-on-activities, a mapping game showing where Frederick Douglass lived and traveled, story time with Shauna Beulah „Ÿ Talbot County Free Library's St. Michaels branch manager „Ÿ face-painting, stickers, prizes, and the opportunity to have your picture taken with Frederick Douglass.The Children's Village is open from 11:30 a.m. to 3 p.m.Frederick Douglass Day will also serve as the kickoff event for a new children's program at the library: the Frederick Douglass Reading Challenge. The challenge is simple: young people from 6 to 18 years of age will have the chance to enter a raffle to win one of three $50 Target gift certificates every time they successfully read a biography of Frederick Douglass.The library has plenty of these „Ÿ suitable for all ages „Ÿ at both its St. Michaels and Easton branches.The Frederick Douglass Day Live Entertainment Stage will be relocated to the Avalon Theatre. Mistress of Ceremony Charlene DeShields will present an amazing lineup of entertainers, including hip hop artist Baba Bomani, the Covenant Gospel Choir, Randall Butler, and DJ Allen Butler.It's a great time to sing along, dance and enjoy terrific music.In the vendors' area near the library, attendees will find delicious regional food and beverages. The vendors' area will also feature retailers, as well as, representatives of local organizations sharing their community initiatives and volunteer opportunities.Robert S. Levine, author of "The Failed Promise, Reconstruction, Frederick Douglass, and the Impeachment of Andrew Johnson," will sign copies of his book at 11:30 a.m. at Flying Cloud Booksellers, 26 W. Dover St. Levine, a professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, is the general editor of "The Norton Anthology of American Literature." At the Talbot County Free Library, Autumn Redman will show attendees how they can have fun on her Girl Scout Gold Award Action Project: "The Frederick Douglass Geocache Trail." The fun begins with a passport book that includes a map and geocache coordinates.At each stop, along the way, geocachers can read about the location's connection to Frederick Douglass and stamp their passport.When all stops have been visited, geocachers will receive a commemorative coin and a picture of Douglass.The 2023 Frederick Douglass Lecture (1 p.m. at the Talbot County Free Library) features distinguished University of Delaware Associate Professor and Cochran Scholar Derrick Spires, who specializes in early African American print culture, citizenship studies and African American intellectual history.His first book, "The Practice of Citizenship: Black Politics and Print Culture in the Early United States" (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2019), traces the parallel development of early black print culture and a distinct African American concept of U.S. citizenship.Spires appeared in the recent film, "Becoming Frederick Douglass." A book signing will follow his lecture.

title: New digital comics at Smithsonian explore lives of women artists
content:
New digital comics at Smithsonian explore lives of women artists

 September 25, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 496
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Smithsonian American Art Museum has published 10 new digital comics, each celebrating a woman artist represented in the museum's permanent collection.The trailblazing artists featured in the 2023 set of the series "Drawn to Art: Tales of Inspiring Women Artists" are Laura Aguilar, Tanya Aguiñiga, Emma Amos, Chitra Ganesh, Barbara Jones-Hogu, Sister Gertrude Morgan, Miriam Schapiro, Lilly Martin Spencer, Wendy Red Star (Apsáalooke/Crow) and Consuelo Jimenez Underwood. This latest group of comics marks the third installment of the museum's online series since launching in 2021."Seeing the stories of women artists made central in this creative project from the nation's preeminent museum of American art gives girls and women a chance to see themselves represented and to draw inspiration from these shared experiences," said Stephanie Stebich, the Margaret and Terry Stent director of the Smithsonian American Art Museum. "The 'Drawn to Art' project captures wonderfully SAAM's role, whether in person or online, as a place that creates connection, wonder and understanding."Inspired by graphic novels and web comics, these short takes on artists' lives were drawn by 10 student-illustrators from Ringling College of Art and Design as part of the college's INDEX (Industry Experience) program. The participating illustrators are Sky Chandler, Ati Gor, Stephanie Hunton, Elena May binti Saini Jeffery, Zahra Merchant, Irene Pae, Ana Parra, Sami Sulzer, Tyler Tjaden and Catherine Vo. The project provides valuable professional experience for Ringling students who learn to work collaboratively, meet deadlines and address formatting and accessibility requirements.Through this digital storytelling project, the museum is connecting with middle-grade readers and their adult teachers and caregivers who may share the comics with younger people in their lives or use them as teaching resources.The life stories of the selected artists provide readers with a chance to identify with the struggles and the triumphs of the women artists depicted in the comics, to see elements of their own stories reflected and to draw strength from that visibility.Since its debut, the digital series has featured the stories of American women artists from throughout the 20th and 21st centuries, including Berenice Abbott, Anni Albers, Romaine Brooks, Maria Oakey Dewing, Carmen Herrera, Corita Kent, Edmonia Lewis, Kay Sekimachi, Alma Thomas and Mickalene Thomas. The museum published a second set of comics in 2022, featuring Judy Baca, Tiffany Chung, Sonya Clark, Sarah Goodridge, Ester Hernandez, Loïs Mailou Jones, Jaune Quick-to-See Smith (Confederated Salish and Kootenai Nation), Nellie Mae Rowe, Augusta Savage and Kay WalkingStick (Cherokee Nation). All 30 comics are available on the museum's website.Several of the artists celebrated in the series - Baca, Chung, Herrera, Jones-Hogu, Morgan, Schapiro, Alma Thomas, Mickalene Thomas, Underwood and WalkingStick - are represented in the museum's new modern and contemporary art galleries, which reopened to the public Sept. 22. This resource extends the museum's commitment to creating and making widely accessible digital content that enhances and complements the permanent collection reinstallation project.

title: Artist says, 'That's where my joy is' - Naluai paints military-themed mural on Southern Maryland American Legion
author: Michael Reid; mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Artist says, 'That's where my joy is' - Naluai paints military-themed mural on Southern Maryland American Legion

 September 26, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid; mreid@somdnews.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 849
 Words 

 Read News Document

 She may not be Wonder Woman, Catwoman or the Black Widow, but artist Jamie Naluai definitely has a superpower, and she tapped into that recently while painting a military mural for American Legion Post 221 in Avenue.The Great Mills artist was commissioned to paint on the side of the Post headquarters and had to go to her special skill set while outlining the mural."I like to joke that my superpower is painting fine lines with a 20-foot pole," said Naluai, who is also an art teacher at Bay Montesorri School in Lexington Park and an adjunct professor at St. Mary's College of Maryland in the Career Pathways Program.Naluai painted various members of different branches of the military along with a C-130, U.S.Coast Guard helicopter, U.S.Navy destroyer and a satellite to represent the Space Force program."I think it's turning out great," Americanisms Program Chairman Mike Barbour said. "With the vibrant colors you can see it going down the road. I think [it's turning out better] maybe more [than I thought]." "It is great to see we have that kind of talent in our county and to be able to see it every day going back and forth from home really fills me with pride," Commissioner Scott Ostrow (R) said at the Aug. 29 county commissioners' meeting. "[And also] that we have these organizations in the county and that they are so proud of our nation and all of our service members." Naluai said she immediately began to process the 34-by-10-foot blank wall space she had in front of her."I take a look at the wall.I take a look at the space and then it's a composition piece," she said. "Where do I want things? Where will they fit? [I knew the] helicopter was going to be the focal point." She added the C-130 when a Legion member looked at the wall and told her he wanted the plane he flew to be included."I wanted [the mural] to show movement and different activity," she said.She said because specialty golden acrylic paint costs about $100 a gallon - it can withstand UV rays and last up to 20 years - that she purchased just four colors: Phthalo Blue, Pyrrole Red, Burnt Sienna and Hooker Green."I'm a master color theory mixer," she said, adding that she purchases orange because it is the hardest to mix.She began the mural by using her "superpower" to make a brown outline, which a friend's father later saw and mistakenly thought it had been graffitied.She said she did "lots and lots" of research to get everything just right, particularly the insignias.Naluai was recommended to the Legion from some of her past murals, and she said she immediately liked the space."We floated the idea and asked if she would be able to do it," Barbour said, "We made a site visit and she said, 'Yeah, I think I could do some creative things.'" Naluai originally intended to use red, blue and white and then paint silhouettes and vehicles in black."After she presented, everyone said, 'Wow, that's fantastic,'" Barbour said."And then she said, 'Well, you know it may not cost you anything because the Maryland State Arts Council has grant money. It was a real nice bomb she dropped." Naluai is expecting to finish the mural by the end of October."I told by husband I could come back and work on it a whole year just because I'm that particular, but there has to be a balance because it has to get done," she said."It really makes my heart feel good when people say 'It looks amazing.' I am so proud of it. And it makes me happy to do these things in our own backyard." She is also painting a mural on the other side of the Legion, which will depict a Continental soldier with modern children holding their hands over their hearts.Naluai is also currently working with a group of artists from a recent mural workshop in conjunction with the St. Mary's Arts Council, the county's recreation and parks department and Yellow Line on public murals at Dorsey Park, Chaptico Park and Lexington Manor Passive Park in Lexington Park."Anytime I can get my hands on a new wall and work with clients and collaborate," she said, "that's where my joy is." Twitter:@MichaelSoMdNews

title: North Caroline band participates in exhibition
author: Laura Tayman
content:
North Caroline band participates in exhibition

 September 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman | Page: 21 | Section: News 
 
 733
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE - The thumping of the bass drum and the melodic lines of brass soared throughout Kent Island on Saturday as the high school band hosted Maryland's first marching band exhibition of the season.Bands from Wicomico, James M. Bennett, and Parkside high schools in Salisbury, as well as North Caroline in Ridgely, joined the Kent Island High School Band in performing their own ten-minute show on the football field. Each band received comments in the categories of Visual Effect, Music Effect, Ensemble Music, Visual Analysis, and Percussion."The Kent Island Marching Buccaneers started their season in May, rehearsing throughout the summer with weekly rehearsals and a Band Camp," said Kent Island band director Kimberly Scully. "They currently rehearse two nights per week in addition to playing in football games and competing in Maryland Marching Band Association competitions on Saturdays throughout September and October."Their season will culminate at the State Championship at Towson University on November 4.Scully, who came to Kent Island in 2015, grew up in New Jersey and participated in drum and bugle corps for years. She has spent the last six years as a music and visual instructor with the U.S.Naval Academy Drum and Bugle Corps in Annapolis.As in athletics, students who play and practice together experience a strong bond and a myriad of life skills such as commitment, perseverance, collaboration, and leadership. "Students can continue their passion for the marching arts in college, oftentimes with scholarship opportunities," said Scully.Events like this would not be possible without the high school's Band Booster volunteers as well as the support from the Kent Island High School administration. Band parent volunteers did everything from staffing the ticket booth and welcome tent, to directing parking lot traffic, to announcing the bands."Our job is to focus on the bands and make sure they have everything they need," said Band Booster President Noemi Navarro.In a side parking lot, the participating bands arrived early, and began their preshow drills, warm-ups, and show reminders.Clifton Griffin, Band Booster President at James M. Bennett High School, was one of many parents busily unloading equipment before the event, making sure that the band would be ready with their show when the time came."We would do anything for these kids. It's hard to explain what being in the band means to them," said Griffin. "They have found their people. It is a place where they belong, and that is very powerful."Tailynn Miron is this year's drum major for the North Caroline High School in Ridgely. Dressed in an all-black dress and boots (as was the entire color guard), she is supporting the show's theme based on the Netflix show "Wednesday" from the "Addams Family.""Being a drum major taught me a different mentality," said Miron. "I'm learning how to be a good leader, that patience is the key. I want to be great for my peers."Spencer Koppenol, director for the Parkside High School Band in Salisbury, said this "preview" show was important for the improvement of the band throughout the fall. "It's important to get initial feedback so the students can be more successful.The Parkside show's theme is "Echols from the Sea" with a focus on the environmental disasters to the earth's coral reefs, with Mother Nature trying to restore what humans have done."I'm so thankful for the work the students have put in, especially after the devastating effects of Covid," said Koppenol. "It's wonderful that students and parents are starting to come back and commit to the season."James M. Bennett High School's Douglas Myles is enjoying his 44th year as a music teacher. He is Eastern Shore born and bred, having graduated from Easton High School and Salisbury State.He has taught music for all grade levels throughout the years, including James M. Bennett for 25 years."I wouldn't do anything else," said Myles as he congratulated each student when they came off the field."I have wonderful support from the parents and such commitment from the students."Kate Fachet, last year's Drum Major for Kent Island and who is now a Naval Academy plebe, was wearing her whites as she viewed the band rehearsing before their scheduled time. "It's nice to come back and visit the students and Ms. Scully," said Fachet. "It brought back good memories."

title: Capturing life on the water - Photographer's image featured on Rock Hall FallFest poster
author: Bob Ford
content:
Capturing life on the water - Photographer's image featured on Rock Hall FallFest poster

 September 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bob Ford | Page: 5 | Section: News 
 
 846
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ROCK HALL - Continuing the Rock Hall Fall-Fest tradition of honoring the waterman's heritage of this bayside town, the Fall-Fest committee announced that the annual event poster this year features an image by the late Heather R. Davidson, an award-winning local photographer and longtime chronicler of life on the water.With cooperation from her family, Davidson's "Carole Ann at Dawn" is the centerpiece of the poster to promote the 26th annual Fall-Fest, which will be held Saturday, Oct. 14 on Main Street from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m."It feels wonderful to have people there still remember her and include her pictures in local events. She would be thrilled," said Gail Iler, Davidson's daughter. "She took pictures of many wonderful things, a lot of which don't exist any more."Rock Hall FallFest is a non-profit street fair that features live music on two stages throughout the day, with lots of great music and plenty of food and drink. A portion of proceeds from this year's event go to support the Kent County Waterman's Association scholarship fund, and to the The Mainstay, the iconic music venue that is the beating heart of Main Street.Heather Davidson, who died last year at the age of 92, left behind a treasure trove of photographs concerning the water and watermen.She lived on Eastern Neck Road for 25 years and her work was featured in National Geographic, Field & Stream, Ducks Unlimited, Washingtonian, and many other publications. A exhibition of her photographs hung in the rotunda of the Smithsonian Institution, and she produced the cover for two Sierra Club books on the Chesapeake Bay, and authored two books of photographs, including her seminal work, "Maryland's Chesapeake Bay Watermen, 1985-2005."Davidson began photographing watermen at the suggestion of her husband, Tuck Davidson, in the 1980s."He felt very strongly that things were changing on the water and things were becoming modern, and that there should be documentation of the old ways," Davidson said, in an interview. "He found a waterman, paid the man, came home and told me I was going to take a boat ride."Davidson took many rides over the years and captured the ways of commercial fishermen, crabbers, eelers, clammers, and oystermen.They loved being subjects of the photographic history being compiled by a celebrated photographer."The watermen seemed to sense that things were changing quickly, and they appeared anxious to have their part of the story documented on film," Davidson wrote, in the epilogue to one of her books. "I remember stopping by Martin Legg's welding shop in Rock Hall one day with my camera in my hand. He was busy repairing a clam rig. As I started to introduce myself, he turned to me and, in a very disappointed voice said, 'What took you so long to get to me?'" The image chosen for this year's poster is of the workboat "Carole Ann" with one of the crew checking the bottom for a promising oyster bed. It is a classic example of Davidson's innate sense of composition, letting the colors of the sunrise, as it emerges from the tree line, put the boat, and a nearby companion workboat, in gentle, timeless silhouette."In her mind, that was her legacy, a way to give back to the community," said Iler, Davidson's daughter. "It's there forever. She loved going out with the watermen, and felt she was preserving that legacy."A limited run of numbered poster prints featuring an authentic reproduction of Davidson's signature will be offered at the FallFest merchandise booth on Main Street, and visitors can own a piece of festival history. The prints, suitable for framing, sealed in a protective, backed slipcase, are offered for $25.Also available, in an extremely limited amount, is the 2021 poster featuring an image painted by the late local artist Jack Fancher, and the 2022 poster featuring a dramatic bulkhead photo by JP Henry. Both of those past collectibles are signed and numbered and are offered at $20 each. The entire set of three posters is available for $50.There are FallFest T-shirts on sale, with the event logo on the front and the poster image on the back, and, new this year, FallFest hats in beautiful brushed denim. All sales are cash-only, but there are two ATMs within a short walk of Main Street.The FallFest will be Oct. 14. In addition to our traditional mix of live music from blues to bluegrass - and don't forget the Catonsville High School Steel Band - we will celebrate the annual "return" of the oyster, with approximately 6,000 oysters shucked on site.Admission and parking are free, and there are lots of free activities for the younger set at Kids Kourt, with prizes, games, face-painting, animals and more. The street, which becomes a pedestrian concourse during FallFest, is lined with artisan crafts and gift ideas. If you need to work up an appetite, the Run For Character 5K race kicks off at 9 a.m. at the harbor.For more information, visit rockhallfallfest.org.Make sure to stop by the FallFest booth on Main Street to help support our community and friends.

title: David Buxton retires from Chesapeake Music
content:
David Buxton retires from Chesapeake Music

 September 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 10 | Section: News 
 
 801
 Words 

 Read News Document

 By In 1985, a dedicated group of chamber music lovers on Maryland's Eastern Shore was approached by the late Ralph Bloom to establish what was initially called the Eastern Shore Chamber Music Festival.Assisted that year by clarinetist J. Lawrie Bloom and later by cellist Marcie Rosen, Artistic Director Donald Buxton of Royal Oak became the organization's founding executive director. The festival continued to blossom over the next 38 years under their leadership. In August, Buxton retired from Chesapeake Music, the festival's parent organization, leaving a musical legacy he hadn't dreamed could happen.Buxton, a Julliard graduate, first helped found the Talbot Chamber Orchestra, which did concerts at the Talbot County Historical Society Auditorium. He served as Associate Conductor of the orchestra and he and his wife Merideth played with the orchestra.Over the years, he was also conductor of the Dover Symphony and along with others founded the Mid-Atlantic Symphony Orchestra and served as its conductor."The personal journey to make the arts important in Talbot County was a journey of love and necessity.When Meredith and I moved here in 1982, there was not a lot happening in the arts. I felt there needed to be a robust arts community in Easton and the surrounding area. Building that legacy has been one of the greatest joys of my life," Buxton said.Over the years, the Eastern Shore Chamber Music Festival grew into a twoweek event in early June, including concerts, recitals, and open rehearsals in venues ranging from concert halls to churches, museums, and waterfront estates across the Mid-Shore. The organization was one of the first organizations to do concerts in the renovated Avalon space and Buxton helped Ellen General become the Avalon's first executive director while also serving on its board.In 2002, the organization expanded its operation to include the Chesapeake Chamber Music Competition, a competition for young emerging chamber music ensembles. In 2004, the first biennial Competition became international in scope, drawing from international conservatories.Concerts between the annual Festivals joined the programming mix in 2004.In 2006, the organization was approached by musician Merideth Buxton, Don's wife, who made a presentation about an outreach program that became the First Strings Program.The program helped elementary school students in third or fourth grade to improve listening, gain self-confidence in performing, use teamwork to exhibit cooperation and self-control, and have fun while learning the skills needed to play the violin. In 2006, Chesapeake Music's Youth-Reach program was developed as a response to an ongoing nationwide decline of funding and lack of prioritization for music education, bringing musicians into the schools for live and virtual work with students.In July 2008, Eastern Shore Chamber Music Festival became Chesapeake Chamber Music Inc. to better reflect the organization's geographic location and scope near the Chesapeake Bay. In 2009, Chesapeake Chamber Music offered a single concert featuring the renowned jazz pianist Monty Alexander, creating the Monty Alexander Jazz Festival over Labor Day weekend.Chesapeake Music soon added its Interlude concerts which feature chamber music stars of the next generation and jazz greats. The organization's move in 2021 to the Ebenezer Theater enabled Chesapeake Music to acquire its own 9-foot Steinway Concert Grand piano something the festival musicians wanted for many years. At the Ebenezer Theater, Chesapeake Music now had an opportunity for yearround programming.Running such an ambitious music program over the years with only a parttime staff has had its challenges.According to Buxton, "It took a village to run an organization this large - in particular a volunteer cadre of 150 people. In addition, I relied on a dedicated board of 19 members with diverse professional backgrounds, who brought energy, talent, and treasure to the organization."Don added, "Chesapeake Chamber Music is a much broader organization today because it has continued to grow and evolve strategically while bringing renowned musicians to delight, engage, and surprise today's audiences and educate, inspire, and develop tomorrow's."Barry Koh, president of Chesapeake Music, reflected on Don's impact and said, "Chesapeake Music will continue to grow in its offerings of fine music and musicians thanks in large measure to Don having built a robust arts appreciation in our mid-shore community."During his career, Buxton served with his wife Merideth on the faculty of Washington College. Buxton served on the Talbot Arts Board and as a reviewer for the Maryland State Arts Council for 12 years. He and his wife also taught lessons through their home studio in Royal Oak.Based in Easton, Maryland, Chesapeake Music is a nonprofit organization whose mission is to bring renowned jazz and classical musicians to delight, engage and surprise today's audiences, and educate, inspire, and develop tomorrow's.They have been doing it for more than 35 years. To learn more about Chesapeake Music or to purchase tickets to this concert, visit their website at chesapeakemusic.org.

title: '10' Trippe Gallery celebrates 10 years with with special exhibit, anniversary reception
content:
'10' Trippe Gallery celebrates 10 years with with special exhibit, anniversary reception

 September 28, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: A4 | Section: News 
 
 305
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Trippe Gallery in downtown Easton will celebrate its 10th year in business with a special month-long exhibit in October entitled "10". The gallery is one of the cornerstones of the local art scene in Talbot County.The gallery will also hold a special reception to ring in its 10th anniversary during Easton's First Friday Gallery Walk on Oct. 6 from 5 p.m. to 8 p.m. Cake and champagne will be served."My goal was to have a gallery where the art appealed to all tastes by exhibiting different media as well as a comfortable venue for the beginning collector to the seasoned one," said gallery owner Nanny Trippe.Throughout October, the gallery will feature works based on a theme of "10" to commemorate its anniversary.Works can be of 10 subjects or can simply be sized 10x10. Trippe plans to exhibit a "Best of the Last 10"-a fine art photograph chosen from each of the past 10 years, according to an announcement from the gallery.The Trippe Gallery features works by contemporary artists including oils, watercolors, etchings, fine art photography, printmaking and mixed media of American Impressionism, botanicals, Plein Air paintings and abstract art.The Eastern Shore gallery is home to more than 40 artists including those from Easton as well as California, Canada and Norway. Fresh works are rotated on a monthly basis featuring a different theme or artists Recently on exhibit has been a show called "Variations 2.0: 1 Photograph 16 Paintings".Trippe submitted a scenic photograph to gallery artists who competed in Plein Air Easton to paint a variation of the photograph.There were no rules, just "paint as inspired," according to the gallery.The Trippe Gallery is located at 23 N Harrison St in Easton. For more information call 410-310-8727 or visit thetrippegallery.com

 In early September, career nonprofit professional and consultant Margaret Enloe-North assumed the leadership at one of Talbot County's premiere organizations for bringing amazing artists and performances to the Mid-Shore."We are very pleased to welcome Margaret as part of the Chesapeake Music team!" says Board President Barry Koh. "I know that her nonprofit experience will prove to be invaluable as we move forward and ultimately search for a new, permanent Executive Director in the spring."Enloe-North has spent her 30-year career entirely in the nonprofit sector. Having launched her new business, the Firebird Coaching & Consulting in 2021, she now serves as a coach for individual clients and small businesses and provides nonprofit clients with expert support in the areas of leadership, master planning, strategic communications, programming and fundraising."I really love serving as an Interim ED for organizations that are doing great work! My role allows a Board of Directors the opportunity to deeply reflect on the organization's future while also knowing that daily operations will continue to work smoothly," explains Enloe-North. "And I am really looking forward to working alongside the Board as we envision and lead Chesapeake Music into a new era. I have always appreciated both jazz and classical music and am delighted to help them bring renowned and up-and-coming musicians to the MidShore that delight and surprise our audiences."Based in Easton, Chesapeake Music is a nonprofit organization whose mission is to bring renowned jazz and classical musicians to delight, engage and surprise today's audiences, and educate, inspire, and develop tomorrow's. They have been doing it for more than 35 years. To learn more about Chesapeake Music or to purchase tickets to this concert, visit their website at chesapeakemusic.org.

title: Don Buxton retires from Chesapeake Music
author: Amelia Blades Steward
content:
Don Buxton retires from Chesapeake Music

 September 29, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Amelia Blades Steward | Page: 10 | Section: News 
 
 802
 Words 

 Read News Document

 By In 1985, a dedicated group of chamber music lovers on Maryland's Eastern Shore was approached by the late Ralph Bloom to establish what was initially called the Eastern Shore Chamber Music Festival.Assisted that year by clarinetist J. Lawrie Bloom and later by cellist Marcie Rosen, Artistic Director Donald Buxton of Royal Oak became the organization's founding executive director. The festival continued to blossom over the next 38 years under their leadership. In August, Buxton retired from Chesapeake Music, the festival's parent organization, leaving a musical legacy he hadn't dreamed could happen.Buxton, a Julliard graduate, first helped found the Talbot Chamber Orchestra, which did concerts at the Talbot County Historical Society Auditorium. He served as Associate Conductor of the orchestra and he and his wife Merideth played with the orchestra. Over the years, he was also conductor of the Dover Symphony and along with others founded the Mid-Atlantic Symphony Orchestra and served as its conductor."The personal journey to make the arts important in Talbot County was a journey of love and necessity. When Meredith and I moved here in 1982, there was not a lot happening in the arts. I felt there needed to be a robust arts community in Easton and the surrounding area. Building that legacy has been one of the greatest joys of my life," Buxton said.Over the years, the Eastern Shore Chamber Music Festival grew into a two-week event in early June, including concerts, recitals, and open rehearsals in venues ranging from concert halls to churches, museums, and waterfront estates across the Mid-Shore. The organization was one of the first organizations to do concerts in the renovated Avalon space and Buxton helped Ellen General become the Avalon's first executive director while also serving on its board.In 2002, the organization expanded its operation to include the Chesapeake Chamber Music Competition, a competition for young emerging chamber music ensembles. In 2004, the first biennial Competition became international in scope, drawing from international conservatories. Concerts between the annual Festivals joined the programming mix in 2004.In 2006, the organization was approached by musician Merideth Buxton, Don's wife, who made a presentation about an outreach program that became the First Strings Program. The program helped elementary school students in third or fourth grade to improve listening, gain self-confidence in performing, use teamwork to exhibit cooperation and self-control, and have fun while learning the skills needed to play the violin. In 2006, Chesapeake Music's YouthReach program was developed as a response to an ongoing nationwide decline of funding and lack of prioritization for music education, bringing musicians into the schools for live and virtual work with students.In July 2008, Eastern Shore Chamber Music Festival became Chesapeake Chamber Music Inc. to better reflect the organization's geographic location and scope near the Chesapeake Bay. In 2009, Chesapeake Chamber Music offered a single concert featuring the renowned jazz pianist Monty Alexander, creating the Monty Alexander Jazz Festival over Labor Day weekend.Chesapeake Music soon added its Interlude concerts which feature chamber music stars of the next generation and jazz greats. The organization's move in 2021 to the Ebenezer Theater enabled Chesapeake Music to acquire its own 9-foot Steinway Concert Grand piano something the festival musicians wanted for many years. At the Ebenezer Theater, Chesapeake Music now had an opportunity for year-round programming.Running such an ambitious music program over the years with only a parttime staff has had its challenges. According to Buxton, "It took a village to run an organization this large - in particular a volunteer cadre of 150 people. In addition, I relied on a dedicated board of 19 members with diverse professional backgrounds, who brought energy, talent, and treasure to the organization."Don added, "Chesapeake Chamber Music is a much broader organization today because it has continued to grow and evolve strategically while bringing renowned musicians to delight, engage, and surprise today's audiences and educate, inspire, and develop tomorrow's." Barry Koh, president ofChesapeake Music, reflected on Don's impact and said, "Chesapeake Music will continue to grow in its offerings of fine music and musicians thanks in large measure to Don having built a robust arts appreciation in our midshore community."During his career, Buxton served with his wife Merideth on the faculty of Washington College. Buxton served on the Talbot Arts Board and as a reviewer for the Maryland State Arts Council for 12 years. He and his wife also taught lessons through their home studio in Royal Oak.Based in Easton, Maryland, Chesapeake Music is a nonprofit organization whose mission is to bring renowned jazz and classical musicians to delight, engage and surprise today's audiences, and educate, inspire, and develop tomorrow's. They have been doing it for more than 35 years. To learn more about Chesapeake Music or to purchase tickets to this concert, visit their website at chesapeakemusic.org.

title: The Digital Renaissance - Re-Imagining classic artistry in The age of Technology
author: Melanie Allen; Wealth of Geeks
content:
The Digital Renaissance - Re-Imagining classic artistry in The age of Technology

 October 2, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Melanie Allen; Wealth of Geeks | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 1260
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The idyllic image of a painter, easel bathed in sunlight, is giving way to a new form. Today's art ist hunches over his laptop, frantically clicking his mouse to form perfect lines.Computers drastically changed art in form and function, forcing modern artists to adapt. Many yearn for the simplicity of ink on canvas while others love the ease o use and instant connectivity modern programs provide.Artists must find ways to bridge the gap to thrive in this ever-changing industry.TECHNOLOGY'S IMPACT ON ARTISTIC EXPRESSIONTechnology has a massive impact on the arts. Novice photographers can take professional quality shots in seconds with their phones, then edit them immediately with an app. Advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) allow companies to create logos and images for branding with the click of a button, limiting job opportunities for artists who bought into digital trends. Fakers and hacks flood internet marketing channels with low-quality works, drowning out the talent.It's not all bad news for artists, though. They no longer depend on galleries and wealthy patrons, but can now set up online shops and connect directly with customers. Livia Ochmann, artist and founde of how-to-art.com, uses modern technology to share her passion for the arts with others. She says contemporary artists have numerous ways to earn a living from thei work, including print-on-demand shops, courses, tutorial websites, affiliate programs, and sponsorships. None of these income avenues existed 30 years ago.Technology has also changed what we consider to be art. Data scientist Kat Campbell, an expert on digital technology, says modern tools have allowed artists to create immersive experiences, making art interactive and multidimensional, and offering a host of new mediums to explore, from digital painting to 3D models.THE CASE AGAINST DIGITAL ARTSome traditionalists, however, view digital creations as imposters not worthy of the "art" designation "I have seen digital artists being sometimes unfairly judged," Ochmann says, adding the common refrains include statements such as "digital art isn't real art," "people working in this medium are lazy," and "anyone can do what they do."Critics also lament the ease of entry into the market that digital tools create. When anyone can be an artist, everyone becomes an artist, crowding the marketplace."While technology makes art more accessible, it also floods the market," explains Campbell. "Standing out amidst this digital noise becomes a challenge."ART AND AIArtists also express concern ove AI and its potential impact on their work.Illustrator Aimee Cozza explains, "Professional artists are losing their jobs already to LLMs [Large Language Models, commonly called generative AI]," she says. "Many long-time artists are feeling quite uneasy about the gen eral attitude of the Internet agains artists, including the fragmentation of social media and the introduction of LLMs."Noting the impact generative AI models are already having on artists, Cozza adds, "I have watched many of my professional artist friends making less money on projects and at conventions throughout the declining economy, with closures due to the pandemic wreaking havoc for many of them. Many friends have turned to picking up side jobs or have qui doing art as a full-time job entirelyALL FORMS OF EXPRESSION HAVE THEIR PLACEHowever, most artists say the judgment is unjust. "Digital artists like us traditional artists, require a deep understanding of anatomy, perspective, and various artis tic principles to create good art. The skills they employ are no less valid, and their dedication to their craft is just as genuine," Ochmann points out.Joseph Taveras, an American roboticist-turned artist, agrees. "Drawing a line between artists who use computers/graphic design and those who stick with traditional mediums isn't necessarily productive - it's all art, just differ ent forms of expression," he says.Despite the stigma, most artists, even those who produce work in traditional media, use modern technology in some fashion.Mikhail Belanovich, lead designer with CoinsPaid Media, thinks it's silly not to take advantage of technology. "Surely it would be ridiculous to ignore tech nology as a phenomenon in 2023, he says; adding that every artist should use social media to share their work.However, connecting with an audience is only a small part of how artists embrace modern technology.ARTISTS COMBINE DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES WITH TRADITIONAL MEDIUMSMany use a combination of traditional and digital mediums to complete their work.Drawing tablets provide an easy way to bridge the gap. Artists can use their natural drawing ability to produce images directly on the screen, which they can then retouch or enhance as needed.Sarajean C, an artist with leading drawing tablet manufacturer Wacom, says, "Traditional art-ists value being hands-on and intimate with their art. Wacom tablet allow traditional artists to maintain the quality of their work in digital form, may it be transitioning into digital art, or retouching their scanned-in pieces."She adds that drawing tablets enhance features in software appli cations that mimic traditional mediums, making these applications more accessible to classical artists.Drawing tablets aren't the only way to transform classical forms of expression into digital media. Ingenious artists use numerous methods of combining the two competing forms.Terena Bell, visual artist and writer, hand draws her work and then combines the drawing with printed photos to make a collage, using the original drawings as an underpainting. Next, she photographs the collage and uses the basic Apple Photos app to refine the lines and colors.Taveras uses digital resources to enhance, not replace his creativity. "I use the programs Sketch, Adob Premiere, Adobe After Effects, and Logic Pro X in my practice to help me with conceptual research and aesthetic studies, but a majority of my artworks (98%) are physical paintings. I also use holo-grams, robots, and projectors to assist with the process," he says.Some use older technology to bridge the gap. Ochmann works with traditional mediums like pen cils, colored pencils, and watercolor on paper, then uses an old scanner to turn them digital. Once there, she uses Adobe Photoshop to remove dust or blemishes before uploading them to her website.TRADITIONAL MEDIUMS WILL ALWAYS HAVE A PLACEDespite the rapidly changing landscape, classical forms of expression will always remain relevant, though how we interact with art may vary.Cozza points to the most famous painting in the world as an example. "Many people do not have the means to visit the Mona Lisa in person, but with the assistance of technology converting this legendary artwork into pixels, they can enjoy the artwork from anywhere in the world," she explains.Belanovich says traditional artworks are just as popular as ever. "Sotheby's hasn't closed, and museums are up and running too. Art academies keep recruiting talented people every year."Taveras explains further, "There is an irreplaceable, tactile quality to physical artworks that digital forms, as of now, cannot replicate. The weight of a brush stroke, the texture of paint on canvas - these are sacred elements that collectors, enthusiasts, and artists alike hold in high esteem."AS TECHNOLOGY EVOLVES, SO WILL ARTISTIC EXPRESSIONAs humanity advances in science and technology, artists will adapt to the new forms. Artistic expression will never disappear, but new generations of artists will find innovative ways to combine technology with creativity, unveiling works that today's patrons can't even fathom.However, traditional mediums will always have their place. The best artists of the future will find ways to walk between both worlds, using modern technology to enhance classical forms while expressing the essence of the human condition.This article was produced by Media Decision and syndicated by Wealth of Geeks.

title: Music for the soul - Church choirs come together for special compline service Oct. 5.
author: Laura Tayman
content:
Music for the soul - Church choirs come together for special compline service Oct. 5.

 October 2, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 356
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE - With the busyness of the fall season already in full swing, the choirs of Christ Church Kent Island and St. Margaret's Church in Annapolis will join in providing an evening of quiet music and prayer to promote spiritual peace.The compline service will be held at 7:30 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 5, at Christ Church Parish, Kent Island."Compline" takes its name from the Latin word com-pletorium, meaning completion, as it marks the completion of the working day through its focus on prepar-ing the body for temporal rest. Those taking part, both the musicians and guests, are led to still the body, mind, and spirit."It's an Episcopal service not offered in most places and is very different from the regular Sunday morning services we lead each week," said St. Margaret's music director and Stevensville resident Jim Douglas. "The church is lit only by candles and [the service] is mostly sung, not spoken."When Christ Church's music director Gary Van Essen asked Douglas if he wanted to do some sort of combined choir event, Douglas suggested joining together for a service of evening Compline, offering one at St. Margaret's and a second one at Christ Church.The varied music selections range from the works of Thomas Tallis, who served as a composer and performer for Henry VIII and Elizabeth I, to Bernadette Farrell, contemporary composer widely known for her gift of writing richly meaningful lyrics and comforting, prayerful melodies.The service will also commemorate the life of St Francis of Assisi, the patron saint of animals and the environment."This program is giving the choir members a chance to collaborate and work with singers from another congregation while at the same time providing a beautiful, ancient worship experience for those who attend the service," said Christ Church Music Director Gary Van Essen. "Compline is quiet, peaceful, and set in twilight, something very different from most people's daily experiences. The service is a meaningful. way to disconnect and end the day on a contemplative note."

 Still one of movie history's greatest comedies, though it has its share of pathos as well, "The Apartment" claimed the Oscar as the best picture of 1960. An MGM+ Drive-In attraction on Monday, Oct. 9, and Tuesday, Oct. 10, director and co-writer Billy Wilder's tale casts Jack Lemmon as an office drone who's quite popular with much of the management at his workplace thanks to his relatively tiny apartment, which he loans out to the bosses so that they can have romantic trysts there.The company's main chief (Fred MacMurray) discovers what's going on and cuts himself in, but his affair is with the office building's elevator operator (Shirley MacLaine) - who is greatly liked by Lemmon's character, forcing him to develop more of a conscience about what he's been facilitating. This simply is a great film that not only has held up on its own over 60-plus years, it also inspired the hit stage musical "Promises, Promises." title: Author publishes 10th novel - BOOKS & AUTHORS
content:
Author publishes 10th novel - BOOKS & AUTHORS

 October 5, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 6A | Section: News 
 
 1031
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Louise Gorday published her latest book, "Letter of the Law," in late August through Amazon's Kindle Direct Publishing.Many of Gorday's 10 novels center on life in a small fictional Southern Maryland town based loosely on Chesapeake Beach.The award-winning author has started writing her 11th novel, a historical fiction murder mystery set in 1923.Gorday lives in Dunkirk with her very patient husband, two Shelties, and Emmett, an African Grey who can sing the "SpongeBob SquarePants" theme song."I could blame it on a stapler," she said of writing. "Or maybe it was the Scotch tape, the dog ear, or the occasional white paste. Whatever it was, once I found I could join pieces of paper and write stories, I was forever enthralled by this great adventure called writing." "Letter of the Law" can be found at Amazon.com or for more information about Louise Gorday, go to How long have you been writing, and how did you get started?Creative writing - poetry and short stories - has been a passion of mine since grade school. I attempted my first novel when I was 14, and throughout the years, writing a book was always an ambition.Professionally speaking, I have been writing since 2010.About 13 years ago, I was thinking about how my mother used to refer to me as "Annie off the pickle boat." Suddenly, I realized that I had no idea what that meant, so I started researching the saying.Fishing boats that pickled their catch would slow down as they returned to port. Hence, my mother's phrase referred to someone bringing up the rear.Then the literary muse stepped in and paired pickling boats and the nickname of a historic, unrenovated, old beach house in Chesapeake Beach (Orphan Annie), and voila, my first novel "The Pickle Boat House" was born.From there, I've branched off into nine other novels that include historical fiction and fantasy.What inspires you to write?Everything. I love tying bits and pieces of information together - letting my mind wander and create. In Southern Maryland, we are blessed with stunning landscapes and so many natural wonders (Battle Creek Cypress Swamp, Calvert Cliffs), and fabulous history (the amusement park at Chesapeake Beach, Moll Dyer witch tale) is all around us. I write about these things, spinning them into stories with hopefully likable fictional characters.I also often write with underlying themes: grief, sibling rivalry, jealousy, and selfishness, for example. "Letter of the Law" tackles issues of father-son relationships.And then there is my sense of humor. Humor underlies much of what I write because I'm tickled by a lot of things.Do you consider writing to be a career?Yes, a second career. I've been writing continually for 10 years and I'll continue as long as the muse keeps shoving stories at me.What kind of writing process do you use?Typically, I get up every morning, eat breakfast, and then open up my laptop to my latest work in progress. I read through what I wrote the previous day, usually hate most of it, and start revising. Before I know it, I'm putting down new material. I usually work with a goal of writing a certain number of words each day. When I reach that number, I close up shop and walk away to do other things.My first novel took 2½ years to write. Later ones have taken as little as six to seven months.It all depends on how giving the muse is. I've spent the last 10 years working with the same editor. He's terrific and taught me a lot about writing.I would never publish a book without an editorial review.Who are some of your favorite authors and why?I love Michael Connelly's "Bosch" and "Lincoln Lawyer" series. His writing is so crisp and clear, and his plots are always fresh. Neil Gaiman is another favorite. His imagination is spectacular. They have a substantial impact on how I write, but maybe not in the way one would think. I look at their sentence structures, the way they move characters around, change scenes, end chapters; the technical stuff.That's what I retain and how I improve my writing skills. I try to learn from the masters.What do you want readers to know about you?I'm a quiet, reflective person with a wild imagination and a sly sense of humor, and these traits readily show up in my stories. Also, that I'm an intensely proud Marylander.I grew up in Clinton and I've lived in Calvert County for over 25 years. I love sharing Southern Maryland through my writing.And finally, I want to share that I work hard at what I do with the intent of providing an entertaining immersive experience. Story development, editing, and book cover designs, I want to put out the very best book that I can for readers to enjoy.Please include a brief description of your book: "Letter of the Law" is in the fantasy genre about Hamelin Russell, an immortal who is assigned to run messages between the Weigh Station (a purgatory-like place in the afterlife) and the pearly gates.Hamelin has been stuck in the afterlife for over 700 years; not good enough to enter heaven, and not bad enough to be condemned to hell. He hopes that this latest assignment will finally get him to the promised land.Please include an excerpt from the book: Chapter One: The Door This was the view that greeted those God saved?Hamelin looked right, then left, then straight ahead again.He saw no St. Peter marking names off a list so long and unwieldy that it spilled off his desk and stretched endlessly into the distance. No twinkling stardust or chorus of angels singing anthems of praise just inside gates of glistening pearl, and no white, shining city bathed in ethereal light on the other side of a tall marble wall. There simply was no other side. He stared off into black, limitless space. He had delivered judged souls to paradise for eons, but he had never come this far. He had transferred them into heavenly care at the portal entrance some hundred yards away. How him as Ezekiel, although he probably went by many names.

title: Fitzgerald writers show 'A Tale of Alcohol and Excess' - BOOKS & AUTHORS
content:
Fitzgerald writers show 'A Tale of Alcohol and Excess' - BOOKS & AUTHORS

 October 5, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 5A | Section: News 
 
 1679
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Maryland Writers' Association created the Writers' Round Table Program to encourage writers, poets, playwrights and authors through monthly articles and activities.The Notable Maryland Author articles and associated Fun With Words writers' prompts are the centerpiece of the program. Each month, Southern Maryland Newspapers will feature a Maryland Writer's Association article about an author. Marylanders are encouraged to read the articles and try their hand at the writing prompts each month.Author: F. Scott and Zelda Fitzgerald Genre: Fiction. Fiction refers to a story that comes from a writer's imagination, as opposed to one based strictly on fact or a true story.In the literary world, a work of fiction can refer to a short story, novella, and novel, which is the longest form of literary prose. Every work of fiction falls into a sub-genre, each with its own style, tone, elements, and storytelling devices.Sample reading list: "The Great Gatsby," "The Beautiful and the Damned," "Save Me the Waltz," "Tender Is the Night" and "The Last Tycoon." "So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past." - F. Scott Fitzgerald Zelda Fitzgerald was an imaginative and ambitious Midwest writer kid from St.Paul, Minn. born to an established Rockville family. She was a Southern belle and the daughter of a judge. Artistic like Scott, she had aspirations to become a ballerina, painter and even a professional novelist like her husband.They met when he was drafted to serve in the U.S.Army in World War I, sent to a training camp in Alabama, but destined never to be sent overseas to see action in a war zone. They would marry and have one child, a girl Scottie.In a brilliant if erratic trajectory like a skyrocket, he shot to fame as a novelist and short story writer. He became the great chronicler of the Jazz Age, writing such classics as "The Great Gatsby" and "The Beautiful and the Damned." Both Fitzgeralds had a special fascination with the rich, such as the fictional shady Jay Gatsby and Tom and Daisy Buchanan.Born Sept. 24, 1896, to a middle-class Catholic family, Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald was named after his distant cousin, Francis Scott Key, who wrote the lyrics for the song that in 1931 became the country's national anthem, "The Star-Spangled Banner," about the September 1814 British bombardment of Fort McHenry in Baltimore which Key witnessed from a ship in the Patapsco River.Rampant alcoholism would impair Scott's career while Zelda wrestled with mental difficulties; although in 1932 she succeeded in publishing a novel of her own, "Save Me the Waltz." Scott Fitzgerald described the Jazz Age as racing "along under its own power, served by great filling stations full of money." In his view, the era represented a morally permissive time when Americans became disillusioned with prevailing social norms and became obsessed with self-gratification. Given what was going on around them in Manhattan, alcohol fueled the Fitzgeralds' life as they consumed gin and fruit cocktails. Privately it led to bitter quarrels.By the 1930s, Zelda had been in and out of psychiatric facilities, and her husband was stalled writing his next work; he had not produced a novel since "Gatsby" in 1925. After an episode of hysteria, Zelda was admitted to Phipps Clinic at Johns Hopkins Hospital in East Baltimore on Feb. 1, 1932. As part of her recovery, she spent at least two hours a day writing.When she was institutionalized at Shepherd Pratt Hospital in Towson, he rented La Paix, a country house owned by the Turnbull family which stood where the power plant for St. Joseph's Hospital on Osler Drive now stands.During this time, Scott wrote magazine stories to pay for Zelda's psychiatric treatment.Later they moved to Baltimore and in 1934, Fitzgerald completed "Tender Is the Night." Scott predeceased Zelda on Dec. 21, 1940, at the age 44 while struggling to make it as a scriptwriter in Hollywood.While he was able to write about Hollywood (his last, incomplete novel was "The Last Tycoon"), he wasn't adept at producing the nifty scripts directors wanted. Just over eight years later, Zelda died tragically in a fire at an Asheville, N.C., mental asylum on March 10, 1948, at the age of 47.The above biography was written by Christopher T. George The couple rests at Old Saint Mary's Catholic Church Cemetery in Montgomery County's Rockville.For more information, go to www.findagrave.com/memorial/344/f-scott-fitzgerald. To sign up for the AARP Maryland Book Club discussion of "Call Me Zelda" by Maryland writer Erika Robuck on Oct. 10, go to https://events.aarp.org/d/xpqnk2/.FUN WITH WORDSThe MWA invites readers to have fun being a writer and revel in the Jazz age like F. Scott and Zelda Fitzgerald.Using 100 words, set two characters in the Jazz Age who are morally permissive and obsessed with self-gratification. Title your work and submit to: https://marylandwriters.org/Notable Maryland Authors by the 22nd of the month to receive an MWA Fun With Words submission certificate.Selected responses will be published next month.Last month readers were asked to have fun being a biased historian like John Thomas Scharf and pick an American historical event or time-period and use newspaper sources and describe the event while inadvertently letting your bias about the event show.The MWA is a 31-year-old statewide association (501c3) dedicated to encouraging and mentoring Maryland writers, poets, playwrights, and authors. Go to www.MarylandWriters.org for more info.Here are some regional selections: Baltimore BurnsThe Great 1873 Clay Street Fire raged for 10 hours, destroying 113 buildings. The first arriving Steamers at the Joseph Thomas and Sons sash and blind factory, unable to control the blaze, sent for additional units. The water stream generated by the coal-fired steamers could not reach beyond the buildings' second story, and wind-driven embers leaped across streets to ignite roofs of neighboring structures. In contrast, the devastating Great 1904 Baltimore Fire destroyed 1,500 buildings. The Clay Street fire to was relegated to second rank status, unless you were among the business or homeowners that suffered in the $750,000 loss.-Ken Stepanuk, Prince Frederick GunnahangeBelow is a recently discovered excerpt from the 19th-century chronicle entitled Unfortunate Happenings.The text being regarded as notably mysterious, this new blurb, unfortunately, does little to clarify itself: "On July 4th, [1865,] Guy Gunnahange was brought before the gallows," read one yellow-press paper [the newsprint here referenced is unknown]; "Only a day prior was his death warrant officialized."Just twenty-four hours! What permissible cruelty is this? Mr. Gunnahange ought to have lived a little while longer. The same bulletin even says, "Because of his crimes, he was offered no last meal."Hadn't they a clue how hungry I was!-Eric Waldow, La Plata Binjimen VictorJanuary 14, 2023: At 26 years old, 6 foot, 4 inch Binjimen Victor was finally going to get a chance at a playoff game. The Baltimore Ravens had promoted him to their active roster for their 2023 playoff game against the Cincinnati Bengals, his third time to be called up as a wide receiver. He had one tackle on just two special team snaps; he played 4 out of 68 offensive snaps, but he failed to log a target.Ravens lost.The famous quotation, "To the Victor belong the spoils" will hopefully happen for Victor who becomes a free agent this upcoming year.-Cindy Herndon, Sunderland Corruption - Not in New York CityThe New York Times reported November 16, 1873, "William Magear Tweed, or Boss Tweed, was convicted on 204 of 220 counts of stealing between $25 million and $45 million from New York City taxpayers from political corruption, graft and embezzlement."The trial tried to prove this occurred through Tweeds manipulation of New York City's Tammany Society, a benevolent society created to ensure citizens received public services. The Post reported, "Tweed used the Tammany Society to control political patronage in New York City and create voter loyalty through jobs he could dispense on city-related projects." Corruption of this type is rare in our city and New Yorkers can be proud that Tweed and Tammany Hall, accomplished the development of upper Manhattan. The Herald's reporting that the project "tripled the city's bond debt to almost $90 million" is just the cost of doing business.-Jim Brewster, Pomfret Peaceful Transition of PowerJanuary 6. An insurrection, a violent attempt to overthrow the legitimate government of the U.S. Or so we hear following the breaking (yeah, right) news on the cable outlets."Nothing like this has ever happened before." Think back to January 20, 2017.Police officers assaulted. Hundreds of violent protestors were arrested in Washington DC., and in other cities across the country. Cars burning in the streets. Dozens of Democratic congressmen boycotted the inauguration in protest. Later, Trump was referred to as an "illegitimate president" by Hilary and former president Carter. You reap what you sow.-Leslie Dickey, Calvert County The Law of RetributionTruth falls first in war. War next claims civility. Yet, during the War of 1812, British officers demonstrated civility toward Americans in general and Marylanders in particular.Take, for example, British Rear Admiral Sir George Cockburn (pronounced civilly: "co-burn"), who incinerated Fredericktown in Cecil County. Refugees described in The Weekly Register dated May 22, 1813, how Cock-burn savored the flames "like Satan[[---]] when he saw[[---]]murdered Abel[[---]], exulting at the damning deed[[---]]." Other witnesses, The Weekly Register reported, overheard Cockburn obsessing about torching Baltimore house by house.War demands civilized savagery, but it is no less civil, for there lies truth.-Lawrence McGuire, Waldorf Titanic HoaxOn April 14th, 1912, the Titanic reportedly sank. Shortly thereafter, White Star executives touted a press release alleging that their unsinkable vessel "sank after hitting an iceberg."However, experts close to an ongoing investigation (who wish to remain anonymous) cite reliable sources attesting the Titanic was actually "disappeared by an inept vaudeville magician" who lacked the necessary talent to "make the Titanic RE-appear."White Star executives also vehemently deny that survivors were paid hush money to secure a massive corporate cover-up. There has also been no comment from White Star about whistleblower testimony maintaining footage of the "found wreckage" is actually an elaborate hoax conjured up by vagabond filmmakers using a secret Hollywood soundstage.-Steve Baker, Waldorf

title: Museum celebrates oysters at OysterFest
content:
Museum celebrates oysters at OysterFest

 October 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 ST. MICHAELS - The Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum will celebrate the Bay's favorite bivalve at OysterFest on Saturday, Oct. 28, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.CBMM's OysterFest features oysters served a variety of ways, along with other local fare, craft beer, and spirits, plus live music on two stages, an oyster stew competition, a full schedule of demonstrations and presentations, children's activities, and more.Guests can savor Chesapeake Bay oysters, with both raw and cooked options available, from the Talbot Watermen Association and other local oyster farms.There will also be a variety of Chesapeake delicacies and other food offerings via local vendors available for purchase, plus a beverage selection that includes specialty cocktails and an array of local craft beer options.For OysterFest, guests will enter campus through CBMM's new Welcome Center, getting a first look at the new building overlooking Fogg's Cove and the chance to shop in the new Museum Store inside. (Please note that the exhibition spaces within the Welcome Center are not yet open to the public.)Purchase your tickets in advance now for this rain-or-shine event and learn more at cbmm.org/oysterfest.The always-popular oyster stew competition invites guests to sample offerings from various local restaurants and then vote for their favorite to decide which chefs will claim the coveted title.There will be live music on both sides of campus all day long, with stages on both the Tolchester Beach Bandstand and Fogg's Landing. Swamp Donkey Newgrass will be playing the historic bandstand, bringing its unique "newgrass" sound with a combination of genre-spanning original songs and covers to OysterFest for the fifth time.Guests can head to Van Lennep Auditorium throughout the day to hear from a variety of guest speakers sponsored by the Upper Shore Regional Folklife Center through the Maryland Traditions Program of the Maryland State Arts Council. The offerings include a series of panels related to CBMM's special exhibition The Changing Chesapeake and a history presentation from Dr. Clara Small.The American Chesapeake Club will be on hand to discuss Maryland's official dog, the Chesapeake Bay retriever, and showcase its retrieving ability, while the 100 Hundred Shores Project will offer the opportunity for guests to dye their own shirts using water from the Miles River.There's also an oyster slurp-off contest to add to the friendly competition, plus a wide range of Chesapeake-themed children's activities, including games, model boat building, and story time.Guests can get in the festive spirit by purchasing OysterFest gear in the new Museum Store, showcasing this year's featured historic oyster tin from CBMM's collection. The one-gallon tin, packed in the 1940s by W.E. Rigging & Co., out of Crisfield, Md., is emblazoned on shirts and stickers, as well as the commemorative mugs that will be used for the oyster stew competition.This year, OysterFest is generously sponsored by M&T Bank with support from Eastern Shore Tents & Events, Kelly Distributors, and What's Up Media.OysterFest admission is $7 for museum member adults and active and retired members of the military (with ID); $19 for non-member adults; $16 for seniors (ages 65 and up) and college students (with ID); $7 for non-member children ages 6-17; and free for member children 6-17, and all children 5 and under. CBMM members at the Family & Friends level and above can also receive the $7 discounted admission for two adult guests.Tickets can be purchased online in advance or at the gate the day of the festival. Additional free event parking will be available at St. Michaels Middle/High School, with a complimentary shuttle service to and from CBMM running throughout the day.Food and drinks are available for an additional cost, with carry-on alcohol prohibited. For safety reasons, non-service dogs need to be kept home during museum festivals, including OysterFest.

title: Sculptures grace Chestertown's walking trails
content:
Sculptures grace Chestertown's walking trails

 October 10, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 CHESTERTOWN - Chestertown's downtown has gotten a little brighter with the addition of two new sculptures from the Peter and Hanna Woicke Sculpture Collection. The Ball and Red Arches has been installed at the southwest end of Cross Street and Taking the Hill has been placed not far away along the Wayne Gilchrest Trail.Adam Walls, the creator of both works, will visit Chestertown the weekend of October 6-7 to talk about his work.Walls, a professor of art at The University of North Carolina at Pembroke, creates sculptures that often evoke children's toys and play structures.The Ball and Red Arches, he says, "represents the ups and downs expected in life with the suggestion to keep one's eye and mind fixed on the top to push for something better." Taking the Hill is part of a larger series of works featuring cartoonish toy tanks and offers a reminder of the pitfalls that can come with blindly following leaders.An informal "opening" for the sculptures will take place along the Gilchrest Trail from 5-7 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 6, in conjunction with the Downtown Chestertown Association's First Friday events. Walls will then present an artist talk on Saturday, October 7 at 11 a.m. in the Kent Cultural Alliance's Raimond Cultural Center at 101 Spring Ave. in Chestertown.Installation of the sculptures was coordinated by the Chestertown Public Arts Committee, which was established in 2019 with the goal of helping to promote and implement the installation of artwork in public places for the enrichment of the community. The committee also seeks to foster educational programming and activities that engage the community and increase the understanding and enjoyment of public art by residents and visitors.Since 2021, it has been coordinating the installation of the Woicke Sculpture Collection, an extraordinary gift of twenty-four outdoor sculptures donated to the town by Peter and Hanna Woicke of St. Michaels.More information about public art in Chestertown can be found at chestertownpublicarts.com.
