Hispanic Heritage Month celebrated in Kent County

 October 10, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 679
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - The lilting chorus of Cuban folk song "Guantanamera" filled the cafeteria of H.H.Garnet Elementary School in Chestertown Thursday, Sept. 21.Local resident and artist Fredy Granillo strummed his guitar as he taught the song to students that morning as part of the Celebración del mes del la Herencia Hispana in the county.The Celebration of Hispanic Heritage Month was brought into schools during September through partnerships with the Kent County Local Management Board and the Kent Cultural Alliance.The two organizations were joined by others in holding a variety of community events including art programs and a block party centered around Hispanic heritage."The Kent Cultural Alliance was honored to work with the Kent County Local Management Board and E(Ñ)E: Alianza para la Cultura y Comunidad Hispana, to create a month long celebration of the contributions of Kent County's Latino community," said John Schratwieser, executive director of the Kent Cultural Alliance."Celebrating those who contribute so much to our economic health and our quality of life, and doing that through art, music, food, dance and the written word, is paramount to the mission of the KCA." For Granillo, who also is a Kent County Public Schools parent, getting to share his family's cultural touchstones with students is a valuable experience.Granillo grew up in El Salvador. He and his wife Kent County Local Management Board Director Rosemary Ramsey Granillo moved to Chestertown when their son, a fourth grader at Garnet, was 2.Granillo found the community friendly and inviting, but he still faced hurdles - first being the language.He learned English and he helped his son with the language.There were additional cultural differences for Granillo as well, such as food, and he sees other families having similar experiences when they move here."I was lucky because I had the opportunity to visit Chestertown first," Granillo said. "So I knew about the artistic community in town and that was something that made me feel like I could live here." For students who move to Kent County from other countries, school can pose a big challenge.Beyond learning math standards, science, social studies and other subjects, they also have a new language to learn - and Kent County Public Schools has staff members dedicated to helping those English language learners.Granillo said programs like Hispanic Heritage Month are important for both students born and raised here and those who have moved to the area from other countries.It gives those students from other countries an opportunity and a space to share their culture with their new peers.Granillo spoke about how celebrations in other countries are often built around specific foods, activities and games - not unlike the American custom of eating turkey on Thanksgiving."I think it's really important for schools to have a space where these kids can show other kids what they like to do in their countries, because that gives you a perspective on the world," he said."When you are a kid, you need to understand the world is more than Chestertown or the town where you live." As part of Hispanic Heritage Month in Kent County Public Schools, there were lessons and school announcements teaching students about the culture.Galena Elementary School, for example, held a daily Hispanic Heritage contest, with questions that students could answer by looking at information posted throughout the building.Teacher Tracey Kendall-Parent works with local English language learners in Galena Elementary School. She took to the morning announcements throughout the month to provide information about countries where students' families are from."I think that's a beautiful experience for everybody, not just for the kids," Granillo said of the Hispanic heritage lessons. "And it's going to make these kids from other countries feel like they live in a space where they can celebrate their culture and their identity too."

title: Dancers bring Hispanic culture to Chestertown - Ballet Folklorico la Esperanza from Cambridge highlights program
author: Laura Tayman
content:
Dancers bring Hispanic culture to Chestertown - Ballet Folklorico la Esperanza from Cambridge highlights program

 October 10, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 623
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - Stunning costumes, festive dancing, and heartfelt songs were joyfully celebrated at the Kent County Alliance's final event celebrating Hispanic Heritage Month at the Raimond Cultural Center last weekend.Events throughout the month included an exhibit for art and poetry featuring paintings by Granillo, poems by Iris Figueroa, and textiles of Latin America; an outdoor festival with Talavera painting workshops for children, a dance party, and food trucks with Latino offerings; along with Saturday's music events. All were supported by the Kent Cultural Alliance, the Kent County Local Management Board, and E(Ñ)E: Alliance for Hispanic Culture and Community founded by Granillo.Highlighting Saturday's program were performers from the Ballet Folklorico la Esperanza from Cambridge who performed popular dancing styles from Mexico, while the second dance group led by Maria Lopez from Delaware were based on Guatemalan dances.Lopez said the colorful costumes and masks were the typical, long-standing costumes used by Guatemalans even at the time of the Conquest. The second dance's music was from a marimba, which, Lopez said, pays homage to their forefathers that began this rhythm.Originally from Argentina, vocalist Sergio Cilla shared with the audience three tangos and three folklore songs from different parts of his country. "When you think of Latin music, you think of something fun and colorful," Cilla said. "Tangos, which began in the 1920s, are generally melancholy, with lyrics that usually have something about loss." His first two pieces were titled "Nothing" and "The Simple Things." Next came the sambas, with the first "Samba to Forget" with a typical melody that comes from the northwest part of Argentina.He also performed a more festive "Ballad for a Crazy Man" that represented the freedom that can come from letting go of one's inhibitions.His final number was titled "Song with Everyone" and was shared in the different countries of Argentina, Chile, Peru, and Brazil."It was meant for all voices to sing as one," said Cilla.At the end of the evening, Granillo who learned to play at the age of 14, took up his acoustic guitar.The first piece he learned, he recalled, was a song he kept hearing again and again.Not knowing any English, he imagined what it could mean, and tried to make the same sounds he heard in recordings.He began playing the song for the evening's audience and everyone recognized it at once - "Let it Be" by the Beatles.Granillo also shared one of the first songs he had written."When I reached out to my colleagues in the community about possibly doing these events, they were ready to start work," said Fredy Granillo, local artist and musician and the coordinator for the programs in September."I believe we all need to learn from each other." "In all that we do at the Alliance, we maintain a sharp focus the role arts and culture plan in connecting people," said Kent Cultural Alliance Director John Schratwieser."By allying the arts and humanities together, we can build stronger communities through those things which connect us."

title: Adkins Arboretum fills with fairies for festival
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
Adkins Arboretum fills with fairies for festival

 October 11, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 10 | Section: News 
 
 566
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY - Toadstools, unicorns and pixies all passed by the fairy king and queen, who sat in thrones and held scepters.Adkins Arboretum had its annual Fairyfest in a light rain on Oct. 7. The soft rain dampened no one's spirits as live music filled the pavillion and crafts were made in the main building. Drawing inspiration from pre-Christian Great Britain and the Celts, the woods were alive with magic fairy houses.In past years Adkins has been overrun with fairy fans, so now they put a cap on how many can attend. Even with that they had over 500 people attend. There were food trucks including Scottish Highland Creamery. The musical talent included Ampersand and Allegra Choir, who gave some rich harmonic a cappella singing.There was even belly dancing put on by the Sammati Dance Troupe.Little children with unicorn hats got to ride horses with their grandparents and parents closely monitoring the journey. A lot of the festival is geared toward little girls. They are perfectly suited for this kind of magic.Jenny Houghton is the assistant director at Adkins, but today goes by "Queen Fairy." She has monarch butterfly wings to match her braided red hair.She said, "Fairfest was my brain child. I came up with it about eight years ago, and it has become our most well attended event.We are sold out today at over 400. Our first year we had over 700 but realized we didn't have enough parking." She focused on Adkins' mission and how it fits well with the event."It is just a fun day getting kids outside in nature and helping them realize how magical it is. We had a lot of 4 to 6 year olds, but that said we are seeing older kids. We have a lot of teen volunteers who enjoy it as much as the kids. It is with our mission, which is to create exceptional experiences outside," Houghton said.There is a bridge that serves as an entrance to Adkins. All along the walkway there were ornate floral structures built by sponsor Chesapeake Blooms.One aspect of the event is a collection of fairy houses that are placed along a woodland path.This year six people were recognized for their building efforts. They are: Cristina Swaine, Dawn Folmer, Sheri Lynch, Clara Terry, Connie Schroth and Nancy Bennington.Charlotte Reyes, 6, of Cambridge was getting face painting. Mom Deenie Reyes, said, "It is very whimsical. It is almost like you are in another world. It is very hands-on for the kids. It is creative and fulfills little girls' fantasies." One of the woman painting faces and dressed as a bumblebee was Nancy Reid from Trappe. She said, "We are sharing the magic right here. The only thing we don't have is glitter.I think the glitter is in the woods." 
 
 Caption: TOM MCCALL/STAR DEMOCRAT/
 
Claire Burneston, 9, and her sister Stella, 4, said in unison, "The best part is getting to see all the fairy houses." There is one next to the pumpkin.
 
TOM MCCALL/STAR DEMOCRAT
 
Lorelei Fisher, in the rainbow maypole tent, said, "It is good. I want to play rocket ship in this." Later as a finale to the Fairyfest, the strands were unanchored and woven around the tree by many people moving in a circle.

title: Forging a Path - 20 years after the publication of 'Purple Hibiscus,' a generation of African writers have followed in Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's footsteps
author: Simon Lewis; College Of Charleston The Conversation
content:
Forging a Path - 20 years after the publication of 'Purple Hibiscus,' a generation of African writers have followed in Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's footsteps

 October 12, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Simon Lewis; College Of Charleston The Conversation | Page: 6A | Section: News 
 
 1269
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Twenty years ago, in October 2003, 26-year-old Nigerian author Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie burst onto the North American publishing scene with her debut novel," Purple Hibiscus." Since then, Adichie's literary fame has only grown: She's published two more novels and a collection of short stories, while two of herTED talks have garnered tens of millions of views. In September 2023, she published her first children's book - a joyful celebration of mother-daughter love - under the nom de plume Nwa GraceJames.But the October 2003 publication of "Purple Hibiscus" didn't just signal the start of a single author's brilliant career. It also forged a path for a whole new generation of African novelists who had come to America as immigrants or students and who have been mining that experience in their writing.The struggles to get published by prior generations of African authors are almost legendary.Thirty years apart, Chinua Achebe and Tsitsi Dangarembga have both described how close their manuscripts of "Things Fall Apart" (1958) and "Nervous Conditions" (1988) came to being lost. Achebe's only copy of the manuscript was a handwritten draft. He sent it to a typing agency in London that nearly dismissed it as a joke. Dangarembga's manuscript sat unread in the basement of a British publishing house for years. Only when the writer stopped by the offices during a work trip to London did the editors agree to read it.Through attending American MFA programs, however, Adichie and her contemporaries were able to tap into the networks of agents and found their work snapped up by American publishers.Writers born in Africa who studied at American universities - Teju Cole, Yaa Gyasi, Uzodinma Iweala, NoViolet Bulawayo and Akwaeke Emezi, to name just a few - have followed in Adichie's footsteps."Purple Hibiscus" has been to these writers what Gabriel García Márquez's "One Hundred Years of Solitude" (1967) was to aspiring Latin American writers during the Latin American literary boom of the 1960s and 1970s, and what Salman Rushdie's "Midnight's Children" (1981) was to the proliferation of Indian writers in English from the 1980s on.While it would be reassuring to think that the current surge of African novelists represents a wider American interest in all things African, the success of these novels may also have to do with the fact that so many are actually set in the U.S.The recurrent theme of immigration to the U.S. gives many of these works direct - and instructive - relevance to U.S. readers. As Black outsiders in the U.S., African immigrants have a particularly acute insight into the way race and racism affect daily life in this country.One of the common features of these novels is the way in which they explore the tension of racial solidarity and mutual misunderstanding between African immigrants and Black Americans.When I first started teaching African literature, I often had difficulty finding books in print. Now my problem is deciding who to leave out of my syllabus. Here is a very brief list of some of the books that I would consider must-reads.1. Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, "Americanah" (2013) As its title suggests, Adichie's fourth novel, "Americanah," is arguably the definitive novel of contemporary African immigration to America.It tells the story of Ifemelu, a young Nigerian woman overstaying her student visa, and how she negotiates the new Black identity forced on her by the blunt instrument of American race-construction.In a brilliant metafictional move, Adichie has Ifemelu achieve internet fame by writing a blog dedicated to non-American Blacks: "Dear Non-American Black," Ifemelu writes, "when you make the choice to come to America, you become black. Stop arguing. Stop saying I'm Jamaican or I'm Ghanaian.America doesn't care. So what if you weren't 'black' in your country?You're in America now." Ifemelu's experience of racism is simultaneously hurtful and baffling to her. On the one hand, her illegal status makes her both psychologically and physically vulnerable. But at times American racism is almost comical; Ifemelu doesn't understand why an innocent reference to eating watermelon might be misconstrued, for instance, and she is totally bewildered by a shop assistant's attempt to avoid distinguishing between two shoppers by reference to their skin color.2. Yaa Gyasi, "Homegoing" (2016)Ghanaian-born Yaa Gyasi's debut novel takes the form of a series of skillfully interwoven stories set on either side of the Atlantic.Beginning with two half sisters, Effia and Esi, in the Gold Coast in the middle of the 18th century, the stories trace the two sets of the sisters' descendants through six subsequent generations in West Africa and the U.S. In the final two stories we meet the young teenager Marjorie, who, as the Americanborn daughter of Ghanaian parents, struggles to come to terms with her identity as one of Ifemelu's "Non-American Blacks." She finds herself ostracized by her Black classmates for "acting white" but is unable to enjoy a normal relationship with a white classmate. One of the only Black teachers at her high school tells her, "You're here now, and here black is black is black." 3. NoViolet Bulawayo, "We Need New Names" (2013)When "We Need New Names" appeared, Nigerian novelist Helon Habila accused NoViolet Bulawayo of peddling "poverty-porn" by pandering to American stereotypes of Africa.However, for Bulawayo's teenage protagonist Darling, it's American culture that is dangerously dysfunctional - and personally discombobulating. Darling finds American high school ridiculously easy, is horrified by the laxness of American parenting and is generally unimpressed by the urban blight she sees around her in the city she calls Destroyed, Michigan.Late in the novel, her mentally ill countryman Tshaka Zulu is shot to death by police when off his meds and ranting in his home language.You might think that such a violent, tragic event would be a major plot driver. Sadly, it seems to exemplify just one more random peril - little different from being hit by a car or struck down by cancer - that many Africans coming to America have to endure.4. Uzodinma Iweala, "Speak No Evil" (2018) Even wealth and class status offer no protection from such perils.In Uzodinma Iweala's "Speak No Evil," the main character, Niru, is the high-achieving son of high-achieving Nigerian parents in supposedly cosmopolitan Washington, D.C. The first three-quarters of the book appear to be exploring Niru's dilemma: how to come out as gay to his conservative parents.It turns out that Niru's gayness - an invisible characteristic, after all - is not the problem; his Blackness is. When he gets in a row outside a bar with his best friend, Meredith - an equally well-off, well-connected, high-flying white female classmate - someone calls the cops. In the space of a paragraph the inevitable has happened: Shots are fired. "You're safe," someone says to Meredith."He can't hurt you." By extraordinary coincidence, Adichie grew up in the very house that Chinua Achebe had lived in on the campus of the University of Nigeria in Nsukka.She, and the other writers of her generation, grew up in the house of fiction that Achebe and his generation established. The writers of that older generation were concerned with the material and cultural despoliation of colonialism. In Achebe's words, their task was to let their African readers know "where the rain began to beat" them.Today's African writers demand readers' attention by letting them know that for African and African-descended people in the U.S., although the winds may have shifted, the storm is far from over.Simon Lewis has been teaching African and Third World Literature at the College of Charleston since 1996. title: Author takes to the seas with 'The Pirate Series'
content:
Author takes to the seas with 'The Pirate Series'

 October 12, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 7A | Section: News 
 
 552
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Maryland author Elizabeth Gagné recently self-published her second book "Evangeline Shores Forever" in July through Amazon Kindle.The book is her second book, and first in The Pirate Series after "Shores of Forever Search for Blackbeard's Treasure" was rewritten and changed to "Evangeline Shores of Forever." The 60-year-old Gagné, who writes under the pen name Bitsey Gagné, graduated from Charles County Community College (now College of Southern Maryland) in 1982 from the licenses practical nurse and registered nurse programs in 1984.Gagné retired in May after a 40-plus year career as a retired nurse in Charles and St. Mary's counties, the last 33 years as a dialysis nurse.Gagné's third book, "Angie's Soulmate," which was released in book and eBook form Sept.21, is available along with the other books at www.amazon.com.How long have you been writing, and how did you get started?I started writing back in 2016 while I was recuperating after having surgery for breast cancer, but I had an idea for this book long before that.What inspires you to write?I visit the Outer Banks in North Carolina several times a year. I love the story about the mystery about what happened to the lost colonists of Roanoke Island. Hence, this is where the idea for my story transpired and blossomed, somehow into the novel that it is now.Do you consider writing to be a career?I consider it my career now after retiring from nursing.What kind of writing process do you use?I used Microsoft word/One Drive initially after I wrote out my document for my first two books but am now just using my laptop.Who are some of your favorite authors and why?Nora Roberts, Diana Gabaldon, Deborah Harkness are three of the authors that I like to read. I enjoy reading and writing romance, paranormal suspense novels.What are you working on now?"Angie's Soulmate" is the sequel to my first book. It's a romance, suspense and paranormal novel about a young country singer who moves to Ocracoke Island and is visited by her ancestor's spirit, Evangeline.Evangeline leaves her with the clues to the whereabouts of Blackbeard's treasure and guides her to her soulmate.And to add a twist, have they stumbled upon what happened to the Lost Colonists of Roanoke Island?Please include a brief description of your book "Evangeline Shores Forever." Angie Harriott, an upcoming country singer/songwriter grew up in a small town called Ripley, Maryland. She spent her summers vacationing on Ocracoke Island listening to tales about Lost Loves and Blackbeard's treasure. After a difficult breakup with her boyfriend and sudden death of her father, she follows her dreams and moves to Ocracoke Island.Angie has always called the island the Shores of Forever, because of its rich and mystical history. She becomes entwined in a mystery and a romance as her new life begins. Evangeline, Angie's long ago ancestor's spirit, roams the shores looking for her lost love. She leaves Angie and her friends clues to the whereabouts of Blackbeard's treasure map and guides Angie to her true love. Angie wonders if there is such a thing as soulmates that can pass from one lifetime to another.

title: Lessons from the heartland - What live theater can learn from Branson, Missouri
author: Joanna Dee Das; Washington University In St. Louis The Conversation
content:
Lessons from the heartland - What live theater can learn from Branson, Missouri

 October 12, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Joanna Dee Das; Washington University In St. Louis The Conversation | Page: 3A | Section: News 
 
 1393
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In summer 2023, the publication American Theatre declared unequivocally that live theater was "in crisis" - particularly regional, nonprofit theaters. Writing for The New York Times, Isaac Butler preferred the phrase "on the verge of collapse." The numbers are stark. Not only have dozens of theaters across the country closed their doors since the COVID-19 pandemic hit in March 2020, but those that are still open have also contracted their seasons massively, producing 40% fewer shows than in 2019.What can regional, nonprofit theaters do to survive?One place to look for ideas is the tourist town of Branson, Missouri.Scholars and theater critics have ignored this mecca of live entertainment that attracts millions of people a year, largely because of its reputation for cheesy performances and political conservatism.I'm a theater and dance historian at Washington University, a liberal arts institution in a city. My politics differ from that of most Branson residents. But that's precisely why I am in the process of writing a book about the town's entertainment industry. In an age of polarization, could I challenge myself to approach the place with an open mind? I expected to feel discomfort; I did not expect to feel envy. In Branson, people really seemed to believe in theater's power.And nowhere more so than at Sight & Sound, a for-profit Christian theater. On a Wednesday afternoon in May 2023, I joined 2,000 other patrons to watch their performance of "Queen Esther," a musical retelling of the biblical story of Hadassah.In "Queen Esther," Hadassah adopts the name Esther and conceals her Jewish identity in order to marry the Persian emperor Xerxes.She faces challenges in the royal court and doubts herself. Eventually, she learns to trust in God that she was "made for such a time as this" and bravely saves the Jewish people from annihilation.The Old Testament story is not as well known as those of Noah or Moses, nor does the musical feature any celebrity performers. Yet approximately eight times a week, 40 weeks a year, Broadway-sized crowds watch "Queen Esther" in a town of 12,000 people in the Ozark Mountains.Embracing the spectacle Sight & Sound's formula is seemingly simple: "spectacle meets story." In one scene of "Queen Esther," over a dozen women in bejeweled gowns twirl with lengthy scarves, turning the stage into a hypnotic, swirling sea of color. In another scene, 45 cast members sing from windows and doorways across a 300-foot-wide set that wraps around three sides to immerse the audience in live surround sound. At several points in the show, Xerxes and his men gallop up the aisles on real horses. Members of the royal court also ride a mechanical, fullsized elephant across the stage.Nonprofit theater has long resisted the siren call of spectacle.For artists who have adopted the theories of cultural critics Theodor Adorno and Max Horkheimer, outlandish, flashy performances reflect cynical pandering to the sensory pleasures of the masses to make money.But spectacle creates an experience that only live performance can offer: a visual, auditory and even - in the case of the horses in "Queen Esther" - olfactory. The effect transports an audience to another world, drawing people off their couches with the promise that they, too, can become part of an experience to remember.While some theater owners are beginning to recognize the value of spectacle, there's another lesson from Sight & Sound: the value of offering hope that seemingly insurmountable obstacles can be overcome.What do audiences really want?In the wake of the commingled disasters of recent years - the COVID-19 pandemic, George Floyd's murder, climate change and an insurrection at the nation's capitol - university dance and theater departments, as well as nonprofit theaters, have changed their mission statements to include social justice as an explicit aim of their programs. They promise productions that confront racism, homophobia and authoritarianism head-on.Musicologist Jake Johnson has written about today's dominant impulse toward "theater to make the present dystopia even more real." But theatergoers have not necessarily responded positively. Since 2020, some audiences and critics have complained that theater is tilting too far toward preachy messages.And when staring out at empty seats, practitioners cannot help but question their faith in theater's power to effect social change.Sight & Sound's success suggests that the problem is less with the message of social justice and more with the approach."Queen Esther" is an ancient story of antisemitism, after all.But as Sight & Sound Chief Creative Officer Josh Enck explained in a 2022 podcast, the shows seek "not just to inform or educate" but "to inspire" - particularly since "inspiration is at the core of who God is." The animatronic elephant lumbering across the stage with a jeweled headdress is not a distraction from the serious business of salvation, but rather a way of unlocking an audience member's sense of awe and wonder.People flock to Branson Sight & Sound is also earnest, a feature that fell out of favor with high-art theater at the dawn of the 21st century, when the sense that everything was fake led to productions that dripped with irony and cynicism.Today's compounding sociopolitical crises have shaken the theater world out of complacency. But in the fierce urgency to confront the world's myriad problems, earnestness is still seen as simplistic, naïve or even duplicitous.Sight & Sound expanded to Branson in 2008 because its earnest approach fit with the town's long-standing entertainment industry, which began back in 1907 with the publication of Harold Bell Wright's wildly popular novel "The Shepherd of the Hills." Tourists flocked to see the real-life inspirations for the characters, and local residents often obliged by performing versions of themselves. In 1959, the Mabe family began performing the Baldknobbers Hillbilly Jamboree to provide nighttime entertainment to tourists who had come to boat and fish during the day.The following year, an outdoor drama based on Wright's novel opened, as did a theme park called Silver Dollar City that recreated an 1880s Ozark village.Over time, dozens of theaters were built, featuring variety shows that combined country, gospel, Broadway tunes, comedy, magic tricks, dance numbers, acrobatics and even animal acts. Musicals that fit Branson's brand of familyfriendly, Christian entertainment also popped up along its strip. Many shows featured singers such as Andy Williams, whose greatest hits had been released decades earlier.Some of Branson's performers didn't qualify as stars at all. "The Shoji Tabuchi Show," arguably the most popular in town during the 1990s, was headlined by a fiddler who had never produced an original hit song or been featured on the radio.Branson performers - whether acrobats or singers or comedians - shared something in common: earnest messages of appreciation for their audiences, whom they greeted in person during intermissions and after shows.Ignoring the sneers In 1991, the Ozark Mountain tourist destination burst onto the national scene when it was featured on "60 Minutes." Reporters from the coasts flocked to the Ozarks in disbelief after the segment aired.Wasn't America supposed to be obsessed with youth and celebrity, not aging or unknown singers? And wasn't earnestness merely hucksterism in disguise to dupe audiences into parting with their hard-earned money?The coastal critics scrambled to come up with the wittiest insults. One called Branson a "cultural penal colony." Another preferred the term "Town of the Living Dead." Even "The Simpsons" couldn't resist piling on.The show went on, undeterred: In 2021, a record-breaking 10 million people came to visit.While not every show has survived the COVID-19 pandemic, clearly some performers are doing something right.Comedians like Stephen Colbert have continued to mock Branson, but live theater is in too much of a crisis to dismiss the town's approach.The town demonstrates that theater can return to the mission of imagining new, better worlds onstage and inviting audiences to join in that mission with them. It can be the stuff of spiritual transcendence - even if it grabs your attention by galloping down the aisle on a horse.Joanna Dee Das is an Assistant Professor in the Performing Arts Department at Washington University in St. Louis.This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article here: https://theconversation.com/what-livetheatercan-learn-from-bransonmissouri-213534. The Conversation is an independent and nonprofit source of news, analysis and commentary from academic experts.

title: Millington native to take stage at FallFest
author: Bob Ford; Special To The Kent County News Star Democrat
content:
Millington native to take stage at FallFest

 October 12, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bob Ford; Special To The Kent County News Star Democrat | Page: 2A | Section: News 
 
 839
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ROCK HALL - When guitarist Blake Thompson takes the stage at Rock Hall FallFest on Sat.Oct. 14, it will mark more than just a homecoming for the Millington native, it will be a virtual family reunion, picnic, and jam session all rolled into one.FallFest, the annual street fair that features nonstop live music on Main Street during the 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. event, will host the Blake Thompson Family Band on the Mainstay Stage at 2 p.m. Accompanying Thompson, the lead guitarist, will be his wife, four of his children, and a drummer who snuck into the family act somehow."Everybody's got to work. We're just poor musicians," Thompson said, with a laugh." The band is a hard-rocking ensemble, reflecting Thompson's guitar-driven passions that are heavily influenced by Stevie Ray Vaughn, Eric Clapton, Jimmy Page, Alvin Lee, and Billy Gibbons.When the family is together, however, the selections also drift all over the musical map."The littlest girl (vocalist daughter Rachel) will do some Dolly Parton and Linda Rondstadt, and we'll throw in some Monkees, like "Daydream Believer," Beatles, and kind of go from Dire Straits to Johnny Cash to 60's rock. In an event like that, you really want to mix it up a lot," Thompson said.Thompson's wife Kate plays keyboards and electric violin; his son, Blake Jr., plays keyboards and drums; daughter, Sarah, is a rhythm guitarist and vocalist, along with Rachel; daughter, Josie, is a bass guitar player; and Russ Reinacher will be sitting in on the drums.During his long career, the 57-year-old Thompson, who is also an accomplished recording engineer and mixer, has played regularly with his own band and with Bit O Jane and the Elliots. He's also toured in conjunction with the Steve Miller Band, Dave Matthews Band, The Gin Blossoms, David Crosby, Little Feat, and others.It is a career that got its start when he bought his first guitar at Dixon's Auction in Crumpton when he was a 15-year-old freshman at Kent County High School."I played ninth-grade football and I met a guy on the team who I talked music with all the time, and he played guitar, and I said, 'I'll get a guitar, too,'" Thompson said. "I bought a cheap guitar at Crumpton and it only had four strings and I played it like that for about three months. It just went from there. I worked and practiced and got some books, and I watched other local bands, and wrote down what they were doing, and ran home and practiced." By the end of high school, he had his own band with other musicians from the Massey area, where his family had relocated. And, as he said, his career went from there."It was wild. The whole band was from about a one-mile radius," Thompson said."In that band, and others after that, we played all over the area before I started traveling the country.I think I'm related to half of Kent County. I've got relatives in Chestertown, Rock Hall, Worton.This show at FallFest is like coming home, big-time. The whole event has a great vibe to it." While the Thompson Family show is can't-miss, it has some company on Main Street during FallFest. Also keeping things lively is Wicked Sycamore, an all-female acoustic Americana trio that recently won a Wammie Award, presented by the Washington Area Music Association; The High and Wides, a traditional bluegrass group that has long been a local favorite; Pat Wictor and Bob Beach, who play dobro, slide guitar, and harmonica to turn out haunting bluesbased rock; and The Good Stuff, a new country-tinged band led by Phil Dutton, who also fronts the Cajun-flavored group, The Alligators.And, of course, no FallFest is complete without an appearance by the Catonsville High School Steel Band, which plays the traditional tuned pans from Trinidad and Tobago.The group has been an annual FallFest highlight since 1999, and the band comes back bigger and better than ever this year.That's a great day of music, but FallFest is about more than music.In celebrating the opening of the commercial oyster season, approximately 6,000 oysters will be shucked onsite, and there is all manner of other street fair food, including fried oyster platters, burgers, dogs, tacos, fries, ice cream and, all the rest.Main Street becomes a pedestrian thoroughfare for visitors to stroll and explore our shops and take a look at the offerings of dozens of artisan vendors. There is also Kids Kourt at The Village at the foot of Main Street with games, prizes, animals, painting, clowns and much more for the younger set and all of it free.Admission and nearby parking is also free. So, come join us for a great day of music, food, and fun that benefits our local community projects. Some proceeds from our non-profit event support the Kent County Waterman's Association scholarship fund, and we also help fund improvements for The Mainstay, the iconic music venue at the heart of Main Street.See you on Oct. 14 at 10 a.m. for all the festivities. Bring your appetite and bring your dancing shoes.It's a family affair, especially for Blake Thompson.

title: Contemporary art galleries to open in Easton
author: Contributed
content:
Contemporary art galleries to open in Easton

 October 13, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 10 | Section: News 
 
 441
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Two new galleries have joined forces as contemporary art galleries at 5 N. Harrison Street in Easton.Spiralis Gallery, owned by Gail Patterson, features Contemporary Afro-Caribbean art, and The Zebra Gallery, owned by Susan Schauer John, an award-winning local fiber artist.The Spiralis Gallery launched its opening with some of its artwork being featured at the show "Things Fall Together" held at Out of the Fire Restaurant in Easton this past summer.John's fabric art was recently featured at the Smithsonian Craft Show in Washington, DC, and at the Oxford Fine Arts Fair."When I met Susan there was an instant connection. I think we both were searching for a way to bring a fresh perspective to the already wonderful art scene here in Easton," said Patterson "We believe collectors are inspired and informed by having a variety of art to experience, and the sophisticated collector enjoys the challenge of watching emerging artists unfold." "We hope to bring fresh, contemporary art that showcases the talents of remarkable contemporary artists from the area and around the world," John added."We will highlight Afro-Caribbean artists as well as fiber artists, and modern art that are catalysts for experiences and new perspectives." Both Patterson and John say their galleries will be actively involved in community-building with charitable organizations that fit within their mission.The space will have a new show every 10 weeks.A physician and art lover, Patterson launched her original gallery at Art Basel Miami and the Outsider Art Fair in 2012 and 2013. For 10 more years, her demanding medical career forced her to put her art gallery dreams on hold - until now."Afro-Caribbean art has always resonated with me, with its vibrant colors, exquisite patterns, and strong spiritual imagery," she said. "I am drawn inexorably to outsider artists, whose creations come directly from their souls." John has been an artist all her life, gaining inspiration and recognition in many art forms, including woodturning, portraiture and fiber arts.Her work has been exhibited and sold in galleries from Washington, D.C., to San Francisco and she has work in the permanent collection of the White House.Her work features animals, specifically species of birds native to the Chesapeake Bay region.Through fabric collage and creative stitching, she combines abstract and realism."Art is how I see the world, and what I see continues to evolve.This medium puts everything together," said John.The Gallery will be open for the first show, "Woman, Phenomenally," on Oct. 28, with a reception from 4:30 to 7 p.m. and an artist talk at 5 p.m. featuring Ernesto Beckford, a collage artist.A ribbon cutting and official opening will be held on First Friday, Nov. 3, from 4:30 to 7 p.m.

title: Adkins Arboretum to host second plein air event
author: Contributed
content:
Adkins Arboretum to host second plein air event

 October 18, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: A2 | Section: News 
 
 328
 Words 

 Read News Document

 "En plein air," a French term that means "in the open air," refers to the practice of painting entire finished artworks outdoors.Where an observer may see only a glimpse of a landscape, an artist sees light and atmosphere, shape and color, subject and form, all combining in a blaze of inspiration that compels the artist to capture it in paint.On Sat., Nov. 4, Adkins Arboretum will host the second annual Plein Air Adkins, a plein air paint-out, exhibit and sale, on the Arboretum grounds.The public is invited to explore the forest, meadows and wetland and observe as artists paint their original works.Artists will begin painting at 10 a.m. At 12:30 p.m., they will bring their completed works to the Visitor's Center for exhibition and judging.The juror is Alison Berry, a painter who exhibits in Maryland and Virginia and has participated and placed in numerous plein air events.Prizes will be awarded for first, second and third places and for honorable mentions. An Artist's Choice Award will also be given.Beltway Bistro, Blue Monkey Street Tacos and Ten Eyck Brewery will have food and drink for sale beginning at 11 a.m., and Fine Times will provide music during the exhibition and sale.All works created during Plein Air Adkins will be for sale during the exhibition.The event is open to any artist who wishes to participate. The artist registration fee is $20, and artists may register in advance or on the day of the event at adkinsarboretum.org. Observers are admitted free of charge.The event will take place in light rain or shine. In the event of heavy rain, it will be rescheduled for Sunday, Nov. 5. For more information, visit adkinsarboretum.org or call 410-634-2847, ext. 100.Plein Air Adkins is sponsored in part by the Caroline County Council of Art, Choptank Electric Cooperative and Unity Landscape Design|Build.

title: Catalysts and Collaborations: Galleries partnering in Easton - Local ART
content:
Catalysts and Collaborations: Galleries partnering in Easton - Local ART

 October 19, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 2 | Section: News 
 
 448
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Two art galleries are teaming up as Contemporary Art Galleries at 5 N. Harrison Street in Easton.Spiralis Gallery - which is owned by Gail Patterson and features contemporary Afro-Caribbean art - is partnering with The Zebra Gallery, which is owned by Susan Schauer John, an award-winning local fiber artist.The Spiralis Gallery launched its opening with some of its artwork being featured at Out of the Fire Restaurant in Easton in the summer with the show, "Things Fall Together."Susan John's fabric art was recently featured at the Smithsonian Craft Show in Washington, and at the Oxford Fine Arts Fair in Oxford, Maryland."When I met Susan there was an instant connection. I think we both were searching for a way to bring a fresh perspective to the already wonderful art scene here in Easton. We believe collectors are inspired and informed by having a variety of art to experience, and the sophisticated collector enjoys the challenge of watching emerging artists unfold," said Patterson."I think of a gallery as not just a place to sell art but a physical space where we engage in relevant conversations, build community, and celebrate creativity."John agrees."We hope to bring fresh, contemporary art that showcases the talents of remarkable contemporary artists from the area and around the world. We will highlight Afro-Caribbean artists as well as fiber artists, and modern art that are catalysts for experiences and new perspectives," she said.The collaboration will include social justice components and work with local charitable organizations.The gallery space will have a new show every 10 weeks to keep the content fresh for collectors, the owners said."Afro-Caribbean art has always resonated with me, with its vibrant colors, exquisite patterns, and strong spiritual imagery. And I am drawn inexorably to outsider artists, whose creations come directly from their souls," Patterson said.Patterson previously operated the Art Basel Miami gallery and the Outsider Art Fair. John's work has been featured in galleries in San Francisco and Washington D.C. and has works featured in the permanent art collection of the White House."Art is how I see the world, and what I see continues to evolve. This medium puts everything together," saidThe gallery will be open for the first show, "Woman, Phenomenally," on Oct. 28, with a reception from 4:30 p.m. to 7 p.m. and an artist talk at 5 p.m. featuring Ernesto Beckford, a collage artist. A ribbon cutting and official opening will be held on First Friday, Nov. 3. from 4:30 p.m. to 7 p.m.For more: https://spiral-isgallery.com/and https://www.thezebragallery. 
 
 Caption: Two new galleries, The Spiralis Gallery and The Zebra Gallery, have joined forces as "Contemporary Art Galleries" at 5 N. Harrison Street in Easton. Easton resident Gail Patterson's deep affinity for Afro-Caribbean art will be featured at The Spiralis Gallery.

 OXFORD - The Tred Avon Players will host auditions for "You Have The Right To Remain Dead," an audience-participation murder mystery which will be performed February 15-25, at the Oxford Community Center in Oxford, Md.Auditions will be held on Nov. 2 at 7:30 p.m., Nov. 4 at 11 a.m. and Nov. 7 at 7 p.m.TAP will be casting 5 men and 5 women. All ethnicities, body types, abilities and skill levels are welcome to audition and will be considered for parts.The play's narrator, Harnell Chesterton, takes the audience to visit a small community theater group staging a play set in the Deep South. The characters are all in an uproar because Fat Daddy, the patriarch of the family, is about to change his will.Is Fat Daddy the target of the killer? Is his wife, Sweet Mamma, looking to do him in? Or is it his son Earl, daughter-in-law Savannah or daughter Hyacinth?Maybe it's the hired hand Clete! But - is it really Fat Daddy who is dead? Just wait until local police sleuth Officer Bainbridge begins his investigation!Rob Sanchez will be directing "You Have The Right To Remain Dead."Auditioners are asked to come prepared to read selected scenes (sides) from the script, which will be provided. Email rsanchez@goe-aston.net for any special accommodations.TAP also needs a stage manager and production crew (sets, lights, sound, costumes, props and stage crew) for the show.Founded in 1982, Tred Avon Players is a nonprofit organization whose purpose is to enrich, educate and entertain its community by providing a high-quality theater experience.Hundreds of local performers, stagehands, audience members and donors have been the backbone of its success throughout the decades.For more information or topurchase tickets for Upcoming shows, visit www.tredavonplayers.org.

title: Photo talk to explore junction of science and art
author: Contributed
content:
Photo talk to explore junction of science and art

 October 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 9 | Section: News 
 
 278
 Words 

 Read News Document

 If it's the aim of the fine arts to give insight or inspiration, then the scientific image is worthy of consideration as an artistic medium, argues Norm Baker, a professor of pathology and art as applied to medicine at Johns Hopkins University.Baker will be speaking at the Tidewater Camera Club's Nov. 6 meeting, to be held at Unitarian Universalist Church in Easton from 7 to 9 p.m., on the subject, delving into the history of photography as a scientific discipline.Ironically, photography was invented by a scientist and not an artist.It was the scientists who realized the importance of this new and novel process to document and to elucidate their scientific activities. The idea of having objects draw themselves on a plate without the aid of an artist's hand is a concept that is foreign now, but that's exactly how one of the early inventors, William Henry Fox Talbot, described his Calotype process.Baker will make his case on the subject at the meeting, which is free and open to the public. This talk will examine how the context in which a photograph is viewed can have an effect on how the image is interpreted.Baker's photographs are in the permanent collections of more than forty museums, including The Smithsonian, The George Eastman Museum, The American Museum of Natural History, The Nelson-Atkins Museum and The Science Museum in London.He has published 9 books and numerous scientific articles and book chapters.His current traveling exhibition "Hidden Beauty: Exploring The Aesthetics of Medical Science" shows the beauty of medicine and the human body and will be going on a museum tour in 2014-2023. His latest book "Perambulations" was published in 2022 by Man & Lion Press.

title: From Overseas to Arm Sleeves - How Elkton's Massimiano marries art, community and service
author: Matt Hubbard; mhubbard@chespub.com
content:
From Overseas to Arm Sleeves - How Elkton's Massimiano marries art, community and service

 October 24, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Hubbard; mhubbard@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1862
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ELKTON - Being, simultaneously, a town commissioner, tattoo artist, band member and military veteran may not be common for many people, but for Rob Massimiano, it is his life."I am grateful to have been able to make a living through my art because I have been an artist since I could walk," Massimiano said. "But I really enjoy being a part of the community and helping my friends and neighbors - I always have." Massimiano, 64, moved from the outskirts of Philadelphia to Elkton at the age of 17 with his mother, younger brother and younger sister in 1976. The family of four settled into a home at Locust Point.Massimiano finished high school at Bohemia Manor and went on to join the Navy in 1979 at age 20.In the Navy, Massimiano served as a Seabee where he operated heavy machinery building infrastructure all over the world for the US military. Massimiano recalled that the most common structures he and his comrades built outside of combat were runways, since they kept getting bombed."In combat, we were digging foxholes for the guys," Massimiano said. "We were in combat like everyday but the bombs never stopped hitting the runways either." One of Massimiano's most memorable moments from his time in service occurred when he was in Beirut where he said he was tasked with constructing underground bases for marines in the desert.His battalion would dig a huge hole, then place shipping containers in the hole before covering the containers with a layer of dirt, sandbags, lumber and chain link fencing.According to Massimiano, the chain link fencing covering the base caused incoming mortar rounds to scatter upon impact rather, than explode downward onto the containers."The fencing worked well because like the runways, those bases were hit several times and the marines were safe," Massimiano said. "It was cool." Between deployments, Massimiano was stationed at his home base in Gulfport, Mississippi. While in Mississippi during his first year in the military, he bought a guitar from a local pawn shop along with a book that he said he used to teach himself how to play guitar.Almost all of Massimiano's free time - prior to, and during his time in the military - was spent drawing.The addition of playing the guitar forced him to divide his free time between playing guitar and creating art which he said he loved."Drawing has occupied much of my time because I have been doing it since I could hold a pencil," Massimiano said. "Picking up a guitar was great because drawing and music all come from the same side of the brain." In 1984, Massimiano, who was 25 at the time, completed his five years of service in the Navy, during which time he received several medals. He recalled that the two he is most proud of are a Combat Action Ribbon from his time spent in combat in Beirut and a Marine Corps Expeditionary Medal that he received for his support of the Marine Corps.Massimiano returned to Elkton in 1985 where he bought the house he still lives in today.For the next year, he worked a variety of construction and heavy machinery jobs while filling his free time with drawing and guitar. Then, in 1986, Massimiano began a tattooing apprenticeship and discovered a new passion."I would frame houses all day and do my apprenticeship all night," Massimiano said. "It was like that for about a year." Massimiano noted that tattooing is the hardest art medium he has ever worked in, which is why he enjoys it so much."I have tried just about all art forms and if you ask any tattoo artist: tattooing is the hardest because you can not mess up," Massimiano said.Later that same year in 1986, Massimiano and his older brother opened a tattoo shop on East Main Street in downtown Elkton.The shop was one of three locations the brothers opened, the other two located over the border in Delaware.Massimiano ran all three locations on his own - changing the name to Tidewater Tattoos - after his brother moved down south.After 18 years at the small shop attached to the back of the Minihanes building in Elkton, and complications with keeping the Delaware locations staffed, Massimiano said he got the idea to consolidate Tidewater's operations to one shop directly across the street from the Elkton location."I was standing in the Elkton shop one day and I saw a for sale sign out front of the spot we currently own and I said, 'you know what, I'm going to close my Delaware shops and bring those artists here' and I've been operating here for 19 years since," Massimiano said.Massimiano runs the shop with his 28 year old son David, who Massimiano says "really keeps the flame under me." "He does great work," Massimiano said. "He is going to be better than me." As a professional tattoo artist, Massimiano is well known for his portraiture, wildlife and Polynesian tribal work. This has not only granted him the opportunity to travel the United States giving seminars on his technique, but he's also served on the board of directors for the National Tattoo Association as well as the board of directors for the Alliance of Professional Tattooists."I am always looking to help and counsel fellow tattoo artists and clients, and even legislation regarding the industry," Massimiano said. "It has been a pleasure of mine." After becoming a fixture in the Elkton community, Massimiano said he was approached by the Elkton Arts Council and asked to serve on the board of directors.Massimiano took the position and served on the board for about six years before moving to serve on the board for the Elkton Alliance.Massimiano said that serving on those boards were great experiences as they helped him better understand the town of Elkton and how he might be able to help move the town forward."There are people who sit back and live their lives and then there's the people who step forward who at least want to try to do the right thing and that's what I have wanted to do since I moved here," Massimiano said.Massimiano spent approximately seven years on the Elkton Alliance's board, balancing his board duties, tattoo shop operations and playing in his band, Plan B, before the passing of former Elkton Commissioner Mary Jo Jablonski in 2019.Jablonski and Massimiano were great friends, as they served on the Alliance board together prior to her becoming a commissioner, Massimiano recalled.Shortly after Jablonski passing, Massimiano paid tribute to his friend by drawing a portrait of her. Copies of the portrait were hung in the Elkton Administration Building and the Elkton Alliance offices.Since Jablonski had passed one year into her four year term as a commissioner, the Elkton Mayor and Commissioners held interviews to find a candidate to fill her position. Massimiano was one of 10 candidates.During the interview process, Massimiano remembers that Commissioner Earl Piner asked him: "if awarded the position as commissioner, what would you do to improve Elkton?" "Instead of trying to buffalo my way through the answer, I told them that I honestly didn't know what I could do because I didn't know what my powers or abilities would be as commissioner and what tools would be at my disposal," Massimiano said. "I said that once I figured it out, I would use every tool available to make Elkton a better place." Massimiano believes he was selected to finish Jabonski's term due to his ability to be honest and admit when he didn't know something."They appreciate my honesty and my ability to admit when I didn't know something, which I have always been that way," Massimiano said.Around the time that he became commissioner, Massimiano was still playing music, but Plan B had fallen apart due to the COVID-19 pandemic.With no band to play in but a passion for music still flourishing, Massimiano began solo performances in 2021. He said he was nervous for his first solo performance at the North East VFW so he brought his son David - who "shreds on the guitar" - and his friend who plays drums to turn the solo act into a band.While Massimiano, his drummer friend Box Turtle Bob and his son David were performing at the VFW, the former bass player from Massimiano's band Plan B walked in and saw the trio of musicians."He had his bass in his car so he grabbed it and got set up and just like that we became a four-piece band," Massimiano said. "We called ourselves The Nightcrawlers and now we are busier than Plan B ever was.The Nightcrawlers primarily play in and around Cecil County, but have gone as far as Newark, Del. and Harford County to perform classic rock.Now balancing his role as a town commissioner, a newly-formed band and Tidewater's ever-busy schedule, Massimiano chose to run for, and win, re-election as commissioner during Elkton's 2022 election - securing his current four year term.As commissioner, Massimiano said he is proud of the annual fishing rodeo he organizes and hosts each year, his part in bringing Southfields to fruition in Elkton and his ability to bring in a local flood control group to help Elkton alleviate flooding issues.Massimiano said he is happy with the direction Elkton is headed and would like to see more growth in the town, especially the arts."Being down here for so long, I have seen Elkton in many different stages," Massimiano said. "When I first came here, downtown Elkton was nice, lots of businesses, quiet, we all knew each other, and it was very nice and clean, and I think we are headed toward that again." Massimiano noted that Elkton is one of Maryland's designated art's districts and that he enjoys the abundance of creativity coming to the town. He aims to continue working with the Elkton Arts Council and the Elkton Alliance to further the town's artistic growth."I love the energy of downtown Elkton and being around other artists of all disciplines," Massimiano said. "We have a lot of artists here and I feel like I am just immersed in it and it is great and I would like to see that momentum continue and for more art to come in." He explained that Elkton's growth will only remain a positive thing in the town if the next generation of leaders are strong.Massimiano said that he hopes to implement a program where the town works with local high schools to get students involved with leadership in the town because "future leaders need to come from somewhere." Massimiano hopes to inspire Elkton town members to do the right thing when no one is looking because those are the acts that move a community forward."I painted the gazebo at the ballfields near Main Street, I pick up bottles when I see them on the sidewalk and I see other people doing the same things, and it is great," Massimiano said. "If there is something that needs to be done, we should do it regardless of if anyone sees us do it because that is the true measure of a good person."

title: CBMM launches new construction buyboat
author: Contributed
content:
CBMM launches new construction buyboat

 October 25, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 10 | Section: News

 Bay Maritime Museum's Shipyard has completed its latest project with the launch of the 36-foot Chesapeake Bay buyboat Mr. Dickie.The Shipyard team began work on the new construction build last fall after finishing up its build ofMary-land Dove and worked over the past year under the direction of Shipyard Foreman Jeff Reed to bring the vessel to life.A contract build for owners Grigg and Cindy Mullen of Lexington, Va., Mr. Dickie will be on display later this month at the Sultana Downrigging Festival in Chestertown before returning to dock at CBMM."Grigg provided the opportunity for us to have our Shipyard team do a complete build from start to finish, creating a unique object in a way that realizes Grigg and our dream of a comprehensive construction that allows for public and Shipwright education," said Vice President of Shipyard Operations Christian Cabral. "It's been an incredible experience."The construction of the unique vessel in CBMM's Shipyard offered a glimpse into the past while highlighting the future for a historic style ofvessel vital to the story of the Chesapeake Bay.Buyboats are cross-planked workboats that were traditionally used for hauling oysters from skipjacks to market in season and anything else that needed transporting the rest of the year.Today, there are estimated to be fewer than 30 buyboats that continue to ply the Bay's waters.Mr. Dickie pays homage to the 60-foot buyboat Mundy Point, designed to bring the buyboat look to a scaled-down 36-foot version. It was constructed from heart pine, white oak, Atlantic cedar and western red cedar, and outfitted with a restored late-1930s Buda diesel engine.A retired engineering professor, Grigg Mullen maintained a hands-on role throughout the yearlong construction, working alongside CBMM's Shipyard crew whenever his schedule allowed.He and Cindy were on hand for a CBMM Member Night on Oct. 12 celebrating Mr. Dickie and the Oct. 20 launch for the new buyboat that is named in honor of the late Dickie Whaley, Mullen's neighbor growing up in Queen Anne's County."It's been a wonderful year building Mr. Dickie and working with the Shipyard folks," Mullen said. "Every time there was a decision to make, it was always - if we do it this way, it's going to be better. It's turned out wonderfully."With Mr. Dickie completed, CBMM's Shipyard will stay busy with a variety of projects heading into the winter months, including ongoing work on a pair of buyboats in its historic floating fleet.Winnie Estelle, CBMM's passenger-carrying 1920 buyboat, is amidst a refit that includes the removal, fabrication, and replacement of its structural timbers. 1938 buyboat Choptank is undergoing a final fit out, which involves building out the interior with cabins and heads for expedition-style overnight trips and outfitting it with modern safety equipment and a new rig.Findmore information about CBMM's Shipyard and itsprojects at cbmm.org/ship-yard.

title: Halloween tricks and treats
author: Mabel Savage; Country Cooking
content:
Halloween tricks and treats

 October 25, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Mabel Savage; Country Cooking | Page: A4 | Section: News 
 
 1211
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Halloween Celebrations have changed through the years, but the fun ofthe young children getting dressed in their favorite attire has not.Attending the school parties and watching the children parade down the halls is priceless. Some towns still hold the annual Halloween parades through the downtown streets, complete with fire trucks, different businesses and clubs with displays, and candy being thrown to the children.The parade ends with Santa getting the early Christmas list from each child in exchange for that candy cane!Trick or treaters love getting lots of candy, which can be purchased at the big name stores by large bags. But for the school parties and other events, everyone loves homemade sweets and treats.My favorite treat to make was always sugar cookies, to which I added a mixture of red and yellow food coloring to reach a light orange color. Just before baking, I would place one candy pumpkin, candy corn or other Halloween candy symbol in the center of the cookie. Use your imagination, and have fun watching the children's faces light up!Today, I will include some of the recipes from years gone by, along with a few new ones.HALLOWEEN FUDGELine an 8 inch square pan with foil and spray with cooking spray. Open one bag - 12 ounce size-Nes-tle Toll House Halloween morsels and separate the orange pieces from the semi-sweet pieces. Starting with the semi-sweet morsels, measure how many were in the separated pile and add enough semi-sweet chips to make 1 1/2 cups total. You will get about 1 cup chips from the bag so you need to add more chips to make the 1 1/2 cups total. Add the semisweet chips to a saucepan with 1/2 cup sweetened condensed milk. Heat over low heat, stirring constantly until smooth. Remove from heat and stir in 1/2 teaspoon vanilla. Spread this in the foil lined pan with a spatula, spreading to fit the pan. Place this pan in the refrigerator for 10 minutes before starting the next step. Measure how many orange chips and add enough white chocolate chips to equal 1 1/2 cups. Add these chips to a pan with remaining 1/2 cup sweetened condensed milk. Heat over low heat until smooth, stirring constantly. Remove from the heat and add 1/2 teaspoon vanilla. Spread this carefully over the layer in the foil lined pan, spreading over the top to the edges. Immediately press at least 24 pieces ofcandy corn on the top. Chill to harden, remove and cut into slices and serve at room temperature.POPCORN BALLSPlace 7 quarts offresh popped popcorn in a large bowl and set aside. In a saucepan place 1 cup light corn syrup, 1/4 cup water and 1/4 teaspoon salt. Cook over medium heat until it forms a soft ball. Remove from heat and add 3 tablespoons butter, 1 teaspoon vanilla extract and orange food coloring, optional- stir until butter is melted. Immediately pour in popcorn and stir until evenly coated. Shape into 3 inch balls. Kids love these popcorn balls.RICE KRISPIES TREATSIn a large saucepan, melt 3 tablespoons butter over low heat. Add one package - 10 ounce size - marshmallows and stir until completely melted. Add 6 cups of Rice Krispies cereal and stir until well coated. Using a buttered spatula evenly press mixture into a 3 x 9 x 2 inch pan coated with cooking spray. Cool and cut into 2 inch squares. You can press a candy corn or other candy into the top of each square.HALLOWEEN SUGAR COOKIES1 and 1/2 cups all-purpose flour, 3/4 cup unsweetened natural cocoa powder, plus more as needed for rolling and work surface, 1 teaspoon baking powder, 1/8 teaspoon salt, 3/4 cup unsalted butter, softened to room temperature, 1 cup granulated sugar, 1 large egg at room temperature, 1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract, Easy Cookie Icing, optional: gel food coloring for tinting icings. Whisk the flour, cocoa powder, baking powder, and salt together in a medium bowl. In a large bowl using a hand mixer or a stand mixer fitted with a paddle attachment, beat the butter and sugar together on high speed until completely smooth and creamy, about 2 minutes. Add the egg and vanilla and beat on high speed until combined, about 1 minute. Scrape down the sides and up the bottom ofthe bowl and beat again as needed to combine. Add the dry ingredients to the wet ingredients and mix on low until combined. Dough will be soft. Ifthe dough seems too soft and sticky for rolling, add 1 moreTablespoon offlour.Divide the dough into 2 equal parts. Dust 2 large pieces ofparch-ment paper or 2 silicone baking mats with cocoa powder (or flour). Place a dough halfon each. With a rolling pin lightly dusted with cocoa powder (or flour), roll the dough out to about 1/4-inch thickness. Use more cocoa powder/flour ifthe dough seems too sticky. The rolled-out dough can be any shape, as long as it is evenly 1/4-inch thick. Lightly dust one ofthe rolled-out doughs with cocoa powder or flour. Place a piece ofparchment on top. (This prevents sticking.) Place the 2nd rolled-out dough on top. Cover with plastic wrap or aluminum foil, then refrigerate for at least 1-2 hours and up to 2 days. Once chilled, preheat the oven to 350°F (177°C). Line 2-3 large baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone baking mats. Carefully remove the top dough piece from the refrigerator.Using cookie cutters, cut the dough into shapes. Re-roll the remaining dough, using more cocoa powder or flour to lightly dust your work surface and rolling pin, and continue cutting the dough until all is used. Work quickly so the dough doesn't become too warm or soft. If it does, stop what you're doing and place any unused dough back in the refrigerator for 10 minutes to stiffen up again. Repeat cutting into shapes with the 2nd half of the dough. Arrange shaped cookies on baking sheets 3 inches apart. Bake for 11-12 minutes or until edges are set. If your oven has hot spots, rotate the baking sheet halfway through bake time. Allow cookies to cool on the baking sheet for 5 minutes and then transfer to a wire rack to cool completely before decorating. Prepare the easy cookie icing. Divide the icing into separate bowls ifyou wish to tint it different colors using gel food coloring.Plain or decorated cookies stay soft for about 5 days when covered tightly at room temperature. For longer storage, cover and refrigerate for up to 10 days.GHOST S'MORES DIP1 bag ghost marshmallows,2 c. semi-sweet chocolate chips, 1/4 c. heavy cream, warmed, Graham crackers, for serving, Mini chocolate chips, for ghost eyes. Preheat the oven to 450°. In the bottom ofa 9" ovenproofskillet, baking dish, or pie dish, spread out chocolate chips and pour cream on top. Cover completely with a single layer ofghost marshmallows. Place mini chocolate chips over eyes and mouth. Bake until the chocolate has melted and the ghosts are golden, 8 to 10 minutes. Serve warm with graham crackers for dipping.REESE'S BATS1 bag of Reese's cups 1 package of Oreo cookies, 1 jar ofcreamy peanut butter, 1 bag ofcandy eyes. One ofthe easiest recipes and that is great to throw together for a snack or treat. Separate the Oreo cookies from the cream. Next, slice them in half. There may be some casualties as Oreos can be a bit crumbly, I suggest using a serrated paring knife. Next, attach them to your Reese's with a dab ofpeanut butter. Apply the same peanut butter method for the eyes and you've got your bats!

 AMERICAN CORNER- Following a five-year hiatus because of the COVID pandemic, a popular concert and top country and bluegrass stars will return Saturday, Nov. 18, to the Curtis Andrew Auction Facility in American Corner.Billed as a "Bluegrass Country Concert," three acts will be featured, with Rhonda Vincent and the Rage headlining. Vincent is a Grammy Award winner, a member of the Grand Ole Opry and the "Queen of Bluegrass.""We love the Andrew family, and I've been performing there over 20 years, so it's like coming home," Vincent said."We've had a good relationship from day one, and the public really loves her," auctioneer and owner Curtis Andrew said of Vincent. "She's an easy person to please when she comes here. What you see - that's the real Rhonda."The opening act will be Wilson Fairchild, billed as the "Ambassadors of Country Music." Wil Reid's father is Harold Reid, and his cousin Langdon Reid's dad is Don Reid of the legendary Statler Brothers.As the Fairfax Trio, U.S. Navy Band musician Haley Stiltner, Matthew Songmaker Ziesing and his wife Sally Sandker create close harmonies and craveable bluegrass Gospel music.Andrew and his family have hosted the family-friendly country and bluegrass music concerts at the auction facility since 1997.He values the opportunity to give back to the community and bring smiles to the faces of friends, neighbors and those as far away as Kansas and Canada who comprise the toe-tapping audience.Despite the enormous amount of hard work and coordination the concerts require of him and his family and staff, Andrew said he enjoys "watching the fans having a good time and an enjoyable evening."The musicians and singers he's met through the years prompt fond memories. Artists like Hank Williams III, John Anderson, Marty Stuart have graced the stage of the large auction building, which is completely emptied of auction tables and transformed into a concert hall with professional stage, lighting, sound system and curtains.Tickets are $60 each. Recordings and videotaping are prohibited.The facility's restaurant and staff will serve reasonably priced dinners and lighter fare. title: Replica Spanish armada ship on display at maritime museum
author: Contributed
content:
Replica Spanish armada ship on display at maritime museum

 October 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 9 | Section: News 
 
 365
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - The Nao Trinidad arrived in St. Michaels on Oct. 25, when it docked at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, where the replica historical boat will serve as a display of maritime heritage.The Nao Trinidad was the flagship of what was called Armada del Maluco (1519-1522), captained by Ferdinand Magellan.Five ships (naos) departed from Seville, but only two made it to the Spice Islands. Nao Trinidad was one of them.This beautiful replica weighs 150 tons, is 93 feet in length and has a 26-foot beam, three masts and a bowsprit. The height of the mainmast is more than 82 feet, with five sails and five decks, built with exquisite work in Iroko (an African hardwood) and pinewood.This ship has sailed to many different ports across the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic European Coast as a training vessel and floating museum.Naos have a unique and original design that made them the most advanced in naval engineering for their time, used first as cargo ships in Spain and then taking the lead as exploring vessels.The Nao Trinidad currently docked in Talbot County is a fullscale replica, faithful to the original's design and dimensions.More than a hundred artisans of the sea worked on its construction, including ship carpenters, rope masters and naval engineers.Visitors will be able to tour four decks to get a feel for how life was onboard during the ship's heyday and how it is to live today on an historical ship of these characteristics.They will be able to learn about the maneuvering and rigging of the boat and interact with the crew, who have the most amazing experiences from their long voyages.The boat will be available to visit at the maritime museum until Oct. 31 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.A ticket to enter the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum must be purchased to access the ship, except for museum members.IN addition to this ticket cost, the cost to board the ship is $12 for adults, $5 for children ages 6 to 17 and free for children 5 and under.

title: New mural brightens Preston
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
New mural brightens Preston

 November 1, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 1B | Section: News 
 
 622
 Words 

 Read News Document

 PRESTON - The rural farming scene painted at Mike's Liquors last week is large - at least 60 feet across - a scale fitting for the project, which town officials say is part of a larger effort to enhance downtown Preston."The town of Preston was interested in doing an art project. It is part of our Sustainable Community certification process, along with enhancing our parks and rec and everything downtown," said Amber Korell, the town manager. "We were able to secure a planning grant through the Maryland State Arts Council for $10,000 in collaboration with the Caroline County Arts Council." Korell said there were two designs submitted for this mural, along with four for a meditation wall, which will be completed at a later date.All the designs were put online, and the community voted for their favorite. At a commissioner's meeting, the artist's statements about their project were read aloud.111 votes were cast for Tindall's piece."This is exciting because it is the first Preston public art installation," the artist said. "I am super grateful to be able to do something like this.The community involvement has been extremely encouraging." Tindall used around five cans of paint and 10 spray paint cans to realize his folk art vision of a sunny day in Preston, including a red tractor, brilliant sun and rolling green farm land.Mike's Liquors was a cantaloupe orange before Tindall began his work, and there were lots of chips and imperfections in the surface of the wall.Tindall caulked and primed the surface to allow the art to stick to something. He even painted on a base primer before he could get creative.After painting for five days, he will apply polyurethane to weather seal it."I started sketching it in with spray paints and going in and fine tuning the details with a little artist's brush," he said on Monday. "I am 90% done.It is exciting to do larger works and be outside and engage with the people that stop by that are curious." People who drove by and saw the mural gave a supportive honk on their way by, Tindall said."I tried to pick subject material that was fitting for the area and that resonated with the community - something that was really going to brighten up the side of this building," he said."This is a prominent corner that receives so much traffic. It has turned almost into a folk art piece. What I am going to do this afternoon is go to the studio and cut out stencils. I am going to put up 'Preston' up in the sky. It will fit perfectly." Korrell and the town council have another art project in mind for a meditation wall and mural to be built in the James T. Wright Memorial Park.Jennifer Lenderking, with the winning design, went through the same voting process as Tindall."I want to get things done. I want to see that we are making progress," Korrell said. "We are really going to try to get what the community wants done. I am applying for a Maryland State Arts Council project grant. I have my project, I have my artist.I am going to apply for $30,000 to see if I get awarded for that."

title: Sultana Downrigging brings in the crowds
author: Laura Tayman; ltayman@chespub.com
content:
Sultana Downrigging brings in the crowds

 November 1, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman; ltayman@chespub.com | Page: 6A | Section: News

 Words
