title: Reimagining Thanksgiving leftovers
author: Marie Savage; Country Cooking
content:
Reimagining Thanksgiving leftovers

 November 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Marie Savage; Country Cooking | Page: 4A | Section: News 
 
 1228
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Thanksgiving leftovers are just as good the next day or a couple of days later.Even Thanksgiving Eve, folks are looking in the fridge or under the covered dishes for a bite.I used to make individual platters, consisting of each food to be heated in the microwave, carried to work, or sent home with someone.Check on that elderly neighbor, or shut-in, or just someone living alone, and deliver a plate. As you sit around the table with family and friends give thanks for all our blessings, no matter how great or how small.Remember those who are serving our country at home and abroad. Remember those working Thanksgiving so we can be home.Remember the law enforcement officers, the hospital staff, the firemen and fire women, the EMT personnel - anyone who volunteered to work today so others could enjoy this day with family and others. We are all thankful for your continued service to us and our families.I know the cooks have already decided what type of meat to cook for Thanksgiving dinner, so I decided to do the leftover recipes today in preparation for the days after the big meal. We all tend to cook more than needed for two reasons - better to have more than needed rather than run out and we can eat leftovers for the rest of the weekend!Maybe you had turkey for dinner with the possibility of many dishes to create - turkey soup, hot turkey sandwiches with gravy, turkey salad, turkey chili and one of my favorites, the Bobbie sandwich.Maybe you cooked a large beef roast with plenty left over to make beef vegetable soup, hot roast beef sandwiches and beef cubes with gravy over rice. Enjoy the leftovers with much less stress. Now, let's get to some Black Friday shopping!TURKEY CARCASS SOUPPut parts of the turkey carcass in a large pot with 8 cups of turkey or chicken broth, 1 head of garlic (halved), 2 bay leaves and 2 sprigs of thyme.In a large Dutch oven, cut carcass to fit in the pot and add enough water to cover only by an inch. Bring to a boil over medium high heat.Simmer, uncovered about 40 minutes. Remove the carcass and add 2 cups dry diced turkey meat, 2 cups frozen corn, 2 cups frozen green beans (cut into 1-inch pieces), salt and pepper to taste, and 1 cup small dry pasta. Cover and cook for another 15 minutes.I usually add 1/2 cup chopped celery and 1/2 cup diced onions.TURKEY POT PIE2 tablespoons butter, 1 onion (chopped), 2 stalks celery (chopped), 3 carrots (chopped), 4 tbsp flour, 4 cups chicken or turkey stock, 2 potatoes (peeled and diced), 2 cups shredded turkey, 2 tablespoons chopped parsley, 1/2 cup frozen peas (thawed), 1 prepared pie crust, 1 egg (lightly beaten). Preheat the oven to 350 degrees.Melt butter in a saucepan, and cook chopped onion until tender. Stir in celery and carrots and cook for 2 minutes. Stir in flour and cook for 2 minutes. Add chicken stock and bring to a simmer. Add potatoes and simmer until tender.Stir in turkey, parsley and peas. Pour mixture into the casserole. Top with pie crust and brush with egg.Bake for 30 minutes until the crust is golden.THANKSGIVING LEFTOVER HAND PIESOne 14.1-ounce package store-bought pie crust, all-purpose flour for dusting, 1/4 cup leftover mashed sweet potatoes, 1/2 cup leftover stuffing, 1/2 cup 1/4-inch diced leftover roasted turkey, 1/4 cup leftover cranberry sauce (plus more for dipping), 1 large egg, 1 teaspoon whole milk, leftover gravy (for dipping). Preheat the oven to 350 degrees and line a baking sheet with parchment paper. Roll out the pie crusts with a rolling pin on a lightly floured surface to 1/8-inch thick. Cut out rounds of dough with a 4 1/2-inch round biscuit cutter and transfer them to the prepared baking sheet. Gather and re-roll the scraps if necessary; you should have a total of 12 rounds. Spread 1 tsp sweet potato in an even layer over half of each round, leaving a 1/4-inch border around the edge. Top each with 2 tsps stuffing, then 2 tsps turkey, and finally 1 tsp cranberry sauce. You may redistribute some of the filling among the rounds so all the piles are even. Whisk together the egg and milk in a small bowl to make an egg wash. Brush the egg wash around the edges of each dough round. Fold over each dough round to cover the filling, creating 12 half-moon shapes.With your fingers, press the edges together to seal, and then press with a fork to seal securely. Brush the top of each hand pie with the remaining egg wash. Make 3 small slits with a small paring knife on the top of each pie to let the steam escape. Bake until the dough is cooked through and golden brown, about 30 minutes. Serve warm with extra cranberry sauce and gravy on the side for dipping.BOBBIE SANDWICHSandwiches are extremely popular for leftovers because there's usually so much turkey or ham! What makes these simple and easy is because you already have the major ingredients. A popular one in my family is the Bobbie.It's a turkey hoagie or sub with stuffing, cranberry sauce sub. Grab a bag of your favorite sub rolls or buns and use your leftover turkey dinner dishes.The ingredients you need are mayonnaise, slices of roast turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, salt and pepper to taste. Using a 9-inch to a 20-inch sub roll, lay the sub roll open and smear with mayonnaise.On top of the mayo, place thin slices of turkey - as much as you like. Try shredding the turkey so it looks like shredded beef or pork. On top of the turkey, place leftover stuffing and on top of the stuffing place cranberry sauce. Put as much of the fillings that you want. Roll the sandwich together and serve immediately. This sub does not need to be warm and tastes better cold.THANKSGIVING LEFTOVER NACHOS1 cup sour cream, 1 tbsp minced chipotle chili in adobo (plus more sauce for serving), 10 cups tortilla chips, 2 cups shredded leftover turkey meat, 3 cups shredded cheddar, 2 cups shredded Monterey jack cheese, 2 cups thinly sliced leftover cooked Brussels sprouts, 1 1/2 cups leftover cubed roasted butternut squash, 1 cup packaged french-fried onions, 1 cup lightly packed cilantro leaves or parsley leaves, 1/2 cup sliced black olives, 1/4 cup chopped pickled jalapenos.Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Stir the sour cream and chipotle chili together in a small bowl. Cover with plastic wraps and refrigerate.Scatter half the chips on a rimmed baking sheet.Top with one-third of the turkey, cheeses, Brussels sprouts, butternut squash and fried onions. Scatter the remaining chips on top followed by the remaining two-thirds of turkey, cheeses, Brussels sprouts and fried onions. Bake until the cheeses are melted and bubbly, about 5 to 7 minutes.Drizzle the nachos with chipotle sour cream and extra adobo sauce. Garnish with cilantro, black olives and jalapenos.I'd like to wish everyone a safe, happy and healthy Thanksgiving! Please take the time to check on your shut in or elderly neighbors as they might not be as fortunate as others. There is nothing that puts a smile on someone's face like a nice big plate of food!As you sit down together at the Thanksgiving dinner table give thanks for all that we have and bless the hands who prepared this meal. Next week we take a trip back in time to the family farm. I'm thankful for all my readers, and God bless you all.

Thanksgiving leftovers can be reimagined in a variety of ways.

title: Tour five regional museums through virtual reality
content:
Tour five regional museums through virtual reality

 November 23, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 4 | Section: News

 CHESTERTOWN - Washington College's Center for Environment & Society (CES) and the Digital Scholarship in Museum Partnerships (DSMP) project are proud to invite local and regional visitors to virtually "tour" the collections from several regional museums, all in one place. Housed in the community space at 210 South Cross Street in downtown Chestertown, the exhibit includes interactive exhibit banners from the DSMP's collaborations with Kent County museums over the last six years, including Betterton Heritage Museum, the Worton Point Schoolhouse, the Waterman's Museum, the Kent Museum, and Sumner Hall.With the goal of preserving and providing greater access to the local histories of our community, the exhibit offers digitized looks into each museum viewable through virtual reality with 360-degree virtual tours of the museums, a look at digitized collections from each site, oral history interviews, and more. The exhibit also features a new curved projection theatre which creates an immersive environment in which to experience the virtual tours.The panels were created by Washington College students participating in the DSMP project and serve as a continuation of their work which was curated under the guidance of Sara Clarke-De Reza, Associate Professor of Education and Director of the Museum, Community and Field Education Minor; Julie Markin, Professor of Anthropology and Director of Archaeology; and Raven Bishop, Assistant Director of Educational Technology and Lead of the Virtual/Augmented Reality Digital Imaging Studio at the Millier Library. After a successful one-day pop-up showcase of the project last fall, an opportunity to put the work on display for a longer period, and for a wider public audience, emerged at the Cross Street space."Working with these museums affords our students the opportunity to apply concepts and best practices learned in the classroom to a project that makes a real impact for the local community," said Bishop. "Students and community stakeholders are immediately able to see the real-world impact of this work as it improves access to the history and culture of Kent County within and beyond our community." Bishop added that community partners often report that their organizations feel reinvigorated by the energy and enthusiasm that DSMP students bring to the project. The reciprocal relationship advances the common purpose of providing greater access to the important cultural heritage of the Eastern Shore that is held in so many small, rural community museums."It would be easy to say that the technology is the most interesting part of this project," said Bishop. "But what is most exciting about this project is the way students are able to authentically contribute to a community-engaged digital scholarship project with real-world impact.Bringing students off of the Washington College campus and into meaningful partnership with community members is one of the most important goals of our work. Students benefit from feeling a stronger connection to place and feel-good knowing that they can contribute to Kent County in a small way." The exhibit is located at 210 South Cross Street and is open to the public through January on the First Fridays of each month from 5:00 to 8:00 p.m., as well as every Saturday from 9 to 11 a.m. The collections may also be viewed by appointment. Scanning the QR codes on the exhibit's exterior windows will allow access to digital versions of the exhibit even when the space is closed. Cultural Heritage organizations are encouraged to reserve time in the space to hold meetings.More information about the Digital Scholarship in Museum Partnerships Project can be found here: https://www.dsmpproject.net/

title: Revisiting 'Australia': Film gets a revamp in new series 'Faraway Downs'
author: Sarah Passingham
content:
Revisiting 'Australia': Film gets a revamp in new series 'Faraway Downs'

 November 23, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Sarah Passingham | Page: 9 | Section: News 
 
 634
 Words 

 Read News Document

 We all roll our failures over in our minds from time to time, so it would make sense that even blockbuster film directors are no different. In cultural memory, the 2008 epic drama "Australia" has remained a dim corner in director Baz Luhrmann's spectacular filmography, which includes massive hits such as "Romeo + Juliet" (1996) and "Elvis" (2022). Luhrmann went back to the drawing board to give "Australia" a second chance and came away with the new miniseries "Faraway Downs," premiering Sunday, Nov. 26, on Hulu.Using additional footage cut from the original movie, "Faraway Downs" spans four hours, split into six episodes, adding new layers to the story told in "Australia." The series, like the film, stars Nicole Kidman ("Special Ops: Lioness") as Lady Sarah Ashley, a British widow who inherits her late husband's sprawling cattle station, called Faraway Downs, on the cusp of the Second World War in 1939. Having made the trip to Australia to convince her husband to sell the property before he died, Lady Sarah has a man known simply as The Drover (Hugh Jackman "The Son," 2022) lead the cattle to Darwin for sale.The pair lead a team and the cattle on a risky adventure across the outback and manage to thwart a rival rancher looking to achieve a meat monopoly in the region of Northern Australia. Lady Sarah and Drover find love on their trip to Darwin and return to Faraway Downs intent on making the station the success that her late husband couldn't.Trouble comes for them when the well-being of Nullah (Brandon Walters, "Operation Buffalo"), the Indigenous Australian boy that the two have been caring for like an adoptive son, is threatened and acts of war loom over Northern Australia.When the reworked miniseries was announced in June 2022, Luhrmann shared in a statement the intent behind both the original film and "Faraway Downs," saying, "I originally set out to take the notion of the sweeping, 'Gone With the Wind'-style epic and turn it on its head - a way of using romance and epic drama to shine a light on the roles of First Nations people and the painful scar in Australian history of the 'Stolen Generations.'" In the film, Nullah is left orphaned after his mother dies trying to evade police, who are attempting to forcibly separate him from his family.The Stolen Generations of mixed-race Indigenous children were removed from their homes to live in church-run missions throughout the latter half of the 19th and into the 20th century, as late as the 1970s in some parts of Australia.Luhrmann added in his statement: "While 'Australia' the film has its own life, there was another telling of this story; one with different layers, nuances and even alternative plot twists that an episodic format has allowed us to explore." Luhrmann alludes quite clearly to what "Faraway Downs" will expand on with its longer runtime and segmented installments. More depth will be paid to Indigenous history in the series and Luhrmann's original ending, cut in favor of a happier final act in "Australia," will finally be seen by audiences.The first episode of "Faraway Downs" screened at SXSW Sydney Screen Festival in October, and The Guardian reported that the soundtrack was "given a contemporary First Nations overhaul," including a song from Budjerah ("Ready for the Sky"), whose music plays over an opening credits sequence animated by Indigenous artists."Faraway Downs" also stars Bryan Brown ("Darby and Joan") as Lesley (King) Carney, a rival cattle farmer; David Wenham ("Pieces of Her") as Neil Fletcher, the station manager at Faraway Downs who is secretly working with King Carney; Jack Thompson ("High Ground," 2020) as Kipling Flynn, accountant of Faraway Downs; David Gulpilil ("The Leftovers") as King George, an elder and Nullah's grandfather; and David Ngoombujarra ("The Circuit") as Magarri, Drover's brotherin-law.

 The Academy Art Museum in Easton has announced two new winter exhibits and has also named the winners of its Annual Members's Exhibition.An exhibit of the works of Baltimore based sculptor Sebastian Martorana started earlier this month and runs through March 24."Sebastian Martorana: Public/Private" features various pieces carved out of marble.Martorana grew up in Virginia and is now an adjunct professor at the Maryland Institute of College of Art after receiving his master's degree there."A Fire That No Water Could Put Out: Photographs of the Civil Rights Movement from the Collection of The High Museum" runs Nov. 30 to March 10, 2024.The exhibition takes its name from Martin Luther King Jr.'s final speech before his assassination in April 1968 - two months before the killing of Robert F. Kennedy.The AAM exhibit reflects on the 55th anniversary of the tumultuous year and features photos from Atlanta's High Museum of Art."Historical works of iconic moments from the movement by Gordon Parks, Danny Lyon, Doris Derby, Ernest Withers, and others are juxtaposed with contemporary photographs by Dawoud Bey, Sheila Pree Bright, Matthew Brandt, and others that speak to the past's reverberations into the present and future," AAM said in an exhibition announcement.The Academy museum also announce the winners of its annual Members' Exhibition Nov. 14.The members event invites artists to submit new works across mediums which are then judged and potentially offered for sale.The exhibition is open through Nov. 26."The Museum has organized an annual Member's show since our founding year in 1958. It's a wonderful testament to our exceptionally creative community and the unusually high concentration of talented artists who live in the region," said AAM Director Sarah Jesse.The winners of awards given for this year's Members' Exhibition include:· Best in Show: Susan Schauer John, Cooper's Cousin, 2023, fiber· Catherine Cripps, Cailleach the Scottish Winter side of the Celtic Triple Goddess, 2023, homegrown gourd, paper mache, paint· Nancy South Reybold Award for Contemporary Art: Gentry Pack, God's Little Secret, 2022, acrylic on canvas· M. title: Local author releases second book in American Heritage series
author: Contributed
content:
Local author releases second book in American Heritage series

 November 29, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: 21 | Section: News

 Read News Document

 The second book in a series by Caroline-County base author Rebekah Colburn has now been released.The American Heritage series follows the fictional Bloodsworth family from the 1770s through the 1860s, highlighting the history of the United States through three of its most formative eras.Book one, "Adrift on Winds of Change," documents the founding of the nation through the eyes of Elias Bloodsworth and his wife, Charlotte. They had created their own paradise on Bloodsworth Island in the Chesapeake Bay just prior to the Revolutionary War, only to find themselves under attack by the infamous pirate and personal rival of Elias, Joseph Wheland, acting as a British privateer.During this dangerous time of intrigue, despite accusations of being a traitor, Elias Bloodsworth steps forward as a voice to the public through his letters to the editor, outlining the reasons why they must take the daring step of breaking away from Britain and forging their own nation.This novel chronicles the formation of the Republic, and the chaos, fear and violence that erupt during this period of uncertainty. Under the flag of the Crown, men like Wheland could privateer without ramifications, legally continuing their ways of piracy and destruction.Book two in the series, "Driven by the Prairie Wind," is told through the eyes of their great-grandchildren."Weaving two storylines together, I wanted to share the broader picture of Westward Expansion and its impact on the developing nation as well as those who originally inhabited the continent," the author said. "While Risdon and Lucy share the excitement of new opportunities and the perils of the wagon trains, his cousin Jane and her Cherokee husband live the consequences of the ideology of Manifest Destiny as they are removed from their established home and forced to walk the Trail of Tears." Both books can be purchased on Amazon.com.Book three, "Wooed by the Dixie Wind," will be released in 2024.

title: Port Tobacco Players celebrate 75th anniversary
author: Ted Black; tblack@somdnews.com
content:
Port Tobacco Players celebrate 75th anniversary

 November 30, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ted Black; tblack@somdnews.com | Page: D8 | Section: News 
 
 614
 Words 

 Read News Document

 As they make the transition from performers to co-directors for the next three weekends of the Port Tobacco Players 75th anniversary celebration "An Evening of Song," Becky Norris Kuhn and Tara Waters noted the collaboration of musical numbers deviates from the norm of scripted performances.In a production that commenced with three shows last weekend, the Port Tobacco Players anniversary celebration includes songs from past musicals such as "Singing In The Rain," "Guys and Dolls," "Beauty and the Beast," "Annie" and "Oklahoma," and several of them remind both Kuhns and Waters of their own performances on stage, although from a different perspective."This is so much different than anything that we did on stage," Kuhns said. "Normally everyone sticks to the script, but with this show we wanted to highlight a lot of the songs from musicals here and just blend them together. I remember doing 'Beauty and the Beast' here and now I get to lend my hand as a director to the performers."Waldorf resident Amanda Hastings, a 2018 St. Mary's College of Maryland graduate and current teacher at nearby Lackey High School, has the chance to display her talents in a solo number early - "You Can't Get a Man with a Gun" from "Annie Get Your Gun" - as well as in a duet with Melina Raynes later and in various numbers when the entire ensemble is on stage, including a pair of songs from "White Christmas" to close the show."This is only my first year with Port Tobacco Players, but I love being a pair of it," Hastings said. "I really only do musicals. This one is different because you don't have a set script. Usually most plays the actor fits the part, but in this one the songs fit the performers. I really enjoy my duet with Melina. She's so talented."Although not entirely a show with Christmas themes, there are more than a dozen songs in each act on both sides of the intermission and performers maintain a lively tempo throughout, aided by the musical accompany of a band that takes its spot elevated on stage rather than in the customary pit below."We wanted to make the show lively and entertaining for the whole audience," Waters said."There are so many songs that remind me of being a performer.Now I get to see what it's like being a co-director with Becky and it's really fun for the cast and for the whole audience."IF YOU GOThe Port Tobacco Players production of "An Evening of Song" will feature songs from more than a dozen musicals and will run every Friday, Saturday and Sunday through Dec. 17. Friday and Saturday offer evening performances beginning at 7:30 p.m. while the Sunday shows begin at 3 p.m.Co-directed by Becky Norris Kuhn and Tara Waters, "An Evening of Song" highlights many of the memorable songs from past musicals offered at the Port Tobacco theater over the past 75 years and includes feature songs from "White Christmas" that are designed to bring holiday cheer to the occasion.For more information, visit www.ptplayers.com or call the box office at 301-932-6819 for ticket availability and prices.

In particular, I like malapropisms. Mrs.Malaprop was a character in Richard Brinsley Sheridan's "The Rivals." She had the habit of using a word close to the one she really should have employed. See how many malapropisms you can find in the rest of this column.Today's deal comes from a rubber bridge game in which the stakes were expansive, very extensive. title: Moving the mission forward
author: Niambi Davis; Special To The Bay Times Record Observer Star Democrat
content:
Moving the mission forward

 Author/Byline: Niambi Davis; Special To The Bay Times Record Observer Star Democrat | Page: A4 | Section: News 
 
 842
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Kennard Alumni Association honoured board members past and present during their annual gala luncheon Nov. 11 at the Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center in Centreville.This year's honourees were Melvin Shorter Jr., Cecelia J. Shorter and John C. Wright.In his remarks to attendees of the sold-out event, current board President Clayton Washington described them as deserving of honour for "being on the battlefield" long before he became part of the effort. He expressed gratitude that last year's gala honoured the late Charles Nesbitt, who died this past Oct. 23.Washington thanked the sponsors, donors and current board members who have helped to move Kennard's mission forward.He described ongoing and upcoming programs at the Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center: community mentoring in collaboration with Minary's Dream Alliance, Institute of Adult Learning Center classes, upcoming summer camp programs with the County and a summer STEM program. Under the direction of Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center library director Michael Sampson, plans are in motion to open the library at least one Saturday of each month beginning in January 2024.Washington then introduced Madelyn Hollis, who began her Kennard career in 1951, as "still going strong." Hollis praised the honourees for their work on behalf of their alma mater lightly joking, "I never had any trouble from any of them as students." After an invocation and grace offered by the Rev.Alice Hutchins, lunch was served by Special "Catering.After the meal, the entire audience joined in singing "Oh, Kennard High," followed by the school cheer that was a staple at every KHS sporting event.Before their introductions by family members, Washington described the honourees as people "who worked to make sure that Kennard was not forgotten. That's why we're here today." In a video tribute to Melvin Shorter Jr., his daughter Shelia Shorter shared highlights of her father's life and accomplishments. The reel began with Shorter's youth on a Burnsville farm, his sporting achievements in basketball, track, touch football and his prowess in baseball that led to Shorter's induction into the Eastern Shore Negro League Baseball Hall of Fame.The film honored Shorter as a man committed to his family, church, Masonic Lodge, and community organizations, many of whom benefited from his famous fish fry and catering skills. In 2016, Shorter was recognized as Citizen of the Year by the Centreville Rotary Club. In 2017, the Queen Anne's County Commissioners honoured Shorter for Outstanding Service to the Community."That's why you are a living legend in our eyes," Shelia concluded.Carolyn Rochester, one of four daughters of Cecilia J. ("Sissy") Shorter, spoke of her mother's many years of service and dedication to the Kennard High School Alumni Association as treasurer, assistant treasurer, president, and later as activities director. Aside from her work with Kennard, Shorter is renowned in her family and community for her white potato pie, macaroni and cheese, and homemade apple sauce.A niece of Shorter shared memories of a family Thanksgiving dinner held at the Queen Anne's County 4-H Park. Although approximately 75-100 people were in attendance, Shorter made sure that everyone left with their own container of apple sauce. To the amazement of many in the audience, Rochester shared Shorter's impressive work record - one that spanned 47 years at Campbell Soup/Chestertown Foods, 14 more at USA Fulfilment, followed by work at Sodexo Food Services until she decided to retire in 2022 at the age of 86."She is truly blessed to be here at 86," Carolyn said. "It is an honour to introduce my mother." In her tribute to John Wright, daughter Natalie Wright praised both her parents as examples of the education and hard work that inspired many in the Wright family to pursue careers in education. She spoke of his early education at Kennard High School, his military service and entry into the workforce. But education was his true calling, Wright said, leading to degrees from the University of Maryland Eastern Shore and Bowie State University.His career began at Centreville Middle School as a student teacher, where he progressed from instructor in industrial arts to assistant principal and finally as supervisor of buildings and maintenance for the Queen Anne's County Board of Education before retirement in 2011. For his work on the betterment of his community, Wright was awarded the Community Involvement Award from the NAACP.Family, community, church members and colleagues praise John Wright for his fairness and good humour."At heart, he is a family man whose life has always been guided by his faith," shared Natalie.The afternoon of honor and celebration ended with a raffle drawing conducted by Zoom to support the programs and scholarships of the Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center. Visit Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center to learn about the organization's history, mission, and programs.

title: A view from behind the cameras - Filmmaker talks metaphors, process and independent films
author: Matt Hubbard; mhubbard@chespub.com
content:
A view from behind the cameras - Filmmaker talks metaphors, process and independent films

 December 5, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Hubbard; mhubbard@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 1190
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ELKTON - For most of his life, filmmaker Samuel White has been focused on captivating audiences through the thought-provoking narratives and community-building aspects of his films, a drive that recently brought him recognition at the 2023 Cecil County Independent Film Festival."Through creating art, my hope is to get people wanting to talk about the art," said White. "Even if they disagree, I want people to communicate, talk about ideas and get to know each other and I think that's the reason I make films." White, 33, of Elkton, developed an interest in filmmaking after he saw the 1960 film "Psycho" when he was 11 years old. White recalls seeing certain shots within the film the artistic intention of which peaked his interest.From that point forward, White took his enjoyment for writing stories and began to think of them as films until he began playing with his grandfather's camcorder to bring his ideas to life. Now, White says filmmaking is his favorite form of storytelling."I cannot picture a time in my life where I didn't think cinematically," White said. "I don't know if I showed any talent as a filmmaker when I was a kid but at that time, I learned that the camera is an important storytelling tool." In high school, White was homeschooled under an umbrella program that granted him the opportunity to meet fellow students who were also interested in filmmaking. Based on their shared love of film, White and his friends created the Cinematography Club, where they would get together and practice different filmmaking techniques.From 2004 to 2008, when White was in high school, video production technology was rapidly evolving with the introduction of HD video and video cameras.After White's senior year of high school, digital single lens reflection (DSLR) cameras took over the market."With the DSLRs, it was like an 'oh my god, we could actually do this,' moment for me with filmmaking because of how video friendly and available DSLRs became," White said.DSLR cameras often have interchangeable lenses, shoot on compact flash or SD cards and are capable of both still photography and shooting high quality video. To learn more about video technology, White attended Cecil College where he majored in video production."When I was at Cecil College, I didn't have an interest in the actual degree, I wanted to get as much hand on tech experience as I could and I did," said White. "It was fantastic because they gave me the tools and opportunities to work and learn with the technology and techniques." White said that his favorite course at Cecil College was called Gorilla Filmmaking, where he had the opportunity to to work with top of the line filmmaking equipment while receiving guidance and criticism on his work from professional photographer and videographer Floyd Dean.During that class, White created his first short film that documented a female character suffering from an unknown problem that was slowly destroying her body. The horror film utilized only music - no dialogue - which White says was intentional, as it left much of the film up for interpretation."For me, the girl running around with her face falling off asking for help and being ignored was kind of like personal feelings I have had throughout my life relating to personal things," said White. "I enjoy films that are abstract that invite you to feel and interpret what you want." White graduated from Cecil College in 2012 and has gone on to build himself a filmmaking portfolio of 14 independent films; six of which he wrote and directed on his own.His most recent film, "Safewords," follows a soonto-be bride and her adventure into an alternative lifestyle.The film won best full-length feature and best scriptwriting."Safewords" took three weekends for White and his crew of three to create, which he said took about 10 years off of his life expectancy due to stress."I didn't give myself enough time, and it was a massive learning experience because of the amount of stuff I didn't know about while making an hour and a half long feature film," White said. "I am proud of the film, and I am glad it turned out the way it did." White often holds his new films up against his 2020 film "The Day Bingo Died," as he said it is his favorite film that he has made to date.The film follows a brother and a sister who return to their childhood home to euthanize their family dog.Both siblings grieve the loss and decide to go to a bar after burying the dog. The siblings later end up intoxicated and arguing over who loved the dog more, which White said is the "weirdest mix between two adults acting like spoiled drunk children." Odd mix aside, White considers "The Day Bingo Died" to be his favorite film because it presents viewers with an uncomfortable, yet relatable, view of grief and family."It plays on the power behind words and the expression of grief and how the differences between the two speak to human nature," White said. "I love putting people in that uncomfortable space where they don't know if they should laugh or not because the uncomfortable feelings come from situations being relatable." Much of White's inspiration comes from directors Alfred Hitchcock, Lars Von Trier and David Zucker, as well as his personal competitive streak to build and improve film ideas using metaphor.White explained that he often views everything in his life as a scene in a movie, which helps him grow as a filmmaker because it allows him to connect metaphors to true meaning."When something emotional or interesting happens to me, I ask what it would look like visually and how would that fit into a story," said White. "If it's a fear of commitment, my metaphor would be a wedding ring stuck on a finger that irritates the skin - stuff like that." White's consistent hunt for metaphors to add into his films is what he says is the base of traditional filmmaking and is what makes his films art. But to keep the sense of traditional filmmaking alive, White said film festivals are essential as art on the big scene is slowly fading into the background."If you want to be a filmmaker, from now throughout the future, there will be less chances to get your film on an actual big screen, which is why I go to local film festivals - to keep the traditional art form of filmmaking alive because of streaming," said White.Looking to the future, White is working to grow his production company, Outsider Film Company, to a point where it can help independent filmmakers produce their work. The film company currently offers a variety of professional video services and can be found on Instagram or Facebook."I will be making art for the rest of my life," White said. "If you're considering making movies, Cecil County is a great place and you're in a great time period.Get out and give it a try."

title: It'S Time For Christmas Casseroles
author: Marie Savage; Country Cooking
content:
It'S Time For Christmas Casseroles

 December 6, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Marie Savage; Country Cooking | Page: 16 | Section: News 
 
 1361
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Remember the excitement on Christmas morning when we were children - getting out of bed at 4 or 5 a.m. trying to come downstairs.The fun began and soon we had to dress and go to Grandmom and Grandpop's house to gather with the rest of the family to have a large country style breakfast.A lot of time was lost being away from our gifts at home those mornings until the later breakfast casserole was born.Christmas morning became perfect. Families would gather mid-morning (around 10 or 11 a.m.) bringing their favorite breakfast casseroles to share.The children of all ages got to enjoy their gifts before traveling. Some years, it would be at the grandparents' place but other members began taking turns also.Enjoy today's recipes to share with everyone and send some of your favorites to me at mmsavage21145@gmail.com so I can share with the readers.PANCAKE CASSEROLE Cooking spray, pancakes, 6 large eggs, 1.5 cups heavy cream, 1 cup whole milk, 25 cup granulated sugar, 1 tsp vanilla bean paste, .25 tsp kosher salt, unsalted butter and maple syrup (for serving).Lightly coat a 13-by 9-inch baking dish with cooking spray. Arrange pancakes in a baking dish in three rows, overlapping slightly, starting at a long end. Whisk together eggs, cream, milk, sugar, vanilla and salt in a bowl. Slowly pour mixture over pancakes.Cover and refrigerate for at least 8 hours or up to overnight. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees.Bake the casserole, covered, in a preheated oven for 25 minutes. Uncover and continue baking until the center is set, about 25 minutes. Let stand for 5 minutes. Dot with pats of butter; drizzle with syrup.CHEESY SAUSAGE, EGG AND HASH BROWN CASSEROLE 3 tbsps olive oil (divided), 8 ounces ground pork sausage, 1 sweet onion (diced), 1 poblano pepper (seeded and chopped), 1 red bell pepper (seeded and chopped), 1.5 tsps kosher salt (divided), 2 cups refrigerated diced potatoes, .75 tsp garlic powder, 4 ounces your favorite shredded cheese, 5 large eggs, .25 cup heavy whipping cream, 1 tbsp minced fresh chives. Preheat the oven to 425 degrees with an oven rack about 6 inches from heat. Heat 1 tbsp of the olive oil in a 10-inch cast-iron skillet over medium-high.Add sausage. Cook, breaking up sausage into pieces with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and just cooked through, about 4 minutes. Remove sausage to a medium bowl with a slotted spoon; set aside. Do not wipe the skillet clean. Add sweet onion, poblano chile, red bell pepper, and .5 tsp of the salt to the skillet. Cook over medium-high, stirring occasionally, until onion is tender and peppers have charred in spots, about 8 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon to bowl with sausage. Wipe the skillet clean.Heat the remaining 2 tbsps of olive oil in a skillet over medium-high.Add diced potatoes to the skillet in an even layer.Cook, undisturbed, until browned on bottom, about 5 minutes. Add ½ tsp of the salt. Continue cooking, stirring occasionally, until golden brown and crispy on most sides, about 5 minutes.Remove from heat.Return sausage and pepper mixture to skillet and add garlic powder. Stir to combine. Stir in ½ cup of the cheese until just combined.Whisk together eggs, cream, and remaining ½ tsp salt in a medium bowl. Pour over mixture in skillet, and tilt pan to allow eggs to distribute.Top with remaining ½ cup each of the cheeses. Bake in a preheated oven until eggs have set and cheeses have melted, about 8 minutes.Increase oven temperature to broil, and broil until cheeses have turned golden brown, 2 to 3 minutes. Remove; let stand for 5 minutes.Sprinkle with chives. Slice and serve immediately.BISCUITS AND GRAVY CASSEROLE 1 (1-lb.) pkg. ground pork sausage,1/2 cup chopped yellow onion (from 1 small onion),1/4 cup plus 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1/3 cup (about 1 1/2 oz.) all-purpose flour,3 cups whole milk,6 ounces pepper Jack cheese, shredded (about 1 1/2 cups),3/4 tsp kosher salt,1/2 tsp black pepper, Cooking spray,1 (25-oz.) pkg. frozen Southern-style biscuits (12 count) (such as Pillsbury Grands),2 tbsps minced fresh chives. Preheat the oven to 350°F.Place sausage and onion in a large skillet over medium, and cook, stirring often, until sausage crumbles and is no longer pink and onion is translucent, 6 to 8 minutes.Transfer mixture to a plate lined with paper towels to drain. Wipe the skillet clean. Reduce heat to low, and add 1/4 cup of the butter to the skillet; cook, whisking often, until melted. Whisk in flour until smooth. Cook, whisking constantly, 1 minute. Gradually whisk in milk; increase heat to medium, and cook, whisking constantly, until thickened and bubbly, 5 to 6 minutes. Whisk in shredded cheese, and cook, whisking often, until cheese is melted and mixture is smooth, 30 to 40 seconds. Stir in sausage mixture, salt, and pepper.Transfer mixture to a lightly greased (with cooking spray) 13-x 9-inch baking dish. Arrange biscuits on top of sausage mixture. Bake in a preheated oven until biscuits are golden brown and gravy is bubbly, 30 to 35 minutes. Microwave remaining 1 tbsp butter in a small microwavable bowl on HIGH until melted, about 20 seconds.Remove the casserole from the oven; brush biscuits with melted butter, and sprinkle with chives.Let stand for 10 minutes before serving.SLOW COOKER CINNAMON ROLL CASSEROLECooking spray,1/2 cup granulated sugar,1/2 cup packed light brown sugar,1 tsp ground cinnamon, 2 (16.3-oz.) cans refrigerated southern homestyle biscuits (such as Pillsbury Grands!Southern Homestyle), biscuits separated and cut into fourths (about 64 biscuit pieces total),1/2 cup (4 oz.) salted butter, melted, plus 2 Tbsp. butter, softened, divided,4 large eggs,1/4 tsp kosher salt,2/3 cup plus 2 to 3 Tbsp. half-and-half, divided,2 tsp vanilla extract, divided,1/2 cup chopped toasted pecans,1 (3-oz.) pkg. cream cheese, softened,2 1/4 cups (about 9 oz.) powdered sugar, divided. Line bottom and sides of a 6-quart slow cooker with aluminum foil; lightly coat foil with cooking spray. Stir together granulated sugar, brown sugar, and cinnamon in a small bowl. Toss together biscuit pieces and 1/2 cup melted butter in a large bowl until biscuits are coated. Working in batches, add biscuits to granulated sugar mixture, and toss to coat; transfer biscuits to prepared slow cooker. Sprinkle any remaining sugar mixture over biscuits in a slow cooker.Whisk together eggs, salt, 2/3 cup of the halfand-half, and 1 tsp of the vanilla in a bowl until well combined; pour over biscuits in a slow cooker.Sprinkle with pecans.Beat cream cheese and 2 tbsps softened butter with an electric mixer on medium speed until thoroughly combined, about 30 seconds. Add 1 cup of the powdered sugar and remaining 1 tsp vanilla; beat until smooth, about 1 minute. Gradually add remaining 1 1/4 cups powdered sugar to cream cheese mixture alternately with 2 tbsps of the half-and-half, beating on high speed until frosting is smooth, creamy, and a little loose, about 1 minute, adding remaining 1 tbsp half-and-half, 1 tsp at a time, if needed to reach desired consistency. Drizzle half of the frosting over the biscuit mixture in the slow cooker. (Cover remaining frosting and set aside until ready to serve.)Cover slow cooker; cook on low until center of casserole is set and biscuit bottoms are browned, 3.5 to 4 hours. Drizzle casserole with remaining frosting; serve warm.TEXAS TWO STEP CASSEROLLE11 oz canned mild chiles (drained), 8 corn tortillas (cut into strips), 12 oz bulk breakfast sausage (cooked and drained), 1 medium yellow onion (diced), 1.5 cups shredded pepper jack or cheddar cheese, 8 eggs, .5 cups heavy whipping cream, .5 tsp salt, .5 tsp freshly ground black pepper, .5 tsp garlic salt or powder, 1 tsp ground cumin, 2 small Roma tomatoes sliced, .5 tsp paprika, sour cream (optional), pico de gallo (optional). Lightly coat a 13-by 9-inch baking dish with non-stick spray.Spread half the amount of chiles in an even layer in the bottom of the dish.Add half of the tortilla strips. Add half of the sausage and onion. Add half of the cheese. Repeat a second time. In a medium bowl, whisk the eggs, cream, salt, pepper, garlic salt and cumin together until well combined.Pour over the casserole.Arrange the tomato slices on top. Sprinkle with paprika. Cover and refrigerate overnight. The next morning, heat the oven to 350 degrees. Uncover and bake the casserole 40 minutes or until the center has set and the edges are lightly browned. If desired, serve with sour cream and pico de gallo.

title: Storytelling in collage - Artist exploring her Eastern Shore Roots and the history of Caroline County during residency
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
Storytelling in collage - Artist exploring her Eastern Shore Roots and the history of Caroline County during residency

 December 7, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 758
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON - Yolanda Vanise Acree's medium to explore issues of identity, Afro-Christianity and family lineage is collage.Give her some scissors and a stack of magazines, and she explores what it means to have grown up Black in Caroline County.Acree is the new artist in residence at Caroline County Arts Council, and for her, art is an expression of history, both personal and of her community.Caroline County, located at the northern tip of the Confederacy during the Civil War, has a deep history of slavery, the underground railroad and the abolition movement."We are the northern South. We are the tippy top," Acree said. "The Eastern Shore tried to secede from Maryland a few times to become part of the Confederacy.To become its own state. I have a piece of my grandmother and her two friends standing in front of Mount Zion Church in Marydel. A lot of our family is buried there in the cemetery across the street. That is where the Mason Dixon Line is."Acree has studied some art, but her major at the University of Delaware was anthropology and Latin American studies."The African diaspora was my focus with my anthropology studies," she said. "I studied African Americans and Africans in other countries and how slavery impacted them.""How they combined their African culture remnants with the Catholic religion (in Central and South America), they used Catholic saints to disguise their African deities," she said. "Syncretism. That didn't happen as much here because the Protestants don't revere the saints the way Catholics do."The mixture of African and Protestant religions in the United States produced a different belief system, she said."Even though they didn't have any saints to disguise their deities, here in the US, they did develop their own religion called Hoodoo," Acree said. "The development of Black Christianity started with Hoodoo. It is a way for me to acknowledge and honor my ancestors.A central tenet of Hoodoo is you are because of your ancestors. Everything they are is carried on within you."As in traditional Christianity, not every soul who has gone before is considered an ancestor in Hoodoo. Acree said ancestors had to have lived a life worthy of being acknowledged."Living a right life is about living in community, supporting your community. Mutual aid, mutual support. It is also about being in the right relationship with the Earth," she said. "You can ask permission of herbs to help heal you and keep you alive and keep you alive and give messages and protect you."This history is central to Acree's collage, and she highlights many of stories of those who lived this history in her work.But she includes her personal history as well, learning to incorporate a mental health struggle into her work.After she gave birth, Acree developed generalized anxiety."I want to explore that during my residency," she said. "Not just the anxiety, but my transformation over the past few years going through the pandemic and becoming pregnant. After my experience at the hospital, I started experiencing panic attacks. I had never had that before, so I thought I was having a heart attack. I feel like this is going to be some art therapy, this process."Acree considers herself, like a novelist or a filmmaker, to be a storyteller."I am telling stories like the flight to freedom and also telling my own personal family history within these art pieces," she said. "I am highlighting narratives that aren't always prominent. Aren't always told."Among the works she plans to create during her residency, she highlighted several."One area I want to work on is my transformation and rebirth over the past several years," she said."I am working on a piece called, 'Flights of Freedom.' So I am imagining, interpreting escapes from Caroline County on the Underground Railroad," she said. " Another series is going to be scenes and dreams.It is all just paper and glue for now."Her residency lasts from Nov. 15 to Jan. 31, and her show will be in February. She plans to have at least 30 pieces created.Acree will be teaching a class at The Foundry on Jan. 12 and 26 on abstract landscape collage.

title: What to know about Hanukkah and how it's celebrated around the world
author: Giovanna Dell'Orto
content:
What to know about Hanukkah and how it's celebrated around the world

 December 7, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Giovanna Dell'Orto | Page: D8 | Section: News 
 
 593
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Hanukkah - also spelled Chanukah or other transliterations from Hebrew - is Judaism's "festival of lights."On eight consecutive nightfalls, Jews gather with family and friends to light one additional candle in the menorah - a multibranched candelabra.In Hebrew, Hanukkah means "dedication," and the holiday marks the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem in the 2nd century BC, after a small group of Jewish fighters liberated it from occupying foreign forces.With the tiny supply of ritually pure oil that they found in the temple, they lit the menorah - and it stayed lit for eight days. The ritual of lighting a nightly candle, as well as the emphasis on cooking foods in oil such as potato pancakes called latkes, memorialize this miraculously long-lasting oil.WHEN IS HANUKKAH 2023?The dates of the holiday are based on Hebrew month of Kislev, which usually coincides with November-December in the Gregorian calendar.This year, Hanukkah will be celebrated from Dec. 7 through Dec. 15.DOES HANUKKAH OBSERVANCE VARY?Jews across the religious observance spectrum - from Reform to Conservative to Orthodox - focus on the same theme of bringing light into the darkness and emphasizing that even a small, againstthe-odds effort can have a transforming effect.For this reason, even though the Talmud reflects a dispute over the order of lighting, most start with one candle and increase the lighting by one more candle each night while reciting or chanting special blessings.The candles are added from right to left, but lit from left to right on the menorah, thus always starting with the newest light.The special menorah used for Hanukkah has eight branches, with a ninth place for the candle called shamash from which all others are lit.The tradition calls for candles with a real flame, though some also use electric ones in public displays, such as in hospitals, for safety reasons.HOW IS HANUKKAH CELEBRATED?A menorah is lit in each household and traditionally is placed where it can be seen from the outside, such as a doorway or windowsill, to symbolize the spreading of God's light to all nations.The lighting of menorahs in city streets and parks has become more prominent in recent years in countries around the world, including in front of public landmarks.In addition to menorah lightings, giving to charity and social works are also part of the celebration for many, reflecting the belief that the Jewish people are called by God to help make the world better for all.Associated Press religion coverage receives support through the AP's collaboration with The Conversation US, with funding from Lilly Endowment Inc. The AP is solely responsible for this content.

 The Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture celebrates Kwanzaa throughout December.From Dec. 26 through Jan. 1, 2024, NMAAHC will feature its first-Kwanzaa display in Heritage Hall, including a kinara, mkeka mat and a Kwanzaa playlist.Created in 1966 by Maulana Ron Karenga, Kwanzaa is an African American and Pan-African holiday that celebrates history, values, family, community and culture.An annual celebration beginning the day after Christmas, Dec. 26 and continuing through Jan. 1, Kwanzaa emphasizes seven principles, written in the language of Swahili: Umoja (Unity), Kujichagulia (Self-Determination), Ujima (Collective Work and Responsibility), Ujamaa (Cooperative Economics), Nia (Purpose), Kuumba (Creativity), and Imani (Faith). Kwanzaa gets its name from the Swahili phrase, "matunda ya kwanza" and is rooted in first fruit celebrations found in cultures throughout Africa in both ancient and modern times. Virtual visitors can check the museum's website for more information about Kwanzaa, including history and traditions, recipes and a reading list.Dec. 16 marks the 20th anniversary of signing the federal legislation that created NMAAHC.The museum is commemorating this milestone by posting an interactive web feature from Dec. 15 through Dec. 25 online at nmaahc. si.edu that documents 20 key facts about the development of the museum. Through film, still photos and computer-generated graphics, the page will exhibit how the building was constructed, how collections were built, what exhibitions were created and much more.On Dec. 30, guests can attend "Kwanzaa & Watch Night: Visions of Freedom," a celebration of both Kwanzaa and Watch Night, a tradition that started on Dec. 31, 1862, when free and enslaved African Americans gathered, many in secret, to ring in the new year and await news that the Emancipation Proclamation would take effect on Jan. 1, 1863.Additional December programming includes a panel discussion of the documentary Stamped From the Beginning, based on Dr.Ibram X. Kendi's New York Times bestseller, and a screening and panel discussion of American Fiction, written and directed by Cord Jefferson and based on the 2001 novel Erasure by Percival Everett.From Dec. 22 to Jan. 4, 2024, the Sweet Home Café presents Executive Chef Ramin Coles' holiday menu, which includes beef pot roast, herb roasted Cornish hen, smoked ham hock succotash, scalloped potatoes, spoon bread, and more. Visit the museum's website for details.The museum also continues the Dine & Shop Pass program in December. Visitors can reserve a Dine and Shop Pass for specified entry to the Sweet Home Café or to shop in the museum store, from 11 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. Visitors can reserve up to four Dine & Shop passes per day and can reserve up to seven days in advance. In observation of Christmas, the museum is closed on December 25.DECEMBER PROGRAMMING HIGHLIGHTSThrough the African American Lens: American Fiction - Friday, Dec. 8, 7 p.m., Oprah Winfrey Theater Join for a screening of American Fiction, written and directed by Cord Jefferson and based on the 2001 novel Erasure by Percival Everett. Jeffrey Wright stars as Monk, a frustrated novelist who is tired of the establishment profiting from "Black" entertainment that relies on tired and offensive tropes. To prove his point, Monk uses a pen name to write a satirical "Black" book of his own, which propels him to the heart of hypocrisy and the madness he claims to disdain. A panel discussion following the screening will be livestreamed.The event is free; however, registration is required.Kwanzaa & Watch Night: Visions of Freedom - Saturday, Dec. 30, 11 a.m. - 3 p.m., Explore More! Gallery, L2; History Galleries, concourse Kwanzaa is a celebration created to provide a cultural grounding in and a reaffirmation of African American culture. During this event, participate in activities that honor the last three principles of Kwanzaa - Kuumba (creativity), Imani (faith) and Nia (purpose).The museum will also have special activities that focus on the history of Watch Night, and visitors can learn more about the role of the Black Colored Troops in the Civil War. The event is free; however, registration is required.ABOUT THE NATIONAL MUSEUM OF AFRICAN AMERICAN HISTORY AND CULTURESince opening Sept. 24, 2016, the National Museum of African American History and Culture has welcomed more than 10 million visitors. Occupying a prominent location next to the Washington Monument on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., the nearly 400,000-square-foot museum is the nation's largest and most comprehensive cultural destination devoted exclusively to exploring, documenting and showcasing the African American story and its impact on American and world history.For more information about the museum, visit nmaahc.si.edu.

title: Church Hill Theatre thrives after being saved
author: Tamara Forte
content:
Church Hill Theatre thrives after being saved

 December 7, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tamara Forte | Page: 6 | Section: News 
 
 919
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHURCH HILL - Saved from a wrecking ball demolition in 1983, the Church Hill Theatre is a preserved piece of history and home to many.Since its inception, the theater has hosted over 140 shows on its stage. On Oct. 27, the CHT celebrated 40 years of being "saved from the wrecking ball" with celebratory ribbon cutting.With a DJ, hors devours, theatre memorabilia and a multitude of stories, members celebrated with a champagne toast the past 40 years and all those who helped to save, renovate and make the theatre the success it is today.Located on Walnut Street in the somewhat sleepy small town of Church Hill, built in 1929, the theater boasts a history of card parties, dances, films, and even organ playing - as it was a community building before it was a theater.In 1944, a fire damaged the building, and it was renovated in the Art Deco style that still exists today.Fast forward to 1983, the local bank wanted to knock down the building for a parking lot. Friends for Church Hill Preservation began with Howard and Jan Burns, Suzanne and John Gutting and Howard and Mary Wood through much fundraising - selling chair nameplates raised $13,000 - the team was able to buy the building on Feb. 26, 1985. A plaque with the original name plates is still on display in the lobby.Donations also came from the Church Hill High School, no longer in existence.Under the newly organized Friends group, Mary Wood wrote their first theater production "1787."To date, Church Hill Theatre is one of the few remaining theaters, self-owned and not renting space. With owning a historic building comes lots of upkeep and general maintenance.Over the years, many things have had to be fixed, replaced, or renovated including the stage curtains, the chairs (2021), the floors, and the boiler - to name a few.The rich emerald and gold wall fabric is also new, as it was replaced and recreated specially to mimic the original Art Deco with the same coloring and shapes - exaggerated in size to impress the guests. This past August 2023, the marquee outside was also replaced.Juanita Wieczoreck, CHT business manager, says the marquee is " beautiful now. It's just gorgeous."Currently, the theater has a six-year plan to replace the almost obsolete gel lighting with LED lighting, expand the light panel, add a dimmer pack and lighting strip and replace the lighting fixtures. "Upgrade, fix, replace: a historic building always needs something," Wieczoreck explains. Donations are needed to help make this plan become a reality.Decades later, the magic is still happening. Becca VanAken, former CHT board member, current volunteer, and founder of the Green Room Gang Jr., not only met her husband at the theatre but also got married on the CHT stage surrounded by cast, complete with all the props and details: poster, playbills, and given speeches. With tears in her eyes, VanAken explains that this theatre is a "special place with special people."During COVID, the theater remained open virtually for some online classes. VanAken shares that the theater's virtual classes and involvement helped with overall community mental health and was a "home and family for many."Throughout the year, theater activities are available for all ages. Some activities include two five-week summer camps for kids that are in the Green Room Gang and Green Room Gang Jr. Starting Feb. 5, the B.A.S.K. Basic Acting Skills for Kids classes will run for five Saturdays for age groups first through fifth grades and sixth through 12th. Adult acting classes (18+) and intern and staff programs for high school, college, and beyond are also available.As a nonprofit, every dollar helps. Board member and theater Director Sylvia Maloney explains "Since profits from the shows are not enough to run the theater, we rely on grants, donations, and fundraising also." The annual Giving Campaign runs from November 2023 to January 2024. The easiest ways to give to the CHT is to call the office with a credit card, send a check made out to Church Hill Theatre, or come see the shows! Maloney emphasizes the importance of theatre by saying, "It's a gift. The gift of theater.You don't outgrow it because you get older or you get aches and pains the way it is with sports. It's something you can do your entire lifetime.There's so much to do in theatre. You can act, be a director, be a stage manager.If you like running around and doing errands, you can do props. You can do lighting.If you like sewing, the big major thing is costuming.You can do carpentry and build wonderful sets. [Theater] is also introducing the public to so many thoughts, ideas, positions, and understanding of what this world is all about."One of the best ways to support CHT financially, is to come and see this historic playhouse in action. The new renovations bring both more comfort and elegance to the playhouse. The next 2023 show is Orson Welles' radio version of "A Christmas Carol" on stage Dec. 15, 16 and 17. CHT Director, Kathy Jones has rewritten it to be held "in the round," which means the action will surround the audience. Families are welcome with both matinees and evening shows available. Upcoming shows for 2024 include: Charley's Aunt, March 8-24; My Fair Lady, June 7-23; Osage County, Sept. 13-29 and Ride the Cyclone, Nov. 8-24.The theatre will go dark for more renovations in late December 2023 until Jan. 12, reopening with a fundraising Cabaret Night.

title: Filmmaker talks metaphors, process and cinematography
author: Matt Hubbard; mhubbard@chespub.com
content:
Filmmaker talks metaphors, process and cinematography

 December 7, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Hubbard; mhubbard@chespub.com | Page: D3 | Section: News 
 
 1171
 Words 

 Read News Document

 For most of his life, Maryland filmmaker Samuel White has been focused on captivating audiences through the thought-provoking narratives and community-building aspects of his films, a drive that recently brought him recognition at the 2023 Cecil County Independent Film Festival."Through creating art, my hope is to get people wanting to talk about the art," said White. "Even if they disagree, I want people to communicate, talk about ideas and get to know each other and I think that's the reason I make films."White, 33, of Elkton, developed an interest in filmmaking after he saw the 1960 film 'Psycho' when he was 11 years old. White recalls seeing certain shots within the film the artistic intention of which peaked his interest.From that point forward, White took his enjoyment for writing stories and began to think of them as films until he began playing with his grandfather's camcorder to bring his ideas to life. Now, White says filmmaking is his favorite form of storytelling."I can not picture a time in my life where I didn't think cinematically," said White. "I don't know if I showed any talent as a filmmaker when I was a kid but at that time, I learned that the camera is an important storytelling tool."In high school, White was homeschooled under an umbrella program that granted him the opportunity to meet fellow students who were also interested in filmmaking. Based on their shared love of film, White and his friends created the "Cinematography Club," where they would get together and practice different filmmaking techniques.From 2004 to 2008, when White was in high school, video production technology was rapidly evolving with the introduction of HD video and video cameras. After White's senior year of high school, Digital Single Lens Reflection (DSLR) cameras took over the market."With the DSLRs, it was like a 'oh my god, we could actually do this,' moment for me with filmmaking because of how video friendly and available DSLRs became," said White.DSLR cameras often have interchangeable lenses, shoot on compact flash or SD cards and are capable of both still photography and shooting high quality video. To learn more about video technology, White attended Cecil College where he majored in Video Production."When I was at Cecil College, I didn't have an interest in the actual degree, I wanted to get as much hand on tech experience as I could and I did," said White. "It was fantastic because they gave me the tools and opportunities to work and learn with the technology and techniques."White said that his favorite course at Cecil College was called 'Gorilla Filmmaking,' where he had the opportunity to to work with top of the line filmmaking equipment while receiving guidance and criticism on his work from professional photographer and videographer Floyd Dean.During that class, White created his first short film that documented a female character suffering from an unknown problem that was slowly destroying her body. The horror film utilized only music - no dialogue - which White says was intentional, as it left much of the film up for interpretation."For me, the girl running around with her face falling off asking for help and being ignored was kind of like personal feelings I have had throughout my life relating to personal things," said White. "I enjoy films that are abstract that invite you to feel and interpret what you want."White graduated from Cecil College in 2012 and has gone on to build himself a filmmaking portfolio of 14 independent films; six of which he wrote and directed on his own.His most recent film, 'Safewords,' follows a soon-to-be bride and her adventure into an alternative lifestyle.The film won Best Full Length Feature and Best Scriptwriting.Safewords took three weekends for White and his crew of three to create, which he said took about 10 years off of his life expectancy due to stress."I didn't give myself enough time and it was a massive learning experience because of the amount of stuff I didn't know about while making an hour and a half long feature film," said White. "I am proud of the film and I am glad it turned out the way it did."White often holds his new films up against his 2020 film 'The Day Bingo Died,' as he said it is his favorite film that he has made to date.The film follows a brother and a sister who return to their childhood home to euthanize their family dog. Both siblings grieve the loss and decide to go to a bar after burying the dog. The siblings later end up intoxicated and arguing over who loved the dog more, which White said is the "weirdest mix between two adults acting like spoiled drunk children."Odd mix aside, White considers 'The Day Bingo Died' to be his favorite film because it presents viewers with an uncomfortable, yet relatable, view of grief and family."It plays on the power behind words and the expression of grief and how the differences between the two speak to human nature," said White."I love putting people in that uncomfortable space where they don't know if they should laugh or not because the uncomfortable feelings come from situations being relatable."Much of White's inspiration comes from directors Alfred Hitchcock, Lars Von Trier and David Zucker, as well as his personal competitive streak to build and improve film ideas using metaphor.White explained that he often views everything in his life as a scene in a movie, which helps him grow as a filmmaker because it allows him to connect metaphors to true meaning."When something emotional or interesting happens to me, I ask what it would look like visually and how would that fit into a story," said White. "If it's a fear of commitment, my metaphor would be a wedding ring stuck on a finger that irritates the skin - stuff like that."White's consistent hunt for metaphors to add into his films is what he says is the base of traditional filmmaking and is what makes his films art. But to keep the sense of traditional filmmaking alive, White said film festivals are essential as art on the big scene is slowly fading into the background."If you want to be a filmmaker, from now throughout the future, there will be less chances to get your film on an actual big screen, which is why I go to local film festivals - to keep the traditional art form of filmmaking alive because of streaming," said White.Looking to the future, White is working to grow his production company, Outsider Film Company, to a point where it can help independent filmmakers produce their work. The film company currently offers a variety of professional video services and can be found on Instagram or Facebook."I will be making art for the rest of my life," said White. "If you're considering making movies, Cecil County is a great place and you're in a great time period. Get out and give it a try."

 From Jan. 4 tho Feb. 25, the Main Street Gallery in Cambridge will be showing the works of their member artists in a special show called "Serendipity." title: Dickens Festival summons the Christmas spirit in Chestertown
author: Will Bontrager; wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Dickens Festival summons the Christmas spirit in Chestertown

 December 12, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Will Bontrager; wbontrager@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 825
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - It was kismet this year's Dickens of a Christmas festival resembled foggy London.Kicking off the annual event, there were 145 runners for the 5k Run Like the Dickens this year; record-breaking participation numbers, said race organizer, Renee Bench.Around 8 a.m., Saturday, participants donned elves costumes, reindeer sweaters, striped stockings, even tutus and dashed through the starting point.The course took them through Wilmer park, around the cemetery, where they were greeted by the Ghost of Christmas Future, onto High Street. Jimi Kinstle, portraying Charles Dickens, encouraged racers at the finish.The quickest time for the men's race was from Theo Penders at 19 minutes and 24 seconds. The quickest time in the women's belonged to Zuleyka Martinez at 21 minutes and 31 seconds.As farmer's market vendors opened up so did the Dickens Welcome Center at 211 High Street.People were greeted at the entrance by Paul Heckles dressed in the fashion of a Victorian gentleman.Patrons could purchase a women's bonnet, have a silhouette of their likeness cut out, make a Christmas star decoration or buy a natural fragrance.Outside, the music kicked off at 10:30 a.m. with the O'McPub Band.Joe Basso and Ryan Allen McKinney took requests from the crowd, singing pub tunes and Celtic-infused pop melodies.After an hour, Kinstle returned, still as Dickens. He read "The Christmas Carol," a classic, which drew people to the ornate furniture placed about for those gathered to sip hot drinks.Kids were thrilled that Santa Clause was at his temporary Chestertown residence near Fountain Park.On Park Row, Kent County 4-H brought horses, goats, rabbits, cows and bunnies for their petting zoo.For those working up an appetite strolling about High Street, vendors like Happy Chicken Bakery and Chester River Spicerie, whose top seller was traditional cider and Masala Chai, were on hand to satisfy their cravings. Oysters were a huge demand as every year.Happy Chicken owner said this year they offered drinks, desserts and meals.Ham Pie, sold out quickly, he said.In the neighboring tent where alcohol was served, the mulled wine was a big hit with the crowd.The refreshments warmed everybody, making them full of good cheer to enjoy the multifaceted performances.After the stand-up comedy by Robert Mac, The American Rogues were greeted with loud cheers. An international Celtic band, the group is known for its multi-instrumental sound including reels, hornpipes, ballads, originals, covers, soundtracks, patriotic and military music and Irish foot-stompers.The six band members showed how versatile they were. Whether it was performing a dancing, upbeat Irish jig, a Guns N' Roses rock n roll cover with bagpipes or doing crowdwork, they had the audience drawn in.Good food, good music, and rousing entertainment was had by many.There were educational opportunities during the festival as well.At the Raymond Arts Center people met Assistant Professor of Literature, Katie Charles, lecturing on "The Making of A Christmas Carol," by Michael Norris.Nina Fleegle, executive director of Mainstreet Chestertown and organizer of the event, said this year was a better turnout than last. The rain stayed away and she was glad to see people coming out in the London-like conditions.She added this year was a little different because they left room for the various performers by choosing not to have as many vendors.This allowed patrons to take in performances like the carolers from River Voices, enjoy music from the Baltimore City Pipe Band and take in a riveting street performance on the steps of the Chesapeake Bank and Trust.There was ample space to see all that capped off by The American Rogues, who were urged by the crowd to keep playing into the night.Chestertown Police Chief Ron Dixon reported there were no issues during the festival. "Everyone was respectful and polite, on the festival grounds and throughout the whole town itself," he said.Pleased with this year's results and thanking the planning committee, volunteers and public, planning for the 2024 Dickens starts almost immediately, Fleegle said.Chestertown Mayor David Foster offered his commendations to Fleegle as well. "Thank you for soldiering through with the rain delay on Friday, and what I saw on Saturday was wonderful," he said.

title: Easton Edc Seeking Information On Black History Month Events
author: Contributed
content:
Easton Edc Seeking Information On Black History Month Events

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Contributed | Page: B6 | Section: News

 EASTON - The Easton Economic Development Corporation is requesting organizations planning events for Black History Month in February 2024 to contact their office and share plans so that they can help communicate to the public what will be happening in the community.Communications will include a website landing page at DiscoverEaston.com, press releases and general marketing support for events during this time.
Events must be free and open to the public. Coordinators of events are encouraged to share their information by emailing welcome@discovereaston.com.
In 1926, historian and scholar Carter Woodson, then the president of the Association for the Study of African American Life and History, launched this recognition in the second week of February to coincide with the birthdays of two notable men - Talbot county native, Frederick Douglass and former president Abraham Lincoln.
Black History Month was officially recognized nationally in 1976 by President Gerald Ford.
The Easton Economic Development Corporation was launched in 2013 to drive economic vitality, smart redevelopment and business creation in the historic Town of Easton to foster a healthy quality of life for all generations. The EEDC works to catalyze Greater Easton's continued prosperity as a diverse and healthy "smart town," leading innovation where the land and water meet.
