title: Lidia'S Life: Celebrity Chef Bastianich Reflects On Career With 'Culinary Jubilee'
author: Dana Simpson
content:
Lidia'S Life: Celebrity Chef Bastianich Reflects On Career With 'Culinary Jubilee'

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Dana Simpson | Page: A9 | Section: News 
 
 663
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Despite its ties to culture, religious practices, family economics, environmental concerns or political statements, food has a distinct way of bringing people together and encouraging conversation.Few people know this better than chef, author, restaurateur and TV personality Lidia Bastianich, whose catchphrase, "Tutti a tavola a mangiare" - or "Everyone to the table to eat," in English - has united people for the past 25 years. Best known for her countless shows and specials on public television during the past three decades, PBS releases an up-close-and-personal look into the life and work of the celebrated chef; "25 Years with Lidia: A Culinary Jubilee" premieres Monday, Dec. 18.
In honor of this quarter-century milestone in her career, Bastianich welcomed the opportunity to speak with me about her childhood, her career, her own personal relationship to food and culture, and the moments that have meant the most to her throughout her journey thus far.
Caught in what was no doubt a rare moment at her home in Long Island, N.Y., Bastianich joins our video call clad in a vibrant pink sweater and scarf that provide a cheerful contrast to the white bookcases and potted palm behind her. Easy to see why North American audiences have been captivated by her for 25 years, Bastianich begins sharing memories of where her close kinship with food began.
"My grandmother used to make a soup [I loved]," Bastianich reminisces. "It's called yota, and it's unique to the region that I come from, [Pula, Istria], which is right on the border in [what] now is Croatia. It's a bean and pasta soup, but instead of the pasta, she would put in sauerkraut, and I loved it."
While this may be one of her most formative childhood food experiences, the association between food and family was just beginning for young Bastianich. Now 76 years old, the celebrity chef is quick to note that cooking, for her, "goes beyond just nourishing the body."
"It's [about] nurturing the person, the soul and the sentiments that come with it," Bastianich says.
"Food is a communicator no matter what culture, if you sit down, and you eat each other's food, somehow doors open. You are accepting that person - through that food - for what they are."
And there is no denying that this Italian food ambassador knows about people. As PBS's "25 Years with Lidia" shows through interviews with friends, family and colleagues of hers from throughout the years, Bastianich is an excellent communicator herself and values meaningful, deeply human connections above all else. To support this, the hour-long documentary features moments with fellow chef/restaurateurs Jacques Pepin ("Jacques Pépin Heart & Soul"), Mary Sue Milliken ("Too Hot Tamales"), Elizabeth Falkner ("The Next Iron Chef ") and Geoffrey Zakarian ("The Kitchen").
Perhaps the most surprising appearance in "25 Years with Lidia," though, is that of celebrated actor and fellow Astorian Christopher Walken ("Pulp Fiction," 1994).
"I came [to the United States] at 12 years old, as an immigrant, and we lived in Astoria, Queens.
Right across the street was Walkens' Bakery," explains Bastianich as she elaborates on the sense of community among immigrants to New York City at the time.
"Christopher [Walken]'s father was a German immigrant and he was a great baker, so [then] a 16-year-old immigrant I applied and he took me on weekends," Bastianich says. "Christopher's job was to fill the jelly doughnuts with jelly and he used to press them and make a mess. We were friends, you know, the weekends we were there."
Beyond the interviews with Bastianich and those closest to her, "25 Years with Lidia" also features "rare and never-before-seen video and photographs" from the now-established chef 's journey to celebrity, including recollections of milestone moments such as her and her husband's critically acclaimed first restaurant, Buonavia, which opened in 1971, and her career-solidifying dinner with Julia Child and James Beard at her third restaurant, Felidia.

title: Christmas Cheer - Maryland Stories: Cabaret Carolers Warm Up The Winter With Song
content:
Christmas Cheer - Maryland Stories: Cabaret Carolers Warm Up The Winter With Song

 December 14, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: A7 | Section: News 
 
 524
 Words 

 Read News Document

 During a busy month of performances for their talented, youthful group, the Children's Theater of Southern Maryland Cabaret Carolers will continue their merry delivery of glad tidings throughout the area this weekend by hosting a pair of concerts at two Calvert County establishments.Comprised of nearly two dozen elementary and middle school students primarily from Calvert County with several from St. Mary's County added to the mix, the Children's Theater of Southern Maryland Cabaret Carolers will perform on Saturday from 1 to 4 p.m. at Mrs.
Moo's in Prince Frederick then again on Sunday at the Bulrushes Cafe from 9 a.m. to noon.
"The carolers will perform three sets of six to eight songs at each location over those two days," said Southern Maryland Children's Theater public relations and social media manager Lara Reisman, who is slated to be the group's president for two years beginning next month. "Most of the group is from Calvert County, but we have a few from St.
Mary's County. They're a very talented, dedicated vocal group and they love to perform at area venues during the holidays."
In fact, the group's two performances this Saturday at Mrs. Moo's holiday open house and again the following morning at Bulrushes Cafe will put the finishing touches on a very busy month for the carolers.
Last Saturday, Dec. 9, the Cabaret Carolers performed for three hours at the Holidays Tree Lighting in Prince Frederick and several days earlier they performed at Asbury Solomons retirement community.
"The kids love to perform any time of year, but especially around the holidays," said Reisman, who has been associated with the group since its inception in 2001. "They enjoy rehearsing together and they can't wait to perform.
They usually do three sets of six to eight songs beginning at the top of each hour."
While most residents do not associate ice cream with the winter months and upcoming Christmas and New Year's Day holidays, Mrs. Moo's is going to sweeten the pot for the local group by unveiling an ice cream sundae named in their honor on Saturday.
Reisman admits that it is a fitting tribute to a youthful group that provides holiday cheer each winter.
Aly Cross, who has directed the group in "Newsies, Jr.," "A Christmas Story," "Beauty and the Beast" and "Once On This Island Jr." and will be directing "High School Musical" in the spring, also teaches all of the acting classes each semester.
In the spring, the acting classes will be held at the College of Southern Maryland's Prince Frederick campus.
"This group is very, very unique," Cross said.
"We have a great group of kids. There's no pressure on these kids to memorize things. It's a great chance for them all to sing Christmas carols together.
They're learning a little bit of choreography to go along with the songs.
When they performed at the Asbury Solomons they were overwhelmed by the response from the audience."

title: Gunston celebrates 'art for everyone'
author: Laura Tayman; ltayman@aol.com
content:
Gunston celebrates 'art for everyone'

 December 18, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman; ltayman@aol.com | Page: 4 | Section: News 
 
 411
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The extraordinary talents of Gunston School students were on full display for family and friends at the school's mid-year Night of the Arts event.Head of School at Gunston, John Lewis, said the arts are so important that students are required to take art credits every year.
"You see where arts are being cut from schools across the nation," Lewis said. "The arts are not only good for the soul, but they promote collaboration of creativity and communication."
Photographs, woodworking pieces, pottery, drawings, and paintings filled the art room and hallways throughout Everdell Hall. Students in AP Art class offered multiple pieces of their work based on a certain theme.
Junior Isla McCollum chose to create works focusing on changes in life while Emma Sharp chose pieces that contrasted both really colorful subjects along with the starkness of black and white.
"My theme focused on what the world would look like if humans disappeared," student Elena Fraser said. "I included objects that we use every day as well as animals."
All three students said they would like to include art in whatever higher learning they choose to pursue. Marie Thomas, the school's director of External Relations, said they have had numerous students accepted into art schools across the country over the years.
Over on the performing arts side, music was provided by the Gunston Chorale and members of the school's Contemporary Ensemble. Members of the ensemble had collaborated with the Songwriting class to create an original song titled "Different Kind of High."
The school's theater students, the Gunston Players, performed scenes from a collection of Edgar Allen Poe stories, including "The Murders in the Rue Morgue," "The Fall of the House of Usher," The Cask of Amontillado," and the "Tell-Tale Heart."
Poets from the school had recorded themselves reading their own works. Guests were provided copies of the student-produced literary magazine, Debris, a print publication that celebrates the school's student writers and visual artists. The magazine features original artwork, photography, and poetry, and even musical performances (via QR codes).
Several impressive works of environmental art created by Chesapeake Watershed Semester students were on display including an eight foot papier-mâché sturgeon and a sea glass sculpture.
New this year was the "tech art" section which included demonstrations of different types of robotics.

title: Massey Air Museum curator, director retires
author: Laura Tayman
content:
Massey Air Museum curator, director retires

 December 19, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Laura Tayman | Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 484
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GALENA - Don Hooker, Massey Air Museum curator and director, is leaving his position and relocating to South Carolina."Don will be massively missed for all that he has done for the Massey Air Museum," said museum volunteer Bill Dougherty who attended Hooker's achievements with a museum goodbye dinner at the airport this month.
Hooker was born in October 1934, on the Isle of Wight, UK, making him barely 6-years-old during the Battle of Britain in 1940. He remembers seeing the swirling high altitude contrails of air battles between the RAF and the Luftwaffe during World War II.
He emigrated to the United States in the early '60s after having worked for Saunders Roe and national service in the Royal Air Force. He came to Massey after retiring from Boeing Vertol as a project engineer on the CH-46 Sea Knight helicopter.
The Massey Air Museum at the Massey Aerodrome is a grass airfield on the Eastern Shore of Maryland that was transformed from corn fields into a working public use airport with a 3,000 feet grass runway that opened in 2001.
The museum was officially opened in 2002 as a non-profit organization dedicated to the education and the preservation of grassroots aviation in this country.
Hooker first started volunteering at Massey in 2007 after moving to Galena. He gravitated to preparation of the earliest artifact displays for the nascent museum.
"With hands-on expertise, he personally helped restore the donated aircraft, engines, etc., to fine display condition with the assistance of other volunteers here at Massey," Dougherty said. "Don took the DC-3 under his wing for restoration and, just as importantly, to maintain it."
"The large DC-3 made for a great experience to climb aboard a larger plane from days gone by," a tourist once wrote about meeting Hooker. "It was awesome to get in the cockpit and experience how pilots used to fly. The other planes on site showed the kids how planes of all sizes worked, including a great 100th anniversary replica of the Wright brothers plane that was restored on the premises."
"My tenure at the museum was wonderful,"
Hooker said. "Our members are all kindred spirits, and our work was such a rewarding experience for me."
Hooker was the driving force behind Massey's popular summer program for high school students titled "Introduction to Aviation Engineering."
"I believe the we need to start sharing our passion for flying with the younger generation," Hooker said.
When asked about his move, Hooker said there were a couple of reasons.
"We have a young grandson in South Carolina we would like to spend time with," Hooker said. "And we really want to downsize our housing situation."
"It's often said that no one is irreplaceable," Dougherty said, "but I fear that is not the case with our good friend and mentor, Don Hooker."

title: Local artists give longtime nativity new life
author: Doug Bishop; dbishop@chespub.com
content:
Local artists give longtime nativity new life

 December 19, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Doug Bishop; dbishop@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 568
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTER - Every year since 1952, the Kent Island Volunteer Fire Department has posted a traditional nativity scene outside the fire house. It began 71 years ago, when the fire department membership voted to have the late James Ball, a member of the fire department and local school art teacher, build and paint the original project. Ball was a former art teacher at the old Stevensville High School, which was located on the site where Stevensville Middle School stands today.The original fire building was constructed in 1947. Not married at the time, Ball resided at the firehouse which was within walking distance of the high school. If a fire alarm was sounded, Ball started all the emer-gency vehicles and opened the bay doors for the volunteers to arrive and have the equipment ready to roll immediately.
In those days, all communications with the fire department was done by rotary phones. There were no cell phones or digital devices to communicate with volunteer firefighters back then. Ball provided a great service living at the firehouse.
This year, members of the Kent Island Creators Club discovered the original nativity was in need of refurbishment and restoring. Though repainted numerous times over the past 71 years, it needed some tender loving care this time. The club mem-bers - Lee Ayers (who orchestrated this project), along with Robin Craig, Candice Whiting, Pam Kline, Kyle Conway, Mari Ann Donnelly and Darlene Winegartner - performed extraordinary detailed work on each of the nativity figures.
The scene depicts the baby Jesus, Joseph and Mary, the three wise men, shepherds, a donkey, a camel and four lambs.
Shortly after Ball completed the original nativity, his health began to fail. As the hospital bills mounted, Ball was unable to pay. The fire department membership voted to cover his hospital costs. Ball died in late 1954. Minutes from the membership meeting show the fire department voted to pay for a Christmas wreath to be placed on Ball's gravesite in December 1954.
Fire department President Jody Schulz said, "We're thankful we still have the nativity. It's a valued part of our fire department history. We've tried to take care of it over the years. We're also very thankful for these very talented local artists who volunteered their skills and talents to preserve it for us."
The nativity is lighted outside the main doors of the firehouse. It can be seen from Route 18 as you drive past the firehouse each night. If you want a more up-close look at the nativity figures, you can drive into the parking lot. Visitors are cautioned not to park in front of the firehouse bay doors.

title: Sculptor bends metal and wood - Local artist draws influence from past experience and the nature of the Chesapeake
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
Sculptor bends metal and wood - Local artist draws influence from past experience and the nature of the Chesapeake

 December 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 890
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ROYAL OAK - Sculptor Cole Meyerhoff's workshop is full of clamps, power saws and TIG welders. He can cut and bend metal and wood into shapes that please him. He takes pleasure in the color and underlying texture in a board of walnut.He likes a clean solder. He is an avid Log Canoe racer.
Meyerhoff studied art at St. Marys College and has had several interesting and engaging internships from Maine to North Carolina to further his growth and vision.
One even included a stint as a shipwright.
But now he does his work at Darmand Creek Designs, which he relishes. He wears heavily worn Carhartts and a welding helmet.
Meyerhoff got his start when his dad borrowed a welder from a friend. His first weld was in a tractor fender.
"I never saw myself working for someone else. I have always been making or modifying things. I owe a large part of that to my dad," he said. "There is a theme of modification and adjustment. Once you start welding anything could be anything. You can put whatever you want together. It is a ton of fun." "It is like a hot glue gun.
You can go to town," he said.
Meyerhoff makes representational birds and rockfish and anchors. There is a giant metal crab claw at the Trippe Gallery in Easton, a gallery he has worked with for six years.
The art he makes draws heavy influence from his past experiences.
Meyerhoff took a gap year before college. He started that year at the vaunted Haystack Mountain School on Deer Isle, Maine.
"I mapped a year of programs that didn't overlap so it made an apprenticeship.
There were half a dozen studios in session with about 10 people in each one. The ceramics, writing workshops, textiles - they even have a glass hot shop. That was the fun place to hang out at the end of the day because they would just keep working," he said.
"Watching those guys was a lot of fun." After Maine, he went to Penland School of Craft in North Carolina.
"That place was incredible.
A lot of super talented people there. The instructors, the people taking classes all the fellowship artists that were there - that was very eye opening for me," he said.
Like a sailor Meyerhoff stopped in various creative ports before starting his own shop. Mastering craft is the north star that allows him express his vision. And he has a lot of fun doing it.
For the last three months of his gap year, he went to the Island School in the Bahamas for an internship.
This was an ocean based inquiry into native ecosystems.
You can see this appreciation of salty critters in some of his designs.
When he finally got to college he found that there were not many people in the art department doing metal work, which gave him free rein to create.
"My adviser said you have the studio, you have got the budget, nobody else is doing it. Go to town," Meyerhoff said. "That definitely shaped the style of work that I have gotten into now." He points to a 5-foot metal fish on the wall.
"That was the first representational piece that I had done. I have always liked more abstract work that is focused on the monumental, like Mark Di Suvero and Alexander Liberman," he said. "They make these giant metal things. I went to Storm King in upstate New York. It is a sculpture park.
You could spend a couple of days there. The park is huge. To go there and see that stuff in person for the first was spiritual after spending so much time reading about these guys." All this finds its way to what he is doing now, starting with the art trail organized by Mary Lou McAllister in St. Michaels.
"I wanted to do it, but I wanted something that theoretically could be marketable and sell, so I did a heron. It really got me to look more closely at birds.
To really hammer out the details of a heron, there is just so many cool little things. You have to look really hard," he said.
"I have done maybe six or seven birds. A couple of geese, one osprey on a nest.
They have all been in the gallery space with Nanny (The Trippe Art Gallery)," he said.
While his heart is in sculpture, Meyerhoff has a practical side too. He is doing marine fabrication building T-tops for boats.
He has a couple of bending machines to shape the metal for center console boats. One time he fixed a Log Canoe's broken rudder between races.
"I really like making things that you have an interaction with. You can tell when something doesn't feel right, like if you sit on a stool that is a little too small. I learned from making pottery that subtle little things can affect your experience with it," Meyerhoff said.
He is looking to a future of more marine fabrication and creative takes on furniture.
For now, Meyerhoff just likes making things.

title: An Italian seafood Christmas feast
author: Marie Savage; Country Cooking
content:
An Italian seafood Christmas feast

 December 20, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Marie Savage; Country Cooking | Page: A5 | Section: News 
 
 1407
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Recently I attended a luncheon that featured mainly Italian dishes, and I was very impressed with both the number of dishes featured and that you could tell they were a labor of love. Especially my favorite - spaghetti and meatballs!My memory went back to my late Italian friend who served Italian Christmas dinners each year in honor of her Italian ancestry. So, I decided to do an Italian dinner this year in memory of my late friend.
In future columns I will feature others. One of the traditions my old friend's family always celebrated was The Feast of Seven Fishes or, Festa dei Sette Pesci.
A southern Italian tradition known as the "Vigilia di Natale" commemorates the wait for the midnight birth of the baby Jesus. Italian-American families around Christmas time gather together to celebrate Christmas with a huge dinner made up of seven different fish and seafood dishes coming in all different types of forms.
Italian-American immigrants - homesick for the land they left behind - combined classic Italian dishes with seafood. The sea was a representation of the connection between their home country and the new one.
The number seven stems from the biblical importance of the number and its lucky connotation. While many of these symbols are taken from Catholicism and Italian tradition, the Feast of the Seven Fishes is virtually unheard of in Italy and instead is considered an Italian-American tradition.
Baked Clams, Baccala, Mussels, Calamari and Lobster are some of the dishes you'll see being served. Here on the Eastern Shore of Maryland, we have oysters, rock fish and so many other forms of seafood native to our bays and Atlantic coast.
For a holiday so widely celebrated, the traditions surrounding Christmas are as unique as the ornaments that decorate your tree.
From decor, songs, stories and gifts, Christmas looks a little bit different in every home across the world, but the "reason for the season" never changes.
Whether you're having any of the below recipes or baking a chicken or turkey or prime rib with potatoes, the time you are spending with family and friends is the most important.
CLAMS WITH LINGUINE
Kosher salt, 12 oz linguine, 4 tbsp unsalted butter, 4 cloves garlic finely chopped, 2 tbsp chopped fresh parsley, pinch of crushed red pepper flakes, 2 dozen littleneck clams (scrubbed), 1/2 cups dry white wine, juice of 1 lemon plus wedges for serving, freshly ground black pepper.
In a large pot of boiling salted water, cook pasta, stirring occasionally, until al dente according to package directions. Drain, reserving 3/4 cup pasta cooking liquid. Meanwhile, in another large pot over medium heat, melt butter.
Add garlic, parsley and red pepper and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add clams and wine. Cover pot with a tight-fitting lid and cook until clam shells open, 7 to 10 minutes. (Discard any unopened clams.) Add lemon juice, linguine and 1/4 cup pasta water, tossing frequently and adding more pasta water if needed, until glossy and warmed through, about 2 minutes; season with salt and black pepper. Divide pasta among bowls. Serve with lemon wedges alongside.
BACON WRAPPED SCALLOPS
1 lb. dry sea scallops (about 14), Kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 8 oz bacon (about 7 strips, not thick-cut), 2 tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 clove garlic (smashed), 1 tbsp. fresh thyme leaves, lemon wedges for serving.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Line a rimmed baking sheet with foil. Pat scallops dry with paper towels; season with 1/2 teaspoon salt and 1/4 teaspoon pepper. Cut bacon slices in half crosswise so you get 3-to 4-inch long strips. Wrap bacon around scallops and secure with a toothpick. Arrange scallops on a prepared sheet. In a small skillet over medium heat, melt butter. Add garlic and thyme leaves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 1 minute. Spoon butter and thyme over scallops, leaving garlic in the pan. Roast scallops until bacon is crisp and scallops are cooked through, 15 to 20 minutes. Remove toothpicks.
Transfer scallops to a platter and serve warm with lemon wedges alongside.
MUSSELS WITH TOMATO AND GARLIC
2 tbsp. butter, 1 onion chopped, 3 cloves garlic minced, 1 15-oz. can diced tomatoes, 1/2 cup dry white wine, 2 tbsp. freshly chopped parsley, kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 2 lb. mussels (scrubbed and debearded).
In a pot over medium-low heat, melt butter. Add onion and cook until fragrant and soft, 5 minutes, then add garlic and cook until fragrant, 1 minute more. Add diced tomatoes, wine and parsley and stir until combined. Season with salt and pepper. Add mussels and simmer until all shells are open. Discard any shells that aren't open.
Garnish with more parsley and serve with a hard bread such as sour dough.
OYSTERS ROCKEFELLER
2 cloves garlic, 1 cup tightly packed fresh spinach, 1/2 cup roughly chopped green onions, 1/2 cup roughly chopped parsley, leaves and stems, 2 tsp. lemon juice, 1/2 cup (1 stick) butter softened, 3/4 cup Panko bread crumbs, 1/4 cup freshly grated Parmesan, 1 tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 1 lb. coarse salt, 24 fresh oysters (shucked, shells reserved), lemon wedges for serving. Position rack in top third of oven and preheat to 450 degrees. Add garlic, spinach, green onions, parsley, lemon juice, butter and Pernod to a food processor and pulse until finely chopped. In a medium bowl combine, panko, Parmesan and oil. Sprinkle coarse salt over a large baking sheet to a depth of 1/2".
Arrange oysters in half shells in salt. Divide spinach mixture among oysters and sprinkle with Parmesan mixture. Bake until the spinach mixture is bubbling and the Panko is deeply golden, about 8 minutes. Serve with lemon wedges alongside.
GARLIC LEMON MAHI MAHI
3 tbsp. unsalted butter divided, 2 tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil divided, 4 (4-oz.) mahi mahi fillets, kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 1 lb. asparagus trimmed, 3 cloves garlic finely chopped, 1/4 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 2 lemons (1 sliced, 1 zested and juiced), 1 tbsp. chopped fresh parsley plus more for serving. In a large skillet over medium heat, heat 1 tablespoon butter and 1 tablespoon oil until butter is melted. Add mahi mahi; season with salt and black pepper. Cook, turning occasionally, until golden on both sides, 4 to 5 minutes per side. Transfer to a plate. In the same skillet over medium-high heat, heat the remaining 1 tablespoon oil. Add asparagus and cook, tossing occasionally, until tender, 2 to 4 minutes; season with salt and black pepper. Transfer to a plate with fish. SteIn same skillet over medium heat, melt remaining 2 tablespoons butter. Add garlic and red pepper flakes and cook, stirring occasionally, until fragrant, about 1 minute, then stir in lemon slices, zest, and juice, and parsley.
Remove from heat. Return mahi mahi and asparagus to the skillet and spoon sauce over. Top with parsley before serving.
BAKED COD
4 cod filets (about 1" thick), Kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 4 tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 1 cup cherry tomatoes, 1 lemon, 2 garlic cloves (smashed but not peeled), 2 sprigs thyme, 2 tbsp. freshly chopped parsley. Preheat the oven to 400 degrees and pat cod filets with a paper towel until dry. Season all over with salt and pepper. Combine olive oil, cherry tomatoes, lemon slices, garlic, and thyme in a 9 by 13 inch baking dish.
Toss to coat and spread into an even layer. Nestle cod pieces into a baking dish.
Bake until fish is opaque and flakes easily with a fork, 15 to 20 minutes, depending on thickness of filets. Serve garnished with parsley, more lemon juice, and pan sauce.
GARLIC PARMESAN FLOUNDER
1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 fillets flounder, Kosher salt, freshly ground black pepper, 1/2 cup freshly grated parmesan, 1/4 cup bread crumbs, 4 cloves garlic (minced), juice and zest of 1 lemon, fresh chopped parsley for garnish. Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Drizzle 2 tablespoons of oil on a large baking sheet. Season flounder with salt and pepper.
On a large plate, combine parmesan, bread crumbs, garlic and lemon zest. Season with salt and pepper.
Dredge fish in bread crumb mixture, pressing to coat.
Place fish on a prepared baking sheet and drizzle with remaining 2 tablespoons of oil and lemon juice. Bake until golden and fish flakes easily with a fork, 20 minutes. Squeeze a bit more lemon on top and garnish with chopped parsley.
I wish each and every one of you a safe, warm and blessed holiday with family and friends.

title: 'Relatably funny' - 'Grandma Got Run Over by a Reindeer' parody celebrates Dorchester County
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
'Relatably funny' - 'Grandma Got Run Over by a Reindeer' parody celebrates Dorchester County

 December 22, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 576
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE - Henry VanDyke was struck by a creative thunderbolt eleven years ago. His family has been playing his Dorchester version of "Grandma Got Run Over by a Reindeer" every Christmas since.But the parody song, "Grandma Got Run Over by a Sika Deer," gained some broader regional attention recently after it played on local radio station WINX-FM.
"Eleven years ago I was pumping gas and the original song came on the radio, and I just started singing with my words and about three quarters of the song was written right there," he said. "That is what my wife and I do. We are always making up funny lyrics." To capture the yuletide magic of his holiday parody, VanDyke borrowed friends' recorders and laptops.
For the backtracking, he said, "It is just an instrumental. We purchased a karaoke track and then put the words to it." There is a bluegrass bounce to it.
Parody is as old as the ancient Greeks, and VanDyke thinks it takes certain ingredients to work.
"So the secret to any music is relating to people. And when it comes to parody, it has to be funny. You know, relatably funny. I did all four verses like the original, but we noted a lot of Dorchester County things in the song," he said.
"Different businesses and things like that. Old tavern called the Stone House that is no longer in business.
We talked about Hoopers Island Nikes, which are the white boots and hip boots, and muskrat huts. Sika Deer obviously. Danny's Marine, which is a boat dealer. He is still open. Then we had Great Slates in there, which recently closed. It was a pool hall," he said.
"(The parody song) is so old that a lot of those businesses are closed now," Jeannie VanDyke, Henry's wife, said. "Kaley (their daughter) and I called Mark Potter and told him to play it, and he did, because Kaley wanted to hear her dad on the radio. And then everybody is like, 'We heard your husband on the radio'." The song's local references garnered quite a bit of attention from the radio station's Eastern Shore audience.
"Kaley heard it on the school bus.
She was pretty excited about that.
A lot of people don't believe it is her dad. She thinks it is funny," Henry said from his Central Texas style barbecue joint Lil' Bitta Bull on Race Street.
He had run a mechanic shop next door, but the barbecue started to take off.
"I realized that I probably needed to focus more on the food. It was a pretty big hit. I turn hobbies into careers," he said.
"I am afraid if I make too many more parodies, I will turn a hobby into a career, and then there I would go. I would have to get T-shirts and everything," he said. "Somebody took the song and put it on YouTube.
If you search 'Grandma Got Run Over by a Sika Deer,' it will populate in your search. I think that is how the radio guy got it." VanDyke's song speaks to his local culture.
"Locals love it when they figure out you are talking about their hometown, their way of life, south country," he said.

title: Story swap to showcase the stories of the Mid-Shore's watermen
author: CONTRIBUTED
content:
Story swap to showcase the stories of the Mid-Shore's watermen

 Author/Byline: CONTRIBUTED | Page: 6 | Section: News

 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS - The son of a Kent Island waterman, Brent Lewis, has been around men and women who make their living on the Chesapeake Bay his entire life.Lewis said his mother early on shut down any thought that he might follow that path, but over the years, the local author and historian's appreciation for the demanding work and the characters who keep the industry alive has only increased.
It's why Lewis is so passionate about offering watermen a platform to share their stories.
"Living here for so long, I just had this idea that a lot of the people in our community don't really understand the watermen's life or what they do," said Lewis, who will host a Watermen's Story Swap on Thursday, Jan. 11 at 5:30 p.m. in the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum's Van Lennep Auditorium.
Lewis has emceed a handful of similar events over the past decade, and he's realized the power of gathering watermen together to explain their shared experience through enlightening, funny and often profound tales.
At CBMM, Lewis will lead a panel that features both working and retired watermen hailing from around the Eastern Shore.
The suggested ticket price is $8 per participant, with both in-person and virtual options available at cbmm.org/WatermenStorySwap.
The event is funded through CBMM's Regional Folklife Center under the Maryland Traditions program of the Maryland State Arts Council.
Lewis has found certain themes - mentors, bad weather, and unexpected Bay adventures, to name a few - to be universal, but ultimately, it's the panelists' unique memories collected over years on the water and the free-flowing format that make these conversations equal parts entertaining and unpredictable.
"You never know where we're going to end up," Lewis said. "We don't have to stick to the topics as long as everyone's involved and having fun. It kind of runs the gamut between really hearty belly laughs to more emotional storytelling." The author of four books with a fifth underway, Lewis has long helmed an oral history project with the Kent Island Heritage Society, and at the first story swap in 2016, held before a standing-room crowd in Grasonville, he brought together eight watermen who he'd interviewed for that project.
There have been other iterations, including a couple at Chesapeake College's Chesapeake Storytelling Festival, but it's been more than five years since the last one.
Lewis found a partner in CBMM through its Folklife Center to launch the latest Watermen's Story Swap, this time with the focus expanding beyond Queen Anne's County.
He and videographer Josh Willis are recording an ongoing series of oral histories as part of the partnership.
The Jan. 11 Speaker Event, bringing together watermen from the mid and lower Eastern Shore, will be documented among that group.
Lewis said working with CBMM's Director of Curatorial Affairs & Exhibitions Jen Dolde and Vice President of Education & Interpretation Jill Ferris has breathed new life into the project by backing his belief in the importance of capturing these stories - both the ordinary and extraordinary.
"Working with CBMM, their enthusiasm for getting these stories down before they're gone has helped keep my enthusiasm up," Lewis said. "I can tell by talking to Jen and Jill that this is something that they feel is positive and beneficial to the community. If we don't take the opportunity to document these watermen's stories, once they're gone, they're gone." As much as anything, Lewis is excited to reach a new audience with this Story Swap. He's worked hard to assemble a panel that will represent different voices within the industry and bring together watermen from across the Chesapeake.
With the group spanning geography and generations all together on Jan. 11, Lewis will start the conversation and see where it goes.
"It's a lot of fun," Lewis said. "If it goes right - and knock on wood I've never had one go badly - it's very entertaining, it's very informative, and I don't think the audience members forget it very quickly."

title: Massey Air Museum curator, director retires
author: LAURA TAYMAN
content:
Massey Air Museum curator, director retires

 December 26, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LAURA TAYMAN | Page: A4 | Section: News 
 
 488
 Words 

 Read News Document

 GALENA - Don Hooker, Massey Air Museum curator and director, is leaving his position and relocating to South Carolina."Don will be massively missed for all that he has done for the Massey Air Museum," said museum volunteer Bill Dougherty who attended Hooker's achievements with a museum goodbye dinner at the airport this month.
Hooker was born in October 1934, on the Isle of Wight, UK, making him barely 6-years-old during the Battle of Britain in 1940. He remembers seeing the swirling high altitude contrails of air battles between the RAF and the Luftwaffe during World War II.
He emigrated to the United States in the early '60s after having worked for Saunders Roe and national service in the Royal Air Force. He came to Massey after retiring from Boeing Vertol as a project engineer on the CH-46 Sea Knight helicopter.
The Massey Air Museum at the Massey Aerodrome is a grass airfield on the Eastern Shore of Maryland that was transformed from corn fields into a working public use airport with a 3,000 feet grass runway that opened in 2001.
The museum was officially opened in 2002 as a non-profit organization dedicated to the education and the preservation of grassroots aviation in this country.
Hooker first started volunteering at Massey in 2007 after moving to Galena. He gravitated to preparation of the earliest artifact displays for the nascent museum.
"With hands-on expertise, he personally helped restore the donated aircraft, engines, etc., to fine display condition with the assistance of other volunteers here at Massey," Dougherty said.
"Don took the DC-3 under his wing for restoration and, just as importantly, to maintain it." "The large DC-3 made for a great experience to climb aboard a larger plane from days gone by," a tourist once wrote about meeting Hooker. "It was awesome to get in the cockpit and experience how pilots used to fly. The other planes on site showed the kids how planes of all sizes worked, including a great 100th anniversary replica of the Wright brothers plane that was restored on the premises." "My tenure at the museum was wonderful," Hooker said.
"Our members are all kindred spirits, and our work was such a rewarding experience for me." Hooker was the driving force behind Massey's popular summer program for high school students titled "Introduction to Aviation Engineering." "I believe the we need to start sharing our passion for flying with the younger generation," Hooker said.
When asked about his move, Hooker said there were a couple of reasons.
"We have a young grandson in South Carolina we would like to spend time with," Hooker said.
"And we really want to downsize our housing situation." "It's often said that no one is irreplaceable," Dougherty said, "but I fear that is not the case with our good friend and mentor, Don Hooker."

 OXFORD - Tred Avon Players unveiled an exciting lineup for the coming year as it enters its 43rd season of providing live theater to the Eastern Shore.The shows will be performed in partnership with the Oxford Community Center at 200 Oxford Road.

'YOU HAVE THE RIGHT TO REMAIN DEAD'
By Pat Cook Directed by Rob Sanchez Feb. 15-25, 2024 In this hilarious audience-participation murder mystery, narrator Harnell Chesterton takes the audience to visit a small community theater group staging a play set in the Deep South. The play's characters are all in an uproar because Fat Daddy, the patriarch of the family, is about to change his will. Is Fat Daddy the target of the killer? 'THE BOYS FROM SYRACUSE'
By George Abbott Music & Lyrics by Richard Rodgers and Lorenz Hart Directed by Liz Clarke April 18-28, 2024 The Boys from Syracuse is a spirited adaptation of Shakespeare's Comedy of Errors. Antipholus of Syracuse and his servant Dromio embark on a quest to find Antipholus' lost twin in the city of Ephesus, leading to a series of comical misadventures.
Against the backdrop of war between Ephesus and Syracuse, the travelers navigate chaos, encountering mistaken identities and humorous situations.
As Antipholus of Ephesus becomes entangled in debts and love interests, the narrative unfolds in a whirlwind of hilarity. Set in the 1930s, the musical features a fast-paced, funny script by George Abbott and a swinging score with timeless tunes like "Falling in Love With Love," "This Can't Be Love," and "Sing for Your Supper." "The Boys from Syracuse" is a delightful and tuneful tribute to Shakespeare's enduring comedic masterpiece.
'THE HALLELUJAH GIRLS'
By Jessie Jones, Nicholas Hope, Jamie Wooten Directed by Sammie Mooney Aug. 15-25, 2024 Hilarity ensues in the small town of Eden Falls, Georgia, as a group of spirited women decide to transform their lives at SPADEE-DAH!, an abandoned church-turned-day-spa.
Meeting every Friday, the friends, led by the high-spirited Sugar Lee, confront the realities of time and loss after the passing of a dear friend.
Each woman faces unique challenges - from romantic disillusionment and family troubles to stagnant marriages.
As they strive to pursue their dreams and embrace change, the women navigate comic twists involving unexpected ex-boyfriends, unlikely marriage proposals, and a determined rival threatening their beloved spa. Amidst the laughter and joy, this rollicking Southern comedy captures the women's journey overcoming obstacles, forging new paths and celebrating the bonds of friendship.
'BLITHE SPIRIT'
By Noel Coward Directed by Susan Patterson Oct. 24 to Nov. 3, 2024 Blithe Spirit unfolds in the home of writer Charles Condomine and his wife, Ruth.
Charles invites the eccentric medium Madame Arcati for a seance to gather inspiration for his book. Unexpectedly, the seance brings back Charles' first wife, Elvira, causing mischief that only he can witness.
Elvira accidentally causes Ruth's demise, resulting in Charles being haunted by both wives. The trio seeks Madame Arcati's help to send the spirits back, blending farce, emotion, and wit in this intensely funny and character-driven play.

title: 'It takes the whole community' - Academy Art Museum director reflects on Easton experience before leaving for New York
author: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com
content:
'It takes the whole community' - Academy Art Museum director reflects on Easton experience before leaving for New York

 December 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom Mccall; tmccall@chespub.com | Page: 5 | Section: Community 
 
 932
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON - Academy Art Museum Director Sarah Jesse is moving on to the University of Rochester in March after a three-year stint in Talbot County.Although this institute is orders of magnitude bigger, she will continue her focus on community engagement with the arts.
Feb. 23 is her last day before she moves on to be director of the Memorial Art Gallery. She said she has enjoyed living and working in Easton. There is a search committee for the next candidate.
"I love this place. I love the people. I love the staff and the people who support this place. I love how important this place is to the area and how beloved it is," Jesse said. "That has made this job feel very rewarding. This has been a total professional highlight for me coming here. I have learned so much, and it has been excellent training for my next step. It has been so fun. I will miss it a lot." She feels she is leaving the Academy in excellent hands, and it is in excellent shape. Looking forward, her next post is in a larger city and connected to a university.
"It is a bigger institution.
The operating budget is $9 million, and the operating budget of this (The Academy) is $1.6 million.
So with that comes more resources, more bandwidth, more opportunity to do more ambitious projects.
It is bigger. It is a very large museum," Jesse said.
She worked at the museum at her undergraduate alma matter Oberlin College in Ohio, and the experience touched her.
She was first generation to go to college.
The Oberlin museum gave prized artworks, like those by Robert Rauschenberg, to students to live with in their dorm rooms. She wants to give that kind of radical outreach to the students at the University of Rochester.
"I have worked in museums for over 20 years.
Ultimately it comes from my working class background and growing up in a rural part of Michigan.
My parents worked in the automotive industry, and my parents did a lot to expose us outside of our rural isolated world. We did not have much access to art and culture," Jesse said.
But something from the arts hit her deeply, and she was hooked.
"When I did have a seminal experience at the Detroit Institute of Arts, it spurred this desire to want to have art in my life," she said.
She wanted to work at art institutes that reflected her passion for sharing art with all kinds of people.
"That has always been the motivation for working in the museum field.
Not just to serve the traditional audience, but to serve the nontraditional museum goer," she said.
"I would have considered myself nontraditional.
Seeing how museums have completely transformed my life makes me want to give other people the opportunity to have a relationship to art and to museums." This desire to break down barriers has been a guiding core principle in each of her museum jobs in the last 20 years. She worked with the Academy Art Museum board to get rid of the entrance fee.
They agreed. She called this a home run.
Elitism is a stigma that all museums bear, she said.
"We have more than made up the loss in revenue from the donation box next to the front desk.
And people say to me, 'I feel compelled to support this institution.' My mentor told me, 'Be compelling and the money will come.'" This follows through in her belief of what an art institution could be.
"My unapologetic path is to take this thing designed for the public good and make it for the public good. It has been a total collective effort and total partnership for donors, members, staff.
Everyone is on the same page and that makes it so easy," she said.
She wants to tout the current civil rights photography exhibit that came from the collection at the High Museum in Atlanta.
"The show uses contemporary artists who are using their work to talk about race in the United States. The title of the exhibition is 'A Fire That No Water Could Put Out.' It is taken from Martin Luther King's last speech before he was assassinated," she said. "It is a fitting title for the show because that fire still burns today in terms of we have made progress on civil rights, but there is obviously so much more this country needs to go to overcome the legacy of slavery." "It is an easy case to make for the value of art having this exhibition.
This work helped spur the civil rights movement and it not only documented it, it helped shape it," she said.
Like a librarian, Jesse's role as director is to have art speak to people.
"If you spend the time, if it is good artwork, it will reveal itself to you, it's meaning. It does require discipline and the ability to read images. I love doing in gallery programming where we are in front of a work of art or talking about a work of art with a group of people. Art of itself doesn't always speak to people. Having a facilitator and hearing people's observations can help you find meaning in it," Jesse said.
Speaking of her fondness of the Academy, could also mark her direction forward.
"I want to thank the community. Anything we have accomplished here has been because of collective effort. It takes the whole community of people to make this place live up to its public spirited mission," she said.

title: Black-eyed peas, traditions and superstitions
author: Marie Savage; Country Cooking
content:
Black-eyed peas, traditions and superstitions

 December 27, 2023 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Marie Savage; Country Cooking | Page: A4 | Section: News 
 
 1415
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The cooks in my neck of the woods always cooked black-eyed peas for New Year's Day. This carried on for generations and still to this day remains a tradition.Mom bought that bag of peas ahead of time to make sure she had them before they sold out. Then she sat a piece of seasoning meat aside in the smoke house.
The most popular tradition on New Year's Day was to eat the black-eyed peas for good luck all year.
Well, the second biggest tradition of all was that no women were to enter the house on New Year's Day, as that was "bad luck." That did not work for me, as I tried to get out of helping mom cook or do dishes because I lived there and was not entering.
Well years later that changed somewhat to "women who accompanied the men to your house had to let the men enter first.
And I used to say "well let him do the dishes." Mom would cook a large pot of black-eyed peas with her seasoning meat and some potatoes. Then out came the big baking pans filled with homemade biscuits.
Sitting next to the biscuits was a jar of homemade jelly from last summer's canning and a dish with fresh churned butter.
No one asked for dessert, but everyone asked for more peas and biscuits.
From all over the world you find superstitions for New Years Eve and New Year's Day. Here are just a few I have heard over the years.
According to popular folklore or superstition, if these foods are eaten on New Year's Day, they guarantee good luck throughout the year: ¡ Peas or beans are said to symbolize coins or wealth. Choose traditional black-eyed peas, lentils, or beans to make a dish seasoned with pork, ham or sausage.
¡ Greens resemble money, specifically folding money. Make dishes using boiled cabbage or sauerkraut, collard greens, kale, chard, mustard greens, turnip greens or other green, leafy vegetables to ensure good fortune for the coming year.
¡ Pork is considered a sign of prosperity in some cultures because pigs root forward. Many southern New Year's Day dishes contain pork or ham, but feel free to serve a pork roast or baked ham as an entree.
¡ Cornbread might symbolize gold, and besides, it is essential with blackeyed peas and greens.
¡ In other cultures, fish, grapes, and ring-shaped cakes or doughnuts, or cakes with special treats inside symbolize luck.
Some believe that lobster could cause bad luck in the coming year because it moves in a backward direction and could mean setbacks in the year ahead. For the same reason, some believe chicken dishes should be avoided on New Year's Day. Chickens scratch backward, plus they are winged, so your luck could fly away.
Now for some blackeyed pea dishes and dishes people around the United States eat on New Year's Eve or New Year's Day.
BLACK-EYED PEAS
Begin by purchasing a bag of the dried blackeyed peas and soaking them in cold water, covering them. In a large soup pot, place the seasoning meat and cover with water, bring to a boil, let simmer.
After the beans have swollen and doubled in size, rinse in cold water and add to the seasoning meat, add more salt if needed and black pepper. When a rolling boil begins, turn flame back to achieve a steady boil, cover with a lid that is slightly ajar to avoid boiling over. As the beans cook, you can add in the last 45 to 50 minutes some whole corn, dumplings or some peeled white potatoes. Before adding the corn or other additions, check the seasonings.
Serve with your warm breads and enjoy this filling meal any time of the year.
TEXAS CAVAIR
2 14-oz. cans blackeyed peas (drained), 1 15.5-oz. can white hominy (drained), 2 medium tomatoes (chopped), 2 green tomatoes (chopped), 1 medium green bell pepper (chopped), 2 jalapeño peppers (chopped), 1/2 cup onion, (chopped), 1/2 cup fresh cilantro (chopped), 2 garlic cloves (minced), 1 8-oz. bottle Italian dressing, tortilla chips for serving. Stir together the first nine ingredients in a large bowl. Add the dressing to the black-eyed pea mixture, stirring until combined. Cover and chill for 2 hours. Drain. Serve with the tortilla chips.
HOPPIN JOHN WITH BRAISED OXTAIL
1.5 pounds oxtails, 1.5 tbsps salt (divided), 2 tsps black pepper (divided), 6 cups chicken stock, 2 cups dried black-eyed peas (soaked overnight), 2 cups diced yellow onions (from 2 medium onions), 2 cups diced carrots (from 5 medium carrots), 2 cups diced celery (from 4 stalks), 1/4 cup chopped jalapeño chiles (from 2 chiles), 4 garlic cloves (thinly sliced), 5 thyme sprigs, 3 fresh bay leaves. RICE:4 cups water, 1 teaspoon kosher salt, 1/4 teaspoon cayenne pepper, 1 cup uncooked jasmine rice, 1/4 cup unsalted butter (cubed), 1/4 cup apple cider vinegar, 1/2 cup chopped scallions.
Prepare the peas: Heat a Dutch oven over high and add canola oil. Sprinkle oxtails evenly with ½ tablespoon of the salt and 1 teaspoon of the black pepper, and place in the Dutch oven. Cook until browned on all sides, about 4 minutes per side. Remove oxtails from the Dutch oven. Pour off drippings, leaving browned bits in the Dutch oven, and add stock. Bring stock to a boil over high, using a wooden spoon to scrape browned bits from the bottom of the Dutch oven. Return oxtails to Dutch oven; reduce heat to medium-low, cover, and simmer until tender, 1½ to 2 hours. Using a slotted spoon, transfer oxtails to a plate, and let cool slightly.
Add peas, onions, carrots, celery, jalapeño, garlic, thyme sprigs, and bay leaves to stock mixture; reduce heat to low, and cook, partially covered, until peas are soft, about 1 hour. Stir in remaining 1 tablespoon salt and 1 teaspoon black pepper.
While peas cook, pick oxtail meat from bones, and set aside. While the peas finish cooking, preheat the oven to 300°F. Bring water, salt, and cayenne pepper to a boil in a medium saucepan over medium-high.
Reduce heat to medium; add rice and stir. Simmer gently, uncovered, stirring occasionally, until rice is al dente, about 15 minutes.
Drain rice in a fine wiremesh strainer, and rinse under cold water. Spread rice out on a rimmed baking sheet. Dry rice in a preheated oven for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Scatter butter evenly over rice, and continue to dry, stirring every few minutes, until all excess moisture has evaporated, and grains are dry and separate, about 5 more minutes. Add oxtail meat and cider vinegar to peas. Using a slotted spoon, transfer peas to a large serving bowl. Add rice, and carefully toss together. (Pour enough oxtail gravy over the top to moisten the peas without making the dish too soupy, about 1 cup.) Garnish with scallions.
INSTANT POT BLACKEYED PEA SOUP
1 tbsp olive oil, 1 cup chopped yellow onion, 1 cup chopped carrots, 1/2 cup chopped celery, 2 large garlic cloves, (minced), 1/4 tsp crushed red pepper, 6 cups chicken broth (such as Swanson's),3 thyme sprigs, 2 cups roughly chopped and stemmed collard greens, 1 14.5-oz. can fire-roasted diced tomatoes (drained), 1 (3/4-lb.) smoked ham hock, 1 lb. dried black-eyed peas (soaked overnight), 2 tbsps red wine vinegar, 1.5 tsps salt, 1 tsp black pepper.
Select the saute setting on Instant Pot or a pressure cooker. Times, instructions, and settings may vary according to cooker brand or model. Select high temperature setting and allow to preheat 2 to 3 minutes.
Add olive oil to the cooker, and heat until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add onion, carrots, and celery; cook, stirring often, until vegetables are softened, 2 to 3 minutes. Stir in garlic and crushed red pepper and cook for 30 seconds. Stir in chicken stock, thyme, collards, tomatoes, ham hock, and black-eyed peas. Press cancel. Cover cooker with lid, and lock in place. Turn the steam release handle to the sealing position.
Select manual/pressure cook setting. Select high pressure for 10 minutes.
(It will take 10 to 15 minutes for the cooker to come up to pressure before cooking begins.) Let the pressure release naturally for 15 minutes. Carefully turn the steam release handle to the venting position and let steam fully escape the float valve. This will take about 2 to 3 minutes. Remove lid from cooker. Remove ham hock from cooker; pull meat off bone, and chop to equal about 1/3 cup. Discard bone. Stir chopped ham, vinegar, salt, and pepper into soup.
Happy new year to all my readers! Here's to a happy and healthy 2024!

title: Digging through Maryland's past - Historic St. Mary's City fort gives glimpse of Colonial life
author: Michael Reid; mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Digging through Maryland's past - Historic St. Mary's City fort gives glimpse of Colonial life

 January 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid; mreid@somdnews.com | Page: 1 | Section: News 
 
 838
 Words 

 Read News Document

 It lay buried in the earth for more than 300 years.And though it was discovered five years ago, work continues to this day on the 17th-century St.
Mary's Fort in Historic St.
Mary's City.
The fort, which was built by colonists upon their arrival from England in 1634, existed until 1642 in what is now St. Mary's County.
"We have a pretty decent snapshot of where the lines of the fort are. We have suspicions of where some of the major buildings are," Historic St.
Mary's City Acting Executive Director Travis Parno said. "But we have research questions to the moon and back." "I think it's important to get to know the history of how the first colony started, but we also have a much longer period of occupation out here by the Native Americans," Jessica Edwards, site director, said. "We want to tell everybody's story that was out here." Parno said archaeologists have recovered projectile points dating back 10,000 years, in addition to Colonial-era ceramics, cannonballs, religious artifacts and glass beads that were used for trade.
Recently, the firing mechanism of a 17th-century musket was pulled from the ground.
"The Colonial period was a punctuation mark; it's not the start of a sentence," Parno said. "We have archaeological evidence dating back 9,000 to 11,000 years, so the colonists moving through the area is the tail end of it." Arguably the most important find to date was in 2019 when crew chief Stephanie Stevens discovered a Spanish-made Caravaca cross while sifting dirt.
"I saw the cross sitting there [in the dirt], and I freaked out," Stevens said.
"I started smacking Jess [Edwards'] arm. I could tell it was a significant find." "We were able to determine, and I swear I cannot make this up," Parno said of the find during COVID-19, "that these were given out because they believed they would ward off the effects of pandemics." When the approximately 150 colonists arrived in the area, the location made an impression on Father Andrew White, who wrote it had "as good ground as I suppose is in all Europe," and the Potomac was "the sweetest and greatest river I have ever seen, so that the Thames is but a little finger to it." The colonists likely lived in longhouses built by the Yaocomaco while the fort was being built.
The colonists endured malaria and dysentery, and went through what they called "seasoning," which was if they survived their first year their life expectancy would shoot up. Still, life expectancy was merely 24 for males and 27 for women.
"It's a pretty grim time," Parno said, "which is why we have about 400 burials near the church." Later, the colonists started growing tobacco, which Parno said was "the gold rush of the 17th century," and added it was so lucrative legislation was enacted requiring colonies to have a certain acreage of corn or wheat for every acre of tobacco because "they didn't want people to starve themselves." Parno said relations with the Indigenous people were good, "but that doesn't mean everything was all sunshine and rainbows." That was put to the test a few years later when colonist John Elkin shot and killed a Yaocomaco leader.
In 1642, the Susquehanna killed two colonists near what is now Naval Air Station Patuxent River.
That year is the last time the fort is referenced in official documents.
"Why did the fort disappear?" Parno asked. "That's the big question in my mind." The fort was originally thought to be on the St.
Mary's River, but former longtime chief archaeologist Tim Riordan thought it would be near Mattapany Road - colonists referred to it as the Mattaponi Path - which had a freshwater spring and was used by the Indigenous to reach the river.
"It's about surveillance, it's about control, maintaining a real good eye on what's going on," Parno said.
Riordan referenced a May 30, 1634, letter from Leonard Calvert, which said, "
We have seated ourselues, wthin one halfe mile of the riuer, wthin a pallizado of one hundred and twentie yarde square we haue mounted one peece of ordnance in parts most convenient; a fortification (we thinke) sufficient to defend against any such weake enemies as we haue reason to expect here" "It's the lack of data that we have," Parno said on why excavating the fort is vital. "It's like any sort of scientific frontier where you're dealing with an area that is understudied, under-appreciated and understood. When people think history, the 17th century often gets overlooked, [but it was] the laboratory where all of our social, religious, racial ideas [merged]." For more information or

title: Tracking Native American cultural heritage - Washington College's Dr. Julie Markin awarded $40k grant for new archaeological work on Upper Choptank
content:
Tracking Native American cultural heritage - Washington College's Dr. Julie Markin awarded $40k grant for new archaeological work on Upper Choptank

 January 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 3 | Section: News 
 
 610
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN - Dr. Julie Markin, associate professor of anthropology and archaeology and director of archaeology at Washington College, was recently awarded a $40,000 grant through the Maryland Historical Trust to study the indigenous cultural heritage of Maryland's Upper Eastern Shore and its inhabitants' social landscapes prior to contact with European settlers and explorers.The grant will provide for an archaeological survey and excavation of the watershed, conducted by the Washington College Archaeology Lab, as well as paid internships for students, public programming and presentations, and open lab opportunities which will be open to volunteers from the public at large.
Markin's project unites archaeological data with geographic information, environmental reconstruction and historical accounts, with the goal of developing a more robust database from which to ask questions about the nature and complexity of civilizations on the Chesapeake Bay's Eastern Shore, an area that has historically received less study and attention than its counterpart chiefdoms across the Bay.
"The research proposed by Dr. Markin will help fill a critical gap in our knowledge about pre-contact indigenous history on Maryland's Eastern Shore," said Maryland Historical Trust Chief Archaeologist Dr. Matthew McKnight, who noted that most of the archaeological work in the state requires consideration of cultural resources and archaeological sites in project planning.
"In areas like the Upper Choptank watershed that have seen less development, our understanding of prehistory is much more limited than places where more publicly funded construction is taking place. We are happy to have assistance from Washington College in documenting the important resources of the region for the Maryland Inventory of Historic Properties," said McKnight.
Markin views archaeology as a means by which we can ask, and attempt to answer, when and why inequalities arise.
She notes that even though the Eastern Shore received limited attention from early English settlers, mid-17th-century accounts describe Eastern Shore groups living in chiefdoms headed by hereditary leaders receiving tribute from subordinate groups. Traditional markers of complex chiefdoms - structures with status indicators and maize agriculture - are absent however, suggesting that Eastern Shore complexity has a different flavor.
"In terms of historical records, we don't know much of what the social and economic landscape looked like before John Smith made his way to the Chesapeake and modern-day Maryland," noted Markin. "Extensive archaeological investigation can help construct a better social geography of the Late Woodland/Contact period in the Upper Choptank." In addition to the excavations and fieldwork, Markin has plans to develop public programming that will engage students and community volunteers in open lab sessions throughout the 2024-2025 academic year.
Volunteers from the community will also be invited to participate in archaeological investigations conducted over the next two summers and fieldwork conducted throughout the academic year.
The grant will also allow for the development of public presentations and talks to community organizations about the project and its findings as well as an exhibit at the Caroline County Historical Society building in Denton, which would bring together project interns, the Caroline County Historical Society, and Washington College students minoring in museum, field, and community education.
"The research grant to Professor Markin is not only a testament to her stature as a scholar but also to the innovativeness of her approach to addressing important knowledge gaps," said Washington College Provost and Dean Kiho Kim.
Those wishing to follow along with the research and find out how to participate as a volunteer are encouraged to follow the Washington College Department of Anthropology webpage and Instagram account at@wacanthropology for blogs, short videos and updates from the field.

title: Art on a Plate - The Unstoppable Trend of Charcuterie Boards in Modern Culinary Culture
author: Beth Neels; Wealth Of Geeks
content:
Art on a Plate - The Unstoppable Trend of Charcuterie Boards in Modern Culinary Culture

 January 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Beth Neels; Wealth Of Geeks | Page: 6A | Section: News 
 
 1141
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Charcuterie boards are everywhere you look.According to Simplot Foods, 52% of Americans know about charcuterie. Of those who have tried it, 76% love the concept.
These boards are on social media feeds and in magazines or books. More restaurants offer a charcuterie board as a shareable appetizer or main entree. Entire tables decked out with tons of meats, cheeses, bread, fruits, nuts, and spreads.
Why?
Charcuterie boards are gorgeous. Even simple boards can be" works of art," according to Lauren Moss of WNDU News. They're colorful, and no two are ever the same.
According to the Institute of Culinary Education, the term "charcuterie" comes from the French chair cuit.
The literal translation of this word is "cooked flesh." It refers to the preservation of meat and came about before the days of refrigeration.
Today, charcuterie has taken on a whole new meaning.
These boards have become intricate, often stunning, displays of a chef's individuality.
Why is Charcuterie So Appealing?
Charcuterie boards are perfect for holiday entertaining occasions, but are also all the rage at baby and wedding showers, birthdays, and backyard get-togethers with friends. You could even bring one to the beach with a suitable storage container.
Charcuterie platters are easy to put together. They're a stress-free option, as opposed to more traditional meals. The more random they are, the better.
Charcuterie boards scale to any party size. Some are perfect for large crowds, like this seafood charcuterie board, but they're also excellent for an intimate date night with your partner.
These boards require zero culinary skills. If you can slice a piece of cheese, you can make a charcuterie board. Get the kids involved, too. They love to help place all the goodies. Plus, cleanup is easy. You only have to wash a few serving vessels.
Charcuterie boards are great for entertaining since they encourage people to gather, socialize, try new foods, or choose their favorite pairings.
Have a Theme in Mind Charcuterie boards - or grazing platters - should have a theme. A theme will give you a direction for your planning, buying, and building.
Keep in mind that virtually anything goes.
Use the seasons to your advantage. For instance, incorporate turkey, mini pumpkins, or apples as great options for an autumn board. Use foil-wrapped candies, cookies, cranberries, oranges, or chocolate salami for Christmas.
A Valentine's Day board would be great with raspberries or chocolate-covered strawberries. Make it in the shape of a heart to show that special someone you care.
Hosting a baby shower?
The board could incorporate pink or blue foods, along with cute baby favors. Birthday boards should include the favorite foods of the person you're celebrating.
Edible flowers add a unique touch to a board, such as one themed for spring. Seasonal fruits, like strawberries, are also welcome on these boards.
A game day board could include football-shaped cookies decorated with the teams' colors.
Make It Yourself Businesses that focus just on charcuterie boards are cropping up everywhere, taking advantage of the popularity of charcuterie boards and grazing platters. You can even purchase pre-made boards at your local grocery store or online. These tend to be pricey, however, and usually don't have nearly as many ingredients as the homemade versions.
General Rules for Planning a Board The Huffington Post recommends using at least three types of each type of food for a charcuterie board.
Incorporate different types of cheeses, including soft, hard, and semi-soft cheeses.
For more visual appeal, use several different colors of fruit, like berries, apples, and grapes.
Try new things on every platter, whether a new cheese, starfruit, kiwi, persimmon, or a different type of meat.
Use small bowls or ramekins for dips, jams, pickles, and olives. Be sure to provide serving tools like spoons, forks, tongs, and cheese knives. Affordable utensil kits are available online and at home stores.
Decide which board or boards to use to display the charcuterie. A giant board isn't necessary. Several smaller boards are just as effective.
Plan on serving 2-3 ounces of meats and cheeses for an appetizer portion.
For fruit and vegetables, buy smaller quantities. You will only use one or two apples, even for a large crowd.
If you incorporate plants, make sure they're all edible.
Everything on a charcuterie board should be edible unless it is obviously purely decorative, such as a "Happy Birthday" sign.
Don't Break the Bank A charcuterie "board" doesn't necessarily have to be made of wood. Use whatever you have on hand. Serving boards can be marble, china, or even plastic. Buy them at garage or rummage sales, flea markets, or wherever you can find lovely display pieces at a discount.
Don't over-buy. It's easy to get carried away and spend hundreds of dollars on a charcuterie board, but that's not necessary. Check your pantry or refrigerator before shopping, and use what you have on hand.
Your refrigerator's jams, pickles, or olives are perfect for a board. So are the nuts and crackers stored in the pantry. Also, buy at discount stores instead of high-end stores to lower your costs.
The Assembly Process Start with larger items, since they will be focal points, and space them out on the board. The cheeses are an excellent place to start.
Take hard cheese out of the refrigerator about 30 minutes before service for better flavor. Hard cheeses that aren't quite at room temperature are easier to cut, according to Food & Wine.
The next step is placing the bowls with mustards, jams, jellies, olives, and pickles. Bowls are also good for fruit like blueberries to keep them in one place.
For a stunning board, arrange meats artistically.
Meat roses are all the rage, but there are other artistic ways to place them. They should be easy for guests to pick up, so don't just place them flat on the board. Fold the meats into ribbons or rolls or make small clumps, so picking them up with a small fork is easy. Prepare these ahead of time, wrap them in plastic, and place them in the refrigerator until needed.
Fill in spaces with other fruit cut into single-serve portions. Dried fruits work well here, too. Finally, add nuts and smaller items, but save room on the board for bread and crackers. If there are still some empty holes on the board, strategically place small sprigs of fresh herbs or greens, like arugula or baby kale.
The Final Slice Charcuterie boards are not just trendy. They're a testament to the joy of sharing and the art of presentation.
They're more than just a collection of meats and cheeses.
They're a canvas for creativity and a centerpiece for conversation with friends and family. Best of all, there's no wrong way to make a charcuterie.
So gather up your favorite ingredients and let a charcuterie board make your next gathering a memorable one.

title: Old Christmas - History, traditions and celebrations of Jan. 6 holiday
content:
Old Christmas - History, traditions and celebrations of Jan. 6 holiday

 January 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Page: 3A | Section: News 
 
 479
 Words 

 Read News Document

 You might have thought Christmas was over. You might also associate Jan. 6 with the political events of 2021.But Jan. 6 is actually the end of traditional 12 Days of Christmas celebrations.
The 12 days marks the birth of Jesus (Dec. 25) through the Coming of the Magi (the Three Wise Men).
Some customs count the 12 days from sundown Dec. 25 until the morning of Jan. 6.
Early Christians celebrated Christmas on Jan. 6 until the Roman Empire moved the holiday to Dec. 25 in the 336 A.D. during the reign of Emperor Constantine. The late December date took the place of pagan holidays celebrating Roman gods and the Winter Solstice.
Still, Jan 6. continued to be celebrated as Christmas by Britons and other Europeans in the Julian calendar.
The changeover to the Gregorian calendar in 1582 moved Christmas to Dec. 25 and closer to the Winter Solstice.
It was adopted by the British and Irish in 1752 which helped bring the calendar change to the American colonies.
Other European countries, including Russia and its Eastern European neighbors, did not switch over until the early 20th Century. Orthodox Christians still celebrate Christmas on Jan. 7.
Still, Jan. 6 holds a place in Christmas celebrations for Armenians, the Irish as well as folks in Appalachia and some Christian believers such as the Amish and Mennonites.
Armenians - who are among the earliest in the Christian faith - still celebrate Christmas on Jan. 6.
In Ireland, the Jan. 6 celebrations have included women getting together for their own holiday festivities and the men of their households handling the cooking, cleaning and other chores for a day.
In Appalachia, Old Christmas still has a place for some with traditions such as getting together with family and friends, putting candles in windows and holiday food such as versions of fruitcakes (including apple stack cake), mincemeat pies and Christmas hams and serenading friends and neighbors.
There are also Appalachian superstitions that animals can speak at midnight on Old Christmas Day Jan. 6.
That superstition is on top Appalachians' holiday traditions such as eating ham hocks, black-eyed peas and greens on New Year's Day for good luck.
The Amish and Mennonites also celebrate Old Christmas with cakes, pies and other holiday foods as well as religious services. 
 
 Caption: AP PHOTO/JENS MEYER

 Old Christmas is celebrated Jan. 6 in Appalachia and by the Amish, Mennonites, some Irish and other Christians. The birth of Jesus Christ was originally celebrated on Jan. 6 by many Europeans in the Julian calendar before being changed to Dec. 25. Jan. 6 is also the end of the 12 Days of Christmas, according to various customs.

 Christmas was long celebrated on Jan. 6 in Great Britain, Ireland and other part of Europe until the changeover from the Julian to Gregorian calendars. Armenians still celebrate the birth of Jesus on Jan. 6 and Old Christmas is still commemorated in Appalachia and by the Amish and Mennonites.
