title: 'Sailing to Freedom' exhibit opens at Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
'Sailing to Freedom' exhibit opens at Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum

 October 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 523
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum's new exhibit shows changing perspectives of the Chesapeake Bay's relationship with the Underground Railroad by centering stories of freedom seekers."Sailing to Freedom: The Maritime Dimensions of the Underground Railroad" explores the lesser-known maritime aspects of the Underground Railroad and highlights stories of African Americans' journeys to freedom along Atlantic Coast water routes, including the Chesapeake Bay.
The exhibit features art, narrative accounts of freedom seekers, interactive exhibits, boat diagrams and historical maps detailing the routes taken by those seeking to escape from slavery.
Jen Dolde, director of curatorial affairs and exhibitions, said inspiration was taken from University of Massachusetts professor Tim Walker, Dartmouth and a scholarly book with several chapters of essays exploring aspects of freedom seekers along the Atlantic coast and in the Chesapeake region.
"People have this preconceived notion that it's primarily land-based routes, and that's not true at all, especially in coastal regions, places like the Chesapeake, where waterways were always our form of transportation," Dolde said.
According to Jill Ferris, vice president of Education and Interpretation for the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, the leadership team has been intentional on adopting language to center the lived experiences of the freedom seekers.
Ferris said historically people who were self-emancipating themselves were considered to be runaways and were painted with language to depict them as fugitives. Ferris describes the laws freedom seekers were running from as "abusive, restrictive and dehumanizing."
"If you shift from a mindset that somebody is a fugitive, that they're running away, that they're working outside of the law, and you put them at the center," Ferris said. "You give them agency and power. They were freedom seekers, they were active in their own efforts to claim and stake out their own freedom when society was trying to take it from them."
Dolde said freedom seekers would seek passage on whaling vessels or learn of safe communities through watermen. Some even went as far as shipping themselves to freedom, such as in the case of Henry Box Brown, who mailed himself in a wooden crate to abolitionists in Philadelphia.
In the exhibit, under a cartoon of Brown, there is a wooden crate created by local middle school students. The students, participants in the museums' summer program, researched primary sources, visited different museums and gathered research of the size of the crate before making the replica.
In conjunction with opening this exhibit, the museum will host speakers at the end of October and in December, as well as pilot a new student and adult group guided program called Seeking Freedom, which will focus on primary sources and first-person perspectives to uncover stories of freedom seekers.
But what stands out to Ferris is the opportunity "Sailing to Freedom" provides people seeking information and curious about freedom seekers' stories.
"Whenever we're talking about a topic that can be really emotionally challenging to take in," Ferris said. "… everybody needs to come in their own space and in their own time. And I think one of the things that I'm most proud of with this (exhibit) is providing a number of different opportunities for people to engage in the way that they are most comfortable engaging."

 At the First Friday event on Oct. 4, Evie Baskin was the featured artist with The Artists' Gallery in her newest show, "Exploring the Surface." The theme for this show was originally inspired by a workshop Baskin took earlier this year in Alexandria, Virginia which involved painting with oil on copper. The use of copper as a substrate for an oil painting originally began in the Medieval times as Flemish masters favored, copper for its smooth surface which allowed for fine detail and increased durability. Included in Baskin's show in October will be paintings using various surfaces and mediums, ranging from oil on copper, canvas and birchwood panels, pastel on sanded boards and paper, to drawing in silverpoint over coated paper.Over the years, Baskin's work has continued to evolve and change. The subject matter for "Exploring the Surface" includes portraits, both human and animal, along with landscapes on the Eastern Shore and beyond.
As a native Floridian, Baskin graduated from Florida State University in Tallahassee in 1976 with a degree in Visual Art. After raising her family in Key West, she moved to Alexandria, Virginia where she managed a law firm in Washington, D.C. while taking classes at The Torpedo Factory in her spare time. In 2007, she and her husband, Jonathan, moved to Chestertown where she began to work with pastel for the first time under the leadership of Mary Pritchard and Claudia Post. title: Museum preserves history with digital scanner
author: Tom McCall
content:
Museum preserves history with digital scanner

 October 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 524
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — White gloves and intense focus are needed to run the new Danish scanner at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum.Some of the museum's oldest artifacts from the 1780s are run through the contactless machine. No liquids of any kind are allowed in the Norman and Ellen Plummer Center for Museum Collections to protect the invaluable documents.
In July, the museum got a world-class large-format scanner. It can make super high resolution images of mostly flat objects. It will be used to digitize not only the museum's vast holdings of nautical information, but to support other organizations with their databases.
This includes materials that are challenging to handle and reproduce, including ship/sail plans, charts/maps, posters, artworks, framed items behind glass, rolled items and some three-dimensional artifacts.
Museum staff will work alongside volunteers to safely scan the materials, upload reference images to its online catalog of over 85,000 records and make them available to worldwide audiences.
As part of the project, the museum will provide free scanning services for other heritage tourism partners on special days, improving the availability and quality of graphic resources for exhibitions, publications and other historical projects.
The scanner is the HD Apeiron/42, made by Contex, designed in Denmark and first introduced in Europe. The Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum is one of the first sites to use this technology in the U.S.
It has five cameras inside of it and is much bigger than a standard 11-by-17-inch flatbed scanner.
There is a husband and wife team that is cataloging ships plans. AJ Daverede is a retired naval architect, and Heidi is an engineer. He spent 23 years as an archivist at the National Archives. There are tens of thousands of documents to be scanned in the museum's collection, and they are volunteers.
"It is going to be great to get all this stuff online and give people access to it," Heidi said, "to have good quality scans."
Currently they are cataloguing Trumpy yachts that were built between 1910 and 1972. There are ship plans for these stately and sleek yachts.
Some of the drawings are torn or are in bad shape. So the advantage of digitizing is it minimizes handling.
Assistant curator Gabriella Cantelmo said that they look at digitization as a preservation method.
"If they get torn or crumble into dust, which is a possibility, we have them," Cantelmo said.
"It is really important because part of our mission is access to Chesapeake-based culture and history. By digitizing these ship plans and making them available online or at request of researchers, we are furthering that access," Cantelmo said.
She scanned a watercolor of "Wye Island Maryland" by Matthias Bordley, 1781. It showed a long-gone windmill on the island. The resolution is so high, you can look at a tiny portion of the art, and it is clear.
The museum was able to get this machine through a Maryland Heritage Area Authority grant.
"They want to know how we are serving the community. Not only with our collection, which serves the community, but also with this outreach. It is part of our stewardship responsibility and we take it very seriously," said Jen Dolde, director of curatorial affairs and exhibitions.
You can see this work at collections.cbmm.org.

title: Mid-Atlantic Small Craft Festival: A living museum in St. Michaels
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Mid-Atlantic Small Craft Festival: A living museum in St. Michaels

 October 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 574
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — This last weekend the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum was filled with the energetic buzz of dozens of families camping outside with unique watercraft for the 41st annual Mid-Atlantic Small Craft Festival.Sailors and builders from around the region showed off their small craft boats, including sailing, skiffs, rowing shells, kayaks, canoes, paddle boats, prams and one-of-a-kind boats.
Vera England, a longtime attendee, said the event began in 1983, back when the maritime museum had fewer buildings and the well-loved dock was just a beach. She said there were probably 10 to 15 people who attended that first year, and by the second year it had grown significantly.
"It was a living museum. That was our goal," England said. "Small boats were possibly dying out. … We wanted people to get on the water. We wanted children to know what boats were like. The museum was very, very supportive of keeping the tradition of small boats and small boat buildings."
England describes the event as "multigenerational" in its family-friendly approach and encouragement of young children's involvement. According to England, there is no better example of the multigenerational work of the small craft festival than the Blackwell family.
Adam Blackwell began attending the small craft festival when he was in second grade. It soon became a part of his family's tradition. Blackwell said as a child he learned to sail and row with other children (one of whom would later become his wife).
After taking a break from attending due to school, Blackwell came back, met his wife again, got married and has now decided to continue the tradition by bringing his own children to the small craft festival every year.
"It's kind of funny because they're playing with some of the children of the kids that I played with growing up. It's fantastic watching the kids. They're happy. They're running around. They're outside on boats. It's beautiful."
According to England, this festival has created a community of boat lovers. But to keep the community going, people need to invest in events like the small craft festival through not only individual engagement, but also empowering young people to learn traditions, build their own crafts and sail through the Chesapeake Bay.
"Appreciate the water. Appreciate the traditions. Appreciate the fact that these traditions are ephemeral," England said. "If there isn't a place to keep them alive, they will fade and you won't move. And that's very important. That's part of what we try to do, is keep traditions alive, keep the idea of working with your hands to build the small boat."
Blackwell said it is amazing to see the confidence his children have developed through sailing. They're interest began as a shared love learned by their parents and has become something all of their own. They have preferred crafts, have been on the water independently and know when to ask for help. His children's passion reminds him of the pull sailing had on him.
Blackwell said that on his wedding day, his father-in-law read aloud an old log book from the small craft festival when Blackwell and his wife were young. In it were descriptions of his wife and his sister playing outside and enjoying nature.
"(My father-in-law) then goes, 'and the Blackwell boy was out on the water the entire time,'" Blackwell said with a laugh. "And that was my entry in the log book as a child. 'The Blackwell boy was out on the water the entire time. We didn't see him.'"

title: German artist brings powerful pieces to downtown Easton
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
German artist brings powerful pieces to downtown Easton

 October 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 520
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Through visually stunning paintings of zebras made from recycled cans collected in crisis zones to brightly colored paint portraits, Erdman Hummel is able to tell stories about the complexities of war and how to continue moving with hope.The Zebra Gallery hosted Hummel, a German artist and international journalist, last Friday evening. Hummel's paintings will be on display at the gallery through October.
According to Hummel, his path toward being an artist was a challenging one. Hummel, who was born under comunitst rule in East Germany when the Berlin Wall was still up, learned early on the importance of art.
Hummel said in the political context of Berlin, government approval was needed before any artist could practice their craft. At the age of 20, after a few of his artist friends were denied by the government, Hummel secretly opened his own gallery, which was forbidden at the time. Eventually, Hummel had an encounter with the Secret Service in East Germany, and it led to his imprisonment.
While in prison, Hummel read about zebras. To his surprise, zebras, over millennia, have never been domesticated. Hummel said he found inspiration from the animal and used it as a mantra during his time in prison.
"I decided these zebras are a symbol for me," Hummel said.
After spending over a year in prison, Hummel's release was negotiated by the West German government. After the Berlin Wall came down, Hummel decided to devote his life to sharing information and began his career in broadcast journalism. Over the years, Hummel has reported on war zones and crisis areas in Africa, Asia, Afghanistan, Iraq and Gaza.
And now Hummel has come back to art, focusing on the animal that kept his spirit going while he was in prison. His pieces are portraits of brightly colored zebras.
Gail Patterson, owner of the Spiralis Gallery, a separate gallery that occupies the same space as the Zebra Gallery in downtown Easton, said she has a strong appreciation for the uniqueness of the gallery's art, particularly with Hummel's work.
"This is just so unique compared to the waterfowl art and even open air art," Patterson said. "I mean, just everything about it is different for our town… I love (Hummel's) colors and the way there's some camouflaging."
Susan Fay Schauer, owner of the Zebra Gallery, said she was excited to include Hummel in her gallery.
"(Hummel) only paints zebras, and many of them he makes out of aluminum cans that he collects around the world," Schauer said. "He's a German war correspondent, so he collects unusual cans from war zones."
Hummel said he is excited to share his art with the Eastern Shore. According to his biography, the zebras changed the way he viewed his own liberty and the complexities of life.
"Zebras are a symbol of freedom for me," Hummel said. "I translate this freedom into joy of color. As a painter, their stripes give me an opportunity to put complementary colors against one another. Zebras are very individual. No animal is like another. Each has a unique stripe drawing."

title: Folk legend Nash returning to Avalon
author: Tom McCall
content:
Folk legend Nash returning to Avalon

 October 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 527
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A Grammy Award-winning folk legend is coming to Easton in March. He wrote and sang the songs that defined a generation.This is the second time Graham Nash has come to the Avalon Theatre. Within hours, his two-night run on March 29 and 30 was nearly sold out.
The Avalon's 400-seat art deco theater is one of the most intimate places to see him perform. He is playing Wolf Trap and in much bigger markets like San Francisco, Dallas and Nashville.
He calls this this show "Graham Nash — More Evenings of Songs and Stories."
Nash epitomized the creative hotbed of Laurel Canyon, California, and dated Joni Mitchell. Before he was the Nash in the Crosby, Stills and Nash, he played in another vocally rich group called The Hollies. Both groups have been inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
Suzy Moore, house manager and talent buyer at the Avalon, said, "When he was here in 2019 for one night, he was a wonderful and warm performer. When he sang 'Our House' and welcomed everybody to sing along, it was magic. It was my top magic moment in the Avalon Theatre in my 22 years."
She still keeps that moment saved on her phone.
"I have known that song my whole life," Moore said.
Nash's biography on the Avalon's website says, "Legendary artist Graham Nash, as a founding member of both the Hollies and Crosby, Stills and Nash, is a two-time Rock and Roll Hall of Fame inductee. He has seen rock history unfold at some of its seminal moments — from the launch of the British Invasion to the birth of the Laurel Canyon movement a year later. An extraordinary Grammy Award-winning renaissance artist — and self-described 'simple man' — Nash was inducted twice into the Songwriters Hall of Fame, for his work with Crosby, Stills and Nash and his work as a solo artist."
To attract this kind of talent takes some effort.
"It is hard to get him. I have the relationships that makes this possible. This is one of the top agents in the country for venues our size. The artists that the agency represents speak so highly of their experience of the venue, the patrons that come and the town. We are known for providing a really great experience on the stage and while they are here in our community," Moore said.
"These shows are not possible without the support of this community who comes and buys the tickets to make these great experiences happen. It feels good that people are like, 'Yes we want them.'
In over 20 years of booking acts at the Avalon, Moore has seen a lot of talent come and go. She tries to gauge his level.
"At his level? Joan Rivers, Dionne Warwick, Wynton Marsalis, Randy Newman and David Sedaris. These are American icons," she said. "He is a legendary musician and an American icon."
Nash will be joined on stage by Todd Caldwell (keyboards and vocals), Adam Minkoff (bass, drums, guitars, and vocals) and Zach Djanikian (guitars, mandolin, drums, and vocals), performing favorites from across his 60-year career.
Aside from VIP tickets, the house tickets are $125, $100 and $80.
Go to avalonfoundation.org for more information.

title: Recipes for Oktoberfest celebrations
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Recipes for Oktoberfest celebrations

 October 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1103
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Oktoberfest was first held in Munich, Germany in 1810 to celebrate the wedding of Crown Prince Ludwig and Princess Therese of Sansony-Hildburghausse. The original date was Oct. 12, and it lasted for several days.Oktoberfest eventually developed to begin in the middle of September and carry on until the middle of October. The celebration exploded with costumes, all kinds of foods and beverages, dancing, music and parades.
This continual celebration that lasted for weeks was held outside of town in a large spacious meadow. Since 1950, the festival has only started after the official gun salute and the mayor shouting "O' zapft is," which means "it's tapped," and offering the first mug to the Minister-President of the State of Bavaria.
Let us explore some of that delicious food that was piled on several lines of endless tables. One of the most popular traditional recipes is schnitzel.
Schnitzel are thin cutlets and can be made with just about any kind of meat. You can have veal schnitzel most affectionately known as "Wiener schnitzel," pork schnitzel, chicken schnitzel and turkey schnitzel, among many others. The meat is pounded thin with a meat tenderizer, then breaded and fried.
For our next one, a longtime favorite of my family, German Chocolate Cake. German chocolate is not really from Germany. German chocolate is a sweet chocolate invented by a man named Sam German in 1852 for Baker's Chocolate. The moniker stuck, and we still call it German chocolate to this day. If you can't find German chocolate, either milk chocolate or semisweet chocolate will do instead.
WIENER SCHNITZEL4 (5-oz) veal cutlets (or chicken or pork cutlets if you like), 1/4 cup all-purpose flour, 1/2 tsp kosher salt, 2 large eggs (well beaten), 1/2 cup bread crumbs, Oil or lard for frying.
Place veal cutlets between sheets of plastic wrap and use a heavy, flat-surfaced pan, rolling pin or meat mallet to pound the meat evenly to 1/4-inch thickness. To bread the schnitzels, set up 3 shallow dishes: Mix 1/4 cup all-purpose flour and 1/2 tsp kosher salt in the first dish, 2 large beaten eggs in the second dish, and 1/2 cup breadcrumbs in the third dish. In a large skillet, heat at least 1/4-inch of oil to 350 degrees. This takes about 8 minutes, and the oil will just start to shimmer and smoke a bit. Working one at a time, dredge cutlets first in flour until the surface is completely dry. Dip in egg to coat, allow the excess to drip off for a few seconds. Roll quickly in the breadcrumbs until coated. Do not press the breadcrumbs into the meat, as this will moisten them and not make for a crispy coating.
The crust should not adhere completely but form a loose shell around the schnitzel. Immediately place the meat in the pan with the hot oil. Do not crowd the pan. Cook the schnitzel in batches, if necessary. Fry the schnitzel for 2 to 3 minutes on one side, until golden brown. Make sure the breaded meat "swims" in fat. Contrary to instinct, the breading will take on less oil than if the meat is sticking to the pan. Also, the breadcrumb topping has a chance to puff up a little, and your cleanup is easier. You may want to swish them around a little with your fork to make sure they are not sticking to the pan. Turn them over once and fry an additional 2 to 3 minutes or until both sides are golden brown and the meat registers an internal temperature of 145 degrees. Remove from pan and allow the oil to drain off.
PORK CHOPS AND SAURKRAUTThis next recipe is best made in a Dutch oven. 1.5–2 lb boneless pork chops about 1/2 inch thick, 2 tbsps olive oil, 4-6 medium russet potatoes, 1 apple, 18 ounces sauerkraut (undrained), 1 tsp caraway seeds, 1 onion.
Peel and dice the potatoes, apple and onion, Set them aside. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. While the oven preheats, pat the pork chops dry with a paper towel and season very lightly with salt and pepper. Heat a large Dutch oven on the stovetop over medium-high heat. Add the oil. Once the oil is shimmering (about 1 minute), add the pork chops. Brown on each side for about 3 minutes per side. They should easily release once they're ready to be flipped. Set the pork chops aside and add the sauerkraut to the hot dutch oven. With a wooden spoon, gently scrape the bottom to deglaze it. Add the onion, potatoes and apples and then lay the pork chops on top. Sprinkle the caraway seeds. Cover and bake in the oven for one hour. Remove the dutch oven, allow to cool slightly and serve.
GERMAN CHOCOLATE CAKE4 ounces German sweet chocolate (chopped), 1/2 cup water, 1 cup butter (softened), 2 cups sugar, 4 large eggs (separated, room temperature), 1 tsp vanilla extract, 2 1/2 cups cake flour, 1 tsp baking soda, 1/2 tsp salt, 1 cup buttermilk. FROSTING: 1 1/2 cups sugar, 1 1/2 cups evaporated milk, 3/4 cup butter, 5 large egg yolks (room temperature, beaten), 2 cups sweetened shredded coconut, 1 1/2 cups chopped pecans, 1 1/2 tsps vanilla extract. ICING:2 ounces semisweet chocolate, 1 tsp shortening.
Line three greased 9-inch round baking pans with waxed paper. Grease waxed paper and set aside. In a small saucepan, melt chocolate with water over low heat; cool. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. In a large bowl, cream butter and sugar until light and fluffy, 5-7 minutes. Beat in egg yolks, one at a time, beating well after each addition. Blend in melted chocolate and vanilla. Combine flour, baking soda and salt; add to the creamed mixture alternately with buttermilk, beating well after each addition. In a small bowl and with clean beaters, beat the 4 egg whites until stiff peaks form. Fold a fourth of the egg whites into the creamed mixture, fold in remaining whites.
Pour batter into prepared pans. Bake 24-28 minutes or until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean. Cool for 10 minutes before removing from pans to wire racks to cool completely. For the icing, in a small saucepan, heat sugar, milk, butter and egg yolks over medium-low heat until mixture is thickened and golden brown, stirring constantly. Remove from heat. Stir in coconut, pecans and vanilla. Cool until thick enough to spread. Spread a third of the frosting over each cake layer and stack the layers. In a microwave, melt chocolate and shortening; stir until smooth. Drizzle over cake. This is not a cake that requires refrigeration, since the flavors will be best at room temperature.

title: 'Black Panther' author discusses ins and outs of writing
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
'Black Panther' author discusses ins and outs of writing

 October 16, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 657
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Nnedi Okorafor is an award-winning author who has garnered international acclaim for her work on Marvel's "Black Panther" comic book series, but her writing career unexpectedly took off following a life-altering event while in college.Okorafor, who writes African-based science fiction and fantasy novels for children and adults, stopped by Leonardtown High School Oct. 11 to talk about her career. St. Mary's College of Maryland Community Affairs Liaison Kelsey Bush served as moderator.
Building on the work of Stan Lee and Ta-Nehisi Coates — whose "Black Panther" comics were adapted into a blockbuster movie in 2018 — Okorafor authored several issues of "Black Panther — Long Live the King," a continuation of the series and earned Hugo nominee for best novella.
In addition, she authored "Wakanda Forever," which was adapted into a global hit movie, as well as its spin-off, "Shuri."
"I had a problem with Wakanda in general because the concept of it just didn't make any sense to me," she said. But during her early years, the two things that she loved more than anything was track and field, tennis and bugs.
"I loved sports and then bugs," Okorafor said, adding her mom was a Nigerian Olympic javelin thrower while her dad was a nationally known hurdler. "I thought I was going to be an entomologist. I didn't grow up wanting to write at all."
She later excelled at tennis — she said she had a 114 mph serve and she and her sister were "like Venus and Serena before Venus and Serena" — but at the age of 13 was diagnosed with scoliosis.
After playing singles her freshman year at the University of Champagne in Illinois, she was told the disease had compressed her spine and needed surgery. Following the operation, she was paralyzed from the waist down.
"You take an athlete that could do all that and you paralyze them?" she said. "That was my identity."
She sought solace in an Isaac Asimov book and eventually regained feeling in her lower body.
"It was in that moment of pure darkness descending on me that my mind just turned to storytelling," she said. "And as soon as I started doing it, it was like a light switched on and that light pushed all that darkness that was descending on me and went away."
She later took a creative writing class on the advice of a friend, whom she had a crush on, and "it opened up my world."
Okorafor — who moved with her parents to America in 1969 — said the hardest novel she's written was "Death of an Author," which is scheduled to be released in January, though she declined to say why.
She said a close second was "Who Fears Death," which she said she started writing on the night of her father's wake.
"I was very, very close to my father and it's literally autobiographical," she said. "The pain I was going through I just poured it all into that novel and still is the darkest novel I've written."
Marvel contacted her and asked her to write "Spiderman," though she declined.
"It was too much," she said. "I'm not jumping in the deep end when I don't know how to swim. Plus I just can't relate to that [story]. I like to start small. A lot of people would have jumped at that, but for me I like to build my way there and be comfortable and feel natural."
She said working with Marvel was quite stressful.
"The thing about Marvel is that once you agree and say, 'Yeah, I'll do that,' you have days to come up with a summary, which is scary because you have these beloved characters and if you come up with something wrong you'll hear about it in many ways," she said of the three-issue series she authored.
Among Okorafor's other works are the "Binti" trilogy, the "Akata Witch" books — both of which are optioned for the screen — and her latest, "She Who Knows."
To watch the whole interview, go to www.youtube.com/watch?v=MKv-8LS9RC0.

title: Telling stories in 'all caps' — Fresca Frankie creates art from bottle caps
author: LISA J. GOTTO Special to the Kent County News
content:
Telling stories in 'all caps' — Fresca Frankie creates art from bottle caps

 October 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LISA J. GOTTO Special to the Kent County News | Section: News 
 
 1144
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Saturday after Saturday small groups come and gather outside the booth of Fresca Frankie at the Chestertown Farmers' Market because, especially on a sunny day, her colorful and subtly shiny wares catch the light in just the right way that it attracts the eye and draws the marketgoer in for a closer look."Oh, they're bottle caps!" one curious patron said. "That's so cool!"
And that is usually followed up by a lot of "oohs" and "aahs" as they get the opportunity to see what's inside each small circumference of metal— a metal that was saved from the scrap bin at one time or another and now enjoys a second life as a sweet little canvas of Frankie's making. When you consider that the size of that canvas is approximately just one-inch, you become keenly aware that there must be something truly special going on in each one.
Lisa "Frankie" Ford, a Centreville resident, has been gracing the maker's row of the Chestertown Farmers' Market with those eye-catching bottle cap designs for more than a decade now, after spending most of her professional career in health care as an occupational therapist. In that role, she leaned heavily into the part of her personality that enjoys communicating with and helping others, and she said she relished the aspects of the work that enabled her to help patients heal through crafting, which became a vital part of their physical and emotional recovery.
"When I first started there was a lot more emphasis on utilizing crafts as a form of therapy," she said.
She recalled a stroke patient in particular, who really struggled with her fine motor skills.
"The craft was basket weaving," she noted. "And she had a lot of trouble getting the weave [to lay] right, or the material would break off in her hand."
As frustrating as the process was, she said, the patient persevered, eventually completing the project and placing the misshapen vessel on her mantel at home. The patient told Ford her kids would later ask why it was on the mantel when it was less than perfect, and the patient replied, "Because that's my recovery. It represents my recovery. It's the story of it."
Those stories and moments still resonate with Ford. However, there would be less and less of them as the health care industry began to change over the years. There came a point, Ford said, when she realized that she would need to change, as well. With the support and encouragement of her husband, Ford left health care to pursue crafting in various forms.
"My husband told me that he never saw me smile more than when I was at the farmers market," she said, and so her full-throttle adventure into full-time crafting began.
Around that time, she said, someone happened to gift a book of bottle cap art to her.
"I would be the first to tell you that I did not invent this idea," she said. She did, however, improve upon it and lend her own imagination to the task. Working with the caps would prove frustrating at first, she explained, as the glues suggested for the practice did not stand up to real-time wear.
"They were non-toxic and water-soluble; which I thought was a good thing."
And then she said she remembered a little piece of advice that her father had relayed to her often when she was growing up.
"'There's nothing that a good two-part epoxy can't fix.'"
Taking her dad's wisdom to heart she perfected her process of application and the concepts for bottle cap charms came fast and furiously. Each reimagined bottle cap artwork is designed to either be worn on a chain as a necklace or attached to a loop so it can be used as a key chain.
To help her mom present her designs in their best light, Ford said her daughter, Abigail, who was modeling at the time, suggested having the charms professionally styled for a photoshoot.
It is clear when visiting Ford's booth that her daughter had a great idea as this imagery and all the other enhancements that Ford adds to create a unique shopping experience is working. Trays of charms are labeled to convey varying areas of interest and styles, areas like sports, celestial, Maryland-centric, and hobbies. Marketgoers tend to linger and browse longer because there is so much to see; from details that are pinhead-sized to the overall aspect of the experience of shopping there and chatting with Ford, which she said is what she loves most about what she does.
And all that chatter results in a nice return customer base for Ford. In fact, if you're already wearing a Fresca Frankie when you visit the booth, her customer loyalty program kicks in automatically, offering a great discount on any pair from her up-cycled earring line.
In addition to her bottle cap charms, Ford displays her unique earring designs that she creates from recycled vintage jewelry. This aspect of her business has proven to be popular as legions of vintage jewelry lovers who wish to purge their troves, regularly contribute to the cause, so there is no shortage of resource material. And everyone wins because Ford provides discounts off of future purchases to those who donate their costume jewelry.
Rounding out her fashionable offerings are the bright and pretty displays of necklaces and bracelets she makes from soda can beads that she rolls herself by hand. She has a "secret-sauce" process for creating this line of lightweight and stackable accessories, which she admits discovering as a happy accident while trying to solve a design challenge.
Frustrated while trying to make a bracelet from a colorful strip of metal from an Arizona iced tea can, her subconscious fidgety fingers rolled the metal into a cylindrical bead, and eureka, the soda-can bead necklace was born. And you can literally see thousands of these shiny elements in containers catching that sun around her booth, where Ford continues to answer her customers' questions.
"Where do you get your ideas from?"
"Do people save their bottle caps for you?" The quick answer to that one is —"yes!"
And Ford is super grateful to those who do reach out and provide her with resources that would normally just get tossed.
Another customer comes by to take a closer look at a specific design and says, "How clever!" — and then asks about how the charm can be worn. Ford explains about the option to wear it as a necklace and tags her comment with something she explained she often tells a potential customer.
"Get used to people getting a little bit closer to you than they normally would when you're wearing it."
Fresca Frankie's booth will be open at the Chestertown Farmers' Market through the end of the year, and then returning for the spring market. You can check her out at her online Etsy shop and on Facebook. Those interested in donating vintage costume jewelry, can contact her via email at frescafrankie@yahoo.com

title: Mid-Atlantic Symphony Orchestra opens Ensemble Series
author: JOHN MALIN Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Mid-Atlantic Symphony Orchestra opens Ensemble Series

 October 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JOHN MALIN Special to the Star Democrat | Section: News

 A synergistic fusion of the arts occurred on Sunday, Oct. 20, as the Mid-Atlantic Symphony Orchestra launched it's 2024/2025 season Ensemble Series with a woodwind quintet concert at the Academy Art Museum in Easton.The highly accomplished musicians were all members of the orchestra and included Rachael Yokers on flute, Noelle Drews on oboe, Cheryl Hill on clarinet, Karl Shea on bassoon and Beth Lunt on French horn.
The program featured several lesser-known composers, ranging chronologically from the early 19th to the 21st century.
Starting with a very lively and bright piece, "Passacaille" by Adrien Barthe, the program moved through the soft, melodic and haunting "Eyes" by Roma Cafolia to the five joyeus and playful movements of "Quintette en Ut" by Claude Arrieu (actually Louise -Marie Simon), who used a male name so her compositions would beat the gender barriers of the early 1900s.
The concert included five more composers from Japan, France and the United States, and the audience was challenged to identify the five dance rhythms in the "Five Easy Dances" by Denes Agay. These dances were played with a boldness and presence that had plenty of feet tapping.
It was a really delightful and uplifting concert set in the lovely venue of the Academy Arts Museum. The blending of the five instruments was very pleasing, and for me the combination of bassoon and French horn playing counterpoint bass melodies and rhythms was great. The musical skills on show were what we have come to expect from one of our local gems, the MSO.

title: Celebrating Hispanic art and artists with poster contest
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Celebrating Hispanic art and artists with poster contest

 October 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 456
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — From iconic Hispanic icons like Frida Khalo, to colorfully rich portraits of Guatemala landscapes, to a tree with all the Hispanic flags hanging from its branches, the Academy Art Museum was filled with a variety of portraits.In celebration of Hispanic cultural heritage, the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center hosted a poster competition and invited community members to rejoice in the submissions.
Every year, the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center asks the Hispanic community to participate in choosing a theme for the annual celebration. Victoria Gomez Lozano, deputy director for Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center, said the theme for this year is "Ser Hispano, es Ser Valiente," which translates to "Being Hispanic is Being Brave."
The top three posters win prizes, and the first place poster will be used as the official poster for the 2025 Hispanic Heritage Month in Easton.
Roxana Tapia, judge of the competition, said the first, second and third place winners this year came from various ages and ethnicities. But they all had the common goal of celebrating Hispanic heritage.
"You don't even have to be a Latina in order to participate," Tapia said. "What I liked about this year is that we have people from all ethnicities. So if for any kids, I invite them to come over and participate, it's always fun. (Artists) should be proud of their work."
The winners of this year's competition were Piper Hambleton and Ellis Williams for their collaborative work. Their poster portrayed a large tree with flags from every Latin American and Hispanic country attached to its branches.
Alberto Gamez, a judge and ChesMRC board member, called the colorful art piece "The Tree of the Nations."
"I love that it was like a tree of life, but each branch had a different nation, and they covered a lot of them. So I love that it included everybody," Gamez said.
Gamez said he enjoyed all the art submitted this year and the various stories attached to the works, including third place winner Ahias Murillo, whose portrait "I Paint My Own Reality" showed Frida Khalo with an array of Latin American flags behind her. According to Gamez, the piece spoke on the identity and growth of Latinos.
The second place winner Majo Arrivillaga, whose portrait of two faceless individuals was meant to depict the different faces migrants have while traveling to the United States, also included a colorful landscape of Guatemala.
Arrivillaga said she loves drawing because it allows her to show people the beauty within the Latino community and encourages Latino artists of all ages to take the leap and share their work with their community.
"Being Hispanic, for me, is being a person who works, studies and centers their family," Arrivillaga said. "We are multifaceted and we can do it all. That's what makes us brave."

title: Candy corn conflict! The Halloween treat that divides us
author: Anne Jolly Food Drink LIfe
content:
Candy corn conflict! The Halloween treat that divides us

 October 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Anne Jolly Food Drink LIfe | Section: Entertainment 
 
 999
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Love it or hate it, candy corn is a Halloween staple. Some people can't resist candy corn's super-sweet taste, while others think it's too artificial and sugary. Whether you're a fan or a skeptic, there's no denying that this tiny, tri-colored treat has a fascinating history that goes beyond mere snacking.There's a little in-between when it comes to this iconic Halloween candy. The great candy corn debate gets people fired up at parties and sparks social media discussion. It's like the pineapple-on-pizza argument but with candy.
Candy corn's unique texture and flavor make it either a classic favorite or a sugary blunder. But no matter how much discussion it provokes, candy corn is a Halloween symbol that you'll find everywhere, just like pumpkins and costumes.
The sweet debateSo, what's the deal with candy corn's love-it-or-hate-it reputation? It all comes down to the flavor. Candy corn is just a mixture of sugar, corn syrup and honey. It's got a waxy feel and a super-sweet taste.
For some, this combo is a match made in heaven; they love the simple, old-school sweetness, which reminds them of trick-or-treating as kids. As Amanda from Simply Awesome Trips reflects, "I love it — It's the perfect bite of sugar. You can't have fall without candy corn. It's like pumpkin spice or Mariah Carey at Christmas. Love it or hate it, the season hasn't truly arrived without these things."
Others think candy corn is just too much; the sugary flavor seems fake to them. The texture is another point of contention — some find it pleasantly chewy, while others say it is weirdly waxy. "I hate candy corn. It's a sad waste of calories! They're pretty to look at, but they taste like a sugary wax candle," Gena Lazcano, from the blog Ginger Casa, argues.
How you feel about candy corn depends greatly on your childhood memories. If you grew up loving it, you're probably still a fan. But if you never liked it, you won't develop a taste for it as you get older.
Generation gapYour age also affects your candy corn preferences. Older generations tend to view it more favorably, probably due to nostalgia. A survey from the National Confectioners Association (NCA) found that candy corn is most popular with GenXers, with 58% of them enjoying it.
Younger generations are divided; some see it as a retro treat, while others ignore it. The same NCA survey found that only 46% of Millennials enjoy candy corn, showing that the popularity of candy is gradually decreasing.
Candy corn through the yearsCandy corn has been around for over a hundred years, starting in the 1880s in Philadelphia. At first, it was called chicken feed because the pieces looked like corn kernels. The candy was marketed to farmers as a special treat with a farm theme.
Candy corn's connection to Halloween happened gradually. As trick-or-treating became popular in the 1950s, candy corn was a common choice for Halloween handouts. Its orange, yellow and white colors perfectly fit the season's theme. Plus, it was affordable and easy to distribute.
Today, it's hard to imagine Halloween without candy corn, but its popularity has been slowly fading. While Halloween candy sales continue to grow, candy corn sales are slowing, a recent CNN report indicates. Sales of other non-chocolate candies like gummies and marshmallows are taking some of candy corn's market share.
Cultural impactCandy corn's influence goes beyond the candy bowl. It is featured in Halloween decorations, costumes and social media posts. Its distinctive three-color design has become a symbol of fall and the Halloween season.
Food manufacturers have created candy corn-inspired products like ice cream, popcorn, coffee creamers and candy corn cookies. Craft breweries even make candy corn-flavored beers. Love it or hate it, candy corn has cemented its place in American pop culture.
You will also see candy corn used to decorate homes. From the blog Get On My Plate, Casey Rooney has found decorating is the solution to her dislike of candy corn, explaining, "I used to hate candy corn, but my daughters love it. They started filling glass jars with it and putting them around the house. It looked so pretty and festive for fall. Instead of eating it, now I just use it as part of my fall decor!"
Seeing candy corn in Halloween decorations and at parties adds a nostalgic element that brings back all sorts of memories. It's a warm and fuzzy feeling reminiscent of happy childhood times.
Alternatives and variationsThere are creative alternatives if you want to incorporate candy corn into your Halloween celebrations but aren't a huge fan of the taste. Combine candy corn with other ingredients, or try recipes that feature the iconic candy corn look without the overwhelmingly sweet flavor.
Mixing candy corn with peanuts is very popular. The salty flavor of the peanuts goes perfectly with the sugary taste of the candy corn, and the mix of crunchy and chewy textures makes it extra satisfying to eat.
You can also create treats that capture the spirit of candy corn without the flavor. A simple idea is to make a candy corn-inspired parfait. Layer some mango, mandarin oranges and yogurt in a clear glass jar for a snack that looks like candy corn but tastes fresh and fruity.
Or make candy corn fudge. White chocolate and food coloring can create those signature yellow, orange and white stripes in a treat that tastes like chocolate, not candy corn. Add some food coloring to your favorite Rice Krispie treat recipe, and you've got a snack that looks like it came from the candy store.
Halloween classicPeople might argue about how candy corn tastes or feels in your mouth, but one thing is certain — it's a big part of American Halloween traditions. Its one-of-a-kind look and connection to Halloween make it a favorite symbol of the season, even if you don't like eating it. It'll keep sparking smiles, starting conversations and maybe even causing a few arguments for many Halloweens to come.
Anne Jolly is the creator of the food blog Upstate Ramblings. She loves cooking but doesn't love candy corn.

title: A Talbot County actress invited Sonia Sotomayor to her show. Sotomayor came
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
A Talbot County actress invited Sonia Sotomayor to her show. Sotomayor came

 October 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 568
 Words

 GLEN ECHO — In 1974, Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor, then a Princeton student, wrote a letter of complaint to her university to call attention to the low Latino student numbers, the absence of Latino administrators and faculty members, and the lack of any courses dealing with Latino culture.That letter pushed the increase in Latino enrollment in Princeton University and was a critical moment in Sotomayor's life. This event is featured in the musical "She Persisted," a show centered on history's most famous women and how modern girls can take inspiration from their stories.
The musical is showing at Adventure Theatre in Glen Echo, Maryland. Victoria Gomez, a Talbot County resident, plays Sotomayor in the show.
Inspired by her character, Gomez decided to take a lesson from Sotomayor and wrote a letter to the justice.
"I admire your work and perseverance you have that led you to becoming the first Latina on the Supreme Court," Gomez wrote in her letter. "You are a role model for many people but especially for aspiring Latinas who dream big, like myself."
In the letter, Gomez shared her story of coming to the United States with her mother as a child. She wrote how honored she was to play Sotomayor in the musical.
Because of that letter, Sotomayor and her family sat in the front row of the Adventure Theatre Sunday.
Gomez said she is honored to be casted in this empowering musical. For Gomez, her passion for the theater began when she was a student at St. Michaels Elementary School when her class went on a field trip to see a musical.
For Gomez, the theater has opened a new world to explore and grow in. She has learned to advocate for herself and has developed a strong sense of her identity.
While on stage, Gomez jumped and sang with immense enthusiasm as she played a curious young Sotomayor in the Bronx with dreams of being a detective. Then later, as she played a college-aged Sotomayor, she comprised the emotional uncertainty of a young woman who sought to make change for her community.
Gomez said while studying for this role, she learned Sotomayor's strong connection to the women in her family. Like Sotomayor, Gomez was encouraged by her mother and grandmother, who taught her to be "proudly Latina" and to help those in her community.
"(Sotomayor's) mom was always someone who helped everyone in the community, which is something that I immediately related to in terms of my mom," Gomez said. "...She's already helping everyone, but even outside of that, she is such a wonderful role model for me to have. And I just really connected with (Sotomayor) in the way that she saw her mom as such an impactful role model."
"She Persisted," based on the children's book by Chelsea Clinton, follows the journey of Naomi, a fourth-grade girl struggling with perfectionism.
Play director Mary Hall Surface, said her hope for the play was to celebrate not only the historical figures and their stories but to really highlight the central character and her struggles.
"I think that is a pervasive feeling of young women and young boys as well, and not to mention grown women, all of us really, as we struggle to sort of measure ourselves against other people and find our own strengths and power and purpose," Hall Surface said.
After the final song of the play, Gomez's mother and Sotomayor, rose to their feet and gave her a standing ovation.

title: Megalodon teeth exhibit comes to Maryland museum
author: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com
content:
Megalodon teeth exhibit comes to Maryland museum

 October 31, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com | Section: Entertainment 
 
 637
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Calvert Marine Museum this month unveiled a new exhibit featuring a never-before-seen set of teeth from an extinct megatooth shark known as megalodon.The 53 teeth from one individual shark believed to be over 50 feet in length were collected over a period of six years from one location along Calvert Cliffs, according to a release from the Calvert Marine Museum.
The new exhibit, titled "Out of the Vault," opened Nov. 1 in the museum's Mezzanine Gallery and features rare and scientifically significant fossils that reveal a unique glimpse into the prehistoric past of the Chesapeake Bay region.
The extinct shark megalodon (aka Otudus megalodon) continues to be a source of endless popular and scientific fascination. This insatiable interest certainly comes from the large size of its serrated teeth and macro-predatory habits.
Megalodon was one of the largest predators ever, thought to have obtained a body length of up to 65 feet.
Doubtless, megalodon dominated the marine ecosystem for nearly 20 million years prior to extinction about 3.6 million years ago. Remarkably, though, what is mostly known about megalodon has come from studying its many fossilized teeth and few vertibrae.
Many tens of thousands of megalodon teeth have been found around the world, the vast majority having been preserved and found in isolation. However, but exceedingly rare, an individual megalodon died and many of its teeth were preserved together in association. Worldwide, there are fewer than a dozen associated partial detentions of megalodon known.
The marine museum in Solomons recently announced a newly associated set of megaloon teeth found along Calvert Cliffs on the Chesapeake Bay. This set includes 53 teeth from a wide range of tooth positions in the giant shark's mouth, from large front teeth measuring 5½ inches long to remarkably small black teeth only just over ½ inch in length.
This is the first associated set of teeth of megalodon to have ever been found along the fossil-famous Calvert Cliffs.
The megalodon teeth were found by both professional and avocational paleontologists including John R. Nance, who initially discovered the stash of teeth, Victor J. Perez, Robert "Bob" Hazen and Margee Hazen, Stephen Groff, Brian Bartron, William "Bill" Counterman, Marcus Jones, Daryl Serafin and Steven Victor. Matt Blomgren and Cindy Eckerd allowed the museum to cast their finds, while many other individuals helped scour that beach over several years.
Several other collectors have found teeth from this shark, and those remain in private collections.
"During the winter of 2015-2016, we heard a rumor of someone who found a bucket of megalodon teeth from this same location, and probably from the same shark. He has become affectionately known as 'Bucket Guy,'" according to the marine museum, which is hoping to contact the person.
Note that the teeth on display were not found at Calvert Cliffs State Park and trespassing through private communities to get to the cliffs is not permitted. Digging in the cliffs is dangerous and is prohibited on all state and federal lands.
On private land, permission must be granted from the owner(s) before digging. If you see a skull, bone or unusual fossil in the cliffs you can report it to the Calvert Marine Museum paleontology department at 410-326-2042. The museum cannot confiscate fossil finds like megalodon teeth.
if you goThe Calvert Marine Museum is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Admission if $11 for adults, $9 for seniors, veterans, AAA and AARP members; $6 for children ages 5-12; children under 5 and museum members are admitted free.
Highlights of the new exhibit "Out of the Vault" include: fossilized shrimp burrows, teeth from an ancestor of the modern great white shark, skull remains of extinct dolphins, parts of a giant leatherback turtle shell, miocene elephant teeth, fossils of miocene hermit crabs and the associated set of teeth from the megalodon.
For more information about the museum, upcoming events, or membership, visit www.calvertmarinemuseum.com or call 410-326-2042.

title: The animal in our midst at the library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
The animal in our midst at the library

 November 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Columns 
 
 744
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Recently, I read an article about a poultry processing plant on Virginia's Eastern Shore that employed underage immigrants to work overnight shifts servicing machines that rapidly decapitated, declawed and disemboweled chickens.Not surprisingly, all the spinning blades and belts occasionally maimed one of the youngsters, who, because they were miles from home and parents in a strange country whose language they did not understand, had to suffer in silence or risk losing their sole source of income.
The essay reminded me of Upton Sinclair's "The Jungle," which described how, in the early 20th century, Eastern European immigrants were similarly harnessed to Chicago's newly-industrialized slaughterhouses.
Thinking about what Charles Dickens did for people incarcerated in debtors' prisons and John Steinbeck did for seasonal agricultural workers, I wondered why there wasn't a modern equivalent to Sinclair out there who could write a book like "The Jungle" to awaken us to the conditions under which some people in the United State must live and labor even today.
But, then again, maybe it's me. Has television's nightly catastrophe parade so inured me to human suffering that I can't see the forest for the trees? Are such works being written and I've just failed to recognize what their authors are trying to accomplish?
Julia Phillips' new novel "Bear" tells the story of two sisters, Elena and Sam. For years now the women have been caring for their mother, who is slowly dying from an unnamed chronic illness. The family lives on the remote island of San Juan, off the coast of Washington State, in a poorly-insulated, dilapidated house that is on the verge of collapsing under the weight of its years.
Elena is employed as a waitress in the local country club, while Sam works long shifts behind a concession stand in the ferry that moves wealthy tourists to and from the island. During the pandemic, the ferry ceased operations, and their mother's medical bills sunk the sisters deep in debt.
Written in the third-person, "Bear" is told from Sam's point of view. She hates her work, hates the contempt with which the wealthy tourists treat her, hates her bondage to a life with few pleasures other than the love she feels for her sister and mother.
But Sam has a dream. When eventually, inevitably, their mother passes away, Sam and her sister will be free to sell their home (and the valuable real estate it sits upon), which means they'll be able to move to a warmer clime and begin living the sort of life she imagines the tourists she waits upon live.
Then one night, as she is taking a break out on the ferry's upper deck, Sam sees something remarkable in the oily blackness of the water beneath her. It's a bear, swimming alongside the boat, making for the shore of their island.
As it happens, the bear takes up residence in the forest that surrounds the two sisters' home. Elena, who is the older of the two and has borne the brunt of bill-paying, housekeeping and caregiving — Elena who arrives home from work each day exhausted and stinking of griddle grease and fried onions — sees the bear as a sort of other-worldly figure, one that has brought into their threadbare existence a hint of magic and even enchantment.
While the hardship of Elena's life moves her to try to befriend the bear, the hardship of Sam's makes her see the beast as a threat to her dreams. What if her beloved sister strays too close to the thing, what if it kills her, if it takes from Sam the one person she loves besides the mother she knows she will soon lose?
The tension between these two divergent views and the wild animal that instigates that tension creates a narrative force at once both troubling and seductive. We want everything to work out for the sisters. We don't see how everything possibly can.
It is this dilemma that drives "Bear" and made me think that, in a subtle way, a way somehow appropriate for our time, Phillips has written a modern equivalent to Dickens' "Little Dorrit," Steinbeck's "Grapes of Wrath," and Sinclair's "The Jungle." For it is the crushing, inescapable reality of Sam and Elena's poverty that puts them at loggerheads, that drives them toward the bear — one armed only with love, the other with a gun.
You can find Phillips' "Bear" (as well as Dickens, Steinbeck, and Sinclair) at the place we visit to try to reconcile such irreconcilables: the Talbot County Free Library.

title: Tilghman Island Day celebrates maritime Maryland
author: TIMOTHY LLOYD TILGHMAN
content:
Tilghman Island Day celebrates maritime Maryland

 November 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: TIMOTHY LLOYD TILGHMAN | Section: News 
 
 596
 Words 

 Read News Document

 My recommendation is to drop anchor during the next Tilghman Island Day in October 2025. The Chesapeake Bay and Choptank River are the waterways that initially attracted settlers to the region seeking to establish themselves on the waterfront, participate in a marine trade and raise a familyTilghman Island Day is a unique maritime festival sponsored annually by the Tilghman Island Volunteer Fire Company. Tourists enjoyed a unique opportunity to experience the ambiance of maritime Maryland when skipjacks ruled the Chesapeake Bay. Small businesses, historic residences, a maritime museum, an elementary school, a post office and Dogwood Harbor coalesce to validate the hometown charm of Tilghman Island.
Saturday, Oct. 19, highlighted perfect sailing weather under sunny skies for visitors to walkabout the Tilghman Island neighborhood.
Tilghman Island Day celebrates Maryland's Eastern Shore watermen and their livelihood. Tilghman Island embodies the ongoing traditions of a nautical industry that thrives on Maryland's Eastern Shore.
Married couples, young families, groups of friends and single parties turned out in numbers to spend their afternoon enjoying all that Tilghman Island Day has to offer. The Tilghman Country Store provided a special menu in addition to real Maryland crabs. Besides seafood, there was a barbecue pit available in the rear of the park and a fresh squeezed lemonade stand.
Tourism, marinas, agriculture, crabbing and oyster harvesting exemplify the broader activities of Maryland's watermen community. Seafood dining and hospitality are major attractions. Tilghman Island is the picture-perfect weekend getaway destination. No hustle, no bustle, just appreciate the easy-going atmosphere of the close nit village. A splendid time was guaranteed for all.
Seth Foster was granted the island in 1659. Tilghman Island was recognized by Talbot County as Great Choptank Island in 1707. Other names included Foster's Island and Ward's Island before Matthew Tilghman obtained the island in 1741. Early industry on Tilghman Island showcased steamboat service and seafood harvesting employing watermen and establishing a vibrant maritime community.
The Chesapeake Bay was a hotbed of activity during the War of 1812. The British fleet was busy raiding and occupying colonial communities along the shorelines of the Eastern Shore. Tilghman Island itself was subjected to British military interference during 1813 and 1814. The Red Coats had erected a barracks on the island that was later abandoned. Bennett's Point 1813, Caulk's Field 1814 and James Island 1815 each experienced hotspots of engagement.
Later in the 1800s, Gen. Tench Tilghman purchased lands beyond the busy drawbridge that constitutes the locality representing the businesses and residences that signify Tilghman, Maryland. A distinguishing house construction known as the "W" is now a scarce structure on the island. Employment opportunities welcomed relocation to Tilghman Island following the Civil War.
My father drove me and my sister to attend the 1988 Tilghman Island Day celebration. I have returned to sightsee at Tilghman Island, St. Michaels and Oxford infrequently over the years. Specifically, I collect round iron postal cancellations from these post offices occasionally. I bought a couple of Tilghman Island postcards that now promote the date of 1752.
President Ronald Wilson Reagan visited the Tilghman Island Volunteer Fire House during a tour of Maryland's Eastern Shore on July 10, 1984. Residents speak fondly of the presidential visit and are happy to share their personal memories four decades later. Capt. Wade Murphy recalls three helicopters flew onto the island to obfuscate his arrival. Fifty local watermen attended the luncheon.
Consider visiting the village in August as bountiful monarch butterflies descend upon the island before migrating to Mexico. Several restaurants offer top-quality seafood and there are numerous choices to reserve a good night's rest. Tilghman Island scenery offers visiting guests an idyllic vacation.

title: Dia de los Muertos celebration embraces traditions of growing Latino population
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Dia de los Muertos celebration embraces traditions of growing Latino population

 November 2, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 607
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Community members and organizations are finding ways to celebrate and immerse in the different cultural events and traditions brought to the Eastern Shore by the growing Latino population.Dia de los Muertos, a vibrant two-day holiday from Latin America, celebrates and honors departed loved ones. In collaboration with Samantha Martinez and the Talbot County Free Library, the Academy Art Museum hosted a celebration beginning Thursday and ending Saturday evening to embrace the holiday's traditions and bring them to a new audience.
Martinez said she was honoring her two grandmothers in the ofrenda displayed during an intimate event on Friday evening. Ofrendas are home altars created by the family members or loved ones of a person who has died. They are intended to welcome the deceased to the altar setting.
"To me, it is an extension of honoring their life," Martinez said. "So me being able to honor them and celebrate them and bring all their favorite things, is a way for my relationship to continue, even though it's not physical and tangible here on this earth."
It is part of the holiday to display favorite foods and items of the deceased on the ofrendas. Martinez said she brought her grandmother's favorite flowers, Carmex lip balm, nail polish, conchas (Mexican sweet bread) and a bible.
According to Martinez, Indigenous people of Latin America believed that upon death, the individual's soul did not die and continued to live in Mictlan, a place of rest. In time, this pre-Hispanic celebration merged with the Catholic celebration of All Souls Day and has evolved into the present Dia de los Muertos celebration.
On Friday night at the Academy Art Museum, people gathered around marigold flowers and shared traditional pan de muerto (bread of the dead) as they honored loved ones whose photos decorated the ofrendas.
Martinez and several others shared the stories and joys of their loved ones and took time to celebrate the lives they lived.
The night before, the Talbot County Free Library hosted a create-your-own mini altar to contribute to a larger community-wide altar located at the Academy Art Museum on Friday and Saturday.
The ofrendas will be available for the public to view on Saturday evening. Community members of the Eastern Shore are invited to celebrate the holiday and enjoy traditional music and dance performances.
Jennifer Chrzanowski, interim director of the Academy Art Museum, said the museum has been working on outreach to the Latino Community on the Shore through events like Dia de los Muertos as well as initiatives to have translated exhibitions for the Spanish speaking community.
This particular event was done through an initiative where the museum invites community members to create unique and interesting programs for better community building. Martinez collaborated and led the creation of the event as a way to extend community outreach.
"It's important that there are no barriers for people to come in and be a part of this community," Chrzanowski said. "So we just feel this is an extension of making this museum more inclusive, more welcoming for anybody."
Martinez said she would love to expand the event to a parade one day, with face painting, music and catrinas (paper mache female skeleton). Martinez encourages the community to join in celebration and learn more about Dia de los Muertos.
"To be open to see how other people celebrate and honor their ancestors, and to think outside of the box when we think about grief or when we think about death," Martinez said. "This is a way to make it more intimate and make it less scary for people and less finite, but to (also) celebrate in a way that honors our ancestors and the reason why we are here today."

title: 53rd Waterfowl Festival set to begin Thursday
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
53rd Waterfowl Festival set to begin Thursday

 November 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 1641
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Thousands will pack the streets of downtown Easton this weekend for the 53rd annual Waterfowl Festival, the town's much-anticipated yearly tradition.On Thursday, it kicks off with opening ceremonies at the Tidewater Inn on Dover Street. Then on Friday, Saturday and Sunday, festivalgoers can enjoy all that Waterfowl has to offer.
Festival Director Deena Kilmon says, "there's something for everybody," whether it's hunting and outdoors enthusiasts, food lovers, history buffs, families or Eastern Shore natives.
"We try with the festival to tell the story of the Eastern Shore and to showcase how it is to live here, essentially," Kilmon said. "It's all about us."
Kilmon said this year's expected attendance may be "more than ever," noting that ticket sales for Thursday's opening ceremonies and premiere night are higher than in years past.
"We have had record VIP ticket sales," Kilmon said. "We're well into the 700-attendee mark at this point. So we know if that's any indication of the general admission, then yeah, it's going to be the biggest year ever."
A number of expanded offerings and additions make this year's festival unique, Kilmon said.
This year's festival will include an enhanced focus on children's activities. Kilmon said a new "Quackin' Trail" will help kids find activities to do all over the festival instead of just being concentrated in one area. Admission for kids 10 and under is free with a paid adult present.
The PNC Art Pavilion — located at 40 S. Harrison St. — will be "about double in size" compared to last year, Kilmon said. Featured at the pavilion will be the festival's featured artist, Texas-based Ronnie Wells, with sculptures and paintings.
"He is a revered artist. He's got sculptures in pretty much every major city in the United States," Kilmon said. "It's worth it just to come see some of these guys and see their beautiful art, even if you can't afford to buy it."
The Avalon Theatre will be home to the Duck Blind Bar, along with the festival's new brew, "In Flight." The Waterfowl-licensed beer will be available while it lasts, along with other seasonal beers and cocktails.
At Easton VFW Post 5118, the Chesapeake Bay Pavilion will host live music all three days, raptor demonstrations and expanded shopping opportunities.
Festivalgoers can expect to see new Waterfowl merchandise and an expanded bus line, according to Kilmon. She added that attendees are asked to park at Easton Elementary School, Easton Middle School, Easton High School or the Easton Elks Lodge.
In her first year as the festival director, Kilmon was emotional when asked about her favorite part of the Waterfowl Festival.
"For me, it is absolutely just seeing Easton shine," Kilmon said. "It's almost emotional. It is emotional, I guess. It's where Easton comes together and we just showcase the beautiful community that we are. We see our families, we see our friends, and we celebrate going into the fall and the winter season together, and it's just a wonderful experience."

title: Adkins Arboretum hosts plein air painters
author: Tom McCall
content:
Adkins Arboretum hosts plein air painters

 November 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Arts 
 
 417
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGELY — The smell of linseed oil wafted into the forest as over 50 artists competed in Plein Air Adkins at the Adkins Arboretum on Saturday. There was food and drink, nature and art all combining to create a perfect fall day."We had almost 250 attendees and 55 artists," said Ginna Tiernan, executive director of Adkins Arboretum.
There was lots of food and drink.
"Ten Eyck provided mimosas and bloody Marys, and Craft Bakery and Night Kitchen provided great food and drinks including pastries and lunch items," Tiernan said. "Diane Mullaly got us started and is our advisor on this event, and she won first prize," she said.
Mullaly learned a lot about running a Plein Air quick contest from her time at the Plein Air Easton.
"I brought Ginna the idea about four years ago about creating an event like this. I created sort of a slower version of the quick draw. The painters started at 10 and ended at 12:30. A half hour longer than Plein Air Easton. Quite a few sold," Mullaly said.
For Mullaly the passion goes deeper than her creativity.
"I am deeply involved with the arboretum. I am a Maryland master naturalist and a trained docent there. I am there a lot and I just adore that place. I always feel so good when I am there. It is very healing and relaxing. Being able to paint there in that beautiful environment is such a treat," Mullaly said.
Beth Bathe was the judge and was generous with her time with all artists.
Bathe said, "Judging the works of over 50 artists this past Saturday at Adkins Aboretum was a true honor as each painting vividly showcased the rich colors and textures of the autumn season. Live music, wonderful food and drink and beautiful artwork all for sale made a great day for the artists and the community."
There were collectors who have also attended the Plein Air Easton event. They came to see and purchase more great art.
The winners were Mullaly, second place winner Abby Ober and third place winner Maryellyn Lynott.
There were honorable mentions too. These included Lori Yates, Lynn Lewis, Ronaldo Dorado, Stephen Walker and Sheryl Southwick.
There was a tie for Artist's Choice — Nancy Fine and Toni Wolf.
Event Sponsors included Caroline County Council for the Arts, Maryland State Arts Council, Enel and Unity Landscape Design/Build. Live music was provided by Fine Times.
Although the Arboretum got a 20% commission of any art that sold, the main benefit was attracting lots of people to spend time in nature.

title: Marigold Market: a community for upcoming artists on the Shore
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Marigold Market: a community for upcoming artists on the Shore

 November 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 364
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Marigold Market, a community vendor event, made its big debut Saturday at the Talbot County Historical Gardens. The event featured over 25 local artists, live music and family-friendly activities.The Marigold Market, named for its fall theme and coinciding with Dia de los Muertos, aimed to support emerging artists and create community.
Helen Fegan, a jewelry artist and co-organizer of the market, said the idea for the Marigold Market began in April when she reached out to her friend Natalie Calloway, a local artist, asking if she would be interested in putting the event together.
"We wanted it to be something that was a really open-space and people could feel comfortable, whether they have done this 100 times or whether they have never done one, and that was the case for a lot of our artists," Fegan said.
Fegan began making jewelry a couple of years ago and was in a place where she was ready to sell her jewelry at a market. When she began to look for a market to sell at, she noticed a few roadblocks for new vendors, including booth fees and a lack of confidence in selling their work.
Fegan and Calloway sought to change these roadblocks and provide an opportunity for new artists like themselves to encourage each other and find support on the Shore.
Calloway is a ceramic artist and is fairly new to the art community. When Fegan pitched the idea of creating their own market she was thrilled with the idea, and on Saturday morning she was stunned by the immediate community support but most of all happy with the growing confidence she saw with all the new artists selling their work.
"We wanted to start something that is for new, upcoming artists who haven't really been a part of much recently because they're still in the shadows and nervous," Calloway said. "So we wanted a welcoming community for them."
Fegan said she hopes to hold another market in the spring and plans to grow the event into a community for artists around the Shore.
"We're just so stunned and happy with the community support and the feedback," Fegan said. "It was really great to know that everyone loved it."
