title: King Arthur comes to life at Chesapeake Culinary Center
author: Tom McCall
content:
King Arthur comes to life at Chesapeake Culinary Center

 November 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 374
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Legend and actors combined with swords, griffins and maidens at "the Legend of King Arthur and His Knights" literary evening on Saturday Nov. 2.Thespians in medieval garb stood behind 12 lecterns and read from historical texts like "Once And Future King." It was pure storytelling in a reader's theater format.
About 30 guests had the stories read to them and then dined on a period meal provided by the Chesapeake Culinary Center.
Caroline County Council of Arts and Caroline County Public Library presented the show.
The source materials were collected from hundreds of years of writing from people like John Steinbeck, Lord Alfred Tennyson and J.R.R. Tolkien.
Sir Thomas Malory is the principle purveyor of the the Arthurian story, and he wrote from a prison cel, director and writer Keith L. Shaffer said. The holy grail, the round table, Merlin and the sword in the stone have captivated people for centuries.
"It is really the legend of King Arthur from the beginning where he pulls the sword from the stone, to his marriage to Gwynevere, to the final battle and even after the final battle. It is readers theater, so it is all reading the script and gesturing and facial expressions," Shaffer said of Saturday's event.
The community outreach extended into the North Caroline High School art students, who painted banners that went for silent auction.
Debby Bennett is the chair of the literary committee.
"We started meeting in the summer. Keith is our director but he is also the script writer. Kendall (Teague) organized the silent auction. We will continue the silent auction for a couple of weeks at the Foundry. We have a lot of talent in this county," Bennett said.
She said this is the first time that they have not picked an author for their literary event. They chose a character that several people had written about.
"Keith has read a lot of authors about Arthur. It is a project of love. It has got the arts. It has got literature It is about books and reading, and community," Bennett said.
There were sponsors sitting in the audience.
"The arts is always something we want to support, because we believe it teaches people how to think and how to put themselves in someone else's shoes," sponsor Michelle Christopher said.

title: Museum to host building bricks lighthouse challenge
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Museum to host building bricks lighthouse challenge

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: Entertainment 
 
 388
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Friends of St. Clement's Island & Piney Point Museums, the nonprofit organization that supports the St. Mary's County Museum Division, recently announced an exciting competition in honor of the oldest lighthouse on the Potomac River."To really celebrate Piney Point Lighthouse during the holidays, we thought this competition would be a fantastic way to get families and the community involved," St. Mary's County Museum Division manager Karen Stone said in a release. "What's even more fun is that everyone will be able to see their creations on display at the museum."
Participants will create a lighthouse model using interlocking building bricks and bring it to the Piney Point Lighthouse Museum for display and judging.
The rules are as follows:
All entries must be made with interlocking building blocks in any variety or brand
The final size for entries must be no bigger than 12-inches wide by 12-inches deep by 24-inches high
Entries must be placed on a sturdy base, such as plywood, foam core or heavy cardboard. The base should be able to support the weight of the entry without bending
No pre-assembled or lighthouse kits may be entered. The entry must be constructed as a completely unique creation; and
No electronics or other materials are allowed. All components must be interlocking building blocks.
The challenge has two age group categories: ages 12 and under and ages 13 and up.
Models should be brought to the Piney Point Lighthouse and Museum's main building at 44720 Lighthouse Road Piney Point between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. Nov. 25-30 (closed Thanksgiving Day).
Winners will be selected by popular vote. Individuals who attend the Evening Tides event, Holiday Open House at Piney Point or visit the museum during December — the museum is closed Christmas Eve and Christmas Day — will receive a ballot.
Regular museum admission applies.
Additional tickets may be purchased at the museum store at five tickets for $1, with proceeds going toward the museum.
Winners will be notified Jan. 2, 2025. The overall winner in each age group will receive a $25 Amazon gift card and bragging rights.
Models will be on display throughout December for voting, and can be picked up between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. from Jan. 2-12, 2025.
Registration is free. For more information or to register, contact 301-475-4200 ext. 1832, or janet.cooper@stmaryscountymd, or go to www.facebook.com/events/1418049026250622.

title: Mayor Megan Cook brings down duck gavel, officially opening 53rd Waterfowl Festival
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Mayor Megan Cook brings down duck gavel, officially opening 53rd Waterfowl Festival

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 324
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The 53rd annual Waterfowl Festival officially began Thursday evening at the Tidewater Inn, where Megan Cook, mayor of Easton, was welcomed onstage to officially open the festival with the banging of the duck gavel.This three-day festival welcomes thousands of waterfowl enthusiasts to Talbot County each year to appreciate local wildlife, art, heritage, food and community.
Throughout the Thursday evening ceremony, citations were given to organizers of the festival, longtime volunteers were honored for their service and a featured artist unveiled new work.
The ceremony began with opening remarks by Eric Milhollan, president of the executive board for the Waterfowl Festival. He welcomed all attendees, recognizing them for joining the festival and supporting conservation efforts.
In his speech, Milhollan shared his long history with the festival. Beginning with volunteering with his father and later becoming involved with his own family as an adult, Milhollan shared his pride for the countless families who have long-standing traditions of volunteering for the festival.
"I'm proud to have my oldest son cheering for the second year. He's joined by his two brothers and sister, all coming home from college to help for the weekend at the festival that's been part of my life and my family's life," Milhollan said. "I believe in the crowd and see that many who have similar stories in passing the tradition of the festival to their families. This is what allows us to celebrate 53 years."
Throughout the evening, several people were honored, including a memoriam for Kim Perry Whiteley and Hall of Fame presentations for Blenda Armistead, Ron Flohr and Butch Townsend. A waterfowl statue was unveiled by this year's Waterfowl Festival Featured Artist Ronnie Wells.
As Cook held the opening gavel in her hand, she looked to the leaders of the Waterfowl Festival, and they all smiled.
"Are we ready? All right, we're ready. Let's go," Cook said before banging the duck-shaped gavel against the podium and officially opening the Waterfowl Festival's 53rd year of celebration.

title: KCA donates to instruments to school music program
author: Staff Writer
content:
KCA donates to instruments to school music program

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 426
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The music department at Kent County High School received a donation last month for new instruments.John Schratwieser, executive director of Kent Cultural Alliance, announced a $10,000 donation to the music program at a Kent County Board of Education meeting Monday, Oct. 14.
The money will be used to purchase instruments including saxophones and a performance piano for the Tom McHugh Black Box Theater at Kent County High School. Remaining funds will be used for instrument maintenance and parts.
Schratwieser said he was "standing on the shoulders" of Leslie Prince Raimond and the late Tom McHugh who, through the Kent County Arts Council, began supporting the arts in Kent County Public Schools decades ago.
"We're happy to continue that tradition," Schratwieser told the Board of Education members. "We know that you do the best that you are able to do with the resources that you have. We are happy to build upon that."
Raimond was the longtime director of the Kent County Arts Council, which is now the Kent Cultural Alliance. McHugh founded the Mainstay music venue in Rock Hall after retiring from a teaching career that included Vassar College in New York.
The Kent Cultural Alliance has contributed $25,000 to the schools' music program over the last two years, including funding from the Robert F. Schumann Foundation, a family foundation named for the father of local musician and environmentalist Ford Schumann. Additional support came from the Shared Earth Foundation, led by Caroline Gabel.
The Kent Cultural Alliance has also donated about $10,000 to the school system's visual arts programs over the last five years as well, including funding for two new kilns, digital drawing devices, field trips and more.
"Know that Kent Cultural Alliance will always be there to advocate for the Kent County Public Schools," Schratwiser said. "Because we believe in the power of arts education."
Mary Boswell-McComas, superintendent of Kent County Public Schools, thanked the Kent Cultural Alliance for its continued support of the arts programs, saying she is deeply grateful.
She said that the county's small student enrollment creates budget challenges.
"It's a testament that as a community, we refuse to allow fine arts to be marginalized," McComas said. "And we could not continue to offer the programming and resources that we do without our partnerships."
Gina Jachimowicz, director of teaching and learning for Kent County Public Schools, agreed.
"Without the generous support of our community, we would not be privy to the amazing advantages that our students have seen and the generous donation that the Kent Cultural Alliance has provided," Jachimowicz said.
Discover more about Kent County Public Schools and its programs at www.kent.k12.md.us.

title: The story behind this year's Waterfowl Festival poster and artist
author: Tom McCall
content:
The story behind this year's Waterfowl Festival poster and artist

 November 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 566
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Ronnie Wells has been coming to the Waterfowl Festival for 28 years. But this year is a little different — he has been chosen as the featured poster artist.When this Texan got the call for this monumental honor, he realized he had to make the art. He was asked to create a sculpture and a painting to be made into the 2024 poster. The two works are of canvasback ducks landing in water only to discover that there is a stiff-looking decoy they have come to.
"They asked me would you be willing to do the poster as well as the sculpture. I said I would be honored," Wells said.
Wells based the works on a Ward Brothers 1936 canvasback duck decoy. Wells thinks 1936 was decoy carvers' peak year of expertise and creativity.
"I have always admired the Ward Brothers and their contribution to the art of decoy carving. I recently collected a 1936 model Canvasback Drake, which I used in the sculpture and the poster. They were artists and didn't even know it," Wells said.
Wells calls the canvasback the king of ducks. He loves the distinct noise their shorter wings make when they fly.
Wells is a hunter, and he said there are canvasbacks that make it to Texas.
"I have never killed a canvasback. I actually knocked one down and never found it and it bugs me to this day," he said. "It is one of my favorite ducks to paint and sculpt. They are such a magnificent looking ducks. They have a wide body and a Roman nose as far as a beak. Thick neck, they call them bull necks."
His inspiration for the poster and the sculpture was clear to him.
"When they called, I first thought of ducks as kind of my forte, and then I thought canvasbacks. The third thing I thought about was the Ward Brothers," he said.
After he got the call from the festival to create the poster, he started making thumbnail sketches of ducks. He sent that pencil sketch in for approval. Ultimately he created the final image in oil.
Wells has had a long career in the arts. He got an art degree and made a living as a medical illustrator. At the hospital where he worked, young doctors kept buying the miniature bronzes that he brought in to the office and put on his desk.
Wells will have an exhibit set up in the clear-roofed tent across from the Waterfowl Building during the festival. While still getting ready, he and his wife Patricia are unloading the art to be displayed. She handles all the driving and cleaning the sculpture with a Swiffer.
"He sculpts while I drive the box truck," she said.
Wells made three big sculptures for the festival. One has already sold.
The official festival sculpture was taken to the Tidewater Inns Crystal Room for the unveiling Thursday night. He made copies, and each one sells for $35,000.
As a market, a cultural event and a community of friends, the festival, "is such a fun thing to do. I have two of my old duck hunting buddies that we hunted in East Texas for 30 years. They came just for this event. I was shocked when they said they are going to be there. They are staying at the Tidewater. That is an honor in itself,' said Wells.
"This is kind of my swan song," he said, "even though it is a canvasback."

 EASTON — Standing near his cast bronze birds in the Waterfowl Festival's PNC Pavilion on Harrison Street, wildlife sculptor Paul Rhymer talked about a skill that has aided his trade: taxidermy."A lot of wildlife sculptors started out as taxidermists," he said, adding that it's a common enough practice that a whole article could be written on it.
Although Rhymer took up taxidermy as a kid because his father did it, painting and drawing were Rhymer's first true loves. In the '80s, while working as an entry-level illustrator at the Smithsonian, Rhymer discovered an opening there for an entry-level model maker and taxidermist.
"I had the experience as a taxidermist with my dad," he said. "And so that taxidermy experience, messing around the basement with my dad, led to this career."
Rhymer fell in love with his new career. In the late '90s, he traded in his paints for clay and took up sculpting. And after a 25 years, he retired from the Smithsonian, giving him more time to sculpt.
For Rhymer, understanding an animal and its anatomy is helpful when it comes to sculpting.
"When you skin an animal out because you're mounting it, then you really know the anatomy," he said.
And Rhymer isn't alone. Sculptor Don Rambadt, who creates mixed metal welded sculptures, said taxidermy experience can give "a better sense of what's inside."
"Because I was actually looking at how the bones are articulated," said Rambadt, who did bird taxidermy as a volunteer at the Milwaukee Public Museum for a few years.
Both Rhymer and Rambadt consider these outside experiences important in their art careers.
Rambadt, who grew up loving nature, animals and art, started his college career studying natural resource management. After getting kicked out of college and taking a few years to work, he went back to college on a general biology track. At that time, he took a few art classes and was introduced to welding as an art form.
"By the end of that semester I had changed my major, transferred schools and was showing in galleries by the time I graduated," he said. Rambadt's knowledge of science has helped inform his art.
He said his career combines his two loves: science and art.
For Rhymer, who is a Marylander, a lifetime of outdoor activities — from hunting to birdwatching to fishing — has contributed to his work.
"You can watch the mannerisms of how things move, and what they do and their behavior," he said.
Rhymer, who started showing his art at the Waterfowl Festival in 2004, appreciates the tradition of it all.
"It's the granddaddy of wildlife art festivals," he said. "Because it's the Waterfowl Festival and I started out as a duck hunter, I love those roots that it started out as a waterfowl show. ... And I love the hook of art and conservation."
Both Rhymer and Rambadt's art can be found in the PNC Pavilion during the festival. Their work can also be found on their websites, rhymerstudio.com and donrambadt.com.

title: Why are decoys so expensive? Artists, collectors share the value of carvings, community
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Why are decoys so expensive? Artists, collectors share the value of carvings, community

 November 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 653
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON – Decoys have long been used in hunting communities, but to the crowd at the Waterfowl Festival, the wood carvings serve more than just a utilitarian purpose.According to Cooper Rossner, a Talbot County decoy carver, the imitation birds and mammals can also be used as historic art pieces for nature lovers.
As a teenager in south New Jersey, Rossner was mesmerized by a carving demonstration in a natural sciences high school class. Rossner said right before his eyes, a carver turned a piece of wood into a Canada Goose.
This demonstration would be the first step into his lifelong passion for carving decoys. The carver at his school would soon become his mentor, and the following weekend he met an additional mentor during a Ducks Unlimited event.
"I was probably 15 years old, and here I am turning 30 in a week, and I'm still obsessed with it, still carving every chance I get," Rossner said. "... carving is my world, and is my mind, and is my heart and soul. It puts everything that I love together: working with my hands, artwork, the history of it, the wildlife, the hunting aspect — it wraps it all up."
The hours of labor and craft artists like Rossner put into the carvings mean sometimes decoys come with a hefty price tag.
Jon Deeter, co-owner of Guyette and Deeter, a decoy auction firm, said his firm surpassed $200 million in total sales during 2020. In his experience, decoys at his firm would minimally be sold at $300. The most his firm had sold a single decoy for was $480,000.
According to Deeter, pricing on decoys depends on a variety of factors. Vintage decoys made between 1850-1950 tend to be more valuable than contemporary decoys made after 1962. Additionally, the history and ownership of a decoy also impacts its value, similar to how provenance affects the value of fine art.
Rarity and originality also play a large role in the pricing of a decoy. The decoys made by renowned carvers like the Ward Brothers from Crisfield, Maryland can fetch prices in the six-figure range. Limited production, unique design or age can often command premium prices at auction, with the record being $1.144 million for a pair of decoys.
Deeter emphasized that decoy collecting is an expensive hobby, but many collectors are not purchasing the high budget decoys and are there for the simple pleasure and admiration of skilly crafted decoys and the history behind them.
Tyler Bryan, an Eastern Shore collector and hunter, said he has around 75 decoys and enjoys the story and history associated with the decoys he purchases.
Bryan said he came to collecting naturally, influenced by his upbringing on the Eastern Shore and his fascination with nature. But one of the main reasons he continues to collect is the close community of decoy collectors.
"The decoy collecting community is really a fantastic group of people," Bryan said. "It's tight-knit. Everyone knows each other. Most people know what everyone collects, and they're very helpful."
Bryan recommends decoy newcomers seek out a mentor because there are facets to collecting that will be much easier to someone if they have a trusted mentor to guide them along the way. According to Bryan, plenty of people within the decoy collecting community are happy to take on a mentee.
Rossner said decoy collecting often gets associated with much older people and can be seen as a "dying craft," but in his eyes, it deserves more recognition for the layers of complexity it holds and the community that has welcomed him.
Rossner said he encourages anyone interested to spend time with other carvers and collectors and learn more about the shared love this community has for decoys.
"There's lots of people still doing it, but not as many as there once were," Rossner said. "So you are living history when you're carving a decoy or you're doing an art form … you're doing something that's been handed down generation by generation."

title: Falconry demonstration wows at VFW
author: Tom McCall
content:
Falconry demonstration wows at VFW

 November 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 520
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Raptors can be taught behaviors with positive reinforcement, says Brian Bradley, the owner of Sky Hunters in Flight and a master falconer.Bradley drove all the way from the Hudson Valley to give a raptor demonstration at the VFW in Easton for this year's Waterfowl Festival. He has been doing falconry for 47 years and he brought 10 birds. Each bird was in a large box with its named taped to the top.
There was a crowd of about 50 people on bleachers. Families and bird lovers were beguiled by the raptors, which provided a thrilling display and highly educational experience. The kids' eyes followed the giant horn owl's every move.
Falconry is over 3,000 years old, and humans have used birds to catch rabbits and foxes for centuries. Bradley said the practice traveled with trade routes. From places like Medieval Europe, to the Middle East, to China. Mongolian horsemen use eagles for hunting to this day.
"As far as the Middle East goes, it is very embedded in their culture. It is a huge thing for them, and it involves a lot of time and a lot of money invested. They take it extremely seriously, but it is practiced around the world," Bradley said. "It was a practical way to bring home meat before firearms."
Being this into falcons is a full-time pursuit. They have to be fed every day, and Bradley weighs each bird down to the gram to know if they are hungry or not.
They come to him when calls out or when he uses a hand clicker.
He brought out a barred owl, a red tailed hawk and the fastest animal on Earth, the peregrine falcon. He described how their wing structure determines what kind of flying and killing they can do. He also explained how an owl's cone-like face helped them to pick up sound like a satellite dish picks up a radio signal.
Many of these birds were threatened by the insecticide DDT in the 1960s and 1970s. They ingested small birds that had eaten bugs who had been poisoned with DDT. The birds' eggs were affected. With shells that were too thin, the babies died.
"At one point there were almost no peregrine falcons recorded east of the Mississippi River. Without passionate falconers, there probably wouldn't be falcons today. They started to breed them in captivity. They got rid of the poison and now the falcons are rebounding. It is probably the greatest conservation success story in our history," Bradley said.
He loved the birds right from the beginning.
"I appreciate what they do in nature and the fact that they do it so dramatically and so athletically. It is just thrilling to watch," he said.
All of his birds were bred in captivity, with the exception is his hunting bird, the red tailed hawk.
He caught it with a net in the wild. He used a live pigeon during the hawk's migration season. It has to be the right age to keep legally. He will train the young hawk for five years and then let it go when it is sexually mature.
"It feels good to let a bird go." he said.

title: States apart, Waterfowl artists build lasting friendships
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
States apart, Waterfowl artists build lasting friendships

 November 11, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 517
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Jim Green and his wife, Kara, traveled from Hermosa, South Dakota, a small town with less than 400 people, to Easton this weekend. He's been bringing his wildlife sculptures to the Waterfowl Festival for around a decade.The South Dakota couple was stationed inside of the Waterfowl's main building for the Art at the Armory display. Directly across sat Carol Heiman-Greene and her husband, all the way from Orange, California.
The two artists and their respective spouses aren't just acquaintances. They're friends, or better yet, family.
"I come back year after year, and these are like my families," Heiman-Greene said of the fellow artists she's come to know. Kara Green used that exact same word — family — to describe her and her husband's friendship with the Heiman-Greenes and others.
Carol Heiman-Greene, who's been an exhibitor at the Easton festival for about 20 years, says there's a "core" of artists who have been at Waterfowl and other festivals for a long time. She said when new artists come, it's a joy to welcome them into the family, too.
On Saturday, Heiman-Greene pointed out her painting of a California condor vulture, laughing since Jim Green had a sculpture of a California condor for sale.
Through the ups and downs of travel, sales and weather, Heiman-Greene said artists have "all sorts of tales (they) can share" with one another.
"You come to these (festivals), and you see your friends from last year and years previous," Jim Green said. "It's so nice to connect with people."
Green says he loves those friendships with fellow artists not just for the relationships, but also to expand his work in an environment rich with creative ideas.
"You have a tendency to think of the world as built on artists when you come to these, because you see so many of them," he continued. "And then you get home and you're in this desert of nobody else around you that does this. So it's really nice to have that creativity, that creative aspect of things to bounce ideas off of other people."
For the Green couple, it's not a competitive environment. Last year, Jim Green said someone stopped by to let him know they recreated his raven coat rack sculpture.
"I know there are other artists that would kind of take that the wrong way," he said. "But I was like, 'Yeah, where are the pictures? I love that.'"
Both Carol Heiman-Greene and Jim Green said the people, atmosphere and weather at Waterfowl combine to make the festival one of their favorites. While Green said his sales are typically solid at Waterfowl, even if they weren't, the three-day event is still his "favorite one of the year."
"I love coming here to see the atmosphere and everything there is about Maryland," Heiman-Greene said. "It's really fun. It has such a small-town atmosphere."
Despite living states and plane rides apart, the annual Waterfowl Festival tradition has helped bring the Greens and Heiman-Greenes together as artists and friends. It's a trend Jim Green hopes continues for years to come.
"Art sells art," Jim Green said. "If you can't have all boats rise, you shouldn't be in the boat."

title: Waterfowl Festival draws crowd of over 25,000
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Waterfowl Festival draws crowd of over 25,000

 November 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 502
 Words

 EASTON — Waterfowl Festival Executive Director Deena Kilmon said Easton's 53rd Waterfowl Festival was not just "spectacular," but record-breaking, too."We know we broke every record we've ever broken," Kilmon said on Monday.
The festival, a combination of wildlife, art, music, Eastern Shore history and more, attracted around 25,000 to 30,000 attendees to Talbot County this weekend, Kilmon said.
She said after talks with the Easton Police Department, it could be roughly estimated that there were 15,000 downtown Saturday and another 10,000 to 15,000 people at the Easton Elks Lodge for the Sportsmans' Pavilion and Dock Dogs competitions.
"We had the highest attendance ever," Kilmon said. "It's hard for us to gauge because not everyone buys a ticket. But we do know that every parking space was full and every bus had about 45 minutes to an hour-long wait, and we had to add three buses on Saturday to accommodate the people."
The executive director said multiple vendors — many of which are already asking about next year — sold out or had record days at the festival.
It all began Thursday evening with the Tidewater Inn's premiere party. Easton Mayor Megan Cook formally opened the festival by bringing down the duck-shaped gavel.
For the next three days, attendees enjoyed clear skies and great festival weather. During Saturday's attendance peak, attendees roamed downtown, many enjoying multiple musical performances that drew large crowds.
According to Kilmon, there were 38 musical performances in total, a focus of this year's festival.
"That made the festival have a different vibe this year, I think," Kilmon said. "Just made it more of a friendly family party on every corner."
On South Harrison Street, an expanded PNC Art Pavilion was a success, Kilmon said. While many artists were stationed inside of the Waterfowl Festival's main building, others had displays across the street in the pavilion's tent, including this year's featured artist, Ronnie Wells.
"You feel like you're in an art museum more than you feel like you're in a tent," Kilmon said. "It was just spectacular presentation."
Over on Bay Street, expanding children's activities and adding a "Beer Wetlands" area were focal points for organizers. Kilmon says she hopes the Bay Street area can grow in future festivals, as well as the Chesapeake Bay Pavilion at Easton VFW Post 5118 on Glebe Road.
"We want to make sure the Chesapeake Bay Pavilion has a little bit of love, because there were incredible educational exhibits out there that I think that some people may not have been able to enjoy," the executive director said.
Kilmon said organizers will work on improving the bus routes for next year, as well as adjusting signage and maps so that attendees, if able, are encouraged to walk to downtown venues for quicker commutes.
Overall, feedback has been "incredibly positive" and Kilmon is excited to begin work on continuing Easton's Waterfowl tradition.
"Fifty-three years of our community coming together just gets better every year," Kilmon said. "And we're already working on next year, believe it or not."
The 54th Waterfowl Festival will be held Nov. 14 through Nov. 16, 2025.

title: Academy Art Museum gets new director
author: Tom McCall
content:
Academy Art Museum gets new director

 November 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Arts

 EASTON — Charlotte Potter Kasic, the new director of the Academy Art Museum, has a lot of ideas. But her first weeks, she said, will be dedicated to completing a listening tour.Her latest post was the Barry Art Museum in Norfolk, Virginia, where she was executive director. Now she has a new challenge with helming the Academy.
"Every time I see a challenge, I lean in," Kasic said.
She was not entirely unfamiliar with the Academy Art Museum before applying for the job.
"When Eric Neil left the Academy in 2012 or 2013, he became the director of the Chrysler Museum of Art, and I was the director of the Chrysler Museum Glass Studio, which was like an annex," Kasic said.
She's been impressed with the museum's existing work and potential.
"When you break it down, there are classes. There are programs and exhibitions. There is collections. There is fundraising. There are galas. It is wild how much happens here with so little. I think this place is doing a great job of hitting a lot of audiences," she said.
Kasic is excited to work with the staff to continue these efforts.
Kasic has past in glass blowing, in which she said she learned about collaboration and teamwork. She created Cirque de Verre (circus of glass), which traveled around the United States to museums and art spaces that had glass blowing furnaces.
"Glass I love because you work in teams. It is hot. It is visceral. There is a lot of strong communication skills," Kasic said. "I like things to be immersive, multisensory and interdisciplinary. When you think of olfactory, that is how you access your deepest memories. Music can change your mood in a minute. Art can do that as well."
Kasic has a masters degree from Rhode Island School of Design and has done residencies at Penland, Oxbow, Pilchuck and in Australia.
After the Chrysler she moved to Vermont to start a family. She ended up being the director at the Yestermorrow Design Build School, which celebrates sustainable design and craft.
The siren song of Norfolk brought her and her family back to the Chesapeake, where she joined the team at the Barry Museum. She says it has become the glass art capital of the East Coast. There, Kasic helmed a 25,000 square foot expansion and closed out a $23 million campaign.
Now at the Academy Art Museum, she sees a collaborative community that brings Plein Air, The Craft Show and the Waterfowl Festival into the institution. She also has a clear-eyed approach to what the Academy can offer the community.
"I would like to see more of our permanent collection on view. We have so much that exists but people don't get to see," she said.
Even with these plans, she realizes that there is a lot of collaborating to be done.
"It is important to say how invested the board is in this place. I have seen more board involvement and more community investment than any other organization I have been in. People are so dedicated. It is really remarkable and it speaks to the strength of this place," she said.

title: Museum opens art-making studio
author: Staff Writer
content:
Museum opens art-making studio

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment

 Read News Document

 Hirshhorn Art School, a first-of-its-kind art education experience, opened inside the Smithsonian's Hirshhorn Museum on Oct. 30. Combining elements of a professional artist's studio, museum galleries and clubhouse, the new and flexible 1,700-square-foot hub will offer structured programming and open-studio sessions guided by museum educators and teaching artists four days a week for visitors of all ages."Hirshhorn Art School asks visitors to 'think like an artist,'" said Melissa Chiu, museum director. "When the Hirshhorn opened in 1974, museum education was in its infancy and largely grounded in observation. We've since found that experiential art learning is both highly effective and in demand."
Designed for varying ages, abilities and interests, Hirshhorn Art School programs will be organized into thematic, artist-focused semesters and will build on the work of Hirshhorn Kids and ARTLAB as well as public programs for adult audiences.
The first semester, "Boundary Breakers," will introduce the biographies, materials, techniques and philosophies of originals such as Anni Albers, Mark Bradford and Barbara Hepworth, whose artworks are on view. In its first year, Hirshhorn Art School expects to host more than 25,000 in-person visitors and 75,000 more virtually with livestreamed lessons and anytime resources.
Hirshhorn Art School offers programs Wednesdays–Saturdays:
Storytime Studio, Wednesdays, 10 a.m.–1 p.m.Children ages up to 8 years will connect an artwork on view with a children's book and engage in hands-on activities that develop self-expression and visual storytelling. Drop-ins welcome.
School Studio, FridaysGuided by museum educators and teaching artists, students in grades three through eight will explore the hows and whys of art-making, inspired by Hirshhorn collections and exhibitions. These weekly morning and afternoon sessions, lasting 60–120 minutes, must be reserved.
Open Studio, Saturdays, 10 a.m.–3 p.m.Guided by museum educators and teaching artists, visitors of all ages will be invited to respond to modern and contemporary art history, with a focus on Hirshhorn exhibitions. Drop-ins welcome.
Emerging Artists, Saturdays, 3–5:30 p.m.Teens ages 14–19 will collaboratively focus on the works of living artists. The debut season invites consideration of Bradford and his monumental work "Pickett's Charge" (2017). This program builds upon ARTLAB, the Hirshhorn platform for teens, which served an average of 4,000 student artists. Pre-registration is required.
As part of Hirshhorn Art School's outreach, art educators will continue to build upon the museum's library of almost 50 online projects and three free in-gallery activity guides. The Art School classroom has a built-in loop system to support visitors who use hearing aids, as well as a quiet area and tactiles.
Hirshhorn Art School is the public expression of Hirshhorn Education, a central pillar of the national museum of modern and contemporary art, whose mission amplifies the importance of the voices of artists on behalf of the Smithsonian Institution.
The Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden is the national museum of modern and contemporary art. Part of the Smithsonian, the Hirshhorn is located on the National Mall in Washington, D.C. For more information, visit hirshhorn.si.edu.

title: Benson's birds: AAM art exhibit explores vintage prints
author: Staff Writer
content:
Benson's birds: AAM art exhibit explores vintage prints

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment

 A new exhibit at the Academy Art Museum in Easton highlights sporting, waterfowl and bird prints from American artist Frank W. Benson.The prints are from AAM's collection and the exhibit runs through Dec. 8.
The exhibit is entitled "Sporting: Frank Benson's Waterfowl Prints."
Here are some details about the artist and his prints from AAM:
"Born and raised on the North Shore of Massachusetts, American artist Frank W. Benson (1862–1951), grew up sailing, fishing, hunting, and birdwatching. These interests persisted throughout his life, and he ultimately became one of the fore- most American practitioners of the genre of printmaking known as the sporting print.
In the early 20th century, Benson established a reputation as a painter of portraits and landscapes inspired by French Impressionism. He joined a group of Boston and New York painters known as "The Ten" who organized carefully curated annual exhibitions of paintings between 1898 and 1918. He was also interested in printmaking, particularly etching. Beginning in 1914, he returned to his early fascination with birds, ultimately creating more than 300 images of the many species of waterfowl native to the beaches and marshes of New England.
Sporting prints by Benson first entered the Academy's collection in 1987 when Berlin Voorhees included two of the artist's waterfowl etchings with a larger gift of late 19th and early 20th century works on paper. The collection grew to encompass more than 30 works by Benson, largely due to the generosity of the late Robert K. Keller, who began donating prints from his collection to the Museum in 2001 and continued with these gifts until his death in 2009."
For more: https://academyartmuseum.org/sporting-frank-bensons-waterfowl-prints/

title: Bringing global flavors to the table this Thanksgiving
author: Kristen Wood Food Drink Life
content:
Bringing global flavors to the table this Thanksgiving

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Kristen Wood Food Drink Life | Section: Entertainment 
 
 1045
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Thanksgiving brings together family and friends over dishes like buttery mashed potatoes and sweet pumpkin pie. This year, add these international flavors to your Thanksgiving traditions and celebrate with diversity on your table.The popular story of the first Thanksgiving tells of Native Americans and Pilgrims coming together to share the bounty of harvest. Over a feast, people of different cultures and beliefs celebrated together.
In 1863, Abraham Lincoln proclaimed Thanksgiving a national holiday. According to State Representative, Wayne Rosenthal, this was the result of a campaign by Godey's Lady's Book to promote unity during the midst of the American Civil War.
Today, Thanksgiving remains a time to come together. It is the busiest travel week of the year, notes the United States Embassy, as families travel across the world to be together. Friendsgiving, feasts on college campuses and celebrations for members of the armed forces stationed abroad bring together those who may not be able to spend time with family over the holiday.
With more people celebrating Thanksgiving from several diverse cultures, new traditions are becoming more common at the holiday table. Turkey, stuffing and pie remain Thanksgiving favorites, but international dishes and flavors are also more at home on a modern Thanksgiving table. This year, bring these global twists to Thanksgiving dinner and celebrate coming together through food.
Thanksgiving traditions around the worldMany countries celebrate their own Thanksgiving holiday. Initially, these holidays began as harvest celebrations, says GoAbroad, giving thanks for a bountiful harvest much as America's first Thanksgiving did. In the years since, these celebrations have taken on their own unique traditions.
For example, in Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people celebrate Erntedankfest on the first Sunday of October. Religious services and lantern parades accompany this holiday. "Mohnstriezel" — a sweet bread with poppy seeds — is a popular treat during the festivities.
Malaysians celebrate Kadazan in May to honor the sacrifice of the goddess Huminodun, whose death provided for an abundant rice harvest. Their celebration is filled with feasting, rice wine, games and music.
Ghanaians celebrate "Homowo" — meaning hooting at hunger — to honor those who died in a historic famine, usher in a bountiful harvest and celebrate the arrival of the new year in Ghana. The people prepare "kpokpoi," a dish made of corn meal, palm oil and seasonings. In addition to eating kpokpoi, local chiefs sprinkle it around the town as an offering.
These traditions and dishes, as well as those from other countries, can be a fun addition to your own Thanksgiving celebrations. Adding African, Asian and European food, and other cuisines to your menu is a great way to learn more about other cultures or welcome an international guest with a taste of home.
Global twists on the main dishAt an American Thanksgiving, turkey is often the main dish of choice. Many traditional recipes call for baking, roasting, frying or even smoking the turkey, often with fresh herbs, salt, pepper and vegetables for flavor.
But turkey's mild taste also makes it a perfect dish for more adventurous flavors. Jamaican jerk turkey combines spices like cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves with herbs and chili for a warm and flavorful dish. Alternatively, a turkey marinade with Chinese five-spice powder — cinnamon, cloves, star anise, fennel and Sichuan peppers — infuses your turkey with fall flavors and a bit of heat.
These marinades are an exciting way to introduce global flavors, but they are only the beginning. Earthy za'atar seasoning from the Middle East, a warm berbere spice blend from Ethiopia or bright herbs de Provence from France can all be inventive additions to turkey.
Turkey mole combines mole, the national dish of Mexico, with your turkey for a rich, chili flavor. Make your own mole or purchase a high-quality sauce to add to roast turkey. You can also try pavo a la brasa, a twist on Peruvian roasted chicken, by marinating your turkey with a sauce with cumin, paprika and other aromatics.
Exotic sides and desserts to expand your Thanksgiving menuSide dishes and desserts are a great way to introduce global influences to a feast with plenty of room for experimenting. Try spicing up traditional sides with international ingredients. Adding shishito peppers to green beans gives the veggies a Japanese flair or you can switch out the sweet potatoes for a delicious yam casserole.
International sides can also bring a nice contrast to common Thanksgiving foods. A Korean cucumber salad is refreshing, spicy and tangy. With a mild heat from the gochugaru pepper flakes, the salad makes a great starter or palette cleanser between courses.
Vegetable korma is a flavorful way to serve veggies at your meal, infusing Thanksgiving with Indian spices. The creamy cashew, yogurt and coconut milk sauce with the korma goes great over turkey and potatoes.
For dessert, bring a twist to classics with pumpkin empanadas or baklava filled with walnuts for a nutty treat. Other exotic desserts, like Chinese moon cakes or melomakarona from Cyprus, both traditional holiday desserts, are great at an American Thanksgiving as well.
Flavorful condiments with international flairCranberry sauce and gravy are Thanksgiving staples. This year, add interest with a variety of condiments. Salsa Lizano, a sauce made with vegetables, cumin and pepper, is a Costa Rican condiment that is perfect on the table or in a rice and bean dish like gallo pinto.
Asian flavors like sriracha or gochujang give a delightful spice to meat and vegetables. Indian mango chutney or the Georgian plum sauce tkemali are sweet alternatives to cranberry sauce.
Serve these condiments alongside the Thanksgiving meal and let your guests tailor their plates to their liking. These are also a great way to spruce up your leftovers.
Bringing it all together at the tableWhether you look forward to visiting with family or enjoying your favorite foods at Thanksgiving, mixing up your menu with international flavors will make for a memorable holiday. Begin with these ideas or explore dishes from cultures that are meaningful to your guests. You might even start some new Thanksgiving traditions to celebrate for years to come.
Kristen Wood is a photographer, food writer, recipe developer and creator of MOON and spoon and yum. She is also the author of "Vegetarian Family Cookbook," "Fermented Hot Sauce Cookbook" and "Hot Sauce Cookbook for Beginners." Her work has been featured in various online and print publications, including NBC, Seattle Times, Elle, Martha Stewart, Forbes, Chicago Sun-Times and more.

title: After exiting the Christian music industry, these artists engage religion on their terms
author: KATHRYN POST Religion News Service
content:
After exiting the Christian music industry, these artists engage religion on their terms

 November 15, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KATHRYN POST Religion News Service | Section: Ap Entertainment 
 
 1606
 Words 

 Read News Document

 When former Christian artist Michael Gungor first hosted a new spiritual community in Los Angeles this year, worship began not with an organ blast or sermon series video promo, but with blowing bubbles.Appropriately dubbed "Play," Gungor envisioned the event — which featured painting, dancing, corporate singing and meditation, but no religious creed — as a celebration that "redefines worship."
"I want to be in a room and see each other's eyes and smell each other and hear each other singing out of key. This is something we've always done as a species," Gungor said. "I think there's something important, really grounding and human about it."
Gungor's idea of worship wasn't always so experimental. In packed churches and concert venues, thousands once sang along to the band Gungor's 2010 hit "Beautiful Things," a song that became a permanent fixture on the setlists of youth group bands. But in 2014, Gungor's critiques of the Christian music industry — as well as his public musings on Genesis as a poem rather than historic fact — led to his exclusion from the Christian music business. Now, after a long process of wrestling with his inherited evangelical faith — documented on his podcast "The Liturgists" — Gungor says he's more interested in embracing the current lived moment than being tethered to a set of religious beliefs, though he describes Christianity as his "native tongue."
For those like him who have "deconstructed" — a popular term today for the process of questioning and sometimes letting go of the teachings of one's faith tradition — Gungor still sees a desire for ritual and for communal gathering. He recognizes the power of the collective — and aims to write non-dogmatic music for corporate, if not religious, worship.
"We've gotten rid of some of the shame-based stuff and some of the dogmas that were oppressing and hurting a lot of us, but now we're kind of just wandering around alone … What are we missing? Is there anything we can find back here?"
In the last two decades, several Contemporary Christian Music powerhouses — Audrey Assad, DC Talk's Kevin Max, Hawk Nelson's Jon Steingard, among several others — have publicly exited the CCM industry. For many of these musicians, questioning the industry's theological parameters meant becoming unwelcome in mainstream CCM spaces. Years later, after interrogating their beliefs, a handful of these onetime CCM artists are revisiting faith in some fashion, trying on elements they'd previously discarded and writing music for listeners who might be more spiritual than religious. In many ways, these artists' break from institutional Christianity and hunger for a broader form of belonging exemplifies national religious trends.
One of the earliest CCM artists to publicly depart the industry was Jennifer Knapp, who burst onto the Christian music scene with her debut album "Kansas" in 1998. But while Knapp was drawn to Christianity's teachings on human dignity and divine love, she soon realized that the Christianity promoted in the CCM world drew hard lines around who belonged, and who didn't. Her lyrics about the Christ's humanity and questions about the necessity of substitutionary atonement — the idea that Jesus died as a substitute for humanity — began to draw criticism.
"I was already getting critiqued at the time and being basically told you weren't a Christian anymore," said Knapp. "And then I was like, oh, well, I'm wondering what you guys are going to think about my sexual orientation."
In 2002, Knapp "pushed the eject button" on the Christian music scene and her faith. When she returned in 2010, it was as an openly gay musician no longer publishing music under the Christian banner.
For longtime Bethel Music recording artist William Matthews, it was in part the rigid homogeneity of the Christian Music industry that ultimately led him to walk away. Raised in a Black Church of God context, he came to Christian music by way of spontaneous worship models promoted by Morningstar Ministries in Charlotte, North Carolina, and the International House of Prayer in Kansas City, Missouri. Though skeptical about the existence of hell, Matthews, who spent his evenings watching Bill O'Reilly on Fox News, largely felt at home in the prophetic corner of the Christian music world. In the early 2010s, he led worship at the conferences of charismatic leader Lance Wallnau, now known for his pro-Trump prophecies.
But by 2015, Williams found non-violent Christian theology a more compelling approach. He watched as anti-immigrant rhetoric and opposition to the Black Lives Matter movement reached a fever pitch in evangelical circles and grew frustrated with what he saw as the Christian music industry's "conservative bias." After spending nearly 15 years thinking he'd been bridging cultures as one of the only Black people in white-majority evangelical spaces, he was shattered to discover that many of those he'd grown close to seemed ambivalent toward racism.
"That led me to really walk away from Christian music," said Matthews.
He attributes the CCM industry's apparent conservative slant to its target audience of "white, suburban, Midwest or Southern moms." In catering to that demographic, Christian radio executives and Christian bookstores are known to censor songs or albums that cross conservative theological or political boundaries.
"What the CCM industry, or Christian music, is selling is security," said musician Derek Webb, founding member of the Christian rock band Caedmon's Call. "The people who run or appear to be gatekeeping the CCM industry are not doing that as a means of holding some kind of moral plumb line." Webb believes the pushback usually has more to do with a company's bottom line than personal convictions.
Despite the Christian music industry's restrictions, exiting the industry often means leaving behind record labels, the Christian music festival circuit and radio play and requires promoting music to a market that's much less defined. While some boundary-pushing Christian artists like Semler and Flamy Grant, two queer artists who've scored top spots on the Itunes Christian charts, have found success via social media and streaming platforms, many onetime Christian artists are labeled "too Christian" for mainstream music spaces and "too secular" for explicitly religious ones.
"It's this kind of no man's land, algorithmically," said Gungor. "I still have more listeners of 'Beautiful Things,' than anything else I make."
Creating music for a more nebulous spiritual audience might not guarantee commercial success, but if it means creating music that feels authentic, for many former Christian artists, it's worth the tradeoff.
Known for his provocative approach to songwriting, Webb says his lyrics cause him to both "shed" about a quarter or third of his audience every 18 months and gain new listeners. After 30 years in the music industry, he's comfortable with the ebb and flow. In 2017, three years after his divorce from fellow Christian artist Sandra McCracken, Webb released "Fingers Crossed," an album documenting his departure from Christianity. But though he still considers himself an agnostic, his latest album, "The Jesus Hypothesis," grapples more explicitly with Christian themes.
"I wanted to go back into the rubble of where all this was pulled down and burned down, and where I was in here with an ax before, I want to come back in with a scalpel," he said of the album.
Webb's return to the debris of his Christian faith coincided with a return to Caedmon's Call, which recently produced a re-record of its self-titled debut album in honor of its 25th anniversary. The 2022 release is emblematic of the ways several former Christian artists have been coming back to reclaim elements of their religious heritage.
More than a decade since her return to the music world, in May, Knapp offered a re-release of her first album, "Kansas 25." She graduated from Vanderbilt Divinity School in 2018, and now views Christianity as a source of wisdom whose teachings on liberation have fueled her own LGBTQ+ advocacy. The outpouring of support for "Kansas 25," Knapp said, caused her to see her early music in a new light.
"If ever I had any bitterness about my role inside of evangelical Christianity, or concern that maybe I tied people down, exposed them to too much religious trauma because of the conservative evangelical space that I came from, this was a real joy to be able to witness, that our faith can teach us something, and it can expand beyond some of the harms sometimes that our smaller religious spaces offer to us," said Knapp.
Gungor's next project has emerged from his desire to see communal songs that trade religious lyrics for more universal themes, like love and unity. This fall, he gathered with over 20 other songwriters in Colorado for a songwriting retreat to begin writing and recording music for the project, called The Mystic Hymnal.
After a long hiatus from Christian music, William Matthews, too, is releasing new, honest songs about spirituality. Earlier this year, he was invited by the evangelical authors of a recent anti-culture war statement to write and produce a corresponding album intended to call the church out of political idolatry. Titled "Return to Love," the September album was recorded by artists from a range of theological and political perspectives and is designed for those who are "full of faith or struggling to believe."
"I'm always in the middle of wrestling. Does church even matter to my life?" said Matthews, who leads worship at a progressive LGBTQ-affirming church in Los Angeles where former evangelicals regularly attend. "I will say, in my life, I've somehow always managed to come back. Maybe it's cyclical. You're always returning home or to a sense of home or to a better expression of home."

title: Country Cooking: Memories of cranberry sauce
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Memories of cranberry sauce

 November 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1179
 Words 

 Read News Document

 We always had cranberries at Christmas and Thanksgiving dinners. Mom used the whole cranberries that you served with a spoon.One time on the Sunday after Thanksgiving Thursday, our parents, my three younger brothers and I were invited to a dinner in a nearby larger town. We were prompted on the way there (or threatened) to be on our best behavior or else — we never tested that "or else."
This strange looking dish came past with red slices of something on it that quivered when shook, and we all four said "no thanks" and passed it on. Oh, but no. Mom said "oh you all love that" and proceeded to plop a piece on our plate.
That is when the trouble started. We rolled it, we slapped it and finally mashed it, leaving the prettiest design ever.
On the way home, we were told that it was canned cranberry sauce. To this very day I have a can of cranberry sauce waiting to be opened, sliced and served on the holiday table. As I look across my kitchen this morning at my can of sauce, I think of Mom standing in her bib apron, smiling and saying, "what did you all think was on that plate?"
The reporter came out of me at an early age, so I said, "Jimmy said it was liver, Ollie said it was brains, Richard said it was jello and I said I would investigate."
GREEN BEANS WITH BACON4 diced bacon strips, 1/2 cup chopped onion, 8 cups fresh green beans (trimmed), water, salt and pepper.
This is tasty, quick and easy. In a large skillet, cook bacon strips with chopped onion until the bacon is crisp. Meanwhile place green beans in a large saucepan and cover with water. Bring to a boil and cook for 8 to 10 minutes or until crisp-tender. Drain well and add the bacon mixture. Sprinkle top with salt and pepper and toss to coat. Serve immediately. This recipe is not the one grandmother or mom made but is great too. Give it a try.
SWEET POTATO N' MARSHMALLOW1 can sweet potatoes, 1 egg, 3/4 cup sugar, 1 1/4 tsp vanilla, 1/3 cup evaporated milk, 1/3 stick margarine, large bag of marshmallows.
For a Small casserole dish size, mix together well with an electric mixer: sweet potatoes, egg, sugar, vanilla, evaporated milk and margarine. Bake in a 350-degree oven for 30 to 40 minutes. Remove from the oven, top with marshmallows and return to the oven just until the marshmallows turn golden brown. Remove from the oven and let set for a while before serving.
CORNBREAD DRESSING WITH OYSTERS2 tbsps unsalted butter (plus more for greasing the dish), 1 yellow onion (diced), 3 stalks celery (diced), 5 cloves garlic (minced), 8 cups crumbled cornbread, kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, 3 1/2 cups chicken stock, 6 large eggs, 1/2 cup chopped Italian parsley, 1 bunch fresh tarragon (leaves stripped and chopped), 2 cups shucked oysters with their juice.
Heat the oven to 350 degrees. Butter a 9-by-13-inch baking dish. In a large skillet, melt the butter over medium heat. When the butter is foamy, add the onion and celery, and cook, stirring frequently, until softened, 6 to 8 minutes. Stir the garlic and cook until aromatic, about 1 minute. Stir in the crumbled cornbread and cook, stirring, until lightly browned, then remove from the heat. In a large bowl, beat the eggs until smooth. Whisk in the chicken stock, parsley and tarragon. Stir in the cornbread mixture and the oysters. Pour the dressing mixture into the prepared baking dish and bake until the dressing is set and golden brown, about 1 hour. (Alternatively, cover and refrigerate overnight before baking.) Let rest for 5 minutes.
GREEN BEAN CASSEROLE2 cans green beans, 1 can golden mushroom soup, half a can of water, 1 cup grated cheddar cheese, one can fried onions.
Heat oven to 350 degrees. In a large bowl, stir together green beans with golden mushroom soup, water and cheese. Lightly mix and transfer to a two-quart casserole dish. Sprinkle top with fried onions. Cover with foil and bake for 30 minutes. Remove foil and bake for another 15 minutes until bubbly.
ASPARAGUS CASSEROLEThis goes great with baked ham. In a buttered casserole dish place a layer of asparagus and then a layer of crumbled cheese nips crackers. Wet with cream of mushroom soup mixed with water according to directions on the can. Finish the casserole with a few more crushed cheese nips. Bake in a 350-degree oven until asparagus is tender.
OLD FASHIONED BREAD DRESSING1 1/2 cups finely chopped onion, 1/3 cup butter, 1 1/2 cups chopped celery, 8 cups dry small bread cubes, 1 1/2 tsp salt, 1/8 tsp black pepper, 1/2 tsp poultry seasoning, 1/2 tsp sage, 1/4 cup water, 1 beaten egg.
In a skillet, cook chopped onion in butter with chopped celery until tender. Add this mixture to bread cubes, which have been placed in a large pan. Sprinkle with salt, black pepper, poultry seasoning and sage, and combine well. Add water and beaten egg. Toss together with a fork. Stuff a thawed bird immediately and bake according to directions on the turkey label.
ITALIAN GREEN BEAN CASSEROLE6 ounces parmesan cheese (grated), 1 1/4 cups Italian-style breadcrumbs, 4 garlic cloves (minced), 1 tsp kosher salt, 3/4 tsp black pepper (divided), 3 (28-oz.) cans Italian-style green beans (drained), 2 (9-oz.) packages frozen artichoke hearts (thawed, drained well and chopped), 2/3 cup extra virgin olive oil, fresh flat-leaf parsley (chopped).
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Combine parmesan, breadcrumbs, garlic, salt, and 1/2 tsp pepper in a large bowl. Reserve 1/3 cup of the breadcrumb mixture then set aside. Add green beans, artichoke hearts, and olive oil to bowl with remaining breadcrumb mixture, and fold to combine well. Pour green bean mixture into a lightly greased 13-by-9-inch baking dish. Sprinkle reserved breadcrumb mixture evenly over the casserole. Cover with aluminum foil, and bake until heated through, about 30 minutes. Uncover and bake until lightly golden and bubbly, about 10 minutes. Sprinkle with remaining 1/4 tsp pepper, and if desired, chopped parsley.
HONEY SPICE BREAD2/3 cup packed brown sugar, 1/3 cup 2% milk, 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1-1/2 tsps baking powder, 1/2 tsp ground cinnamon, 1/2 tsp ground nutmeg, 1/8 tsp ground cloves, 2 large eggs (room temperature), 1/2 cup honey, 1/3 cup canola oil. GLAZE: 1/3 cup confectioners' sugar, 2 tsps 2% milk.
Preheat the oven to 325 degrees. In a small saucepan, combine brown sugar and milk. Cook and stir over low heat until sugar is dissolved. Remove from heat. In a large bowl, whisk flour, baking powder, cinnamon, nutmeg and cloves. In another bowl, whisk eggs, honey, oil and brown sugar mixture until blended. Add to flour mixture; stir just until moistened. Transfer the batter to a greased 8-by-4-inch loaf pan. Bake for 50-60 minutes or until a toothpick inserted in the center comes out clean (cover top loosely with foil if needed to prevent overbrowning). Cool in pan 10 minutes before removing to a wire rack to cool completely. In a small bowl, stir glaze ingredients until smooth, drizzle over bread.

title: Native American heritage honored
author: Madison Bateman Special to Star Democrat
content:
Native American heritage honored

 November 19, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Madison Bateman Special to Star Democrat | Section: State News 
 
 483
 Words 

 Read News Document

 "Native Americans were here first, and they are still here."With that statement, Rod Cofield, executive director of Jefferson Patterson Park and Museum, summed up the reason for the annual American Indian Heritage Day, which drew more than 400 guests to the park on Nov. 2.
"Many gloss over the fact there is still an indigenous population in the area. … Their culture and history is worth acknowledging," Cofield said.
The annual event, usually held on the first Saturday of November, aligns with the national recognition of Native American Heritage Month.
He said programs such as American Indian Heritage Day at the park in St. Leonard provides local Native groups the opportunity to "tell their story, in their words, in their way."
"People really enjoy the event," Cofield said, adding the celebration was supported by Friends of Jefferson Patterson Park and Museum and the Southern Maryland Folklife Center.
Brent Meadows of Port Republic attended the celebration for the first time this year with his 3-year-old son Ian and 5-year-old daughter Isla.
"We like taking advantage of the park's free and educational events," he said.
Meadows and his family spent some time making cordage out of plants, led by Clare Walker from Irvine Nature Center in Baltimore County.
The event featured local Native dancers, demonstrations and educational activities such as clay pot-making, archery, painting, fishing and more.
"We are the original people to inhabit what is known today as the state of Maryland," Mark Tayac, Piscataway Indian Nation chief, said. "We called it home for 15,000 years. Our presence has been documented by anthropologists and archeologists."
Tayac's son, Naiche, spoke and performed at Saturday's program.
"We are not part of the past, relics in museums. … We are human beings, and we are still here today," he said.
Especially during Native American Heritage Month in November, Tayak explained participating in celebrations such as the one held at the park gives them an opportunity to educate people about their culture, a culture that is thousands of years old.
By the time the Europeans embarked on the New World at the dawn of the 17th century, the Piscataway was the largest and most powerful tribal nation in the lands between the Chesapeake Bay and Potomac River, according to the Maryland Department of Natural Resources website.
Traditional territory primarily included present-day Charles, Prince George's and St. Mary's counties, and extended north into Baltimore County and west toward the Appalachian Mountains.
"We are now centrally located in Southern Maryland," Tayac said.
The Piscataway people faced many challenges in Maryland, colonization being among the largest. English colonists began taking over the Piscataway's homelands in 1634, converting them to Catholicism and forcing them to surrender their beliefs.
"There was a time in history when Native people were not allowed to practice their culture," Tayac said. "The history is hard to talk about, but it must be talked about. That's how we begin to comprehend that we are all the same, that we all have the same heart."

title: Historic Sotterley screens, holds panel discussion on 'Grandma's Hands'
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Historic Sotterley screens, holds panel discussion on 'Grandma's Hands'

 November 20, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 665
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Family recipes are passed down through the generations and the film "Grandma's Hands" focuses on six Southern Maryland individuals who cherish those recipes.Historic Sotterley held a screening and panel discussion with the stars of the film along with writer, executive producer, director and narrator Craig Sewell on Nov. 13 at the museum in Hollywood.
"This was a passion project for me," said Sewell. "Kitchens are magic places, whether they're commercial kitchens or home kitchens, because it's about where everything happens. It's where smiles happen and tears happen and stories happen and the aromas happen. Kitchens are places where people come together."
The 58-minute film was funded through a Maryland Heritage Areas Authority grant and filmed by the Southern Maryland National Heritage Area.
"Ask someone about their grandmother and chances are the story will quickly end up in the kitchen. And once there, the real story begins," Sewell said to open the film. "Lives change, but the food will always be with us. Food is powerful. It nourishes our bodies, it excites our tastes, it is infused and marinated in emotion and it provides us with a solid connection to our past. For generations our grandma's hands have made memories, continued traditions and blessed us with the knowledge of who we are."
The film stars six individuals who recreate their grandmother's recipes: Lexington Park's Teandre Thompson (bread pudding), Waldorf's Mary Louise Booth Webb (crackling bread), Newburg's Tiffany Barber (tomato sauce with meatballs), Benedict's Franklin A. Robinson (chili sauce), Greenbelt's LaWann Stribling (macaroni and cheese) and Lothian's Kayla Griffith (sweet potato pancakes).
Thompson said her grandmother Theresa Young would create "a masterpiece dessert using a few ingredients and her hands. She didn't use measuring cups and spoons; she did it just by sight. I'm not that daring yet."
The 98-year-old Webb, who cooked the dish in her grandmother's farm kitchen located near Zekiah Swamp, said it was made as a way to use everything of the pig.
Robinson, who lives at Serenity Farm, said his grandmother would make the sauce at the end of the tobacco harvest.
"For me these recipes are a way of keeping all of these people I've known alive," Robinson said. "Every time I open the cookbook, I remember my grandmother at her wood stove and my other grandmother who lived on another farm. It's remembering them and honoring them."
Barber, who lives on Grace Haven Farm, said her grandmother would take Wonder bread, slather it with the sauce and layer it with Parmesan cheese.
"My grandmother's recipes were the center of my childhood," Barber, who still uses her grandmother's cast iron skillet, said in the film, "and it's something I carry forward with my kids."
Barber said dinner at her two-table dining room — which is essential for eight children and five grandchildren — "became that place where you learned to express yourself, having conversations about what matters to you and those connections. Dinner matters, meals matter. It's the connection you build around that meal."
Griffith, who lives on the family farm, said her grandmother Lillian would make pancakes with chocolate chips, whipped cream, sprinkles, "the whole nine yards"
"She could not sit down for more than a minute or two," she added. "She would get up, make sure everyone had something on their plate. To most of us she would say, 'You don't have enough,' but [to my grandfather it would be] 'Earl, you're eating too much.'"
The film viewing earlier this month was the season finale of Historic Sotterley's Common Ground series.
"Throughout the peninsula that is Southern Maryland, people have gathered, cooked for centuries," Sewell says in the opening minutes of the film. "The recipes are messengers from whence we came. Food and recipes can divide a family, a region, even a culture."
Maryland Public Television will air a 27-minute version of the film — focusing on three of the cooks — at 7 p.m. Saturday, Nov. 23.
The hour-long version of the film will premiere on mpt.org, pbs.org and the PBS app starting on Sunday, Nov. 24.
Find out more about the film at destinationsouthernmaryland.com/discover/grandmas-hands.

title: Wolves arrive at Wilmer Park
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Wolves arrive at Wilmer Park

 November 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Entertainment 
 
 315
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Wolves have arrived at Wilmer Park to art lovers and residents' anticipation. "The Wolves" created in 2000 by Sally Matthews is the 16th sculpture from the Peter and Hanna Woicke collection, and can be seen at Wilmer Park in front of Aunt Sarah's Playground.According to Elizabeth Healy of the Chestertown Public Arts Committee, they were installed in the afternoon of Nov. 13, overseen by Dave Hegland, acting chairman of the Committee, after being stored for minor stability repairs at the Woicke's property in St. Michaels.
Hegland pointed out, the sculpture was repaired and conserved by Howard Wellman of Wellman Conservation and his team, then were de-installed and palletized for transport by Howard Wellman and Ben Herr of Anthony's Flowers and Landscaping.
According to Hegland, the work was well worth it.
Back in early September, he told the Chestertown Council the wolves were one of the most highly anticipated of their pieces.
He later told the Kent News, "This has been our most anticipated sculpture and in the short time since its installation we have seen adults and children enjoy the thrill and mystery of these life size sculptures walking in the tree line at Wilmer Park."
There are five wolves, each weighing 350 lbs., rugged and lifelike from a distance; bronze snouts pointing towards the water, trekking through fallen leaves.
Up-close you see their craftsmanship and appeal.
And very shortly, the wolves will be joined by the next sculpture, Durbar. The sculpture weighs approximately 3500 lbs and is about 15 ft tall, to be installed in the South East corner in Bailey Park. The complex structure will be disassembled and reassembled by an art team.
Durbar will set on a concrete pad installed by the Chestertown Streets and Public Works Department, Hegland said.
The Peter and Hannah Woike Collection consists of 23 outdoor sculptures which are diverse in style, subject matter and origin. For more information about Chestertown Public Art go to chestertownpublicarts.com/.

title: Mid-Shore Community Band celebrates differences
author: Tom McCall
content:
Mid-Shore Community Band celebrates differences

 November 21, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Tom McCall | Section: Local News 
 
 476
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Copper timpani, sliding trombones, heraldic trumpets and a focused baton are just some of the instruments making up the 45-member Mid-Shore Community Band. Band Leader Matt Fullerton keeps all the moving pieces in order.The band brought its music to Thompson Park on Nov. 9 during the Waterfowl Festival, and band members commanded a range from flutes to thundering drums.
But the most significant diversity the band exhibits is not in its musical abilities, but in the ages of its members.
Members of the band range from high schoolers to those in their upper 70s. There are people from all different walks of life who come together to make music.
"We do this because we love music. If nothing else it is therapy. No, it is a lot of fun," Fullerton said.
Fullerton has been conducting since 1975 and has a masters in music. He taught the band at Easton Middle school for 30 years. He said he can play most of the instruments in the band.
Tracie Thomas, who plays clarinet, has been in the band since its founding in 2009.
"One of the best parts is getting to play with my old musical director from middle school, Matt Fullerton," she said. "Just being able to play is the best part. We generally have a season, and we will have a repertoire for the season that we select for each concert. Of course we already have Christmas music out. We have started rehearsing for that."
She said they have everything from jazzy Christmas to sleigh ride Christmas music.
"We really try hard to be a part of the community. Our band is here to serve other nonprofits like we are today. Every concert we have played is no charge and often raising money for another organization. Everybody here is volunteering their time," Thomas said.
There was also a vast expanse of musical choices on display at the Nov. 9 concert, including a theme from the Disney film Fantasia "Night On Bald Mountain," a medley of computer gaming songs, a march and a hoedown.
"It includes themes from Assassin 33, 'Bratja' from Full Metal Alchemist, 'Dragon Born' from Skyrims, 'Sadness and Sorrow' from Naruto and 'Baba Yetu' from Civilization 4," Fullerton said of the gaming medley.
He noted that Hollywood used to produce most music, but the successful gaming industry is paying composers to make the digital worlds come alive.
"The same backing that creates that, as they do for themes for movies. It is possible that more people hear these than some of the pieces more than some of the movie themes," Fullerton said.
Of course the band also played a crisp "Star Spangled Banner" and got the crowd on their feet.
They practice at the Easton High band room every Tuesday at 7 p.m. They always looking for new players, even if they haven't dusted off their tuba in 10 years. To learn more, visit mscb.org.

title: Allegra Women's Chorus produces moving program
author: JOHN MALIN Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Allegra Women's Chorus produces moving program

 November 22, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JOHN MALIN Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Music 
 
 187
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Allegra Women's Chorus, an integral part of the Allegro Academy, is rapidly becoming a choral force to reckon with on the Eastern Shore.Directed and conducted by Amy Morgan, on Nov. 17, the 13 female voices with piano and cello accompaniment produced a very musical and emotive program of 12 songs set upon a theme of nature, life relationships, experiences, sadness and joy within the community of mothers and daughters.
From the words of William Wordsworth in 1798 and music by Elaine Hagenburg to the words and music of Bob Dylan from 1963, the program was creative and moved from melancholy to joy.
St Paul's Pilgrim Holiness Church in Oxford with its wonderful interior and stained glass windows provided an excellent backdrop and sound stage for the concert.
The choir has an impressive range of very talented voices. Under the direction of Morgan, they produced really beautiful multipart harmonies and solos from the softest lullabies to powerful crescendos seemingly impossible for such few voices.
The Allegro Academy is certainly delivering on its mission to "bring exceptional music education and performance opportunities for all" and in doing so enriching our lives.
