title: Art teacher Bridget Whited gets 2024 Fine Arts Award
author: Staff Writer
content:
Art teacher Bridget Whited gets 2024 Fine Arts Award

 November 26, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Life 
 
 241
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Talbot County Retired School Personnel Association Fine Arts Committee Chair Elizabeth Wildasin awarded the organization's 2024 Fine Arts Award to Bridget Whited, the Saint Michaels Middle High School Visual Art Educator, during the group's autumn luncheon.Whited has taught there for the past 17 years. She believes that "art is for everyone" and emphasizes this when connecting programs and lessons with service learning and collaboration among students and the surrounding community.
Currently, she is the AP studio art educator and the National Art Honor Society sponsor. In 2014-2015, Whited was honored as the Talbot County Public Schools Teacher of the Year and was a state finalist. Most recently, she received the Maryland Art Education Association Advocate for Inclusivity Through Art Award, which highlighted her dedication to making visual art accessible to all.
Whited is a Talbot County resident, is married and has two young children.
"She is very deserving of the TCRSPA Fine Arts Award, and we look forward to seeing her for many more years teaching her students and encouraging their creativity," the organization said in a press release. "We are thrilled to present our 2024 Fine Arts Award to her."
TCRSPA celebrated its 60th birthday this year. The organization's primary purpose is informing school retirees and protecting their local and state benefits, providing special social events to socialize with former colleagues, and strengthening participation in community activities. It welcomes retired faculty, administrators and staff to inquire about membership.
For more information, contact jkohn@goeaston.net.

title: Gala at Kennard honors former educators
author: Staff Writer
content:
Gala at Kennard honors former educators

 November 29, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 855
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Queen Anne's County Commissioners have pledged $50,000 in funding for each of the next three years to Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center and Museum (KAACHC), while building upon the $140,000 they received from the African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund, to support the hiring of an executive director to manage their programs and operations. The first installment of the county's pledge, a $50,000 check, was presented to Clay Washington, president of the Kennard Alumni Association Board of Directors, on Nov. 9, at the Kennard Gala Luncheon and Raffle event. The check was presented by County Commissioners Jim Moran and Chris Corchiarino."We are incredibly proud of the work the Kennard Alumni Association has done to preserve and celebrate African American heritage in Queen Anne's County," Moran said. "The Kennard Center has grown into a vital resource for our community, providing educational and cultural opportunities that truly make a difference. We are excited to continue supporting their mission and to see how this new funding will help expand their programs even further. The County Commissioners are committed to ensuring the success of the Kennard Center and look forward to partnering with them for many years to come."
The county assisted the Kennard Alumni Association in applying for and securing a $140,000 grant from the National Trust for Historic Preservation's African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund.
The former high school building served as Queen Anne's County's only all-Black segregated high school until segregation ended in 1966, and integration took place within the county with the opening of Queen Anne's County High School in 1967.
Left in disrepair, continuing to disintegrate over the years, a motion was made to have the former school building razed. Former alumni of the school began fundraising efforts to have the building restored instead. The efforts were led by Kennard Alumni Association President Clayton Washington, formerly of Grasonville. Washington was persistent, organizing and planning for over 15 years, until donations and grants were obtained to begin the literal renovation process.
With restoration completed several years ago, the building was dedicated in 2019. A number of events have been held there since, and the building is open to the public for rental for special private celebrations and uses.
The next big step is to hire the Kennard AAHMCC executive director.
Washington said, "We have information for applying for the position listed on our website, kennardheritage.com . We've already received a couple applications, and hope to begin interviewing people within the next 30-days. It's hoped we will have someone hired to begin work by January 1, 2025."
The KAACHC is one of only 30 sites nationwide to receive funding from the African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund, which awarded a total of $3 million to historic sites representing Black cultural heritage. KAACHC has become a hub for African American history programs, exhibits, and community events in Queen Anne's County. With more than $140 million raised to date, the Action Fund is the largest U.S. resource dedicated to preserving African American historic places.
Since its establishment, KAACHC has played a vital role in providing educational and cultural learning opportunities, in Queen Anne's County. The center offers a variety of programs, including after-school mentoring, exercise classes, and summer camps for youth with special needs. With the hiring of a dedicated executive director, the center plans to expand its offerings to include adult literacy, STEM education, cultural arts, and more.
The Kennard Center is poised to become an even greater asset to Queen Anne's County, fostering connections within the community and preserving African American heritage for future generations.
Also, during the Nov. 9 program, Washington recognized and honored three former Kennard High School educators, Dr. Velma Kennedy Speight, Madelyn Matthews Hollis, and Alveta Smith Jones. Each had extensive careers in education, going well beyond teaching at Kennard.
Speight went on the teach several universities in Maryland, after serving as guidance counselor at Queen Anne's County High School. She was director of alumni affairs at North Carolina A & T University, where she had earned her bachelor's degree. Her service there was so profound, the university named one of the dormitories "Speight Hall".
Hollis transferred to QACHS where she taught until she retired, after teaching in the county for over 30-years. She then served on the county's Board of Education. Hollis was amazed that before segregation ended, African Americans could not try on clothes in stores when buying them, and personal mail could not be delivered to African American homes — they had to go to the post office to get their mail. She was a force in the community to see that the Kennard H.S. building was not torn down, but was restored to further serve the community.
Even as a child growing up on the Eastern Shore, Jones dreamed of becoming a teacher. She began her teaching career at Kennard in 1947, Jones also taught overseas, teaching sixth graders while living in Istanbul, Turkey. She then returned to teach in Prince George's County Maryland Public Schools until she retired in 1981. She, Speight and Hollis have been loyal friends all of their adult lives.
Washington presented all three ladies with plaques thanking them for their dedication to serving in education.

 The Academy Art Museum in Easton has announced the winners of its annual Members' Exhibition.The exhibition is open now and runs through Dec. 29.
The museum's annual Members' Exhibition "invites artists to submit imaginative, traditional, and experimental works in any medium," according to an announcement. Many of the pieces in the exhibition are for sale and can be purchased.
This year's juror is Robyn Asleson, curator of prints and drawings at the Smithsonian Institution's National Portrait Gallery.
"Her exhibition projects at the Portrait Gallery include "Brilliant Exiles: American Women in Paris, 1900–1939" (2024), the team-curated "Kinship" (2022), and "Portraits of the World" (2016-20), a series of spotlight exhibitions featuring individual portraits on loan from international museums, placed in conversation with works from the Portrait Gallery collection. She was also venue curator for the exhibition "John Singer Sargent: Portraits in Charcoal" (2020)," According to AAM.
AAM is hosting the exhibition at the Waterfowl Building (40 S. Harrison Street)
in downtown Easton. Hours for the exhibition are Tuesday and Wednesday, 10 a.m. — 4 p.m., Thursday (Dec. 12 and 19) 10 a.m — 7 pm, Friday, 10 a.m. — 4 p.m., Saturday and Sunday, 12 p.m. — 4 p.m. Closed Mondays, and December 24 through 26.

title: Festival of Trees brings holiday cheer, hope to Talbot County
author: KENIA ITZEP Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Festival of Trees brings holiday cheer, hope to Talbot County

 December 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KENIA ITZEP Special to the Star Democrat | Section: Local News 
 
 370
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Tidewater Inn's Gold Ballroom was once again transformed into a warm winter wonderland for the 39th annual Festival of Trees. Over 100 beautifully adorned trees, small and large, captured the spirit of the season while supporting a cause close to the community's heart — raising funds for Talbot Hospice."The festival has grown exponentially over the years," said Karla Wieland-Cherry, chairman of the Festival of Trees. Since its inception in 1986, the event has raised over $4.7 million, providing critical funding for Talbot Hospice's operating budget.
This year's festival featured 50 beautifully decorated trees sponsored by individuals and businesses, as well as 50 smaller trees, ranging in size from 12 to 36 inches, available for purchase. Each display reflects the creativity and care of the decorators, many of whom return year after year.
One such decorator, Andrea Tull Wilson, has been contributing her talents for 15 years and now includes her two sons in the tradition. This year, their tree's theme is "A Cup of Cocoa," capturing the warmth and comfort of the season.
The festivities began with a formal gala on Friday night, setting a celebratory tone for the weekend. On Saturday morning, attendees participated in a pet-friendly 5K Fun Run/Walk, while that evening brought the magical "Candles by the Candlelight" event. Spectators joined in singing carols by candlelight, sipping hot cocoa and enjoying seasonal treats.
The highlight of the event remains the Festival of Trees itself, with this year's theme, "Holiday Traditions," inspiring creativity and community spirit. Volunteers worked tirelessly to craft each tree's unique display, making the ballroom a true holiday showcase.
Throughout the festival, visitors enjoyed holiday-themed performances by local musicians and artists, while festive gifts were available for purchase. Families made cherished memories in the Garden Room, where children decorated ornaments and shared their Christmas wishes with Santa Claus.
Since its founding, Friends of Hospice has worked tirelessly year-round to support hospice patients and their families through the Festival of Trees, ensuring that the hospice "does not turn anyone away," regardless of their insurance or ability to pay, as Wieland-Cherry emphasized.
Proceeds from the event directly support hospice services, providing compassionate care for those facing life-limiting illnesses.
To learn more about the Festival of Trees and Talbot Hospice, visit festival-of-trees.org.

title: Explore Maryland: A Tuba Christmas returns
author: Staff Writer
content:
Explore Maryland: A Tuba Christmas returns

 December 5, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 527
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In what has become a growing tradition both locally and nationally, the Solomons will host the annual Tuba Christmas Saturday, Dec. 14, where onlookers will be treated to a free concert that features a set list of nearly a dozen Christmas favorites performed by tuba and euphonium players of all ages.Among the primary local events planned Dec. 14 at the Our Lady Star of the Sea in Solomons is a rehearsal slated from 11 a.m. to noon followed by an hour-long concert set to commence at 1 pm. In all, roughly a dozen songs will be performed by musicians whose expertise is either the tuba or euphonium and the event is free for audience members of all ages.
According to the set list provided by organizers of the Tuba Christmas, "Adeste Fidelis" will open the proceedings and then will be followed by "Deck The Halls," "God Rest Ye Merry Gentlemen," "The First Noel," "It Came Upon A Midnight Clear," "O Little Town of Bethlehem" and about a dozen other songs before the musicians can take a graceful bow for the audience.
Conceived exactly 50 years ago in 1974 by Harvey Phillips as a tribute to his teacher and mentor, William J. Bell, who was born on Christmas Day in 1902, the inaugural Tuba Christmas was conducted by Paul Lavalle in the heart of New York City on the famed Rockefeller Center Ice Rink on Dec. 22 half a century ago. Bell is considered a legend in the musical field and this even annually honors his legacy and numerous great artists, according to information provided by Tuba Christmas organizers.
Coincidentally, the first Tuba Christmas featured music arranged by American composer Alec Wilder, who passed away almost exactly six years later on Christmas Eve in 1980. Bell's legacy was honed by years of professional integrity, personal values and a camaraderie envied by thousands of other instrumentalists, regardless of their chosen instrument preference.
Like Bell, Wilder has a reputation that has long outlived him. Although he passed away nearly 45 years ago and one day before his music celebration reached an annual zenith, Wilder is still remembered for his work composing many solo and ensemble compositions for tuba and euphonium. He was also a loyal supporter of every effort to improve the literature and public image of various brass instruments.
Part of the celebration of the 51st Tuba Christmas celebrates Wilder's memory and genius and offers performers in this concert in particular to express their respect and gratitude to all composers who continue to embrace the inherent value of brass instruments through their compositions and allows them the chance to contribute to the solo and ensemble repertoire for tuba and euphonium.
If you go
Tuba Christmas in Solomons will take place Saturday, Dec. 14, beginning at 1 p.m. at the Our Lady Star Of The Sea, located at 225 Alexander Lane. Tuba and euphonium players of all ages are invited to attend, with the registration for players slated for 10:30 a.m. and a fee of $10 is required.
The hour-long concert, which features a set list of nearly a dozen Christmas favorites, is free to audience members. For more information, contact Brian Brown at 443-404-1098 or brownbl@comcast.net.

title: Bringing Latino Christmas traditions to Oxford
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Bringing Latino Christmas traditions to Oxford

 December 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Local News 
 
 347
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — The Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center hosted a Posada Navideña, a Mexican Christmas tradition of community and song, on Friday evening at the Oxford Community Center. The event provided new experiences to Eastern Shore natives and a piece of home to those missing their native countries during the holidays.Posada Navideña involves people, often children, gathering outside and going door-to-door singing Spanish holiday songs in order to reenact the Christian story of Mary and Joseph seeking shelter for the birth of Jesus.
In certain areas in Mexico, people will provide the singers with treats while they listen to the songs. The singers will sing around the neighborhood before going to one house that has food and warm treats awaiting them.
Victoria Gomez Lozano, deputy director of the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center, said this was the first time the center has hosted a Posada and hopes to continue the tradition in upcoming years.
"I think the reason, as with any other activities that we are organizing here, is just so our clients can have a little piece of their countries," Gomez Lozano said. "Some of the traditions that we would like to keep and maintain, so maybe they can also feel at home."
Gomez Lozano said the event received a lot of support from Oxford neighbors who eagerly awaited the crowd of singers to reach their homes.
Throughout the Posada, people of all ages enjoyed the event and especially enjoyed the various treats including tamales, champurrado (a chocolate-based thick drink made with corn flour), chuchitos (Guatemalan tamales), apple Christmas salad, fruit salad, cookies, coffee and apple cider.
The evening provided attendees the opportunity to give back. Gomez Lozano said a table at the event held handmade ornaments that could be purchased through a donation.
The donations will benefit the center's after-school program. People also could sponsor a child of the program for a year. Sponsorships will give the donor an ornament, a thank you card from the child sponsored and a tour of the after-school program.
Gomez Lozano said ornaments still are available. Those interested can call the Chesapeake Multicultural Resource Center for more information.

title: Celebrate Kwanzaa at the Anacostia Community Museum
author: Staff Writer
content:
Celebrate Kwanzaa at the Anacostia Community Museum

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 535
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Smithsonian's Anacostia Community Museum is celebrating the seven days of Kwanzaa with performances, storytelling, and craft and dance workshops. The museum has welcomed the local community to celebrate Kwanzaa for over 50 years, and it will debut archival images of past celebrations with a nightly display on the museum's façade from Dec. 19 to Jan. 2, 2025."The Smithsonian's Anacostia Community Museum has been celebrating Kwanzaa since the early 1970s," Melanie Adams, director of the museum, said. "Museums are spaces for personal reflection and shared connections, and we encourage the community to join us throughout each of the seven days, as we gather family, friends and neighbors to learn, reflect and share."
Activities connect to the theme of each day: Umoja (Unity), Kujichagulia (Self-Determination), Ujima (Collective Work and Responsibility), Ujamaa (Cooperative Economics), Nia (Purpose), Kuumba (Creativity) and Imani (Faith). Visitors of all ages can take part in the free festivities. Each event takes place from noon to 2 p.m. A full schedule is below:
Thursday, Dec. 26 — Kwanzaa Opening Ceremony, Umoja (Unity)
The weeklong celebration kicks off with this afternoon gathering, uniting families and communities. Storyteller and griot Mama Ayo leads the traditional candle-lighting ceremony, pours the libation honoring ancestors and shares the history of Kwanzaa. Taratibu Youth Association, a performing arts group for the youth of the African diaspora, will follow. Registration is requested.
Friday, Dec. 27 — Family Workshop, Kujichagulia (Self-Determination)
A family workshop led by Jessica "Culture Queen" Hebron, a Grammy-nominated teaching artist and children's musician, will encourage self-determination through affirmations, song, dance and hands-on activities. Registration is requested.
Saturday, Dec. 28 — Verbal Gymnastics Workshop, Ujima (Collective Work and Responsibility)
This live interactive storytelling workshop will honor those have inspired visitors' lives, prompting visitors to share stories of their personal heroes. The theater company Verbal Gymnastics will then play back these stories with actors and musicians. Registration is requested.
Sunday, Dec. 29 — Memory Box Craft Workshop, Ujamaa (Cooperative Economics)
Families will decorate and fill their own memory box in this arts and crafts workshop led by artist Tamara Thomas. Participants are encouraged to bring their own photos and trinkets. Thomas will also lead an Ujamaa vision project, discussing what is needed in local communities and the benefits of having a family or community business. Registration is recommended, but not required.
Monday, Dec. 30 — African Dance Workshop, Nia (Purpose)
African cultures imbue every dance with purpose, from rites of passage to communing with the spiritual world. Khepera Wellness, a community-oriented yoga studio, will celebrate Nia through this African Dance Workshop, guiding participants through intentional movements. Registration is recommended but not required.
Tuesday, Dec. 31 — Family Kwanzaa Bag Workshop, Kuumba (Creativity)
Local artist Rain will lead families in this arts and crafts workshop creating and decorating family Kwanzaa bags. The bags can be used in many ways, including carrying handmade Kwanzaa gifts or the fruits of the harvest. Registration recommended but not required.
Wednesday, Jan. 1, 2025 — Spiritual Dance Workshop, Imani (Faith)
A performance and workshop on miming and liturgical dance guided by Crazee Praize starts the new year. Landle and Antoinette Jones will then lead a discussion on what gifts and talents keep participants hopeful despite life's challenges. Registration recommended but not required.
For more information about the Anacostia museum, visit www.si.edu/newsdesk/anacostia-community-museum.

title: 'So many sources of inspiration if we just look”:New art gallery celebrates inspiration
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
'So many sources of inspiration if we just look”:New art gallery celebrates inspiration

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Entertainment 
 
 507
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Showcasing a world of inspiration around us, Stevensville's newest gallery and art studio Abstract Truth held an official gallery opening Nov. 29.A retired architect, gallery artist Ray Moldenhauer, of Grasonville, focuses his attention on creating abstract paintings and sculptures with dimension, noting "art is a natural extension of architecture."
Outgrowing his previous space at My Little Studio, Moldenhauer remarked the new location is proving to be a blessing.
Leaning into layers in his art as well as in his gallery, Moldenhauer designed the space to take full advantage of the existing glass enclosed cubicles and provide natural light.
By staggering the paintings from one cubicle to another, the gallery visually takes on a special 3D experience from one space to another. Many of the paintings are mounted back to back on the glass to create an allusion of them floating in the space, according to Moldenhauer.
"At night, the extensive front glass wall of the building just glows and reflects the beautiful artwork within," he said.
"I love the idea of flowing paintings," he said.
Moldenhauer utilizes many different creative techniques for his work. From traditional brushes and sponges, to business cards to even finger painting, Moldenhauer isn't afraid to try something new with his inspiration. Moldenhauer also incorporates resin, cellophane, and even foam to create something completely new.
For Moldenhauer it is the inspiration behind each artwork that brings forth its beauty and meaning and makes it "more than just another landscape or sunset."
Moldenhauer's work typically starts with a Bible verse and lets his inspiration guide his hand, for instance, Moldenhauer sculptures based on the Pillars of Creation present an abstract look of the universe.
As an accomplished SCUBA diver, Moldenhauer also finds inspiration in the natural world of water, sunsets and sunrises.
Moldenhauer also takes inspiration from the surrounding Eastern Shore, has also incorporated his love of the Eastern Shore into his work.
His very first sculpture "Be Still" repurposed an old sailboat skeg and was selected for the Maryland Federation of Art's Off The Walls 2024 exhibition.
According to Moldenhauer Abstract Truths are works that, "in some way, reveal God," and each art piece has a corresponding Bible verse accompaniment for patrons to take to heart.
For artists just starting out, Moldenhauer encouraged finding inspiration around you in what you enjoy doing and where you enjoy being.
"There are so many sources of inspiration if we just look," he said.
Moldenhauer welcomes everyone to discover the work for themselves, noting the studio gallery isn't for the purpose of business or making money, "it's about sharing art," he said.
Moving forward, Moldenhauer looks to collaborate and connect with the surrounding art community and plans to eventually have rotating monthly artists featured and juried art exhibits.
Abstract Truths is located in the Stevensville Art and Entertainment District at 214 Island Plaza Court. and typically open Monday, Wednesday and Friday from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m.
Special showings are available by appointment at 410-490-6302.
Moldenhauer is an award winning abstract artist and Maryland Federation of Art juried exhibitor. He is also a Christian author and music writer with a Youtube channel and Instagram account.

title: Santa's Workshop in the Land of Misfits continues next 2 Saturdays in Denton
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Santa's Workshop in the Land of Misfits continues next 2 Saturdays in Denton

 December 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 437
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Children gathered at the Wharves of Choptank Visitor & Heritage Center on Saturday for an afternoon full of crafts, wooden toys, painting and more as the holidays quickly approach.In an event put on by the Caroline County Council of Arts and The Foundry, its art gallery, children were welcomed to build their own toys, greet Santa and meet the Grinch. Two more Santa's Workshop in the Land of Misfits Saturdays are scheduled: Dec. 14 and Dec. 21 from noon to 4 p.m.
Caroline County Council of Arts Executive Director George Karos said the event is a "fun way to celebrate the holidays."
"Everyone can make art and spend time with loved ones — especially a win-win as proceeds go towards supporting local youth programs and spreading holiday cheer," Karos said in an emailed statement.
Megan Krizovensky, program manager for Caroline County Council of Arts, said in an interview that last weekend's event was a success. It's the first time the art organization put on Santa's Workshop.
"It was pretty good," Krizovenksy said of Saturday's turnout. "I know the first week we expected to be a little slower. But we actually had at least 50 children there, and we were prepared for over 100. So we're hoping that (Dec. 14 and Dec. 21) can pick it up much bigger just for the kid's sake."
Last Saturday, the Chesapeake Culinary Center participated in the event and donated cookies and cocoa. Krizovenksy said Earth Tones Cafe will be donating food for this Saturday.
Additionally, students from Caroline County Public Schools are volunteering, gaining student service learning hours. The first-time event runs fully on donations, Krizovenksy added.
"The event is completely donation-based with all proceeds going to support local youth programs through the Caroline County Council of Arts," she said.
Krizovensky said local artist Steve Mead, formerly the board treasurer for the arts council, was integral in the event's formulation.
The hope is that Santa's Workshop can continue in the future, with some of this year's proceeds working to fund a second annual Santa's Workshop. Registration is free with a suggested donation of $15 per child.
"The goal is to create a magical experience for kids who otherwise might not have a great holiday," Krizovenksy said. "We want to make sure that it's free. Our mission is to enrich the community through the arts, and Caroline County itself is a unique place anyway with a lot of deep-rooted tradition. So we're trying to create authentic experiences that reflect and celebrate the spirit of that community."
To register for Dec. 14 or Dec. 21, sign up at carolinearts.org/events/santas-workshop-in-the-island-of-misfit-toys/ or visit The Foundry Art Gallery at 401 Market St. in Denton.

title: St. Michaels’ Gingerbread Competition is back to spice up holiday celebration
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
St. Michaels’ Gingerbread Competition is back to spice up holiday celebration

 December 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: Christmas 
 
 412
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — Dozens of gingerbread designers are competing for one of several cash prizes and for the admiration of the community this weekend.The St. Michaels' gingerbread competition is back in full swing after a nearly five-year hiatus. An array of intricately built gingerbread houses will be on show this weekend at the St. Micheals Woman's Club for the Gingerbread "House" Competition and Display.
Proceeds from the sale of these creations support the beneficiaries of Christmas in St. Michaels, including family service organizations, education and child development programs, and community enhancement organizations and programs.
Michele Lowe and Andrea Robinson, co-chairs of the Gingerbread Committee, both said they were fairly new to the area and heard of a St. Michaels gingerbread competition but had never witnessed it themselves.
Lowe said the memory of the competition was incredibly strong among the community and Lowe and Robinson felt a need to step up and bring back the beloved tradition.
"Everybody has been wanting this back since (2019)," Lowe said. "I guess we finally got coerced, and it's been a great success. We had a lot of the donations from the St Michael's Community Center, Critchlow Adkins (Children's Centers), who are also both beneficiaries."
Lowe mentioned that a young girl in the area, who last competed in 2019, had been eagerly awaiting and planning new designs for when the competition came back.
The gingerbread entries are divided into seven categories with cash prize awards. The categories cater to different skill levels and ages, including Master with a $500 prize and Adult with $300 first prize.
Additionally, there are categories for younger participants including young adults with a $100 prize, and children with and without an adult with a $100 prize for the respective categories.
Finally, there are categories for nonprofit organizations, Candy Backus Award (best depiction of the Eastern Shore) and a People's Choice Award.
Judges for the gingerbread competition include Commissioners of St. Michaels President Alfred Mercier, President and CEO of the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum Kristen Greenaway and St. Michaels Police Chief Jeffrey Oswald.
Prizes will be awarded on Sunday at the Woman's Club of St. Michaels at 2 p.m.
Robinson said she is happy with the support they have received this year and encourages people to continue their support into the new year.
"Thank you for your support, and please make gingerbread at home next year," Robinson said. "In order for us to keep doing this we need everybody to be excited next year and participate and start planning their creation for next year."

title: Country Cooking: treats to keep kids occupied
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: treats to keep kids occupied

 December 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1240
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I am sure your major shopping is completed, menus planned, gifts wrapped and that final grocery list waiting to be completed.However, the children are out of school and the excitement is mounting. I have a few suggestions to help keep them busy.
Before that I have a recipe from the past I want to include. My mother loved making pies, and one of her favorites for the Christmas holidays was always mincemeat pie.
HOMEMADE MINCEMEAT PIEPie crust, 4 cups peeled chopped apples, 1 1/2 cups diced cooked beef, 1 1/2 cups raisins, 1 1/2 cups white sugar, 1 cup beef broth, 1 large orange (peeled, sectioned, seeds removed and cut into small bite size pieces), 1/2 cup molasses, 1/4 cup sweet pickle juice, 1/2 cup pineapple juice, 1 tsp ground cinnamon, 1 tsp ground nutmeg, 1/2 tsp ground cloves and 1/2 tsp salt.
This recipe will make two 9-inch pies. Prepare enough crust for bottom and a top crust for two 9-inch pie plates and sit aside. If you only want to make one, just store the extra mincemeat filling in the refrigerator for later use. In a large bowl combine apples, beef, raisins, sugar, beef broth, orange, molasses, pickle juice, pineapple juice, cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves and salt. Mix well and let sit in the refrigerator for at least 30 minutes before placing in pie shells. Preheat the oven at 375 degrees. Place pie shells full, place top crust on, cutting slits in crust. Bake for at least 30 mins. Serve warm. I must tell you that this recipe is somewhat modern, as the recipe from the '40s and '50s used hog meat and whiskey for flavor.
I must tell this story that we siblings still laugh about. When mom made her mincemeat, she would have our farm worker go to the liquor store and get her a half pint of whiskey, and she hid it until ready to use. That day when he gave Mom the whiskey, she placed it in the oven in a small pot. Forgetting this, the next morning she preheats the oven and before she can put the pan of biscuits in, the bottle of whiskey explodes. The stove had to be completely taken apart and the whiskey smell lingered for days. Mom was teased for many years about this.
I have some fun making yummy treats for the kids to help you make. Before we start that portion of the column let me suggest some fun projects for the kids to help past the time.
Purchase a packet of the white paper placemats (no design) and plenty of crayons. Have the kids design placemats for the dinner table, making plenty to use throughout the holiday. Make a contest, and upon completion each child gets a candy cane with everyone being the winner.Take some old Christmas cards/paper from last year, cut and paste the designs on large file cards, write a message and drop them off to shut-ins and nursing homes. Or do a special batch for those serving our country, the first responders in your area and anyone working this holiday.
CHRISTMAS CHEX MIX6 cups cereal, 3 cups of Rice Chex and 3 cups Corn Chex cereal (Store brand works just as well); 2 cups miniature marshmallows; 1 cup mini pretzel twists; 15 oz vanilla candy coating (about 9 cubes from 20-oz package); 3 tbsps holiday-colored sprinkles or nonpareils; 1/4 cup powdered sugar; 1 cup holiday-colored M&M'S.
Line a large rimmed cookie sheet with waxed paper. In a large bowl, mix cereal, marshmallows and pretzels. In a medium microwavable bowl, microwave candy coating uncovered on High 60 to 90 seconds, stirring after 1 minute, until almost melted. Stir until smooth. Pour onto cereal mixture; mix well. Spread on cookie sheet; sprinkle with holiday sprinkles, and cool completely, about 15 minutes. Break into bite-size pieces. In 2-gallon resealable food-storage plastic bag, add coated cereal pieces and powdered sugar. Seal bag; shake to coat. Remove from bag; discard any remaining powdered sugar. In large serving bowl, mix coated cereal mixture and M&M'S.
CRACKER SNACK-WHICHES48 round buttery crackers (such as Ritz), 8 Swiss cheese slices (cut into 1-inch squares, divided), 8 Black Forest deli ham slices (each cut into three equal strips about 1 1/2-in. wide), 1/4 cup red pepper jelly (such as Braswell's), 2 tbsps unsalted butter (melted), 1 tsp Dijon mustard, 1 tsp Worcestershire sauce, 1/2 tsp everything bagel seasoning, 1/4 tsp garlic powder, 6 cornichons (halved lengthwise and crosswise optional).
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Arrange 24 of the crackers, top sides down, on a large parchment paper-lined rimmed baking sheet; top each cracker with 1 piece of cheese and 1 strip of ham, folding ham strip into thirds and lightly pressing down. Layer each ham strip with 1/2 teaspoon pepper jelly and another piece of cheese. Top with remaining 24 crackers, top sides up, to form a sandwich. Stir together melted butter, Dijon mustard, Worcestershire sauce, everything bagel seasoning, and garlic powder until combined. Brush butter mixture evenly on top of cracker sandwiches. Bake in a preheated oven until the cheese has melted and the tops are golden brown, 10 to 12 minutes. Garnish each cracker sandwich with a piece of cornichon threaded onto a wooden pick, if desired. Serve immediately.
PIGS IN A BLANKET12 beef hot dogs, 1 large egg, 1 tbsp water, 1 (17.3-oz.) pkg frozen puff pastry sheets (thawed but cold), All-purpose flour, 2 tbsps Dijon mustard (plus more for serving), 1 tbsp everything-bagel seasoning.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Line two baking sheets with parchment paper. Pat hot dogs dry using paper towels, and pierce each hot dog three times using a fork. Whisk together egg and water in a small bowl. Set aside. Roll out one puff pastry sheet on a lightly floured work surface into a 12-inch square. Cut pastry in half lengthwise; cut each half crosswise into three equal pieces. Repeat the procedure with the second puff pastry sheet. (You will have a total of 12 pieces.) Brush mustard crosswise down the center of each pastry piece; top each with one hot dog. Brush edges of pastry with egg mixture; roll up, and seal overlapping edges. Place seam side down on prepared baking sheets. Freeze until firm, about 30 minutes. Cut each log crosswise into four equal pieces, trimming ends as needed. Brush tops with remaining egg mixture, and sprinkle evenly with seasoning. Bake in a preheated oven, one baking sheet at a time, until golden brown, 20 to 25 minutes. (Keep the second baking sheet chilled until ready to bake.) Serve warm with additional mustard.
CHRISTMAS COAL1 (13 oz.) package oreos, 5 cups marshmallows, 4 tbsps (1/4 cup) unsalted butter.
Line a square baking dish with parchment paper and grease generously with non-stick spray. Also spray rubber spatula with non-stick spray. Place Oreo cookies in the food processor and pulse until finely ground. Place butter and marshmallows in a large, microwave-safe bowl and microwave for 1.5 minutes, stirring every 30 seconds with rubber spatula, until mixture is melted and smooth. Pour Oreo crumbs into marshmallow mixture and stir until everything is evenly incorporated, then press mixture (leaving the top uneven and shaggy) into a greased and lined baking dish. Let the mixture cool and set completely, then break into pieces and place in stockings or paper bag for "serving."
Note: pick up plenty of breakfast foods for next week's annual Christmas breakfast column and a bag of those black eyed peas for my annual New Year column.

Santa lights up 5th annual crab basket Christmas tree

 December 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 GRASONVILLE — The Queen Anne's County Watermen's Association hosted the fifth annual ceremonial crab basket tree lighting honoring watermen at the Crab Deck Dec. 7.Showcasing stories of the community, over 300 hand-painted crab buckets make up the trees with festive scenes unique to the Eastern Shore, commemorating local organizations, civic and school groups, and remembering loved ones lost over the years while honoring local watermen imperative to the Chesapeake Bay culture.
Carolers from Matapeake Middle School brought forth joyful holiday songs.
The Blessing of the Fleet was led by Bob Timms.
At Fisherman's Crab Deck, joyous festivities throughout the day also included a vendor fair for all holiday needs alongside food trucks, crafts and pictures with the Claus family.
The Crab Basket Holiday Trees will be on display to behold in front of the Watermen's Monument between the Crab Deck and Fisherman's Inn through mid-January.

title: Country Cooking: Breakfast on Christmas morning
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Breakfast on Christmas morning

 December 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1372
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Christmas morning has arrived finally, and the kids are having a grand time opening presents, running through the house and trying to play with the gifts all at one time. Mom is trying to keep the parts and pieces in one box while dad is trying to put Legos back in the right boxes.After a couple of hours everyone is getting hungry.
This is the time of morning when Christmas past and Christmas present comes into play. Christmas morning from my childhood is so much different from today. My mother was up Christmas morning early and had the bacon and scrapple cut and ready to fry. The biscuits were made and ready to bake.
As soon as the last gift was opened the gas stove was turned on, iron frying pans ready, oven heating up, table being set, homemade butter and jellies on the table and the big aluminum coffee pot starting to perk.
Oh my — I can still smell that Christmas morning breakfast cooking. There was not an empty chair at the table. The phone was ringing as the family called asking "is breakfast ready?"
Now times have changed, but it's just as much fun on Christmas morning with kids laughing, ripping open gifts, parents hooking up electronics, inserting gift cards in the correct gaming slots and getting air pods in the ears correctly.
Later the grandparents arrive for a breakfast brunch consisting of homemade waffles, microwave bacon and breakfast casserole dishes.
Yes, the world has changed as it does with every generation but the reason for the season is still the same, and families gather to celebrate, no matter how much is under the tree or how little.
Enjoy today's recipes to share with everyone and send some of your favorites to me at my email address so I can share with the readers (mmsavage21145@gmai.com).
PANCAKE CASSEROLECooking spray, pancakes, 6 large eggs, 1 1/2 cups heavy cream, 1 cup whole milk, 1/4 cup granulated sugar, 1 tsp vanilla bean paste, 1/4 tsp kosher salt, unsalted butter and maple syrup for serving.
Lightly coat a 13-by-9-inch baking dish with cooking spray. Arrange pancakes in a baking dish in three rows, overlapping slightly, starting at one long end. Whisk together eggs, cream, milk, sugar, vanilla and salt in a bowl. Slowly pour mixture over pancakes. Cover and refrigerate for at least 8 hours or up to overnight. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Bake the casserole, covered, in a preheated oven for 25 minutes. Uncover and continue baking until the center is set, about 25 minutes. Let stand for 5 minutes. Dot with pats of butter; drizzle with syrup.
CHEESY SAUSAGE, EGG AND HASH BROWN CASSEROLE3 tbsps olive oil (divided), 8 ounces ground pork sausage, 1 sweet onion (diced), 1 poblano chile pepper (seeded and chopped), 1 red bell pepper (seeded and chopped), 1 ½ tsps kosher salt (divided), 2 cups refrigerated diced potatoes, ¾ tsp garlic powder, 4 ounces your favorite shredded cheese (about 1 cup), 5 large eggs, ¼ cup heavy whipping cream, 1 tbsp minced fresh chives.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees with an oven rack about 6 inches from heat. Heat one tbsp of the olive oil in a 10-inch cast-iron skillet over medium-high. Add sausage. Cook, breaking up sausage into pieces with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and just cooked through, about 4 minutes. Remove sausage to a medium bowl with a slotted spoon; set aside. Do not wipe the skillet clean. Add sweet onion, poblano chile, red bell pepper and ½ tsp of the salt to the skillet. Cook over medium-high, stirring occasionally, until onion is tender and peppers have charred in spots, about 8 minutes. Remove with a slotted spoon to bowl with sausage. Wipe the skillet clean. Heat the remaining 2 tbsps of olive oil in a skillet over medium-high. Add diced potatoes to the skillet in an even layer. Cook, undisturbed, until browned on bottom, about 5 minutes. Add ½ tsp of the salt. Continue cooking, stirring occasionally, until golden brown and crispy on most sides, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat. Return sausage and pepper mixture to skillet and add garlic powder. Stir to combine. Stir in ½ cup of the cheese until just combined. Whisk together eggs, cream, and remaining ½ tsp salt in a medium bowl. Pour over mixture in skillet, and tilt pan to allow eggs to distribute. Top with remaining ½ cup each of the cheeses. Bake in a preheated oven until eggs have set and cheeses have melted, about 8 minutes. Increase oven temperature to broil, and broil until cheeses have turned golden brown, 2 to 3 minutes. Remove; let stand for 5 minutes. Sprinkle with chives. Slice and serve immediately.
BISCUITS AND GRAVY CASSEROLE1 lb ground pork sausage, 1/2 cup chopped yellow onion (from 1 small onion), 1/4 cup plus 1 tbsp unsalted butter, 1/3 cup (about 1 1/2 oz.) all-purpose flour, 3 cups whole milk, 6 oz pepper Jack cheese (shredded), 3/4 tsp kosher salt, 1/2 tsp black pepper, Cooking spray, 1 (25-oz.) pkg frozen Southern-style biscuits (such as Pillsbury Grands), 2 tbsps minced fresh chives.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Place sausage and onion in a large skillet over medium, and cook, stirring often, until sausage crumbles and is no longer pink and onion is translucent, 6 to 8 minutes. Transfer mixture to a plate lined with paper towels to drain. Wipe the skillet clean. Reduce heat to low, and add 1/4 cup of the butter to the skillet; cook, whisking often, until melted. Whisk in flour until smooth. Cook, whisking constantly, 1 minute. Gradually whisk in milk; increase heat to medium, and cook, whisking constantly, until thickened and bubbly, 5 to 6 minutes. Whisk in shredded cheese, and cook, whisking often, until cheese is melted and mixture is smooth, 30 to 40 seconds. Stir in sausage mixture, salt, and pepper.Transfer mixture to a lightly greased (with cooking spray) 13-by-9-inch baking dish. Arrange biscuits on top of sausage mixture. Bake in a preheated oven until biscuits are golden brown and gravy is bubbly, 30 to 35 minutes. Microwave remaining 1 tbsp butter in a small microwavable bowl on high until melted, about 20 seconds. Remove the casserole from the oven; brush biscuits with melted butter, and sprinkle with chives. Let stand for 10 minutes before serving.
SLOW COOKER CINNAMON ROLL CASSEROLECooking spray, 1/2 cup granulated sugar, 1/2 cup packed light brown sugar, 1 tsp ground cinnamon, 2 (16.3-oz.) cans refrigerated southern homestyle biscuits (separated and cut into fourths), 1/2 cup salted butter (melted), 2 tbsp salted butter (softened), 4 large eggs, 1/4 tsp kosher salt, 2/3 cup plus 2 to 3 tbsp half-and-half (divided), 2 tsp vanilla extract, 1/2 cup chopped toasted pecans, 1 (3-oz.) pkg. cream cheese (softened), 2 1/4 cups powdered sugar.
Line bottom and sides of a 6-quart slow cooker with aluminum foil; lightly coat foil with cooking spray. Stir together granulated sugar, brown sugar, and cinnamon in a small bowl. Toss together biscuit pieces and 1/2 cup melted butter in a large bowl until biscuits are coated. Working in batches, add biscuits to granulated sugar mixture, and toss to coat; transfer biscuits to prepared slow cooker. Sprinkle any remaining sugar mixture over biscuits in a slow cooker. Whisk together eggs, salt, 2/3 cup of the half-and-half, and 1 tsp of the vanilla in a bowl until well combined; pour over biscuits in a slow cooker. Sprinkle with pecans. Beat cream cheese and 2 tbsps softened butter with an electric mixer on medium speed until thoroughly combined, about 30 seconds. Add 1 cup of the powdered sugar and remaining 1 tsp vanilla; beat until smooth, about 1 minute. Gradually add remaining 1 1/4 cups powdered sugar to cream cheese mixture alternately with 2 tbsps of the half-and-half, beating on high speed until frosting is smooth, creamy, and a little loose, about 1 minute, adding remaining 1 tbsp half-and-half, 1 tsp at a time, if needed to reach desired consistency. Drizzle half of the frosting over the biscuit mixture in the slow cooker. (Cover remaining frosting and set aside until ready to serve.) Cover slow cooker; cook on LOW until center of casserole is set and biscuit bottoms are browned, 3 1/2 to 4 hours. Drizzle casserole with remaining frosting; serve warm.

title: Nause-Waiwash's 1st female chief fights for identity, equality and preservation
author: Andrea Durán Capital News Service
content:
Nause-Waiwash's 1st female chief fights for identity, equality and preservation

 December 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Andrea Durán Capital News Service | Section: News 
 
 1402
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — A little over five feet tall, the chief of the Nause-Waiwash walked quickly. Despite a limp from a recent total knee replacement, she zipped up and down the stairs at the Dorchester County Visitor Center.The chief beamed as the overhead lights caught in her silver dreamcatcher earrings and white-streaked hair. Her blue-gray eyes darted over the various exhibits displaying pieces of her culture and history: a photograph of her uncle fishing, a miniature Nause-Waiwash longhouse and a taxidermied white muskrat.
The Nause-Waiwash tribe is one of the seven Native American tribes that are represented on the Maryland Commission of Indian Affairs, although the tribe is not state-recognized. The tribe, whose origins and traditions were once nearly lost but now are being revitalized, does statewide educational outreach to, as their chief says, "tell their story in their own words."
Chief Donna Wolf Mother Abbott is the first woman chief of a Maryland tribe in known recorded history.
Abbott has now been "Chief Donna" for 10 years. However, when she was first approached to run, she had serious doubts about whether she even wanted to become chief.
"But then I got thinking again, it's not about me," she said. "If I didn't step up and take on the responsibility I felt like that, all that would have just disappeared, and again, we would have lost our history one more time."
As chief, Abbott is in charge of planning the tribe's annual festival, overseeing educational outreach and acting as a liaison between the tribe and conservancy groups.
Deborah Barber, director of land conservation at the Nature Conservancy's Maryland chapter, has worked with Abbott on a handful of projects and said she admired Abbott's willingness to work with others within and outside of the native community.
Barber said a conversation with Abbott made her realize that what she was doing with her own children, being intentional about the values she is instilling in them, Abbott is doing with her own family and the whole tribe.
"She's doing it times 150," Barber said in an interview with Capital News Service.
It wasn't until Abbott was in her 30s and already a mother that she became fascinated with researching and passionate about preserving her culture.
"Growing up, I knew I was Native American, but it wasn't something that we shouted from the rooftops," she said. "It was just who we are."
Abbott said it was her cousin who approached her and told her she needed to join the tribe, but when Abbott resisted, her cousin told her, "It's not about you."
"It's about preserving what we have and learning and teaching and then teaching it for our next generation," Abbott said.
Since then, she has been dedicated to learning about her culture and educating others.
"I myself, I want to learn it all," she said. "Just not enough hours in the day."
However, as she became more involved in the native community, she also encountered stereotyping from both native and non-native people because she passes for white.
"'How much Indian are you?' How much do you want me to be? How much do I have to be? Does it make a difference?" Abbott said. "Not just the Nause-Waiwash—but not all tribes are tall, thin, with black hair and high cheekbones, riding bareback."
However, Abbott said that when she does encounter stereotyping or unfamiliarity with her culture, she turns to optimistic grace.
"I really try to blame it on the lack of knowledge," she said. "I'm like, 'These people don't know any better, so let's teach them.' So, I try not to take it personal. But I go through the 'okay, I'm mad now.' … and then I get over it."
Beyond tackling the prominent misconception that there were no more Indigenous people in the region, Abbott faced a multitude of challenges to increasing tribe membership. One of them is sexism from within and outside of the native community.
"…Here we are (in) 2024, and there's still so much gender discrimination and thoughts out there about, 'Oh, you have to be a warrior to be a chief,' And I'm like, 'Says who? No, you're practicing Western history,'" Abbott said.
Abbott said that some had used her gender against her and shamed her for not being as firm as the previous chief.
"I have been told I'm a pushover. I am a people-pleaser. And 'Who's ever heard of a woman chief? Who's ever heard of a chief or an Indian with blue eyes?'" she said.
Jerry "Gentle Bear" Hughes is 34 years old and serves as the Nause-Waiwash Band of Indians' vice chair and social media administrator. He is also Abbott's son, and he said it was his mother becoming chief that persuaded him to become involved with the tribe in his 20s.
Although Abbott's leadership might be controversial to some, Hughes said it's led the tribe to new opportunities.
"Oh, she's been an inspiration to everyone involved," Hughes said. "We've seen a lot of people who had stepped away because people had rubbed them the wrong way or made them angry or said something out of line. We've seen a lot of those people come back. We've had a lot of olive branches extended to us since she's been elected."
Prospective chiefs in the Nause-Waiwash tribe are nominated by the tribe's council to run, and the tribe's women vote for them. In 1988, the Nause-Waiwash Band of Indians was formed to preserve the Nause-Waiwash culture. A council of elders was created, and the tribe's women elected Fitzhugh as the chief.
Twenty-six years later, Chief Fitzhugh died, and in November 2014, Abbott was elected as his successor.
She has had doubts about making the right decisions for the tribe and questioned her own leadership.
"I have actually considered stepping down, and my son has said, 'If you step down, then who's gonna do it?'" she said. "But if I step down and nobody does it, then I feel I'm going to feel responsible for letting everything go and being a part of what caused us to lose our history again. And I don't know that I would be happy with myself if I did that."
The Nause-Waiwash people have always been in Dorchester County, which is known for its lush wetlands, diverse wildlife and crabbing and fishing on Maryland's Eastern Shore. They are descendants of the Nanticoke and Choptank tribes of modern-day eastern Maryland and Delaware. Unlike other Native American tribes, the Nause-Waiwash escaped persecution and death by hiding in plain sight for centuries and sometimes marrying Europeans.
"When I was in school, there were three paragraphs about the Trail of Tears that didn't apply to us," Abbott said.
However, even within the Nause-Waiwash community and Abbott's own family, people's connections to their Indigenous heritage can be complicated.
"My own sister does not identify as Native American," she said. "It just is not important to her. However, I do. Same mother, same father."
When someone wants to join the tribe, Abbott and other members must do a lot of genealogical research to verify connections to the tribe.
One major challenge for the tribe is getting younger people more involved.
Another is that younger tribal members are moving away from the area because of rising sea levels.
"It is just my opinion, but in the next hundred years, the Eastern Shore is probably not even going to be here based on what I see on our trapping grounds," she said. "That part of the county probably won't be here in the next 50 years."
Dorchester County is one of the regions in the country with the fastest sea-level rises, according to research by the Virginia Institute of Marine Science. In 2020, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration released a study that said, for example, sea levels for the Chesapeake Bay increased twice that of the global average over the 20th century.
For Abbott, who said she feels she's only scratched the surface of her people's history on her ancestral lands, the environmental changes feel especially tragic.
"I think that's going to be a part of our history that we're going to lose, that we can't get back because a lot of our ancestral land will be gone," she said. "There are probably hundreds of cemeteries that have washed away. We are never to get those back."
But Abbott stays optimistic about the future of her tribe.
"I think the culture can survive because the history in the culture, in their traditions, are the ones who practice it," she said. "And I think if we all pull together, then yes, absolutely, it'll survive whether we have our ancestral land or not."

title: Black-eyed peas, traditions and superstitions
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Black-eyed peas, traditions and superstitions

 December 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1472
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The cooks in my neck of the woods always cooked black-eyed peas for New Year's Day. This carried on for generations and still to this day remains a tradition.Mom bought that bag of peas ahead of time to make sure she had them before they sold out. Then she sat a piece of seasoning meat aside in the smoke house.
The most popular tradition on New Year's Day was to eat the black-eyed peas for good luck all year.
Well, the second biggest tradition of all was that no women were to enter the house on New Year's Day, as that was "bad luck." That did not work for me, as I tried to get out of helping mom cook or do dishes because I lived there and was not entering.
Well years later that changed somewhat to "women who accompanied the men to your house had to let the men enter first. And I used to say "well let him do the dishes."
Mom would cook a large pot of black-eyed peas with her seasoning meat and some potatoes. Then out came the big baking pans filled with homemade biscuits.
Sitting next to the biscuits was a jar of homemade jelly from last summer's canning and a dish with fresh churned butter.
No one asked for dessert, but everyone asked for more peas and biscuits.
From all over the world you find superstitions for New Years Eve and New Year's Day. Here are just a few I have heard over the years.
According to popular folklore or superstition, if these foods are eaten on New Year's Day, they guarantee good luck throughout the year:
Peas or beans are said to symbolize coins or wealth. Choose traditional black-eyed peas, lentils, or beans to make a dish seasoned with pork, ham or sausage.
Greens resemble money, specifically folding money. Make dishes using boiled cabbage or sauerkraut, collard greens, kale, chard, mustard greens, turnip greens or other green, leafy vegetables to ensure good fortune for the coming year.
Pork is considered a sign of prosperity in some cultures because pigs root forward. Many southern New Year's Day dishes contain pork or ham, but feel free to serve a pork roast or baked ham as an entrée.
Cornbread might symbolize gold, and besides, it is essential with black-eyed peas and greens.
In other cultures, fish, grapes, and ring-shaped cakes or doughnuts, or cakes with special treats inside symbolize luck.
Some believe that lobster could cause bad luck in the coming year because it moves in a backward direction and could mean setbacks in the year ahead. For the same reason, some believe chicken dishes should be avoided on New Year's Day. Chickens scratch backward, plus they are winged, so your luck could fly away.
Now for some black-eyed pea dishes and dishes people around the United States eat on New Year's Eve or New Year's Day.
BLACK-EYED PEAS
Begin by purchasing a bag of the dried black-eyed peas and soaking them in cold water, covering them. In a large soup pot, place the seasoning meat and cover with water, bring to a boil, let simmer. After the beans have swollen and doubled in size, rinse in cold water and add to the seasoning meat, add more salt if needed and black pepper. When a rolling boil begins, turn flame back to achieve a steady boil, cover with a lid that is slightly ajar to avoid boiling over. As the beans cook, you can add in the last 45 to 50 minutes some whole corn, dumplings or some peeled white potatoes. Before adding the corn or other additions, check the seasonings. Serve with your warm breads and enjoy this filling meal any time of the year.
TEXAS CAVAIR
2 14-oz. cans black-eyed peas (drained), 1 15.5-oz. can white hominy (drained), 2 medium tomatoes (chopped), 2 green tomatoes (chopped), 1 medium green bell pepper (chopped), 2 jalapeño peppers (chopped), 1/2 cup onion, (chopped), 1/2 cup fresh cilantro (chopped), 2 garlic cloves (minced), 1 8-oz. bottle Italian dressing, tortilla chips for serving.
Stir together the first nine ingredients in a large bowl. Add the dressing to the black-eyed pea mixture, stirring until combined. Cover and chill for 2 hours. Drain. Serve with the tortilla chips.
HOPPIN JOHN WITH BRAISED OXTAIL
1.5 pounds oxtails,1.5 tbsps salt (divided), 2 tsps black pepper (divided), 6 cups chicken stock, 2 cups dried black-eyed peas (soaked overnight), 2 cups diced yellow onions (from 2 medium onions), 2 cups diced carrots (from 5 medium carrots), 2 cups diced celery (from 4 stalks), 1/4 cup chopped jalapeño chiles (from 2 chiles), 4 garlic cloves (thinly sliced), 5 thyme sprigs, 3 fresh bay leaves. RICE:4 cups water, 1 teaspoon kosher salt, 1/4 teaspoon cayenne pepper, 1 cup uncooked jasmine rice, 1/4 cup unsalted butter (cubed), 1/4 cup apple cider vinegar, 1/2 cup chopped scallions.
Prepare the peas: Heat a Dutch oven over high and add canola oil. Sprinkle oxtails evenly with ½ tablespoon of the salt and 1 teaspoon of the black pepper, and place in the Dutch oven. Cook until browned on all sides, about 4 minutes per side. Remove oxtails from the Dutch oven. Pour off drippings, leaving browned bits in the Dutch oven, and add stock. Bring stock to a boil over high, using a wooden spoon to scrape browned bits from the bottom of the Dutch oven. Return oxtails to Dutch oven; reduce heat to medium-low, cover, and simmer until tender, 1½ to 2 hours. Using a slotted spoon, transfer oxtails to a plate, and let cool slightly. Add peas, onions, carrots, celery, jalapeño, garlic, thyme sprigs, and bay leaves to stock mixture; reduce heat to low, and cook, partially covered, until peas are soft, about 1 hour. Stir in remaining 1 tablespoon salt and 1 teaspoon black pepper. While peas cook, pick oxtail meat from bones, and set aside. While the peas finish cooking, preheat the oven to 300 degrees. Bring water, salt, and cayenne pepper to a boil in a medium saucepan over medium-high. Reduce heat to medium; add rice and stir. Simmer gently, uncovered, stirring occasionally, until rice is al dente, about 15 minutes. Drain rice in a fine wire-mesh strainer, and rinse under cold water. Spread rice out on a rimmed baking sheet. Dry rice in a preheated oven for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally. Scatter butter evenly over rice, and continue to dry, stirring every few minutes, until all excess moisture has evaporated, and grains are dry and separate, about 5 more minutes. Add oxtail meat and cider vinegar to peas. Using a slotted spoon, transfer peas to a large serving bowl. Add rice, and carefully toss together. (Pour enough oxtail gravy over the top to moisten the peas without making the dish too soupy, about 1 cup.) Garnish with scallions.
CHILI ROASTED BLACK-EYED PEAS
2 cans black-eyed peas rinsed and drained, 3 tbsps olive oil, 1 1/2 tsps chili powder, 1 tsp pepper, 3/4 tsp ground cumin, 1/2 tsp salt.
Preheat the oven to 425 degrees. Combine all ingredients in a medium bowl. Transfer mixture to a lightly greased 17-by-12-inch jelly roll pan. Bake for 45 to 50 minutes or until crispy and dry, stirring every 10 minutes. Let cool for 20 minutes.
INSTANT POT BLACK-EYED PEA SOUP
1 tbsp olive oil, 1 cup chopped yellow onion, 1 cup chopped carrots, 1/2 cup chopped celery, 2 large garlic cloves, (minced), 1/4 tsp crushed red pepper, 6 cups chicken broth (such as Swanson's),3 thyme sprigs, 2 cups roughly chopped and stemmed collard greens,1 14.5-oz. can fire-roasted diced tomatoes (drained), 1 (3/4-lb.) smoked ham hock, 1 lb. dried black-eyed peas (soaked overnight), 2 tbsps red wine vinegar, 1.5 tsps salt, 1 tsp black pepper.
Select the saute setting on Instant Pot or a pressure cooker. Times, instructions, and settings may vary according to cooker brand or model. Select high temperature setting and allow to preheat 2 to 3 minutes. Add olive oil to the cooker, and heat until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add onion, carrots, and celery; cook, stirring often, until vegetables are softened, 2 to 3 minutes. Stir in garlic and crushed red pepper and cook for 30 seconds. Stir in chicken stock, thyme, collards, tomatoes, ham hock, and black-eyed peas. Press cancel. Cover cooker with lid, and lock in place. Turn the steam release handle to the sealing position. Select manual/pressure cook setting. Select high pressure for 10 minutes. (It will take 10 to 15 minutes for the cooker to come up to pressure before cooking begins.) Let the pressure release naturally for 15 minutes. Carefully turn the steam release handle to the venting position and let steam fully escape the float valve. This will take about 2 to 3 minutes. Remove lid from cooker. Remove ham hock from cooker; pull meat off bone, and chop to equal about 1/3 cup. Discard bone. Stir chopped ham, vinegar, salt, and pepper into soup.
Happy New Year to all my readers. Here's to a happy and healthy 2025.

title: Temple B'Nai Israel in Easton celebrates Hanukkah
author: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com
content:
Temple B'Nai Israel in Easton celebrates Hanukkah

 January 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: KONNER METZ kmetz@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 561
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — On Saturday, Temple B'Nai Israel and community members gathered together for a community Hanukkah candle lighting. The celebration and observance is continuing through sundown on Thursday.Rabbi Fred Scherlinder Dobb, interim rabbi for the temple and Satell Center for Jewish Life on the Eastern Shore, emphasized Saturday's candle lighting as a tradition that strengthens Easton and the surrounding community.
Easton Mayor Megan Cook and Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher were two of the community members who attended, Dobb said.
"This is an opportunity to unite the members of Temple B'Nai Israel with the broader community," he said. "Year to year, different area clergypeople, and elected officials and others are able to join us."
Barbara Spector, president of the Temple B'Nai Israel's Board of Trustees, said there was singing, lighting of Hanukkah menorahs and games.
Hanukkah is considered a festival of lights and lasts eight days, in which Jewish people gather to light a candle in a menorah each day. It stems from the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem in the second century B.C.
"This eight-day holiday falls around the new moon that is closest to the winter solstice," Dobb said. "So it comes at the time of greatest darkness, both daytime and nighttime. And in that darkness moment, we introduce light."
This year, Hanukkah began Dec. 25. Temple B'Nai Israel celebrates with latkes (fried potato pancakes), sufganiyah (jelly donuts) and a dreidel (a four-sided spinning top).
As the only full-service synagogue in Talbot and neighboring counties, Temple B'Nai Israel is a sacred place for many that practice Judaism. Since beginning his interim role in November, Dobb has come to appreciate the diversity of those that attend the temple's programs and services.
"I am consistently astounded by not only the depth of thought and positivity of the members of this temple community, but also of the region as a whole," Dobb said. "I have not met someone from Easton and Talbot County who I have not been impressed by in some way.
"Irrespective of faith, or political affiliation or race, folks are sharing a spirit of sorts. And the larger community is clearly stronger for that ethos."
Spector and Dobb admit that distance is a challenge for many, especially in the rural Eastern Shore compared to other parts of the region. Temple B'Nai Israel sees people often come from Centreville, Cambridge, Stevensville and Chestertown, among other areas.
Dobb welcomes the challenges that may come with accommodating a wide range of people and practices.
"People of all backgrounds and ideologies and levels of observance, as well as different comfort and knowledge with tradition and Hebrew, all come together for the same events and the same worship services," Dobb said. "So finding the range of sweet spots that will touch everyone in some way is both a challenge and an opportunity."
Dobb said the Hannukah celebration is about "hope and community."
The rabbi said the theme of Saturday was that "we are all in it together."
"That applies to the civic fabric of our region and the democracy of which we are a part," Dobb said. "It also applies to the natural world for which we are all responsible, and we have to work together to caretake one another, as well as to be good stewards of the land and the day. These things can only be done in unison, and blessingly, that spirit of unity in the broader community is strong and growing."

title: Delaware art exhibit showcases letterpress work
author: Post staff report
content:
Delaware art exhibit showcases letterpress work

 January 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Post staff report | Section: News 
 
 637
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The letterpress studio of Lead Graffiti was voted Newark's favorite artist of 2024 in a recent citizen poll by the Newark Post. That inspired the Newark Arts Alliance to dedicate its January exhibition to an overview of Lead Graffiti's work over the past two decades and its dedication to "printing slowly & patiently via letterpress in Newark, Delaware."The solo exhibition, "Lead Graffiti: An Exhibition of Letterpress and Book Arts" runs through Jan. 17 at the Newark Arts Alliance Gallery, located in the Shoppes at Louviers on Paper Mill Road. A public reception will be held on Jan. 10 from 6 to 8 p.m. The gallery is open to the public Tuesday through Saturday from noon to 4 p.m. daily and noon to 8 p.m. on Fridays.
Lead Graffiti was formed in 2008 by Ray Nichols and Jill Cypher as an experimental letterpress laboratory. The husband-and-wife team of artists/designers focused on public causes, a love of words and typography, passing historical and technical information forward, and a playful disregard for the usual design rules.
Located in a 2,200-square-foot space in Newark's Sandy Brae Industrial Park, Lead Graffiti is packed with cases of wood and metal type, printing presses of all kinds, a working hot-metal Intertype linecaster, and all the gear that Gutenberg would have known.
The studio's letterpress work is included in more than 75 significant collections of libraries and institutions, along with solo exhibitions at The British Library in London, the Hamilton Wood Type Museum in Two Rivers, Wisconsin, and the American Institute of Graphic Arts in Philadelphia. Lead Graffiti has been written up in Sports Illustrated Magazine and makes a grand entry in printer/author Chris Fritton's book The Itinerant Printer, where he wrote, "Lead Graffiti is the incorrigible, unpredictable, and uncompromising brainchild of Ray Nichols and Jill Cypher — a shop where the only rule is there are no design rules, and the thing you learn every day is that there's always more to learn."
Nichols and Cypher have given dozens of talks and tours to various organizations and student groups and conducted numerous in-house and online workshops related to letterpress and bookmaking. One of the studio's major projects was an endurance letterpress series of 115+ broadsides produced over five years (2011 — 2015), visually documenting the daily events of the Tour de France in handset type and ink on paper.
For three decades as a professor and director of the visual communications program at the University of Delaware, Nichols helped lead the program to an international reputation. He was also co-director with his teaching colleague Bill Deering of the program's summer study abroad to London.
Beginning in 2001, the trips were for students in advertising and graphic design to visit design studios, advertising agencies, filmmakers, and museums to provide experiences with design creativity, typography and historical perspectives. A pair of early visits to the letterpress studio of Alan Kitching and the St. Bride Printing Library unexpectedly provided Nichols and Cypher with two life-altering experiences. Their creative focus switched from blink-of-the-eye advertising design to the slow and patient world of letterpress printing and book arts for the next two decades.
In 2002, Nichols, Cypher and Deering founded Raven Press at the University of Delaware. Over the next four years, it became a new teaching tool. Cypher's interests in typography, colorful paste paper painting and exploring various forms of bookmaking also benefited Raven Press externally. Upon Nichols' retirement from teaching in 2006, the couple formed Lead Graffiti, collecting presses and cases of type to continue their creative work.
In 2006, their first major post-teaching project solidified their intellectual connection to Newark. As volunteers, Nichols and Cypher were tasked with designing, photographing and producing the 300-page hardback book "Histories of Newark: 1758 — 2008." The design is highlighted by their photography of a citizen's band of about 4,000 Newark residents that runs through the book.
