title: Country Cooking: Eating like the King
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Eating like the King

 January 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Life 
 
 1157
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Unbelievable that my teenage idol, Elvis, turns 90 today. Millions of fans from all over the world come to Memphis to gather at Graceland to reflect on memories together.The younger generation want to hear about our stories from the early days of Elvis — his music, his singing and moving style, and our parents' thoughts on this "good looking guy" who ripped the music world apart.
I have met some great folks from across the ocean who are in their 30s, 40s and 50s who are so interested in Elvis' early career days and the reaction to his music from the older generation.
Graceland is just a small part of the must-see sights in Memphis. Sun Records studio is open for touring and is widely considered the birthplace of rock 'n' roll. Many famous singers have recorded there, such as Elvis, Johnny Cash, Jerry Lee Lewis and Conway Twitty, just to name a few.
Each time I go it's like my first time — amazing.
Not only is the tour of Graceland awesome, but downtown Beale Street is loaded with great food and sights to see. Whatever kind of food you like is available in and around Memphis. Southern-style eating is everywhere you turn.
HOMEMADE MEMPHIS STYLE BBQ SAUCE2 tbsps unsalted butter, 1 small onion (finely chopped), 2 cloves garlic (minced), 2 cups tomato sauce, 1/2 cup cider vinegar, 1/3 cup rice vinegar, 1/3 cup molasses, 3 tbsps Worcestershire sauce, 2 tbsps packed dark brown sugar, 2 tsps yellow mustard, 1 tsp Louisiana hot sauce, 1 tsp Kosher salt, 1 tsp freshly ground black pepper, 1/4 tsp cayenne pepper.
Melt butter in medium saucepan over medium heat. Add onion and cook until softened, about 5 minutes. Add garlic and cook until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Add tomato sauce, cider vinegar, rice vinegar, molasses, Worcestershire sauce, brown sugar, mustard, hot sauce, salt, black pepper and cayenne, and stir to combine. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low and simmer until slightly thickened, about 15-20 minutes, stirring occasionally. Transfer sauce to the jar of a blender and blend until smooth. Let cool to room temperature, transfer to a jar and store in the refrigerator for up to a month.
SMOKY GRILLED CHEESE2 slices sourdough bread, 1 cup freshly grated Monterey Jack cheese, Memphis BBQ sauce (for serving), 2 tbsp butter.
Prepare the grilled cheese by spreading butter on one side of each piece of bread. Lay one piece of bread butter side down on a skillet, top with cheese, and place the other piece of bread on top creating a sandwich. Turn the heat to medium-high and cook for 4-5 minutes on each side. Before removing the grilled cheese, you can top each side with shredded cheese and cook until the cheese is melted and crispy. Remove the grilled cheese from the skillet and serve hot with the Memphis BBQ sauce to dip in.
MEMPHIS STYLE CHICKEN NUGGETS1 lb boneless skinless chicken cubed, 1 egg, 1/3 cup bread crumbs, 1/4 cup shaved parmesan, Memphis BBQ sauce.
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Cut the chicken tenderloins into small nugget-like cubes. Whisk 1 egg in a small bowl. In a large zip lock bag, combine bread crumbs, and parmesan. Coat each piece of chicken in egg and then place in the bag with the breading. Once you have done this with each piece, close the bag and shake well. Each piece of chicken should be covered in breading. Place the breaded chicken on a sheet pan and place in the oven to bake for 30 minutes. Serve warm with Memphis BBQ sauce for dipping.
MEMPHIS DRY RUB RIBS1 slab pork loin spare ribs (also called baby back ribs), 5 tbsps light brown sugar, 4 tsps smoked paprika, 1½ tsps black pepper, 1 tsp granulated garlic or garlic powder, 4 tsps kosher salt, ½ tsp chili powder, ¼ tsp onion powder, ¼ tsp ground cumin, ¼ tsp dried oregano, ¼ tsp rubbed sage, ¼ tsp dried marjoram, ¼ tsp dried parsley, ¼ tsp white pepper, 1 cup white vinegar, 1 cup water.
Adjust the oven rack to the middle of the oven. Preheat the oven to 250 degrees. Stir together the sugar and all of the spices in a small bowl. Reserve ⅓ of the spice mixture in a separate bowl. Place the ribs on a large baking tray, meat side down. Slide a knife just barely under the edge of the membrane at one end of the ribs and then use that loosened edge to pull the membrane off the ribs. (I find it easiest to grab the edge of the membrane with a paper towel and pull it off that way). Pat the ribs dry with a paper towel. Apply the rub generously to the front and back of the ribs (leaving the reserved amount for later use). Place the ribs meat side up on a large foil-lined baking sheet and cook for about three hours, until the ribs are tender. Pour the vinegar and water into a shallow baking dish. Remove the cooked ribs from the oven and dip them into the vinegar water. Place the wet ribs onto a cutting board or a clean baking sheet and season immediately with a coating of the reserved dry rub. Cut the ribs apart between the bones.
GUS'S WORLD FAMOUS FRIED CHICKENThis next recipe is a 24-hour marinade of the chicken, a full day before you plan to cook it.
1 lb boneless skinless chicken breast cut into three pieces (or, your standard bone-in chicken pieces like Gus's does. I went with boneless chicken breasts for this recipe because they are a challenge), 1 cup corn starch, ¼ cup (4 tbsps) all purpose flour, 1 tbsp ground black pepper, 1 tbsp sweet paprika, 1 tbsp cayenne pepper, 1 tsp Kosher salt, 1 cup water (Note: 1 ½ cups is too much. On my first go, I actually ended up with 1 ¼ cup water and poured off a little water in the morning that had gathered on top of the marinade and that is how I came up with the 1 cup measurement).
Marinade for 24 hours In the refrigerator, keeping everything refrigerated to protect against bacterial growth. Remove the chicken from the marinade/batter and if everything goes well, the batter/slurry will cling to the pieces. You may need to agitate the batter/slurry to assure that it coats the chicken pieces. Fry at 325-350 degrees. Use a neutral vegetable or corn oil. I've become a big fan of sunflower oil as it has a high smoke point, but, yeah, vegetable, corn, peanut oils are fine if that is what you have. I do not recommend canola oil as it smells like frying fish and adds an unpleasant fish taste to fried foods.
There are so many places to visit in Memphis to eat. If you ever make it there, please check out Gus's Fried Chicken, Charlie Vergos' Rendezvous, Central BBQ, The King Jerry Lawler's BBQ, Rum Boogie Café and BB King's Blues Club.

Spreading the love: Centreville welcomes Eastern Shore’s first romance-only bookstore

 CENTERVILLE — Providing a community for romance readers, indie writers, and all those who love books, a small bookstore in a small town is supporting small authors for all those with a big heart as Romance-Landia Bookstore held a grand opening in Centreville Jan. 4.The niche store fills a need, supporting self-published authors and offering a community for romance book readers, according to owner Staci Hicks who considered romance books to be her escape outlet and was excited to share that passion with the community.
Hicks has a background in promoting self-published authors, and noted romance novels are no longer a genre that one has to be ashamed of enjoying and now has its own entire community backing, she said.
Romance books come in an eclectic variety of subgenres from westerns to sports to paranormal.
"Anybody can find something if they open themselves up to it," she said.
In addition to a wide variety of romance books, the store stocks everything a bookworm needs, including stickers, pens, bookmarks, tote bags, and gifts for the bibliophile in your life.
With a degree in graphic design, Hicks designed a number of bookmarks and stickers herself.
Highlighting the importance of a good book, the store is also complete with a sitting lounge and a small self-serve coffee bar to curl up with a new favorite find.
The intimate location is perfect for connecting with others who feel passionate about books.
"We needed this," said Cristi Bruce, of Crumpton, with an armful of indie writings, who noted there was nothing like it in the area and was thrilled by the opportunity of a brick and mortar bookstore in Centreville. The stigma used to be that you never told anyone you read romance, she said, now the genre is becoming more and more popular by readers of all types.
To have a physical bookstore and in-person book clubs that romance book lovers can flock to is nothing short of a dream come true, said Amanda Parsons, of Chestertown.
Romance is a rapidly expanding genre, according to indie author Kristie Wolf, of Bel Air who came out to the ribbon cutting in support of local businesses and fellow authors.
The best part of romance novels, both writing and reading, is the guaranteed happy ending, Wolf said, which fills her days with much needed hope.
Indie author Sarah Blue provided signings and promotions of her latest page turners last Saturday. From paranormal to contemporary, Blue writes a little bit of everything in the genre of romance,"I can't stay in one lane," she said.
The great part of writing romance books is there aren't too many rules to follow and Blue loves the opportunity to write stories that she wants to read.
Local authors supporting a local woman-owned businesses in a small town, "is a match made in heaven," said indie author B.R. Goodwin performing book signings.
Being a self-published author is similar to owning your own businesses and indie authors are always supportive of each other, according to Goodwin.
Indie authors are always sharing, supporting and encouraging each other and readers are vicarious who love devouring anything, author Claire Cain said.
Hicks has been delighted in the new people she has met through connecting over books and as the flocks of the opening day's crowd gathered, community support has been extremely receptive and supportive of the store.
The best thing about romance books is sharing a sense of escapism with other readers, which in this day and age is needed more than ever, Hicks said.
Romance-Landia has a schedule of regular indie author visits and book clubs are held Thursdays once a month
Located at 204 Banjo Lane, more information about Romance-Landia Bookstore, including upcoming author visits and bookclubs can be found at https://www.romance-landia.com.

title: Artists' exhibit honors Historic Sotterley
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
Artists' exhibit honors Historic Sotterley

 January 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: State News 
 
 708
 Words 

 Read News Document

 An exhibit at the Leonardtown library is helping to tell the story of Historic Sotterley."Moments in Time" features the works of watercolor painter Pamela Callen, photographer Damien Wilkinson and multi-disciplinary Joi Lowe.
"I want people to know who Sotterley is, what it is and I just want them to get a glimpse of the history because I don't want that to be erased," said Lowe, who helped set up the exhibit. "I want people to see what it was, but it's also a beautiful site with many, many stories and we help tell those stories. It's important."
The exhibit — which is "acknowledging spiritual connections to the landscape of Historic Sotterley" — will be at the Leonardtown branch through the end of January when it will move to the Lexington Park library.
"It's very exciting," said Susie Glauner, who is the executive director of the St. Mary's County Arts Council, which is sponsoring the exhibit. "We are thrilled to be able to offer the gallery partnerships, both for the benefit of the artists as well as St. Mary's County residents and visitors so that more people can see the local talent we have here in the county."
Callen, who has three paintings in the exhibit — "Slave Dwelling," "Manor House" and "Fall in the Fields" — had a lengthy career as a foreign service member for the U.S. Agency for International Development and spent a number of years in developing countries.
As a result, she said, "The human condition means a lot to me. That's one of the appeals of Sotterley is that you have both sides of the coin there — the slave dwelling and the Manor House."
The Solomons resident said when she was painting "Manor House" a few years back an elderly couple appeared so she painted them in.
"But when I did that they became the main focal point and that really wasn't what I wanted," she said. "I wanted the sky and the house and the beauty so I painted them back out. When you have the brush in your hand you can change the world."
When she painted "Fall in the Fields" last year, she started thinking.
"We have a lot of [hay bales] in Southern Maryland, but at Sotterley it's so special because one of the things you think about when you look at this vast expanse of land and the water is the people who did that work, so you think about them," Callen said. "You think about who lived in the manor house and who kept them going doing all the work in the fields and living in that slave dwelling. You think about that when you're out there and there's nobody around except you and your paint."
Wilkinson took up photography as a hobby a few years back but started getting more invested in it last year.
He has three photographs in the exhibit: "Beautiful Yet Broken," "Reflections of the Past" and "Portals to Relics."
"I would just kind of point-shoot [my camera] and hope it would come out OK," said the 43-year-old Great Mills resident, who said he recently "just fell back in love with photography again. I was really excited to get out there [to Sotterley] and take pictures."
Lowe has four pieces in the show: "This Time, Stephen Marley," "Mariposa" and "Catalpa Piece with Paper," as well as a 10-foot piece made from marbles, gemstones, wood and pieces of a maple tree titled "Born Free."
She said one piece she did titled "Royal" included collecting honey locust seed pods from a tree in front of the Sotterley slave cabin.
"I spent so many days at that cabin collecting those seed pods," the 47-year-old California resident said, "and so many times I felt like I was having conversations. Who else was collecting these seed pods?"
Lowe also has a current show through the end of January at the Lexington Park Library and artist Jay Anderson has an exhibit hanging at the Port of Leonardtown Winery.
The "Moments in Time" exhibit is in the Maryland Room at the Leonardtown Public Library, located 23630 Hayden Farm Lane. The library is open 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. Mondays to Thursdays and 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Fridays and Saturdays.
For more information on the exhibit or to purchase pieces in it, email Joi Lowe at joi_lowe@yahoo.com.

title: Stephen Harvey is bringing jazz to St. Michaels
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Stephen Harvey is bringing jazz to St. Michaels

 January 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 718
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST MICHAELS — When Stephen Philip Harvey is playing the saxophone, the sounds that come from the horn of the golden instrument are lively, rhythmic and attention-grabbing.Harvey, a celebrated and well-decorated musician from the Eastern Shore, has a generational love for music.
Its a love he shares with those running the Windon Distilling Company in St. Michaels, who have invited the musician to be a part of unveiling their newest endeavor.
Having just finished its 11th year of production, the distillery is opening a new event space, Golden Hour, next to its staple tasting room. Harvey will be performing a sold-out show to mark its opening Friday night.
The distillery's founder Jaime Windon said in a press release, "this space is designed for showcasing the things we love the most: rum cocktails alongside brilliant and inspiring music, art and community. To be able to debut it while enjoying jazz along with our friends and neighbors in January is a dream."
Harvey was raised in a family passionate about music and would perform for their local church. Raised on gospel music, he soon expanded his repertoire into jazz and gained an appreciation for gathered sounds and instruments.
According to Harvey, it's not uncommon for someone in his family to break into song.
"My love for music is really a family love for music," Harvey said. "My whole family are singers and musicians… (there are times) we would be on a walk to meet up together in a space, and then someone would be like, 'oh, let's sing this hymn,' and then we break out into four part harmony. My wife was very startled by it the first time she was at a family event."
As Harvey grew up, his curiosity in music began to change away from gospel when his high school band director encouraged him to join the jazz band. From there, his relationship with music took several twists and turns.
When he got to college, his interest peaked in studying music education before choosing to focus on Western European art music, where he learned song styles of Italian, German and French musicians.
But it was American music through idioms of bebop, hard bop, vocal jazz and then big band jazz that made Harvey want to commit the rest of his life in exploring those sounds.
"It's this really interesting hobby/career where I feel like I can just do it forever and always discover new things, even looking back and going forward," Harvey said. "So discovering new things as I write and discovering new things as I listen to people who have performed and recorded in the idiom before me is so cool, especially since you come from this family that loves music so much."
Today, Harvey is a professional musician, composer and bandleader. He has released seven full albums throughout this career, with "Library Card" being his latest release.
Additionally, his compositions have been performed by an array of ensembles across the world including the National Youth Jazz Orchestra, ensembles at the Peabody Conservatory of Music and several universities across the nation.
Harvey sees his upcoming performance as part of an effort to expand jazz music's presence in the area, a mission the distillery's owners are also on board with.
Windon said she is a fan of jazz and was incredibly excited to host Harvey and his trio Sphinx as the first musical act at Windon's new event venue.
For Windon, Harvey has an electric presence.
"I have a great appreciation for jazz music of all kinds of styles, and so I liked that his music felt classic and familiar, but yet fresh," Windon said. "… There's a charisma, to me, that Stephen has that I think is also reminiscent of jazz musicians that I've always known and gravitated towards."
Harvey said he has performed in Easton and his concert will be his first time playing in St. Michaels. He shared that he's excited to establish himself on the Eastern Shore and share his love for jazz.
"My whole vibe since I've moved down here is seeing what a vacuum of jazz and Black American improvised music is on the Shore," Harvey said. "There's like none, and I would love to produce as many shows as possible, whether they are in conjunction with Lyon Rum and the Golden Hour or anywhere else. I'm just excited for any opportunity to play inside of this county."

title: Maryland author releases new historical mystery
author: Staff Writer
content:
Maryland author releases new historical mystery

 January 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 834
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Author Carol McCabe Booker recently released her latest book "The Farmer's Wife" through New Bay Books.The book details the 1877 mystery of why a woman who had just picked a basket of cabbage leaves for dinner was murdered in a field in the village of Friendship in Anne Arundel County.
According to the New Bay Books website, "The Farmer's Wife" is the third in the Lusby resident's nonfiction series exploring historic events in 19th- and early 20th- century Southern Maryland.
It follows 2021's "Cove Point on the Chesapeake" and her 2023 best-selling "The Waterman's Widow," which was one of the Top-10 nonfiction books checked out of the Calvert Library in 2024.
The 129-page mystery is available for $17 at www.newbaybooks.com.
How long have you been writing, and how did you get started?
I started writing as a pre-teen, always focusing on nonfiction. I liked reporting on events either in school or the community. Then, one day I learned of the upcoming scrapping of a luxury cruise ship, the SS Ile de France, and it inspired me to write an essay on the great lady's history on the high seas. It was published by the New York Daily News, and it convinced me that a career as a journalist was indeed possible. A summer internship at the Voice of America while I was in college made it happen.
What inspires you to write?
I am inspired by the discovery of information that seems too fascinating or important not to share with others.
Do you consider writing to be a career?
It was my first career, starting in radio with the Voice of America, covering civil rights. I reported for Westinghouse Broadcasting from the Nigerian civil warfront, and on other stories throughout Africa while freelancing for magazines such as Reader's Digest, Ebony, and Jet. It was a wonderful career, but I also had a fascination with the law. I went to Georgetown Law School with the idea of combining the two.
What kind of writing process do you use?
I think it might best be described as a journalistic approach.
Who are some of your favorite authors and why?
Two of my favorites are historical nonfiction writers, Timothy Egan and Eric Larson. Egan's recent release, "A Fever in the Heartland: The Ku Klux Klan's Plot to Take Over America, and the Woman Who Stopped Them," is a jaw-dropper. Larson's "A Devil in the White City" and "Isaac's Storm" are both unforgettable. And coincidentally, they are both journalists.
What are you working on now?
I'm working on another book about Southern Maryland in the 1870s. It was quite a decade.
What do you want readers to know about you?
I want readers to know that whichever of my books they pick up, they will find within it something they never knew, but which merits some thought in the context of the famous quote carved into stone in front of the National Archives: "The Past is Prologue. Study the Past."
Please include a brief description of the book
In one of the wildest years in the post-Civil War period in Southern Maryland, one story in 1877 captured headlines across the country from May through December.
The press called it "one of the most revolting murders in the annals of crime," and spared no details in their reporting on the arrest and trial of a young tenant farmer for the cold-blooded murder of his wife, the mother of his three children, in the tiny hamlet of Friendship in Anne Arundel county.
Southern Maryland, like much of the country at the time, was recovering not only from the Civil War, but also from the previous November's U.S. presidential election, which had resulted in no winner until a couple of days before Inauguration Day on March 4, 1877.
Perhaps a harbinger of things to come, the year had begun with a frozen Chesapeake Bay imprisoning oyster boats, and leaving frostbitten watermen facing possible starvation until a thaw sent ice floes ripping into some of their hulls, cutting them in half. The Farmer's Wife follows the murder trial and the events that must have left many Southern Marylanders wondering "what next?
Please include an excerpt from the book
"These were tumultuous times, from a contested presidential election to deadly weather extremes, a bloody railroad strike and the actions of national and local legislatures. Reporters in every state covered the news for avid readers, and Maryland historically had several very popular newspapers.
Yet, a single story first reported in The Baltimore Sun captured headlines throughout most of the year across the country. It was a tale of betrayal. Some called it an atrocious breach of faith; a fiendish, brutal violation of trust. Others even called it "inhuman," with hints of demonic possession. It began in May with "one of the most revolting murders in the annals of crime." The victim was a young mother who went to her grave never knowing why, and perhaps not even seeing her cowardly executioner.
Steadily and in excruciating detail, nationally syndicated reports illuminated a cold-blooded crime more chilling than the past winter's paralyzing frosts on the Chesapeake Bay. No detail was spared."

title: Country Cooking: Just need a bowl of homemade soup
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Just need a bowl of homemade soup

 January 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1098
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Schools were closed for three weeks — two weeks for holidays and one for snow.Just when schools are open once again and the normal schedules begin to be in place, the temperatures dive to freezing again and life slows down.
One thing is for sure, appetites have not slowed down, and cooks are scrambling for suggestions to make life easier and keep tummies full.
Well let's go back to farm life. When the temperatures dropped, and the ice and snow fell, Mom always knew what to cook. After spending the day out in the cold freezing weather, we would arrive home to the kitchen windows steamed up, the warm heat of the kitchen falling on our cold faces and the smell of soup bubbling on the stove and bread baking in the oven.
Not only were the warm biscuits good, but there would always be a plate of assorted crackers with sliced sharp cheese to enjoy.
Let's get the soup pot or Dutch oven out.
GREEN LIMA BEAN SOUP WITH DUMPLINGS
SOUP: 1 piece salt pork or ham bone, 1 can whole tomatoes, 6 cups water, 3 cups green lima beans, 1 cup corn, 3 small potatoes (peeled and cubed), 1 tbsp sugar, 1/2 tsp Worcestershire sauce, salt and pepper. DUMPLINGS: 2 cups flour, 1 tsp salt, 2 tsps oil, 2 tsps baking powder, water.
In the pot combine salt pork or ham bone with tomatoes, water, lima beans, corn, potatoes, sugar, Worcestershire sauce, and salt and pepper to taste. Cook slowly for about an hour and in the meantime mix your dumplings to add later. DUMPLINGS: mix flour with salt, oil, baking powder and enough water to moisten. Mix flour mixture well just adding enough water to make a stiff dough. Roll out on a floured surface and cut into two-inch pieces. When lima beans and potatoes are tender, add the dumplings to the soup, tasting the seasonings just before adding the dumplings. Cook until dumplings are tender and serve hot. NOTE: cook your seasoning meat before you start adding any beans, etc. unless you have leftover cooked ham or pork. I always just pre-cook my seasoning meat for a fresher taste.
CHICKEN NOODLE SOUP
2-1/2 pounds bone-in chicken thighs, 1/2 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp pepper, 1 tbsp canola oil, 1 large onion (chopped), 1 garlic clove (minced), 10 cups chicken broth, 4 celery ribs (chopped), 4 medium carrots (chopped), 2 bay leaves, 1 tsp minced fresh thyme or 1/4 tsp dried thyme, 3 cups egg noodles (about 8 ounces), 1 tbsp chopped fresh parsley, 1 tbsp lemon juice, salt and pepper.
Pat chicken dry with paper towels; sprinkle with salt and pepper. In a six-quart stockpot, heat oil over medium-high heat. Add chicken in batches, skin side down; cook until dark golden brown, 3-4 minutes. Remove chicken from pan; remove and discard skin. Discard all but 2 tbsps of drippings. Add onion to drippings; cook and stir over medium-high heat until tender, 4-5 minutes. Add garlic; cook 1 minute longer. Add broth, stirring to loosen browned bits from the pan. Bring to a boil. Return chicken to pan. Add celery, carrots, bay leaves and thyme. Reduce heat; simmer, covered, until chicken is tender, 25-30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a plate. Remove soup from heat. Add noodles; let stand, covered, until noodles are tender, 20-22 minutes. Meanwhile, when chicken is cool enough to handle, remove meat from bones; discard bones. Shred meat into bite-sized pieces. Return meat to the stockpot. Stir in parsley and lemon juice. If desired, adjust seasoning with additional salt and pepper. Discard bay leaves. Once they reach an internal temperature of 165 degrees, set the chicken on a plate, let cool and shred.
EASY BEEF SOUP
1/2 pound ground beef, 2 cups water, 1 can (14-1/2 oz) stewed tomatoes, 1 package (10 oz) frozen mixed vegetables, 1 can (8 oz) tomato sauce, 1 envelope onion soup mix, 1/2 tsp sugar.
In a saucepan over medium heat, cook beef until no longer pink, 3-5 minutes, breaking into crumbles; drain. Add the remaining ingredients; bring to a boil. Reduce heat; cover and simmer until vegetables are tender about 10-15 minutes.
CHEDDAR POTATO SOUP
2 cups water, 2 cups diced unpeeled red potatoes, 1 cup diced carrot, 1/2 cup diced celery, 1/4 cup chopped onion, 1 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp pepper, 1/4 cup all-purpose flour, 2 cups 2% milk, 2 cups shredded reduced-fat cheddar cheese, 1 cup cubed fully cooked ham.
In a Dutch oven, combine the first seven ingredients. Bring to a boil. Reduce heat; cover and simmer for 10-12 minutes or until tender. Place flour in a large saucepan; gradually whisk in milk. Bring to a boil over medium heat; cook and stir for 2 minutes or until thickened. Remove from the heat. Add cheese; stir until melted. Stir the ham and the cheese sauce into undrained vegetables; stir until combined.
TURKEY AND WILD RICE SOUP
1/2 cup uncooked wild rice, 4 cups water, 1/2 cup butter (cubed), 8 oz chopped red potatoes (about 2 medium), 1 medium onion chopped, 1 celery rib chopped, 1 medium carrot chopped, 2 garlic cloves minced, 1/2 cup all-purpose flour, 3 cups chicken broth, 2 cups half-and-half cream, 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp dried rosemary (crushed), 2 cups cubed cooked turkey or chicken.
In a saucepan, combine rice and water; bring to a boil over high heat. Reduce heat; simmer covered, 30 minutes. Meanwhile, in a Dutch oven, heat butter over medium heat. Add potatoes, onion, celery and carrot; cook and stir for 6-8 minutes or until almost tender. Add garlic; cook 1 minute longer. Stir in flour until blended; cook and stir for 2 minutes. Gradually stir in broth and undrained rice. Bring to a boil over medium-high heat; cook and stir 1-2 minutes or until slightly thickened. Add cream, salt and rosemary; return to a boil. Simmer, uncovered, 15-20 minutes or until rice is tender, stirring occasionally. Stir in turkey; heat through.
STUFFED PEPPER SOUP
2 pounds ground beef, 6 cups water, 1 can (28 oz) tomato sauce, 1 can (28 oz) diced tomatoes (undrained), 2 cups chopped green peppers, 1/4 cup packed brown sugar, 2 tsps salt, 2 tsps beef bouillon granules, 1 tsp pepper, 2 cups cooked long grain rice, chopped fresh parsley.
In a Dutch oven over medium heat, cook and stir beef until no longer pink, breaking it into crumbles; drain. Stir in the next eight ingredients; bring to a boil. Reduce heat; simmer, uncovered, until peppers are tender, about 30 minutes. Add cooked rice; simmer, uncovered, 10 minutes longer. If desired, sprinkle with chopped fresh parsley. The skin of bell peppers is thin and easily digestible; peeling them is very rarely required.

title: Water's Edge Museum will celebrate upcoming anniversary celebration
author: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado
content:
Water's Edge Museum will celebrate upcoming anniversary celebration

 January 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Veronica Fernandez-Alvarado | Section: News 
 
 439
 Words 

 Read News Document

 OXFORD — Saturday, the Water's Edge Museum, Talbot County's first African American museum, is celebrating its four-year anniversary with music, art, food and a celebration of leaders on the Eastern Shore.In attendance will be Leroy Potter and his group at the Maryland Spirituals Initiative. They will perform for attendees and talk about the founding Black families and the legacy they left behind.
Kay Brown, a Queen Anne's native and co-director of the museum, said she is honored and proud to be working with such rich pieces of art and history.
According to Brown, from the walls to the staff, every bit of the museum is a part of the living history of the area, and through her time as co-director Brown has enjoyed watching the connection and joy people have visiting for the first time.
"It's just rewarding that we are on to something and people just like and when you come to the museum it's not like we're trying to kick (guests) out but they don't want to leave," Brown said. "They say they're so enamored of everything in the museum. Even our floors have history."
Over its four-year existence, the Water's Edge Museum has cultivated an abundance of programs and different galleries. Included in the galleries is the Environmental Justice as a Civil Right Galleries, where the museum presented photography, paintings, historic maps and high resolution cartography on how climate change is impacting underserved rural communities on the Chesapeake Bay.
In addition to celebrating the museum's four year anniversary, the team at Water's Edge will also honor Tish Moaney, who is described as the backbone of Oxford's Waters Church.
Moaney died this month, and in honor of her legacy the Water's Edge team will be playing some of her songs and a video.
Ja'lyn Hicks, curatorial and graphic designer for the museum, is a fourth generation native to the Eastern Shore. She said this museum empowered her to take pride in her community and embrace the stories of those around her.
More than anything, Hicks hopes the attendees of the event will find comfort in expressing and finding themselves especially during these unsure times.
"We are living in times that are hard and changing and there's a lot of uncertainty and there's also this fear that causes you to want to shrink into yourself and be like, 'I don't want to share my culture. I don't want to put myself out there. I don't know what's at risk by sharing my identity.' And so I'm hoping that by coming to our event, they feel that it's an environment where they can truly be themselves or even see themselves in some of the artwork," Hicks said.

title: Behind the scenes of a production about going behind the scenes
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Behind the scenes of a production about going behind the scenes

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 642
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — English playwright Michael Frayn's "Noises Off," opening Feb. 21 at the Garfield Center, is a play within a play. It features a troupe of American actors putting on a touring play called "Nothing On."In "Noises Off," the audience sees the dress rehearsal of "Nothing On" in Act I. In Act II, they witness the hilarious drama and tension between the actors backstage during the performance. Act III shows how things have comically deteriorated two months after opening night.
This meta storytelling offers an exaggerated glimpse of life backstage during theatrical productions. The play relies heavily on its set design.
Characters must time their responses perfectly, running through multiple doors in the proper English manor set. Like Kramer from "Seinfeld," but with a much larger cast of nine, they break windows, rush down steps, trip, slip, fall, scratch, drink and fight.
The set requires both an English manor setting and a backstage setting. It rotates between acts, with everything on rollers and interchangeable pieces from steps to platforms, all connected by pins and hinges.
"It is well-loved by professional and community theatre audiences, even though it requires a huge, two-story set that rotates between acts to show both the front and backstage areas of a touring play," according to a press release.
The interchangeable set requires meticulous planning and on-the-fly adjustments. Director and scenic designer Steven Arnold has extensive set design experience from his theater studies and his work on "The Play That Goes Wrong" in January 2022.
Like this story, that play featured a two-story set in an English manor. Arnold recalled that at one point, every item on the second story fell off the wall — from coat hooks to large chunks of the wall itself.
"The whole set was rigged," he said. In one scene, while actors stood on a platform, the floor was hinged to fall three times.
He said that while that was his craziest set, "Noises Off" might be the most complex to assemble.
The reason: doors are everywhere — upstairs, on the sides, in the attic, study, bathroom and bedrooms — with platforms and steps mirrored on both sides. Technicians are securing the set to the existing theater framework, and constructing railings and walls to ensure actor safety.
The set is tall enough that gallery viewers are level with actors on the second floor, Arnold noted.
His self-designed plans lie on a table beside the stage. Each floor plan was built to scale, with squares representing one foot, making construction easier for his contractor and workers.
Arnold praised his team: Butch Clark, contracted GCA technical director; Carmen Grasso, who has designed and built the "Noises Off" set for three previous productions; and Benji Price, theater assistant learning from both men.
Production stage manager Allison Jones is instrumental, Arnold said, along with construction help from Jeff Russell, Jim Landskroener and Jim Johnson.
The crew is working steadily on safety features so actors can begin rehearsing.
"The movement of this show is frantic and fast and can be dangerous unless what you have on this stage, with all its components, is solid, built well and safe to use," Arnold said.
Why tackle such an enormous project?
"It's a fun romp," Arnold said, grinning. He noted that audiences called "The Play That Goes Wrong" one of the funniest, most entertaining shows they'd seen.
The actors appreciate the elaborate set, which helps them stay in character, Grasso remarked.
It also helps the audience suspend disbelief and feel transported to a proper English manor.
"There are lots of places that ask their audience to use their full imagination. But when you can give your audience a big, grand set, they love it. It adds a different flavor to their experience," Arnold said.
"Noises Off" runs weekends from Feb. 21 through March 9. Shows are at 8 p.m. Fridays and Saturdays, and 2 p.m. Sundays. For tickets, visit garfieldcenter.org or call 410-810-2060 Wednesday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

title: Garlic to wasabi: Wild chocolate pairings give Valentine's a delicious twist
author: Robin Donovan Food Drink Life
content:
Garlic to wasabi: Wild chocolate pairings give Valentine's a delicious twist

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Robin Donovan Food Drink Life | Section: News 
 
 1158
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Chocolate-covered strawberries and hazelnut cream-filled truffles are classics, but why play it safe this Valentine's Day? There's a world of unconventional pairings that bring out chocolate's rich complexity in unexpected ways. Soy sauce, blue cheese or Kalamata olives may sound like strange partners for sweet chocolate, but that's the point — these daring pairings are bold and delicious, giving standard Valentine's Day offerings an exciting new twist.Why unusual chocolate pairings workThe magic behind these unconventional combinations lies in chocolate's unique chemical makeup. Cocoa contains both bitter compounds, like theobromine, and fats that mellow those sharp edges. When paired with salty, savory or even spicy flavors, chocolate's sweetness becomes more pronounced, and its richness shines through.
Scientists call this effect "taste contrast enhancement," where opposing flavors make each other more vibrant. According to a study in Flavour Journal, the interplay between sweet and savory flavors can enhance our taste experience. For instance, when you combine savory, meaty umami with sweetness, it creates a more complex and satisfying flavor profile.
Chocolate and cheese: A match worth melting forCheese boards and chocolate trays rarely mingle at the same table, but they should. Chocolate, especially dark chocolate with a hint of bitterness, pairs beautifully with creamy, tangy and even funky cheeses.
Take blue cheese, for instance. Its saltiness and pungent flavors contrast perfectly with the deep cocoa notes of dark chocolate. It's the same principle that makes salted caramel irresistible — sweetness tempered by salty and savory undertones.
For a milder approach, try rich brie with milk chocolate. These two creamy ingredients melt together into something unexpectedly lush. Add dried figs or almonds for texture, and you've got a dessert that could replace the standard cheese plate.
Chocolate and soy sauce: Sweet, salty and savorySoy sauce's salty umami highlights cocoa's natural sweetness without overpowering it. There's even a Japanese company that makes chocolate-flavored soy sauce, combining two fermented ingredients — cacao beans and soybeans — into one umami-rich seasoning.
A sprinkle of soy sauce over dark chocolate ice cream — or even just a square of good-quality dark chocolate — is transformative. The umami kicks in just as the chocolate dissolves, adding depth without excess salt. If you're feeling adventurous, a dash of soy sauce in a cup of hot chocolate lends a richer, more rounded flavor profile.
Chocolate and olive oil: A Mediterranean revelationOlive oil is celebrated as a base for salad dressings and marinades, but its potential in desserts is usually overlooked. Paired with dark chocolate, a fruity extra-virgin olive oil adds silky texture and subtle bitterness that enhance the chocolate's depth.
Drizzle olive oil over a slice of flourless chocolate cake, sprinkle with flaky sea salt, and you'll wonder why you haven't done it sooner. For an easy experiment, try dipping pieces of dark chocolate into a small dish of olive oil and topping with a pinch of salt. The combination is addictive.
Chocolate and chili: A kick of traditionWhile chili and chocolate might seem like a modern trend, the combination has ancient roots. The Aztecs and Mayans famously combined cacao with chili peppers to create a bitter, spicy drink known as "xocolatl." It's a powerhouse pairing, with chili enhancing chocolate's bitterness while adding a lingering heat that begs for another bite.
Spicy chili peppers pair best with dark chocolate that contains a high percentage of cocoa. A pinch of cayenne in a cup of hot chocolate is an easy way to test the waters, or you can try chili-dusted truffles for a fiery twist. Other spicy additions include ginger, pink peppercorns and cinnamon.
Chocolate and black garlic: The umami powerhouseBlack garlic might not be a pantry staple, but it deserves a spot on your experimental dessert list. It starts as fresh garlic — sharp and aromatic — and as it ages and ferments, develops a mellow, caramelized flavor.
"The sweet molasses and balsamic undertones in black garlic make it a great flavor addition to many desserts," according to Black Garlic North America, the continent's largest black garlic processor. It's sweet and sticky, similar to a raisin or date, making it a perfect complement to chocolate.
"One of the remarkable things about black garlic is just how many layers of flavor it has," says Katy Heath, founder of Balsajo, a black garlic producer in the United Kingdom. Try black garlic in chocolate ganache or as a secret addition to rich, fudgy brownies. It adds complexity without overwhelming the dish.
Chocolate and Kalamata olivesIf you're an olive lover, don't sleep on this combo. Dark chocolate has fruity notes that complement the saltiness of the olives, and the result is kind of mind-blowing.
"We all know how a pinch of sea salt can enhance dark chocolate, but just wait until you experience what black olives can do," says Food52 writer Cathleen Clarity, who uses Kalamata olives in her molten dark chocolate and black olive cake. "Their brininess and slightly bitter taste are the perfect complement to the molten dark chocolate."
Chocolate and matcha: An earthy fusionCombining chocolate with matcha, finely ground green tea powder, creates an intriguing flavor profile. The earthy bitterness of matcha complements the sweetness of chocolate, creating a delightful balance.
Matcha works especially well with white chocolate, known for its pronounced sweetness and creamy texture. Matcha's bitterness tempers the sweetness of white chocolate, while the chocolate's creaminess softens the tea's intensity, creating a smooth, complex and satisfying flavor profile.
Chocolate and wasabi: An unexpected heatPairing chocolate with wasabi, the Japanese horseradish commonly served with sushi, creates a surprising blend of sweet and spicy flavors. Wasabi's heat differs from that of chili peppers, hitting more in the nasal passages than on the tongue, and it dissipates more quickly. Wasabi cuts through the richness of the chocolate, exemplifying how contrasting flavors can both balance and accentuate each other.
White chocolate-coated wasabi peas capitalize on the addictive quality of the sweet-spicy, creamy-crunchy snack phenomenon. In Japan, you can even find wasabi and white chocolate KitKat bars made with wasabi from the Shizuoka prefecture, famous for its production of the spicy root.
To explore this combination at home, add a dollop of wasabi paste to chocolate ganache, hot fudge sauce or hot chocolate. Wasabi's heat sneaks up on you and can be quite potent, so start with a modest amount and adjust to taste.
The takeaway: Make bold moves this Valentine's DayWhen selecting a Valentine's gift this year, don't default to the same boring heart-shaped box of chocolates everyone goes for. Instead, surprise and delight your Valentine with unexpected chocolate pairings. If nothing else, these adventurous combinations are great conversation starters, and if they strike a chord with your sweetheart, they'll make the gesture — and you — unforgettable.
Robin Donovan is the author of more than 40 cookbooks and the founder and creator of All Ways Delicious, a food site loaded with easy recipes for the best dishes from around the world. Her writing and recipes have been featured in major media outlets including Huffington Post, MSN, Associated Press, Buzzfeed, Cooking Light, PopSugar, Chicago Sun-Times, Fitness, Parade, Mercury News and many others.

title: Julia Child's kitchen at the library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
Julia Child's kitchen at the library

 January 31, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life 
 
 696
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On Monday, March 3, at 6 p.m., in the Easton branch of the Talbot County Free Library, it will be my honor to interview Paula Johnson about her newest book, "Julia Child's Kitchen: The Design, Tools, Stories, and Legacy of an Iconic Space."Full disclosure: Johnson is a lifelong friend of mine. She is also a distinguished curator at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. Among her many curatorial triumphs, it was Johnson and co-curator Rayna Green that brought Julia Child's kitchen to the museum in 2001. Almost a quarter of a century later, it remains one of that institution's most popular exhibits.
I was one of the lucky fellows who received a copy of Johnson's new book when it came out in October.
Initially, truth be told, I wasn't sure what I would think of a book about a kitchen, fool that I am. Anyone who knows Julia Child, read her books or watched her television shows, knows that a book about Julia Child's kitchen is a book about Julia Child.
It's been a long time since I've had so much fun reading a book.
And the word "fun" is apt. Again and again in the book, as people recall cooking with Child in her kitchen or a meal they shared there, the word they use to describe both their host and the place is "fun."
Which is not to say that serious labor did not take place in that kitchen.
The book makes it clear that Child and her husband Paul were both workhorses. In the early television shows, the sponsoring public television station, WGBH Boston, couldn't afford retakes or editing. Julia had to begin upon a complicated recipe, carry it through, instructing all along, and arrive at a finished product that she could take a bite out of in just 28 minutes flat. The cameras shut off at 28 minutes, and there was no going back.
To accomplish this feat of legerdemain, she and Paul would practice for hours at home before a show, choosing which elements of a recipe to demonstrate, deciding how to demonstrate those elements and carefully working out the language to use in explaining them.
The whole thing was choreographed from beginning to end and different stages of the cooking prepared in advance so that, "through the magic of TV," they could be displayed at the proper time as if just pulled from the oven.
Yet somehow, Julia always came across as relaxed and enjoying herself. And it wasn't a guise.
One of the things I found most endearing about "Julia Child's Kitchen" is the way sections on subjects such as the kitchen's organizing principles inevitably end up revealing the love Paul Child felt for his wife, the care he took in setting up that kitchen and showcasing her art. In letters to his brother, Paul sometimes referred to his wife as "Julie."
Julia called her kitchen "the soul of the house," and her nephew, Alex Prud'homme, called the table where meals were served in that kitchen "the center of the universe."
Unsurprisingly for that time and a family of their class, the Childs had a formal dining room, but Julia's preferred place to serve friends a meal was the kitchen. Julia's unpretentious attitude toward entertaining (and herself) is made clear in her explanation for the placement of that kitchen table, "I want the dining table in the middle of the room because, like a sheepdog, I need to be right there in the midst of everyone."
That statement is so characteristic of the woman we meet in Johnson's book. Julia Child never fails to charm, yet somehow she never seems to patronize or fawn.
The book itself is like a party at Julia's house. You meet fascinating people, hear terrific stories, experience a magical place, and, at the very least, get to imagine yourself enjoying extraordinary meals.
Speaking of stories, I can tell you from long experience that the author of "Julia Child's Kitchen" is a great storyteller in person as well as in her writing. And so I ask the pleasure of your company on March 3 at 6 p.m. for an evening in Julia Child's kitchen, courtesy of the Smithsonian's Paula Johnson. Trust me, you're in for a real treat.

 "Bugatti: Reaching for Perfection", an exhibit highlighting the art, technology, race cars and automobiles of the Bugatti family, is currently open at the Academy Art Museum in Easton.AAM's Bugatti exhibit runs through April 13.
"This captivating exhibition showcases a rare collection of Bugatti automobiles, sculpture, and furniture, along with a trove of related ephemera that brings the Bugatti legacy to life. Highlights include five vintage Bugatti cars from the North Collection of Maryland's Eastern Shore, eight striking bronze sculptures from the Arsidi-Scuderi Collection of Switzerland, and iconic pieces of furniture designed by Carlo Bugatti, who pioneered a unique blend of artistic creativity and technical mastery. Visitors will also encounter rare photographs and advertisements, offering a deeper understanding of the Bugatti family's unparalleled influence on the worlds of art, design, and automotive innovation," according to an announcement from AAM.
"Ettore Bugatti, famous for his race cars and luxurious automobiles, and his son Jean, known for their forward-thinking designs, reshaped the world of automobiles into something that was both technically sophisticated and beautifully artistic. From grand prix race cars to the iconic Type 57 touring models and the miniature 'Baby' ugatti, the exhibition immerses visitors in the world of high-performance automobiles that symbolize the dynamic energy of the 20th century. This exhibition is not just about cars—it's a tribute to the intersection of art, engineering, and modernity that defined Bugatti's legacy," the AAM announcement continued.

 Local student artists from Kent Island High School captured all four finalist spots in the visual art category of the esteemed Saturday 'Visiter' Awards, presented by Poe Baltimore.The competition celebrates a new generation of artists inspired by Edgar Allan Poe's life and works, honoring creativity in media, art, performance, and writing.
The awards ceremony took place at Westminster Hall & Burying Ground in Baltimore — an iconic "Poe Place." The evening included a catacomb tour and a murder mystery event to commemorate what would have been Poe's 216th birthday.
Student finalists, are senior Brooke Register, junior Alexis Detamore, junior Grace Hartlove, and senior Mark Monroe, who claimed the top honor with a mixed media piece, "No Pain; I Am Done," inspired by Poe's tale "The Facts in the Case of M. Valdemar."

The Saturday 'Visiter' Awards are named for the periodical that famously launched Edgar Allan Poe's literary career. Poe won the original award for his short story "MS Found in a Bottle" while living in Baltimore. Today, the awards recognize works that adapt Poe's life or writings and original works inspired by his legacy, continuing to celebrate his profound influence on the arts and literature worldwide.

 OXFORD — Surrounded by historic paintings, photos and maps, nearly 100 people packed the tight confines of the Water's Edge Museum Saturday to honor and celebrate Black history on the Eastern Shore.Talbot County's first African American museum celebrated its fourth anniversary in Oxford Saturday afternoon, along with kicking off Black History Month. The galleries around the museum tell the stories of Maryland's founding Black families.
Elinor Thompson, a member of the Maryland Commission on African American History and Culture, spoke in front of the large crowd. She emphasized the importance of passing down and preserving history.
"I'm so glad that we, as a community, this community, can come together and share some of this rich history that we can pass onto the next generation," said Thompson, a Kent Island native.
Kay Brown, co-director of Water's Edge Museum, thanked those who came out, including local leaders and community members. The crowd was welcomed by musician Leroy Potter and his group at the Maryland Spirituals Initiative.
During the anniversary celebration, the museum's team provided tours of the galleries, which dive into Oxford's Black history as well as that of the Eastern Shore. Brown said bringing the younger generations into the museum is a key goal moving forward.
"We need the seed planted," Brown said. "And we are enthusiastic with our team, and I cannot do this without my team."
During the event, Brown asked the Moaney family to stand, honoring the late Tissier Moaney, who died last month. She is described as a founding backbone of the museum's collection.
Jeffrey Moaney is a genealogical advisor for the museum and Tissier Moaney's grandson. He said his grandmother was friends with Water's Edge Museum Founder Barbara Paca for the last 15 years.
The two amassed a collection of work and history before the museum ever existed.
"It is my grandmother who helped make that connection between the historians of our family like myself and a couple of others to bring this collection to life," Jeffrey Moaney said. "And as an exhibition, as well as a book."
While giving a short presentation, Thompson asked attendees to sit down with their families to protect and explore family histories.
"We need to have generational sustainability for the next generation," Thompson said. "We need to put our gifts and talents back into our community. We need to start with our businesses and things like that."
Thompson asked parents to encourage their children to learn cursive writing, as most papers and documents she preserves are written in cursive. "We want to put those things back into our communities, back into our children," she said.
As Black History Month began Saturday, Brown said it's the perfect time for the community to "show off and show out" by commemorating its roots, just like the Water's Edge Museum has been doing for four years
"You all can make your own memories, make your own museum, in your own churches," Brown said. "We need to start pulling out our photos of grandparents, uncles and aunts, and preserve those photos. Our kids need to see what things look like."

title: 'Symmetrical Bodies' on display at St. Mary's College
author: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com
content:
'Symmetrical Bodies' on display at St. Mary's College

 February 6, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Ted Black tblack@somdnews.com | Section: Entertainment 
 
 491
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Longtime St. Mary's College of Maryland art professor Susan R. Johnson remembered the impact that her mother and Hollywood actresses had on her family growing up in Los Angeles, and through the first week of March guests and students will have the chance to get a glimpse of that impact on full display.Earlier this month on a Tuesday afternoon inside the genuinely cozy confines of the Boyden Art Gallery inside the Montgomery Hall on campus, Johnson spoke to a gathering of students and guests to discuss the recent unveiling of her new exhibit "Symmetrical Bodies."
The new show features super-lifelike images of women in various roles adorned on material typically relegated to banners and flags.
"Throughout the centuries there have been so many ways that women have been photographed and visualized in advertisements," said Johnson, who moved from New Jersey in 1993 to begin her teaching career at St. Mary's College. "A lot of them were featured in so many ways in magazines and on postcards and it's amazing to see how the images have changed over the centuries."
As Johnson noted in her presentation to the audience last Tuesday, her "Symmetrical Bodies" project draws inspiration from the ideal of body symmetry, an unattainable perfection and beauty that contrasts with the reality of human diversity. Her work will be displayed on the walls of the Boyden Art Gallery through March 7, offering onlookers to see and appreciate her concepts.
"My mother was a big influence on me in every aspect of my life," Johnson said. "We grew up in Los Angeles, so Hollywood was a big influence on my mom. You can see in the objects that I created, images of Judy Garland, Audrey Hepburn and Liz Taylor, and none of them really appear as though we remember them because each side of their face is different from the other."
In addition to the symmetrical images, the portraits are done on a cloth material that naturally blurs the images. While photos and drawings are basically crystal clear by design on post cards and magazines, Johnson's works on material designed for other purposes, purposely blurs the images of each of the females she has highlighted on works in the gallery.
"In actuality, the images of the women are larger than life," Johnson said. "There is symmetry, but their images are far from perfect and there is a blurred effect created by the material. But that is also done by design. It is meant to highlight the fact that there is no perfect body symmetry. We always look for perfection, but it is really not attainable."
If you go
The new art exhibit "Symmetrical Bodies" created by St. Mary's College of Maryland art professor Susan R. Johnson will be on display in the Boyden Art Gallery located inside the Montgomery Hall, which is on campus of St. Mary's College. For more information regarding the exhibit and operating hours, contact the school during business hours at 410-895-2000 or go to www.smcm.edu/boyden-gallery.

title: 'Subversive' exhibit pushes the boundaries of fiber and thread art'
author: Staff Writer
content:
'Subversive' exhibit pushes the boundaries of fiber and thread art'

 February 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 929
 Words 

 Read News Document

 "The Subversive Thread" — an exhibit and series of events at the Academy Art Museum — "showcases four artists who challenge the conventional boundaries of fiber and thread art."That is according to an announcement from the downtown Easton museum.
"The Submersive Thread" features fiber and threadworks by Han Cao, Jennifer McBrien, Michael-Birch Pierce, and Stacey Lee Webber. The exhibit runs through March 30
Here is rundown of the artists and their work, according to the AAM announcement.
Han Cao infuses found photos with modern narratives, using needlework to add texture and depth. Each piece invites viewers to engage intimately, bridging past and present through stitches that connect distant figures to contemporary observers. Cao's sense of humor adds another layer of depth to her work: through subtle nuances and playful elements, she examines conventional perceptions and invites viewers to approach her artwork with curiosity and joy.i
Jennifer McBrien's striking Warrior Women series features a dramatic departure from the typical confines of embroidery hoops, with vintage toile curtain panels cascading freely from their frames. McBrien's hybrid figures, merging avian and female forms, symbolize the fragility of endangered species, evolving alongside the deteriorating fabric. Complementing the series is the poignant installation Hanging Them Out to Dry, a visceral commentary on the plight of endangered birds. Hung on a clothesline, embroidered vintage napkins evoke a sense of vulnerability, emphasizing the urgent need for conservation efforts to safeguard threatened species from extinction.
Michael-Birch Pierce explores identity through embroidery, blending traditional techniques with contemporary themes. At the heart of Pierce's practice lies an intimate exploration of the self and the narratives chosen to weave around it. Through the medium of embroidery, Pierce delves into the layers of identity, often cloaking their creations in the superficial trappings of high fashion and costume. Their work challenges notions of authenticity, inviting viewers to peel back layers of artifice and notice the essence beneath.
Stacey Lee Webber's choice of American currency as a medium is particularly poignant. By stitching directly onto artifacts of commerce, she forges a tangible connection between past and present, laborer and leader. Ultimately, the act of embroidering through dollar bills becomes an act of defiance — a subversion of the traditional notions of value and representation, making symbols of capitalism available for introspection and critique.
The exhibition is organized in conjunction with the Museum's 27th Annual Craft Show in October. "represents a pioneering initiative for AAM as it embarks on a new path to integrate exhibitions of contemporary craft into its well-established 3-day event. The Museum seeks to enrich the visitor's experience by showcasing examples of modern craft alongside traditional work."
This exhibition was made possible through Westobou Gallery in Augusta, Georgia.
There are a number of other upcoming events at the Easton museum. according to AAM.
AAM Film Series: Unraveling Narratives
Now through March, 2025
(Film pass: $25 members, $35 non-members, per film $10 members,$15 non-members, includes beer and popcorn for members, $5 non-members) .
Dive into the themes of The Subversive Thread exhibition through Unraveling Narratives, a curated monthly film series that brings fiber art's cultural intersections to the screen. Join us for thought-provoking documentaries and narrative features, followed by facilitated discussions connecting the films' stories to the exhibition's exploration of fiber, craft, and culture. From powerful documentaries like Yarn to artist profiles like Outsider: The Life and Art of Judith Scott, this series invites audiences to experience fiber art in an entirely new dimension. Screenings are open to all, with refreshments provided for post-film discussions.
The Subversive Thread Art Cart: Stitching Stories
Every Thursday through March 27, 5-7 pm
Explore the art of embroidery and its connection to storytelling, line drawing, and mark-making. Throughout the exhibition's run, this mobile art-making station will be available to invite visitors to experiment with embroidery techniques. Inspired by the work of fiber artists featured in The Subversive Thread, this drop-in program offers examples of stitches and materials for creating your own textile art. Whether you're a seasoned stitcher or new to fiber arts, this hands-on experience brings a tactile dimension to the exhibition's themes of identity, craft, and creativity.
The Subversive Thread Art Cart: Stitching Stories with Jennifer McBrien
Thursday, February 13, 4:30 - 7 pm
Don't miss the chance to stitch with The Subversive Thread artist Jennifer McBrien at the Art Cart! Whether you're new to embroidery or an experienced stitcher, Jennifer will guide you through basic techniques or help you bring your own design to life. Additionally, please feel free to bring a piece of fabric and a concept to work on. Jennifer will be in the gallery from 4:30 pm until the "Threads of Disruption" lecture.
Threads of Disruption: A Contemporary Craft Conversation
Thursday, February 13, 6 pm
The exhibition's featured artists—Han Cao, Jennifer McBrien, Michael-Birch Pierce, and Stacey Lee Webber—share their unique approaches to fiber and thread art. This dynamic event begins with four mini-presentations from each artist, offering personal insights into their creative processes and the themes driving their work. Following these presentations, a lively discussion, led by the exhibition's curator, will explore the thematic connections of identity, subversion, and value that unite the artists' practices while highlighting the unique perspectives that set each artist apart. The evening concludes with an open Q&A session, offering an opportunity for meaningful dialogue with the artists.
Threads of Sound: Improvisational Music Inspired by The Subversive Thread
Friday, March 28, 5:30–7:30 pm
Experience the intersection of art and music with musicians Robert Hitz and Felicia Harrington in a dynamic, live musical experience directly responding to the textures, narratives, and themes of the exhibition. Guided by the exhibition's curator, this performance will explore the dialogue between visual and auditory art forms, weaving together an evening of creativity, inspiration, and discovery.

title: Real or not, Chessie the sea monster is part of Maryland culture
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Real or not, Chessie the sea monster is part of Maryland culture

 February 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 607
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — In the late 1970s and early 1980s, the Chesapeake Bay gained a mystery.Multiple sitings of an unknown creature stirred concern and intrigue that a sea monster lurked in Maryland and Virginia's waters.
During a presentation at the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum Thursday evening, historian Eric A. Cheezum talked about the "thoroughly modern monster," putting its discovery in context of the times.
Cheezum started off his presentation with a grainy video that fills the screen with blue. Despite the video's poor quality, many in the audience of the event thought they saw something moving in the video.
Taken of the Bay off Kent Island on Memorial Day in 1982, the grainy video launched Chessie "into the international firmament of cryptozoology," or the study of hidden animals, Cheezum said. Although it was not the first Chessie siting, it was a big moment in Maryland pop culture.
Chessie has been described as long, dark creature, smooth like a snake, that moves fast through the water in a motion that is different than other serpents.
Robert and Karen Frew, the couple who captured the video of who they believe was Chessie, were "relatively new transplants" to Kent Island, Cheezum said. They had a waterfront home, and, for them, the Bay was a place for recreation.
Cheezum considers the video camera the most notable part of the Frews' story. He said that having a camera on the Eastern Shore in 1982 was "at least as rare as a sea monster" due to the wealth necessary to afford it.
The video camera was a symbol of the change happening on the Eastern Shore.
After World War II, the areas surrounding the Chesapeake Bay developed very fast, Cheezum said. "And suddenly you have people in rural places who have never been in those places before," he said.
The shoreline also started to shift from a place of work to a place for recreation. Almost all the people who claimed to have seen Chessie were on the Bay for recreation, not watermen who had been working on the water for generations.
Cheezum said this falls into the theme of "natives versus outsiders," with the outsiders being tourists and suburbanites. He also noted that at the time of these sitings, movies like "Jaws" and "Piranha" were popular.
Amateur Chessie investigator Wayne Lawson said the reason watermen didn't see Chessie in the water was because they they weren't sitting there, scanning the water. They had work to do.
In 1993, a manatee was discovered in the Bay after it swam up the coast, Cheezum said. The manatee, which made this journey more than once, was named Chessie.
Cheezum said he thinks there's a strong likelihood the people who spotted Chessie were actually seeing manatees.
"I hate being that on the nose," he said. "Because I want to believe too."
But, even if the creature was a manatee, it has shaped Maryland culture. Cheezum mentioned the Chessie-shaped boats that people can take out in Baltimore's Inner Harbor. He talked about a children's book featuring Chessie that aimed to teach kids the importance of protecting the environment.
In the 1970s, Marylanders started to appreciate the Bay and its heritage more, Cheezum said.
"And Chessie somehow seems to kind of sum all that up," he said, "which is really weird because there's about a million other things that could sum up the Bay besides a sea monster."
After Cheezum's presentation, Joseph Kempf — who now believes Chessie was a manatee that people mistook for a sea monster — asked why watermen never saw Chessie if the creature had been a manatee the whole time.
Cheezum replied that people see what they want to see.
"The thing that is observed is shaped by the observer," he said.

title: Chef of St. Michaels restaurant named James Beard semi-finalist
author: Maggie Trovato
content:
Chef of St. Michaels restaurant named James Beard semi-finalist

 February 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Maggie Trovato | Section: Local News 
 
 571
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — After the cold temperatures of a January morning cut his hunting plans short, Ruse executive chef and partner Michael Correll went home to take a nap before work.When he woke up, text messages from the restaurant's partners were blowing up his phone. Then the general manager of The Wildset Hotel — which houses the restaurant in St. Michaels — called.
"So my first thought is something's wrong," Correll said.
When he picked up the phone, the general manager congratulated him. Correll had been named a semi-finalist of the James Beard Award for best chef in the Mid-Atlantic.
"I was just numb," Correll said about how he felt when he learned the news. He called his mom, who started crying.
"It's the biggest accomplishment an American chef can have," Correll said. "I mean, besides Michelin Guide, James Beard is like the biggest one."
Established in 1990, the James Beard Awards recognize leaders in the culinary arts and food media industries, according to the James Beard Foundation's website. He said the day after he received the news, the entire restaurant cheered for him during happy hour.
"I think the coolest thing about the whole process is just the outpouring of love from people," he said. "Like people I haven't talked to in a long time, people who I didn't even know knew me, people just reaching out."
Correll has been serving elevated fare, switching up menus by the season and scouring the area for the best seafood since Ruse opened on Talbot Street in 2021. From the start, the restaurant aimed to bring a Washington, D.C., caliber of dining to the heart of St. Michaels, focusing on sustainable seafood and local ingredients, Correll said.
For Correll, inspiration comes from trying different foods and keeping a finger on the pulse.
"The restaurant industry is constantly evolving and changing, so it's just being aware of what's going on," he said. "But also it's like, you have to put your own flair on it."
That inspiration doesn't just come from fine dining. Correll said inspiration can come from any good flavor combination. He said he was inspired to create a steak tartare dish after eating a carne asada taco with salsa roja.
When it comes to the quality of seafood, Correll sources from different places to ensure it's fresh.
"I do things the hard way," he said. "Which is like, I find a guy who sells the best of something, and I buy that from that person. ... Just because that's how you get the best product. You have to work for it."
Allie Balin, Ruse's food and beverage director, said Correll and the entire restaurant is all about supporting local watermen, farmers and small businesses. She said Correll is collaborative when it comes to developing the menu too.
"Anyone who's involved in any artistic pursuit, getting feedback on what you're creating can be challenging," she said. "And Mike takes it extremely well. His goal is just to create the best possible product."
As someone who played sports when he was younger, Correll sees the kitchen as a team sport of sorts. He said that a team mentality makes a kitchen successful.
"I think that's what makes us special is the team," he said. "Because, I'm not trying to brag, but food's always going to be good. But the team is what takes it to the next level."
Correll said he will find out in April if he made it to the final round of the James Beard Awards.

title: Frederick Douglass' Valentine's Day birthday honored by his family
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Frederick Douglass' Valentine's Day birthday honored by his family

 February 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 686
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Frederick Douglass never knew his exact birthday.Like many born into slavery, the exact date was never recorded. Douglass knew it was sometime in February but not the exact day.
Douglass chose to celebrate on Valentine's Day because his mother called him her "little Valentine."
"Yes, he celebrated his birthday on Valentine's Day," Douglass' five-time great nephew Tarence Bailey Sr. said. "Feb. 14 through Feb. 20, you can say it's the most important week of Black History Month because that's the week of Frederick Douglass' birth and death."
Douglass has strong roots in Talbot County and throughout the Eastern Shore.
Born in Talbot County in 1818, Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey Douglass was enslaved for 20 years in Baltimore and on Talbot County farms. He fled north in 1838 and changed his name to Frederick Douglass. His brilliance, eloquence and courage, quickly brought him to the forefront of the abolitionist movement.
He was known for his skills as an orator, with many of his speeches remembered to this day.
"He spoke in Denton on Halloween 1883, and Douglas took the train from Wilmington to Denton," author and historian John Muller said. "Then when he was leaving and he spoke in front of the County Courthouse in Denton... there was so many people they didn't fit inside. The crowd had to go outside."
According to Muller, Douglass also spoke in Cambridge, St. Michaels, and many more Eastern Shore locales.
Douglass and his work are inspirational to many Americans, but it goes deeper than just inspiration for the Bailey-Groce Family Foundation, Bailey said.
The Bailey-Groce Family Foundation is run by multiple Douglass family members who grew up on the Eastern Shore. It is one of two family foundations operated by descendants of the Douglass bloodline.
"I think for my family here from Talbot County and from Eastern Shore as a whole, it's a whole lot different for us," Bailey said. "Being raised on the Shore and then having the relative like him, you look at it differently than the average person does."
Three years ago, the foundation started hosting a birthday celebration for Fredrick Douglas between Feb. 14 and 20, close to his birthday and the anniversary of his death. This year's celebration will be held on Feb. 22 due to a scheduling conflict.
The birthday celebration is held to help fundraise for an African American Cultural Center and an African American Historical Society, institutions the foundation plans to establish in Talbot County.
The event will begin at the historic Avalon Theatre at 3:45 p.m.
This year's event will feature a homecoming performance by Ayla Dennis, who was featured on American Idol.
"She's actually a Bailey family descendant," Bailey said. "So it's going to be a history making to have her singing at the Avalon, which was a formerly segregated theater down the street from where the slave auction once was, right there by the courthouse where Frederick Douglass spoke, having his relatives actually headlining for his birthday in a formerly segregated theater."
Other entertainment for Douglass' birthday celebration includes a county group from Atlanta, Georgia; a concert violinist from Philadelphia, Pennsylvania; a featured poet from Brooklyn, New York; and many more.
After the performances, the foundation will host a VIP dinner at the Waterfowl Building in Easton. The foundation wants everyone to wear African-style clothing to honor Douglass' heritage.
"Frederick Douglass was a very classy dude. We like to keep his birthday the way he would want it," Bailey said. "He was John Q when it came to his clothes. Everything he wore was Brooks Brothers. So he was always dressed to the nines. So I know that at his birthday party, he would want everybody in there dressed as well as him."
The Foundation continues to host these types of events not just to raise funds, but to keep Douglass' legacy alive, Bailey said.
"Uncle Frederick is the main reason, the only reason that I that keeps me going, that keeps me pushing," Bailey Sr. said. "The goal is much bigger, Fredrick Douglass himself is the inspiration, because if it wasn't for him I don't know if we would have made it this far."
For more information about the celebration or to purchase tickets, visit avalonfoundation.org/events.
