title: 'Musical time travelers': Slambovian Circus of Dreams brings its eclectic style, inspirations to Easton, Elkton
author: Staff Writer
content:
'Musical time travelers': Slambovian Circus of Dreams brings its eclectic style, inspirations to Easton, Elkton

 February 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Music 
 
 547
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Slambovian Circus of Dreams is coming to Maryland for shows at the Avalon Theatre in Easton on Friday, Feb. 21 and at the Elkton Music Hall in Elkton on Saturday, Feb. 22.The Avalon show starts at 7 p.m. Tickets are $30. The Elkton concert starts at 8 p.m. Tickets are $32.
The band also has another upcoming show on Sunday, Feb. 23, at the Havana in New Hope, Pennsylvania.
The eclectic band has its origins in Sleepy Hollow, New York.
We caught up with Joziah Longo and Tink Lloyd to talk about their musical journey and upcoming concerts.
Tell us a bit about the band and your musical journeys?
Joziah: The band first formed in Sleepy Hollow, New York and have been working our way up the Hudson River ever since. You could say our neighborhood extends everywhere from NYC to Woodstock. As our fan base grew, we began touring the UK regularly since 2008, playing all the major festivals — instead of going west, we headed east to the musical 'holy land' of England. They really 'get us' there as our "Woodstock-tinged psychedelia" has a lot of British folk-rock influences alongside the very Americana.
What should fans expect at the upcoming shows?
Tink: We're celebrating the 25th anniversary of our debut album, "A Good Thief Tips His Hat" which is still a fan fave. Some of those songs will be included for this show, and since the new Dylan movie, "A Complete Unknown" came out, we'll slip in a few choice Dylan tunes for everyone. Dylan was a big influence on Joziah growing up. He thought he was Bob Dylan when he was 12 — that was ok because Dylan thought he was Woody Guthrie.
What stands out about your live performances and musical connections to fans?
Tink: As a band, we're somewhat "musical time travelers", tapping familiar language and textures. Audiences feel like they recognize the songs from a misty, past memory — though the songs are all distinctly 'Slambovian'.
Joziah: The Avalon show will be in the main theatre, our first time on the big stage. This lets us bring our projections (we are ultimately an 'art-school' band, you know). But no matter the size of stage, shows keep an intimate vibe that lets the audience 'tune in' and connect for a tribal musical experience.
Who are your musical influences, inspirations?
Joziah: I grew up playing on Friday nights in my Dad's basement. He could play anything — country, rock and the British Invasion — I attended the ultimate 'School of Rock'.
Tink: As a flutist, I was always attracted to acoustic rock and Celtic music. Influences of Jethro Tull (Ian Anderson is a fan) definitely shine when I pick up my flute or recorder at shows. My main instrument, however, is the accordion! Fellow player, Garth Hudson of The Band was a 'mentor' to me and loved Joziah's songwriting (btw, he passed away in Woodstock just last week). That 'band' vibe is a part of our legacy, and hence, comparisons to The Band — but with Dylan/Bowie as lead singer.
What else is up with the band?
Joziah: We just started work on our 7th studio album, "The Book of Better Things". We'll be playing a few tracks at this weekend's shows... "Everyone's Dumb in Their Own Special Way" is sure to get everyone singing along.

title: Chesapeake legacy honored at Frederick Douglass Day Celebration
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Chesapeake legacy honored at Frederick Douglass Day Celebration

 February 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 355
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Leaders in maritime heritage, arts and social justice gathered at Washington College for the annual Frederick Douglass Day of Acknowledgement, celebrating African American contributions to the Chesapeake Bay region.The ceremony, co-hosted by Washington College and Bayside H.O.Y.A.S (Helping Our Youth Achieve Success) at the Decker Theatre on campus, opened with Maryland Public Television's Emmy-winning documentary "Water's Edge: Black Watermen of the Chesapeake".
Film Director Alexis Aggrey joined a panel discussion alongside Salisbury University Professor Emerita Clara Small, Minorities in Aquaculture CEO Imani Black, and fifth-generation fisherman Capt. Tyrone Meredith. Artist Marc Castelli and Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum Chief Historian Pete Lesher rounded out the panel examining the bay's role as an economic and cultural cornerstone for African Americans.
Composer Marlon Saunders performed selections from "ISAAC: A Musical Journey," commissioned by the Kent Cultural Alliance. The work chronicles Isaac Mason's escape from slavery in Chestertown and his emergence as a community leader.
This year's Frederick Douglass awards recognized Rev. James Jones, convener of Caucus of African American Leaders on the Eastern Shore; Vincent Leggett, author and founder of Blacks of the Chesapeake Foundation; and Saunders, founder of The Seamless Voice.
Social media influencer Tyshawn "YVNG SWAG" Johnson received the Bayside H.O.Y.A.S Shooting Star award. The 25-year-old entertainer, known for his role on Nick Cannon's Wild 'N Out and various brand partnerships, represents a modern parallel to Douglass's own mastery of public image.
Johnson's family, including two sisters and one brother, are all from the Chestertown area and attended schools here. Even before signing a record deal, (he signed with Atlantic Records as a high school senior) Johnson had an active Facebook and Instagram account with thousands of followers. A video of him dancing reached 1 million views on Instagram over the summer of 2016.
The honorees reflect Douglass's diverse legacy, from his early exposure to maritime life near Wye Mills to his later emergence as a prominent public figure who skillfully managed his public persona.
"This was the best event yet," said John Queen, H.O.Y.A.S. president. "The documentary and panel were greatly received. People absolutely loved the Marlon Saunders performance, and the award recipients are always top-tier community leaders and class acts."

title: New sculptures enhance Chestertown's public art collection
author: Staff Writer
content:
New sculptures enhance Chestertown's public art collection

 February 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 255
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Four new sculptures from the Peter and Hanna Woicke Collection have arrived in town, with one already installed and three awaiting placement."Super Duty Yellow," created in 2013 by American artist Jeremy Thomas, now stands in Gateway Park at Route 20 and Flatland Road. Thomas crafted the abstract piece by welding metal sheets together and inflating them with forced air, creating forms that evoke everything from birthday balloons to fortune cookies.
The remaining three pieces are temporarily housed at Robert Ortiz Studios, 207 S. Cross St., where the public can view them weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to noon and 1:30 to 5:30 p.m., and Saturdays from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
"Inchworm (for John Coltrane)," a 2000 work by Lee Kelly, features swirling Cor-Ten steel forms that echo the jazz legend's fluid playing style. The piece's steel wheels offer a subtle nod to Coltrane's nickname, "Trane."
Don Rambadt's "Woicke's Owl," commissioned by the collectors in 2000, continues the artist's minimalist approach to bird sculptures, similar to his local works "Sentinel" at the Cerino Center and "Strength of Community" at Cannon and Mill streets.
"Fully Empowered" by Maryland artist Ella Tulin was featured in the United Nations' "Progress of the World's Women" exhibit in 2000. The 1987 sculpture represents Tulin's significant contribution to the feminist art movement.
The Woicke Collection, now fully gifted to the town, comprises 23 pieces from American and international artists. The Public Arts Committee works with town officials to place the sculptures throughout Chestertown, with installation handled by local artisans Ben Herr, Mat Warrington and Rob Glebe.

title: Learning the story of Harriet Tubman
author: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com
content:
Learning the story of Harriet Tubman

 February 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Matt Wynn mwynn@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 351
 Words 

 Read News Document

 History was brought to life with a performance telling the story of Harriet Tubman, an Eastern Shore native and one of the most significant abolitionists of her era.The Friends of Maxwell Hall, a group dedicated to preserving and bringing to light the history of the hall, put on a performance Feb. 15 featuring Shemika Renee, a first-person historical performer,
Mike Callahan, a member of the Friends of Maxwell Hall, shared a little bit of the property's history with Southern Maryland News.
The historic property was built by George Maxwell, a Scottish immigrant, approximately 255 years ago. Maxwell was a merchant and sold goods to local people and had grown tobacco on his property.
The house, situated on the Star Spangled Banner Trail, was in despair by the 1980s with holes in the ceiling and was purchased and remodeled to become the landmark it is today.
While Maxwell enslaved people, the story told at the house was one of triumph.
Renee delivered a riveting telling of Tubman's life through her perspective.
Renee started her performance by detailing the early years of Tubman, including her life-changing traumatic head injury that caused severe headaches throughout her life and narcolepsy.
She detailed how Tubman actually became "Harriet Tubman" as it was not her given birth name. Tubman was born Araminta Ross and had the nickname "Minty."
When she was older, she took her mother's name — Harriet — and her husband's last name of "Tubman" and became Harriet Tubman.
"I wanted to be free," Renee said while in character. "I will never forget that first sunrise when I knew I had crossed the border. … It was like the sun was gleaming down through the leaves, and the gold was just shining on my hands."
Echoing Tubman's actions of constantly going back to help family, friends and others find freedom, Tubman said, "I feel that I could have saved so many more people if they had even known that they was in bondage."
The Friends of Maxwell Hall hosts an annual colonial fair the third weekend of October every year, spirit investigations and a variety of other events. To find out more, go to www.friendsofmh.com/events.

title: Temple B’nai Israel presents 'a joyous evening of klezmer music'
author: Staff Writer
content:
Temple B’nai Israel presents 'a joyous evening of klezmer music'

 February 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Music 
 
 313
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Have you ever danced the Hora?If you've ever attended a reception for a bar or bat mitzvah or danced at a Jewish wedding, you probably have. This popular dance is perhaps the best known example of klezmer music, a style of instrumental music that dates back centuries.
At 7 p.m. on Thursday, March 6, at Temple B'nal Israel, the Satell Center for Jewish Life on the Eastern Shore, The Seth Kibel Trio will entertain with a program of klezmer music (Eastern European Jewish folk music).
The trio will also take some musical detours into Yiddish theater, Yiddish folksong, as well as jazz and swing.
"Historical commentary and anecdotes from Kibel will provide an insightful context for their selections. A pre-concert lecture presentation from Kibel will make this a true evening of "edutainment," according to an announcement from the Easton synagogue.
"This program is presented as part of the Susan and Barry Koh Music Series. Klezmer, which literally means 'tool of song' in Yiddish, is the secular folk music of Jews of Central and Eastern Europe. In the first decades of the 1900s, this music flourished not only in the Old World but also in the New, in the immigrant community of New York City," the announcement reads. "The result was a quintessentially American sound."
"Seth Kibel is one of the Mid-Atlantic's premier woodwind specialists, working with klezmer, jazz, swing, and other bands. Wowing audiences on clarinet, flute, and saxophone, Seth has made a name for himself in the Washington/Baltimore region, and beyond. He is the featured performer with The Kleztet, Bay Jazz Project, Music Pilgrim Trio, The Natty Beaux, and more," according to the announcement. "His most recent recording, "Clown With A Stick," was released in May 2023 on the Azalea City Recordings record label. www.sethkibel.com."
Everyone is welcome, admission is free. Register at bnaiisraeleaston.org/event/Klezmer or call 410-822-0553.
Temple B'nai Israel is located at 7199 Tristan Drive in Easton.

title: Local students win top honors at state art contest
author: Staff Writer
content:
Local students win top honors at state art contest

 February 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Arts 
 
 330
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Kent Island High School senior Mark Monroe and sophomore Aubrey Kline earned 2nd and 3rd place in The Arc of Maryland's "Together We're Better" Art Contest — marking the third consecutive year that Kent Island students have claimed top awards in the statewide competition.Their winning artwork will be published in The Arc of Maryland's annual coloring book, which will be on display at ArtScene 2025 at KIHS on May 1.
Kent Island art teacher Andrea Schulte was honored in spring 2024 with The Arc of Maryland's Statewide School Inclusion Award for her championing of students with disabilities and fostering a culture of empathy and accessibility in the arts.
For Schulte, this mission has become deeply personal. After suffering profound hearing loss this past year, she has become a member of the disability community herself—an experience that has only strengthened her passion for making art education more inclusive, while inspiring students to embrace their varied abilities. Her leadership in The Arc's "Together We're Better" initiative has not only provided students with intellectual and developmental disabilities greater opportunities in the arts but has also helped all students develop greater compassion, understanding, and inclusivity.
School district Fine Arts Supervisor Michael Bell accompanied Schulte to awards in support of her and her students. He said Schulte has gained momentum as a state arts leader, presenting at numerous conferences on empowering student voice. "Andrea's dedication — while navigating her own hearing loss journey — is nothing short of inspiring. She leads by example, showing students that their voices, stories, and creativity matter," said Bell.
Monetary prizes presented to the school have been used by Schulte's National Art Honor Society to host an annual art party for students with developmental disabilities — further reinforcing dedication to inclusive arts education.
"Mark and Aubrey have used their artistic talent to make a real impact, advocating for students with developmental disabilities through their work. We're proud of their accomplishments and excited to see them recognized at the state level," Principal Dan Harding said.

 EASTON — The Bailey-Groce Family Foundation hosted the 207th birthday celebration for Frederick Douglass. The celebration was held at at the historic Avalon Theatre.Proceeds from the celebration will go toward a planned African American cultural center, an institution the foundation aims to establish in Talbot County.
"It's just getting people to come out," Douglass' five-time great nephew Tarence Bailey Sr. said. "All this is fundraising for an African American culture center. I wouldn't care if only one person showed up here. I'm not cancelling because we have a goal, and we're going to we're going to meet it."
The celebration consisted of a program of multiple performers, headlined by Ayla Dennis — an 18-year-old singer from Talbot county and descendent of Douglass.
Dennis, a student at Salisbury University, was recently a contestant on American Idol.
"So for this year, we featured Ayla," Bailey said. "Ayla is the star this year, and she knocked it out the park. I mean, she should have won American Idol, but it was great to see a relative of Frederick Douglass on stage at the Avalon, a formerly segregated theater."
The master of ceremonies was the 2024 Grace Brooks Award Winner, retired news broadcaster Paul Butler. Butler is from Talbot County.
"It's quite an honor," Butler said. "Being from Easton, being in this theater many years as a young kid, and now coming back and be able to host this event, it's something very special."
The celebration was kicked off by John Coleman singing the national anthem. Coleman has sung the national anthem multiple times at Camden Yards, Home of the Baltimore Orioles, followed by the Black national anthem, "Lift Every Voice and Sing," presented by the Joyful Singers.
Angelic Kreations, who traveled from new York City, performed two poems and a rap about Black history.
"This is not something I take lightly," Angelic Kreations said. "I truly feel that a lot of us are just so extraordinary beyond measures and to be able to carry on his legacy, we're talking about 207 years. But to be a part of something like this, I am happy to be here."
Eboni Strings, a duo of violinists performed multiple songs, followed by Dennis.
"It feels great that so many people hear me and see me as a artist," Dennis said. "To be a descendent of Frederick Douglass is super empowering, and I am blessed."
The performances were followed by a dinner at the Waterfowl Building, where food was served, artwork was shown and Push Play DC performed.
Many people showed up in African style clothing, and Bailey believes it showed solidarity with Douglass.
"Seeing people members of the diaspora and in traditional clothes shows solidarity," Bailey said. "Everybody understood the assignment."

title: Local author encourages 'choose love'
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontragerchespub.com
content:
Local author encourages 'choose love'

 February 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontragerchespub.com | Section: News 
 
 725
 Words 

 Read News Document

 "Kitty the Goat and the Puppy" is the third book of what will be a five-part series from local kid's author Abraham Keys, who resides in Rock Hall.All of Key's children's books are based on his real-life farming experiences growing up in South America with eleven siblings, and all his books involve relationships not normally found in nature which teach lessons of acceptance and love.
For example, his first book is about a hen named Donkey...(it's already starting out confusing) and Donkey is a little glum and depressed. In the story, farmer Abe allows Donkey (the chicken) to not only sit on chicken eggs, but also duck eggs.
Well, Donkey ends up with a new lease on life, and when those ducks hatch, she cares for those ducklings like they are her very own.
Farmer Abe learns a valuable lesson from that. If a chicken can learn to love something so different, he can love people different from him too.
And "writer Abe" can instruct people that a chicken and duck cannot interbreed, and the chicken is simply incubating the duck eggs then loving the ducklings as her own.
This kind of love transcends, and is repeated again in Abe's second book: "Moo Moo the Dog Adopts a Baby Pig," published in December 2023.
The theme is, you guessed it, Moo Moo the dog taking care of a baby pig, even more different than a duck and a chicken, and offers another powerful lesson about acceptance to Farmer Abe.
Key's third book, "Kitty the Goat and the Puppy" has been delayed in shipment, but he is hoping for an Easter release. For his other books, you can find them on Amazon and some local book stores or contact him directly.
This time around Farmer Abe will learn from Kitty the goat, taking care of a puppy.
The story goes, Kitty the goat lives on a farm. He's a prize goat, but retires and like many in the limelight, gets depressed. And like many of us, depression gives way to mischief. Kitty is eating up the flower beds and gnawing on the clothesline as goats often do.
What breaks Kitty from those bad habits is raising a little puppy, and through this puppy, Kitty finds purpose again.
The lesson?
Choose love.
It's a lesson that resounds with many readers to the joy of Keys, especially in schools where love and acceptance is a key focus, he said.
Writing with no expectations, his first book did amazingly well. Within weeks of publishing he had schools waiting to buy 300 books and since then has sold 3-4,000 copies of the book.
His foray into writing began with a challenge from friends, and he is glad he went through with it, Keys said. Finding a local artist to complement his stories, he discovered a very special niche combining children's books and agriculture along with a message of love and acceptance.
With plenty of source material too, drawing from his family owning farmland in Canada, South America and Montana, he's creating the fourth book, where the animal theme will continue. The last book of the series will explore Farmer's Abe's past with a very special horse.
Keys success has continued to grow. He has been featured in four newspapers, including a story in Montana the place of his birth, a paper in Canada, and television broadcasts in Salisbury, Maryland in addition to being invited to several local schools.
As many story tellers will say, there are all kinds of ideas running around in his mind, but he is focusing on finishing out the series first.
And he is honing his craft, drawing inspiration from others like Jay Miletsky, author of 14 books including "Ricky the Rock Who Couldn't Roll."
Keys will further challenge himself as he prepares to attend his first writer's summit in Nashville, Tennessee. He will have the chance to connect with fellow authors, pitch his ideas to professionals and learn from longtime experts.
Thrilled with the possibilities ahead, he takes with him lessons from his latest book. "Farmer Abe was reminded that when given the chance, to always choose love. Because you just never know if the love you give to others might also change your life forever," Keys wrote.
Based on his whirlwind author's journey so far, it seems like he's on to something rather special.
For information about his books, Keys encourages you to contact him directly at 410-708-5164, or find him on Facebook under Abraham Keys.

title: Country Cooking: Time-saving recipes for Daylight Savings Time
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Time-saving recipes for Daylight Savings Time

 March 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1277
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Daylight savings time begins Sunday, March 9. Set those clocks forward one hour before going to bed on Saturday evening.Daylight Savings first started in Germany in 1916 to save energy during World War I. The United States started this change in 1918, but this was repealed after only one year. Then the United States reinstated this practice in 1942 and called it "War Time."
The point behind Daylight Savings Time was to move an hour of sunlight from the early morning to the evening so people could make more use of daylight
No matter if you like the change or not — it is here. Personally, I like and dislike it. Having more time after dinner (supper) to be outside doing chores and yard work with the family is great, but getting small children in bed with daylight is difficult.
What about dinner? It takes a lot of planning ahead with the dinner/supper hour. When the family hits the door, you hear "what to eat?" Everyone is starving, and Mom must be prepared.
Today we will share some quick but filling meals, some pop in the oven casseroles, soups and sandwiches. Please share some of your favorites by emailing me at mmsavage21145@gmail.com so I can share some favorites from other households.
BROCCOLI CHEESE CASSEROLE
Large bunch broccoli, 2 cups chopped sharp cheddar cheese, 2 eggs (lightly beated), 1 can cream of mushroom soup, 1/2 cup mayonnaise, 1/2 cup chopped onions, 4 tbsps softened butter, 1 1/2 cups herbed seasoned stuffing mix.
Rinse and steam broccoli until slightly tender. Grease a 11-by-7-inch casserole dish and arrange broccoli in the dish. Sprinkle cheddar cheese on top and set aside. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. In a bowl combine eggs with cream of mushroom soup, mayonnaise and chopped onions. Mix well and spread over cheese. Combine softened butter with herbed seasoned stuffing mix and place on top of broccoli mixture in a casserole. Bake for 30 minutes.
BISHOPVILLE SQUASH CASSEROLE
2 eggs, 1 tbsp sugar, 1 1/2 cups shredded sharp cheddar cheese (divided), 1/2 cup mayonnaise, 1/2 tsp salt, 1/4 tsp black pepper, 1-pound yellow summer squash (cut into 1/4-inch slices), 1/4 cup plain breadcrumbs.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Coat a 1 1/2 quart casserole dish with cooking spray; set aside. In a large bowl, with a fork, beat eggs and sugar until frothy. Add 1 cup cheese, mayonnaise, salt and pepper; mix well. Stir in squash and pour mixture into prepared casserole dish. Sprinkle with breadcrumbs and bake for 30 minutes. Remove from the oven, top with remaining cheese, and bake for 10 to 15 additional minutes, until heated through and the cheese is golden.
COUNTRY BEAN SUPPER
This is a very hearty combination of different types of beans combined with your choice of hamburger such as turkey or bison or the healthy 90/10 beef. This recipe is easy to make, very filling and simply add a roll to complete the meal. Perfect for a busy day dinner, Saturday lunch or hungry teens.
1 lb beef, 1 cup diced onion, 1/4 cup fried bacon, 45-oz can pork and beans, 15-oz can kidney beans (drained), 15-oz can butter beans (drained), 15-oz can cannellini beans (undrained), 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp black pepper, 1 tbsp vinegar, 2 tbsps water, 1 cup ketchup, 1/2 cup brown sugar, 1 tbsp liquid smoke.
Brown beef with diced onion until well-cooked then drain. In a crockpot place the beef and onion mixture with fried bacon, drained and broken into pieces, pork and beans, one 15 kidney beans, butter beans, cannellini beans, salt, pepper, vinegar, water, ketchup, brown sugar and liquid smoke. Mix slightly, place lid on crock pot, turn on low heat and cook for 4 to 6 hours. Serve with rolls.
POTATO SOUP
4 cups peeled and cubed potatoes, 1 cup diced celery, 1 cup coarsely chopped onion, 2 to 2 1/2 cups water, 2 tsps salt, 3 tbsps butter or margarine, 1 tbsp dried parsley flakes, black pepper, 1 cup milk, 1 cup whipping cream.
Cook potatoes in a soup pot with celery, chopped onion, water, salt, butter or margarine, dried parsley flakes and black pepper to taste. Cook until potatoes, celery and onions are tender then mix in milk and whipping cream, stirring constantly until soup is thickened. Serve immediately.
CROCK POT BEEF ROAST
2-to-3-pound beef roast with fat on the bottom, 1 qt beef flavored stock, salt, black pepper, peeled potatoes (quartered), carrots (unpeeled), several onions (quartered)
Spray the bottom of a crockpot and turn on high to heat the oil. In the meantime, rinse the roast with cool water, drain, and place in the crock with a fat side on the bottom. Pour beef flavored stock juice from a quart container — any brand — reserving the rest. Sprinkle the top of the roast with light salt and black pepper. Place the lid on top and continue cooking. Peel several potatoes, cut them in quarters and place in a bowl of cool water. Add several unpeeled carrots to the water, chopping them into quarters, unless you use the small carrots. Peel several onions, chop them into quarters. Drain water from veggies, place them in a crockpot around the roast. Add more liquid only if needed. Do not cover roast with liquid. Reserve the remaining beef stock. Place lid on, turn to medium heat and cook until beef and veggies are tender. You may need to add additional seasonings — after about 70 — 80 minutes cooking I drop a couple of brown gravy seasoning liquid drops in the stock for further seasoning, continue to cook until tender. Before adding any additional seasoning, taste test to see if it is necessary. When beef and veggies are tender, remove from the juice, in a casserole dish place veggies around the beef, adding a small amount of juice, about 1/2 inch. Cover tightly, save remaining juice to add some dumplings or a thickened brown gravy.
How about breakfast for dinner? Here are a few for just the occasion.
SLOW COOKER CINNAMON ROLL CASSEROLE
Cooking spray, 1/2 cup granulated sugar, 1/2 cup packed light brown sugar, 1 tsp ground cinnamon, 2 (16.3-oz.) cans refrigerated southern homestyle biscuits (such as Pillsbury Grands! Southern Homestyle) separated and cut into fourths, 1/2 cup plus salted butter (melted), 2 tbsps salted butter (softened), 4 large eggs, 1/4 tsp kosher salt, 2/3 cup plus 2 to 3 tbsps half-and-half (divided), 2 tsps vanilla extract (divided), 1/2 cup chopped toasted pecans,1 (3-oz.) package of cream cheese (softened), 2 1/4 cups (about 9 oz.) powdered sugar (divided).
Line bottom and sides of a six-quart slow cooker with aluminum foil; lightly coat foil with cooking spray. Stir together granulated sugar, brown sugar and cinnamon in a small bowl. Toss together biscuit pieces and 1/2 cup melted butter in a large bowl until biscuits are coated. Working in batches, add biscuits to granulated sugar mixture, and toss to coat; transfer biscuits to prepared slow cooker. Sprinkle any remaining sugar mixture over biscuits in a slow cooker.
PANCAKE CASSEROLE
Cooking spray, Pancakes, 6 large eggs, 1 1/2 cups heavy cream, 1 cup whole milk, 1/4 cup granulated sugar, 1 tsp vanilla bean paste, 1/4 tsp kosher salt, unsalted butter, maple syrup.
Lightly coat a 13-by-9-inch baking dish with cooking spray. Arrange pancakes in a baking dish in three rows, overlapping slightly, starting at one long end. Whisk together eggs, cream, milk, sugar, vanilla and salt in a bowl. Slowly pour mixture over pancakes. Cover and refrigerate for at least 8 hours or up to overnight. Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Bake the casserole, covered, in a preheated oven for 25 minutes. Uncover and continue baking until the center is set, about 25 minutes. Let stand for 5 minutes. Dot with pats of butter. Drizzle with syrup.

title: The many faces of Shemika Renee
author: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com
content:
The many faces of Shemika Renee

 March 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Michael Reid mreid@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 681
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A history lesson on Black women was held live and in person during Shemika Renee's one-woman show, "Ms. Story's Living History" at Three Notch Theatre in Lexington Park.The 48-year-old Air Force veteran portrayed 15 living history characters during the four-show run which concluded Sunday and took audience members around the country with in-depth looks at Black women who made their marks in history.
"I try to tell little-known facts and dispel myths because I want people to realize we've been taught certain things incorrectly," Renee said, "or we've been taught things partially, and they were real people. I want to honor who they really were."
The Hollywood resident portrayed a young ancestor's reactions when Black men, women and children were snatched from their homeland and shipped to the United States to be enslaved.
She refers to men with "skin like milk" grabbing her and "squeezing so hard I could not breathe." She said the ensuing voyage in the ship's hold "was hot, it was stuffy and oh, the smells," and added their captors "gave them enough to eat, to live, but nothing more."
When the ship voyage was over and they were purchased, she said in character, "They said we're slaves, we were property. I was in my seventh year [of life]. How could I be property."
"It's more visceral and I want that emotion to be present, even when children are in the audience," Renee said of why portraying "Ancestor" was difficult. "I don't shy away from the hard topics of history. I'm just mindful of how I phrase it."
Renee also portrayed Madam CJ Walker, who attained great wealth and became one of the first female millionaires in the country with her women's skin products.
The actress also took a turn telling the story of Cathay Williams, who changed her name to William Cathay in order to become a member of the all-Black Buffalo Soldiers regiment.
"The physical was pretty much, 'Can you breathe? Can you walk? You're in,'" Renee said in character, and added that when she told her commanding officer the truth, he responded by saying he was "shocked and gave her her discharge papers, stating she was unfit for duty, weak and feeble-minded."
After a portrayal of Stagecoach Mary, who delivered the U.S. mail for almost a decade, Renee portrayed Lorraine Hansberry, who wrote "A Raisin in the Sun."
Over other shows, Renee portrayed several women, including singer Mahalia Jackson, professional tennis player and golfer Althea Gibson, Civil Rights activist Sojourner Truth and Harriet Tubman.
Renee's first portrayal came about a decade ago when she helped out her son's teacher at Southern Maryland Christian Academy.
"I had always loved dressing up so I said, 'I can dress up as any historical figure and do a first-person narrative,' and she took me up on my offer," Renee said.
She said the first person she was asked to portray was Johnnie Appleseed.
"I texted her and asked, 'Are you sure?' She said yes so I put a pot on my head and the kids loved it," Renee said.
She returned year after year and expanded her repertoire — she can now portray more than 25 women. She did her first "Ms. Story's Living History" one-woman show in 2019 at the Black Box Theater in Indian Head.
"A lot of the structure of the show is based on costume changes," she said. "Being a costumer, my brain is always like, 'How do I do a reveal? What's the fastest way to get from one costume to another by layering?' [Changing from Stagecoach Mary to Bessie Coleman] was really just a matter of putting the pants on and the goggles on and I was a completely different person."
In February 2023, the costumer, actress and award-winning makeup artist was highlighted on the Today Show's 3rd Hour segment for her work honoring African American women in history.
"I want to give each figure their due with their persona, the voice, the mannerisms, so it's not like Ms. Story is telling their story like she's memorizing a Wikipedia page," Renee said. "I want the audience to feel like they literally met these women because they were true, breathing women."

title: Author shares her book with kids at Toys for Tots event
author: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com
content:
Author shares her book with kids at Toys for Tots event

 March 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com | Section: News 
 
 374

 The Toys For Tots Foundation — which includes the Cecil County chapter of the United States Marine Corps Reserves group — joined forces with a children's book author, who is originally from the Eastern Shore, to provide free books to children at the Elkton unit of the Cecil County Boys and Girls Club.Kim C. Lee brought signed copies of her book, "The Night Owl Goes to Space" for each child in the after school program at the Elkton Community Center. With the assistance of Allison Brown, Toys For Tots Foundation Youth Ambassador, Lee read her book to the kids.
"This is my second Night Owl book," Lee said, adding her son Jourdan is her inspiration to the stories.
"My son does not like to go to sleep at night," she said of Jourdan Russell, now 11. Even though it was written for him at a younger age, Lee said Jourdan still claims the title. "I am the Night Owl,' she said Jourdan would say.
As the story developed, the youngsters peppered Lee with comments and questions, showing they knew about the planets, their names and unique qualities. To her right, Brown kept up, turning the pages so each of the colorful pages could be seen.
Brown, who is from Centreville and now lives in Baltimore, has been a Toys For Tots Youth Ambassador for three years. She got involved through her American Heritage Girls troop. The lessons she's learned so far have been invaluable.
"I've really learned how to do social media ... how to push a post to get the community involved," Brown said. She's also learned about all the services in her own community and can talk to other teens about how they can get involved or get help.
Valerie Anderson, representing the regional foundation, said Brown — like the 44 other youth ambassadors across the country — is "a stand out person."
"She's been to our Outdoor Odyssey Leadership Camp in Pennsylvania, she goes to monthly meetings and activities and helps us raise brand awareness," Anderson said.
Lee gave each child her book and Brown handed each a Toys For Tots backpack that included such items as bookmarks, rulers, slap bracelets and stress balls.
The Night Owl Goes to Space is available on Amazon in hardback and paperback editions.

title: National Cherry Blossom Festival returns to D.C.
author: Staff Writer

National Cherry Blossom Festival returns to D.C.

 March 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 The Smithsonian American Art Museum is collaborating for the 12th year in a row with the National Cherry Blossom Festival for a series of in-person cherry blossom-themed public programs. The museum's cherry blossom family activities and celebrations are part of its hands-on program series, designed to spark learning, creativity and appreciation for the arts.The museum's popular Cherry Blossom Celebration for children and families will be presented in person Saturday, March 22, from 11:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. Weather permitting, the event will begin on the museum's F Street plaza with a Japanese taiko performance by the drumming group Nen Daiko.
Other performances in the museum's courtyard include an all-vinyl music set of Japanese soul, funk, boogie, pop and disco by Les The DJ. More information is available on the museum's website.
Attendees can create their own cherry blossom-themed crafts and explore the museum's galleries during a spring-themed scavenger hunt. Seasonal treats will be available for purchase at the Courtyard Café. This program is free, but registration is encouraged.
Two cherry blossom-themed in-person workshops, presented as part of the museum's series "Beyond the Studio," are scheduled for Sunday, March 23, and Sunday, April 6, both at 1 p.m. Washington, D.C., maker Miri Artyukhina of Capitol Stich Co. will lead participants through embroidery basics and skills required to create a festive spring artwork inspired by cherry blossoms (cost $15); space is limited, and advance registration is required.
Additional family activities are available on the Family Zone webpage, including seasonal crafts, coloring pages inspired by artworks from the museum's permanent collection, videos and more.
During the National Cherry Blossom Festival, the museum is presenting "Pictures of Belonging: Miki Hayakawa, Hisako Hibi and Miné Okubo," which honors three trailblazing Japanese American women artists. The women were three of the most active and critically acclaimed American artists of Japanese descent in the years that had been underrecognized within 20th-century American art history. The exhibition is free and is on view through Aug. 17.
For more about the Smithsonian American Art Museum, visit americanart.si.edu.
About the National Cherry Blossom FestivalThe National Cherry Blossom Festival is one of the world's great celebrations of spring. The 2025 festival takes place March 20–April 13 and includes four weeks of events featuring diverse and creative programming promoting traditional and contemporary arts and culture, natural beauty and community spirit. Visit NationalCherryBlossomFestival.org or call 877-44-BLOOM for more information.

title: Irish-inspired meals for St. Patrick's Day
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Irish-inspired meals for St. Patrick's Day

 March 11, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: Food 
 
 1248
 Words 

 Read News Document

 St. Patrick's Day is celebrated on March 17, which happens to fall on a Monday. Celebrations including parades and parties are not limited to those of Irish descent but can be enjoyed by all who appreciate the Irish foods, drinks, fun-filled parties and dancing.This day is an observance of the death of Saint Patrick, the Patron Saint of Ireland. What originally began as a public feast day in the 17th century has turned into a variety of celebrations across the continent.
My mother's family was of Irish descent — the McCabe and Hudson clans. I have seen my mother do an "Irish jig" as she danced as she talked about her Irish bloodline.
With the small line of Irish descendants in my family I knew very little about Ireland — until that date in 1970.
I had just begun a career in different aspects of the newspaper world. I started in the composition of the Delmarva News in Selbyville, Delaware. There, I learned many different areas of the newspaper make-up department, and, as they say, "the ink got in my blood."
A few weeks after my training began, a new kid on the block came to work in this department — a kid I will never forget. Muriel was fresh from Ireland and came to the job after marrying a U.S. soldier and becoming a citizen. This job was to be a wonderful opportunity for all of us. Our lunch times were spent showing Muriel around the small town, the hamburger joint we gathered at each day, the Five and Dime store we used and much more.
Of course, we were late going back to work.
Years ago I worked with a lady at a local middle school who had direct descendants who were Irish, and she and her family visited Ireland. Upon returning, she shared many photos and stories with her students and staff.
I may never get to personally visit Ireland, but what a beautiful and scenic countryside they have.
In 2022, about 9.2% of the United States residents were Irish descendants. Cook County Illinois reportedly has the largest population of Irish Americans in the United States. New York City has the largest U.S. St. Patrick's Day Parade each year, and I personally look forward to it.
Before we start experimenting with our favorite Irish foods, I like to share a list of true Irish foods that are a part of Ireland. They include Irish soda bread, cabbage and bacon, Irish stew, Irish coffee, corned beef and cabbage, crubeens (pig's feet), Irish seafood chowder, oysters, cured salmon Dexter beef, cottage pie, black pudding (sausage) and much more.
More of those days will come eventually but let's get cooking.
SHEPHERD'S PIE
2 tbsps extra-virgin olive oil,3 small carrots (chopped), 1 cup frozen pearl onions, 1 lb. lean ground beef, 1 tbsp all-purpose flour, 1 cup frozen peas, 2 1/2 tsp chopped fresh rosemary, kosher salt and freshly ground pepper, 3/4 cup low-sodium chicken broth, 3 cups mashed potatoes. Preparing and making mashed potatoes: 2 pounds baking potatoes, peeled and quartered, 1 cup milk, 2 tbsps butter, salt and ground black pepper to taste.
Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Add potatoes and garlic, lower heat to medium, and simmer until potatoes are tender, 15 to 20 minutes. When the potatoes are almost finished, heat milk and butter in a small saucepan over low heat until butter is melted. Drain potatoes and return to the pot. Slowly add warm milk mixture, blending it in with a potato masher or electric mixer until potatoes are smooth and creamy. Preheat oven to 400 degrees. In a large pan, heat olive oil over medium heat. Add carrots and onions and cook until soft, about 5 minutes. Add turkey and cook, breaking up meat with a wooden spoon, until browned, about 6 minutes. Stir in flour and cook 3 more minutes. Stir in peas and rosemary. Season with salt and pepper. Pour in chicken broth and stir. Bring to a simmer and cook until slightly thickened, about 5 minutes. Season with more salt and pepper. Transfer to a 9- to 10-inch deep-dish pie pan. Spread mashed potatoes atop mixture. Bake until golden on top and heated through, about 25 minutes.
CORNED BEEF AND CABBAGE
Place one medium onion, cleaned and quartered, in a 5-quart slow cooker. Combine 3 cups water, 3 minced cloves of garlic, 1 bay leaf, 2 tbsps sugar, 2 tbsps vinegar, and the contents of the spice packet that comes with the beef brisket. Mix well and set aside. In the slow cooker, place 4 medium peeled and quartered potatoes over top of the onions. Pour the spice mixture over potatoes and place one corned beef brisket, about 2 to 3 pounds, on top. The final layer will be 1 small head of cabbage, cut into wedges. Cover and cook on low for 8 to 9 hours, or until the meat and vegetables are tender. Remove the bay leaf before serving.
IRISH SODA BREAD
4 cups all-purpose flour (plus extra for currants), 4 tbsps sugar, 1 tsp baking soda, 1 1/2 tsps kosher salt, 4 tbsps (1/2 stick) cold unsalted butter (cut into 1/2-inch dice), 1 3/4 cups cold buttermilk (shaken), 1 extra-large egg (lightly beaten), 1 tsp grated orange zest, 1 cup dried currants.
Preheat the oven to 375 degrees. Line a sheet pan with parchment paper. Combine the flour, sugar, baking soda and salt in the bowl of an electric mixer fitted with the paddle attachment. Add the butter and mix on low speed until the butter is mixed into the flour. With a fork, lightly beat the buttermilk, egg and orange zest together in a measuring cup. With the mixer on low speed, slowly add the buttermilk mixture to the flour mixture. Combine the currants with 1 tbsp of flour and mix into the dough. It will be very wet. Dump the dough onto a well-floured board and knead it a few times into a round loaf. Place the loaf on the prepared sheet pan and lightly cut an X into the top of the bread with a serrated knife. Bake for 45 to 55 minutes, or until a cake tester comes out clean. When you tap the loaf, it will have a hollow sound. Cool on a baking rack. Serve warm or at room temperature.
CREAMY POTATO SOUP
This is one of my go-to soups and a family favorite. It is creamy, hearty, comforting soup. While the toppings are optional, I recommend using them for the loaded baked potato style.
Combine 6 cups peeled diced russet potatoes, 1 1/2 cups chopped yellow onion, 1 1/4 cups peeled and diced carrots, 1 cup diced celery and two 14.5-ounce cartons of chicken broth in a large stockpot. Season with salt and pepper to taste. Cover pot and bring to a boil over medium heat and continue to cook about 15 to 20 minutes longer until potatoes are very soft when pierced with a fork. Meanwhile, in a medium saucepan, melt 1/3 cup butter over medium heat adding 1/3 cup all-purpose flour and only cook 1 additional minute while whisking constantly and start slowly adding 2 1/2 cups milk. Cook until mixture lightly bubbles and begins to thicken. When the potatoes are tender, add the thickened mixture to the stockpot with the potato mixture, stirring gently. Remove from heat and ladle into bowls for serving. Have some toppings available for those who want them. Use crumbled bacon, chopped cooked ham, shredded cheddar cheese, chopped green onions or chives. Enjoy this tasty Irish potato soup.

title: Museum effort 'on pause' after project lead fined for falsely claiming to be an architect
author: Lilly Howard lhoward@chespub.com
content:
Museum effort 'on pause' after project lead fined for falsely claiming to be an architect

 March 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lilly Howard lhoward@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 970
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ELKTON — The Elkton Colored School Museum project has been put on hold after the Maryland Board of Architects issued a $20,000 fine against Dale Glenwood Green, the project's architect, for falsely representing himself as a licensed architect for at least 17 years. The board said that his claims have led to Green stealing opportunities from qualified architects, such as the museum project.The ECS Museum project had been working in partnership with an architecture firm that Green was a part of, during which partnership Green gave a tour of the ECS building to Gov. Moore during his visit last year to Cecil County. Due to the fine against Green and his lack of licensing, the project has been put on hold.
"We are on pause right now because we can't move forward until we find out what is going to be done architecturally for the benefit of the group and the benefit of putting the building in place where it's supposed to be," said Town of Elkton Commissioner Charles Givens, an ECS alumni who has been heavily involved in the museum project. "We're dependent upon grants and other finances to move forward…we aren't going to get funds until the mess that we have right now is cleared up."
Green is known for working to preserve the oldest Black communities in Maryland, and Maryland Gov. Wes Moore appointed him to the board of directors for the Maryland African American Museum Corporation.
Green also claimed to have a Ph.D in architecture and historic preservation from the University of Missouri, but the school has no record of his enrollment according to an article by the Baltimore Banner.
Until being fired recently, Green had taught architecture and historic preservation at Morgan State University since 2008, where he earned his undergraduate degree in architecture. Baltimore architect Jerryn McCray was teaching as an adjunct professor at Morgan State when he met Green as an undergraduate nearly 20 years ago.
"He was the best salesman I think I've ever met, but his work was just awful," McCray said.
McCray acted as a mentor for Green in one class, but said "his ego would never allow him to see himself as a mentee. He took the position as if he was already a professional. He dressed the part, wore a bow tie, the suit, the whole get up that he still carries."
Shortly after graduating from Morgan State, Green started a company and listed himself as the principal project architect on the website. McCray recalled confronting him for marketing himself as an architect, and proceeded to file a complaint with the state against Green in 2008 when the website went unchanged.
However, the state did not have a record of the initial complaint and nothing came of it, till now.
McCray said that Green has continued to cause problems for himself and other architects in the community since then.
"He's persisted to find different ways to promote himself as an architect," McCray said. "It had gotten to the point where it was affecting my company, the local economy, my family, my relationships…I had to make it stop."
According to McCray, because of the way Green presented himself and played the part, he became connected with a lot of people in the industry, which took away opportunities from legitimately licensed architects like McCray.
"It's been more of an obstacle dealing with Dale, in terms of my business, than it's been being Black and being an architect," McCray said.
McCray recalled telling several architects who partnered with Green that he is not licensed or trustworthy.
"They look at me like I'm the issue, and it's ruined those relationships for 20 years, and I've persisted to speak the truth. I know that Dale is a con artist," McCray said.
McCray filed a second complaint when a national architectural firm was reviewing Green's application for a renovation project and upon reviewing his credentials, found mismatched fonts and a license that seemed fraudulent. The project manager reached out to McCray, who proceeded to look up Green's license number, which was associated with a woman living in Georgia. After speaking with her, both filed complaints which led to a state investigation on Green.
The investigation into Green began in the spring of 2023, culminating in a final order issued by the board in December of 2024. The board increased the fine from $15,000 to $20,000, insisting on the maximum penalty for each violation because of Green's "incessant bad faith" which persisted for at least 17 years.
The Maryland Board of Architects determined that Green did in fact forge a license to practice architecture, and even created a fake email chain blaming one of his former students for the fraudulent license.
The fine is the largest issued by the Maryland Board of Architects since 2012.
A main focus of the case was on the testimony of Stanford Britt, the president of Sulton Campbell Britt & Associates, that he had hired Green to manage the firm's website and help with technological aspects of the company, a firm at which Green had been claiming to be a vice president and partner.
Britt testified that he never promoted Green to a partner of the firm. Currently, the firm website lists Green as vice president and partner, with Britt the only other listed employee. Britt said that his architecture license had expired three years prior to the trial and he was now working as a teacher in Virginia.
According to Givens, Green reached out to the Elkton Colored School Museum team to set up a meeting and discuss next steps in the upcoming weeks.
"It's thrown a wrench in the plan because he was one of the architects for the company and right now we are at a stand still," Givens said.
Givens compared the situation to buying a Mercedes that breaks down on your way home, unexpected and disappointing.
Green and his firm did not respond to a request for comment.

title: 'Kin: Rooted in Hope' named as One Maryland One Book
author: Staff Writer
content:
'Kin: Rooted in Hope' named as One Maryland One Book

 March 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 439
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Maryland Humanities recently announced that Carole Boston Weatherford's "Kin: Rooted in Hope" is the 2025 One Maryland One Book selection."I couldn't be more excited about 'Kin: Rooted in Hope' as our 2025 One Maryland One Book pick." Maryland Humanities CEO Lindsey Baker said in a release. "This book does exactly what our theme [What We Collect/What We Tell] asks of us; it pieces together history, memory, and loss to reclaim stories that deserve to be told. [The Weatherfords] don't just bring the past to life; they remind us why it matters today. With deep Maryland roots, 'Kin' is a powerful, moving, and necessary read, and I can't wait for people across the state to experience it."
The poetry collection from the Maryland author includes art by her son, Jeffery Boston Weatherford.
A combination of history, art and personal genealogy depicts the author's search for her family tree, which leads her to ancestors who were some of Maryland's founders. Through art and poetic voice, the mother and son impart their family's lives and offer a view into Maryland's African American history.
"Kin: Rooted in Hope is a family affair, a mother-son collaboration on a family saga dating back to colonial Maryland," Carole said in the release. "[The book] conjures the past, reclaims lost ancestral narratives and brings us to the realization that knowing your history is generational wealth."
The collection weaves the personas of the Weatherfords' ancestors, from experiences on the Wye House Plantation in Talbot County through the Civil War and into the twentieth century.
Maryland locations feature prominently in the book, many the subject of their own poems, including the Chesapeake Bay, the port of Oxford, Fort McHenry, and the Wye River where the Wye House plantation sits.
"As a Marylander, I am so proud that [the book's] selection as the 2025 One Maryland One Book will further amplify our ancestors' voices," Carole said in the release. "Their story of bondage and freedom — a history shared by many African Americans — is the American story."
"Kin: Rooted in Hope" is a Coretta Scott King Honor Book and a Boston Globe-Horn Book Poetry Award Winner.
Carole recently received the 2025 Children's Literature Legacy Award from the American Library Association and holds a Newberry Honor and Nonfiction Award from the Children's Book Guild.
A selection committee consisting of Maryland teachers, scholars, librarians, writers, booksellers, and community workers chose the book as the One Maryland One Book selection under the theme "What We Collect/What We Tell."
Maryland Humanities will hold programming that will invite readers to explore histories of African Americans, of Maryland and their families, and will announce an author tour this summer.
For more information, go to www.mdhumanities.org.

title: New virtual museum displays artifacts from home of Harriet Tubman’s father
author: Konner Metz
content:
New virtual museum displays artifacts from home of Harriet Tubman’s father

 March 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 520
 Words 

 Read News Document

 A new virtual collection of historic artifacts is shedding light on the early life of abolitionist Harriet Tubman and her father, Ben Ross.Archaeologists for the Maryland Department of Transportation led efforts in uncovering many items, such as plates, bowls and pitchers, in work done at Ross' home deep in the Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge in Dorchester County.
Experts spent the last four years finding and identifying hundreds of artifacts. Julie Schablitsky, MDOT's chief of cultural resources, said it all began when they found an 1808 half-dollar coin on the site.
"That coin gave us inspiration to keep on digging and keep on working," Schablitsky said.
Earlier this week, the department announced the artifacts and unveiled The Ben Ross Homeplace, an online museum since the physical site isn't open to the public.
Some of the artifacts provide insight into Ross' life as an enslaved person in the 19th century, as well as Tubman's early years, during which she learned how to live off the land.
Archaeologists found a lock to a door, which Schablitsky says may indicate Ross had some form of independence from his enslaver, Anthony Thompson.
"That's a bit of negotiated independence that not everybody would have had who was enslaved," she said.
Schablitsky pointed out a tobacco pipe with a bald eagle. While many may assume it's a patriotic symbol, she says it could be a "subtle signature" of defiance.
"I wondered that, in his hand or the hand of Harriet Tubman and her mother, … if that was somehow a way of resistance — (if) that symbol was there for freedom rather than allegiance to the United States," Schablitsky said.
Schablitsky and MDOT media relations manager David Broughton say the process of working in the wetlands of Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge was demanding due to weather conditions, mosquitos, snakes and more.
While the team knows the approximate area Ross' home was in, it didn't locate the exact markings or corners of the home. The exact location is "lost to time," Schablitsky said, but the online museum preserves as much as possible.
"It could be a valuable tool … for teachers and their children," Broughton said.
'RUSH AGAINST TIME'
Archaeologists aren't just battling the elements. They're working on a limited clock.
"Climate change, sea level rise made digging very, very difficult," Schablitsky said. "Within the next decade, I know that I'm not going to be able to return there."
Schablitsky said even when work began back in 2021, environmental conditions impacted their work. Holes already dug would fill up with water after just a lunch break, Schablitsky said.
Sea level rise makes the preservation and historical work even more pressing, experts say.
"We're definitely in a rush against time," Schablitsky said. "The waters are coming up, they're percolating up through the ground."
Amid the challenges, descendants of Tubman and Ross were able to join archaeologists at the wetlands of Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge. Schablitsky said the humility and gratitude they expressed to be able to dig at the historical site was impactful.
"The most meaningful part of the process was to have the descendants of Harriet Tubman and Ben Ross down on the site, walking where they walked, in her footsteps, in his footsteps," she said.

title: Annmarie Garden prepares to build a greenhouse
author: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com

Annmarie Garden prepares to build a greenhouse

 March 19, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARTY MADDEN mmadden@somdnews.com | Section: News 
 
 446

 Read News Document

 The 30-acre tract known as Annmarie Sculpture Garden and Arts Center continues to undergo value-adds, thanks to its many devotees providing stewardship.On March 18, the Solomons facility hosted a groundbreaking ceremony for its greenhouse project.
Annmarie Garden officials stated in a release that the greenhouse "is being built adjacent to our community garden and will be used extensively by the master gardeners and our own horticulture and grounds team."
The community garden is located on a 20-acre tract owned by the Koenig Private Foundation. Last year, Stacey Hann-Ruff, the director of arts center, announced during a presentation to the Calvert County commissioners that Annmarie Garden officials plan to expand the existing sculpture garden to include the 20-acres.
In 1991, Francis and Ann Marie Koenig donated the land where the facility is located. The expansion plans include a 15,000-square foot welcome center.
The Calvert County Master Gardeners program trains volunteer horticulture educators to support the University of Maryland Extension's initiative to educate locals about best horticulture practices.
Noting that the greenhouse project is being supported by state grant money from the Maryland General Assembly, the Rural Maryland Council and the Cove Point Natural Heritage Trust, Edward Goodman, the local master gardener specialist, called the effort "an amazing collaboration."
Goodman told Southern Maryland News there are about 50 active master gardeners. The training course takes about three to four months to complete and is culminated by a final exam. Then, the master gardener candidate must complete 40 hours of community service.
"There are lots of opportunities," Goodman said.
The fledgling master gardeners share their knowledge at such venues as the North Beach Nature Center, Calvert Marine Museum and numerous other locations.
"The biggest thing of the mater gardener program is to educate others on sustainable horticulture practices," Goodman said.
While he couldn't provide a timeline for when the greenhouse would be completed, Goodman said "the project has crossed the hurdle of permitting and processing."
"This is the first step in the [expansion] plan," Cari DeSantis of Ann's Circle, the nonprofit organization that supports many programs and activities at Annmarie Garden.
In briefly addressing the gathering, Bruce Fall of the Cove Point Natural Heritage Trust commended the garden's staff and volunteers "for bringing people in to our area with events."
Fall said the visitors, who come to the garden for such traffic-jamming events as Artsfest and Halloween in the Garden, spend their cash at local restaurants and other businesses, which bolsters the area's economy.
Before grabbing shovels for some fun in the patch of dirt where the new greenhouse will stand, plastic glasses of champagne and cider were distributed to attendees. Everyone drank a toast.
DeSantis said the toast was "to celebrate the public-private partnerships that make Calvert County such a beautiful place."

title: Megaladon, shark teeth on display in Solomons
author: Staff Writer
content:
Megaladon, shark teeth on display in Solomons

 March 21, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Entertainment 
 
 562
 Words 

 Read News Document

 While fans of the movie and novel "Jaws" might envision an encounter with a 22-foot great white shark as being daunting, historians and marine biologists alike are quick to note that the extinct megatooth shark Otudus megalodon, commonly known as "megalodon," once roamed the oceans spanning a far more imposing 65 feet in length.The megalodon was likely the largest shark ever to exist and is well known for its large, evenly serrated teeth, indicative of its lifestyle as a formidable apex predator. These blade-like teeth were used to prey upon marine animals, such as whales, dolphins and likely other sharks and a new paper published sheds light on the impacts of their impact on other sharks and the teeth are readily on display at the Calvert Marine Museum in Solomons.
Evidence of predatory behavior is well represented in the fossil record, with many examples of shark-bitten fossil bone as seen in images provided by the Calvert Marine Museum. However, shark-bitten shark teeth are very rare, but perhaps proof that the megalodon would attack other sharks in the vicinity including members of their species.
In a paper recently published online in Acta Palaeontologica Palonica, paleontologists from the Calvert Marine Museum in Solomons and the St. Mary's College of Maryland in St. Mary's City describe four megalodon teeth that were bitten by other megalodon teeth. These bite marks are represented by shallow parallel lines marking the surface of the teeth caused by a forceful impact of another megalodon tooth.
Although the authors of this recently released paper describe these rare, meg-bitten meg teeth, they do not know under what circumstances any of the megalodon teeth were bitten. One might imagine that the simplest way to account for megalodon-bitten teeth would be that two teeth in opposing jaws struck each other during occlusion, the serrated cutting edge of one marking the other.
Another possibility is that another megalodon tooth was knocked loose for any number of reasons but remained in the originating jaw of the shark. This shed tooth (while still in the shark's mouth) might then have been struck and marked by another occluding tooth.
A third possibility is that megalodon teeth became marked during a predatory or scavenging event.
Seven years ago, Calvert Marine Museum Curator of Paleontology Stephen Godfrey was the senior author on similar paper published online. It was a collaborative effort between Godfrey, Mike Ellwood, Stephen Groff and Michael Scott Verdin — avocational paleontologists who found the bitten vertebrae. The paper describes fossil dolphin tail bones that were bitten by the mega-tooth shark, Carcharocles megalodon.
Megalodon was the largest predator that lived on Earth two million to 20 million years ago, according to a release from the museum. It was initially estimated that they attained lengths of between 50 and 60 feet, a scale that has since been upgraded to a larger specimen. From time to time, fossil whale and dolphin bones are found along Calvert Cliffs that show megalodon tooth bite marks. Some of them may have been made as megalodon scavenged an already dead whale.
Modern great white sharks are known to disable dolphins by biting their tails, the release states. Megalodon certainly could have done the same, as the fossil tail vertebrae show multiple gouges. This suggests that the tails of these dolphins were jammed forcefully and repeatedly between adjacent teeth by powerful bite forces, according to the release.
For more information, go to www.calvertmarinemuseum.com.

title: En pointe: Carole Cascio Fund welcomes Ballet Theatre of Maryland

En pointe: Carole Cascio Fund welcomes Ballet Theatre of Maryland

 CENTREVILLE — The synchronized movement of professional dancers is reminiscent of the unity of the local community as the Carole Cascio Fund welcomed the Ballet Theatre of Maryland for a free public performance at the Centreville YMCA March 14.Committed to ensuring the accessibility of arts to all, the Carole Cascio Fund supports dance education in schools and communities across the Eastern Shore and there is nothing like the unity of dancers following in one motion seamlessly ties into community connection tied in perfectly with the mission to bring enhanced community engagement to the arts, according to Fund Executive Director Peter Pucci.
Partnerships and support brings experiences right to the community, meeting inspiring dancers and enthusiasts right where they are, Pucci said.
Bringing a full professional dance performance to a familiar space in the community helps spark interest and engagement, he said.
Thirty professional full-time dancers graced the YMCA gymnasium to perform seven ballet dances and with contemporary to classical pieces, including aspects of Swan Lake, Sleeping Beauty, and Concerto Lilla, the free performance promised something for everyone.
The Fund's mission of making the magic of arts accessible to all fits perfectly with the Ballet Theatre of Maryland's mindset, according to Artistic Director Nicole Kelsch.
Leaping and pirouetting at the opportunity to bring their dancers to the Eastern Shore, the company always welcomes opportunities to share their performances with new audiences, she said.
The unique space of the YMCA gymnasium floor allowed a more up close engagement with the audience, said Brenna Mazzara, company community engagement coordinator.
"It's always fun to be in a new location and we are grateful for the opportunity," she said.
A crowd of nearly 300 registered for the show beforehand, with more signing in on the day of, the Carole Cascio Fund officials said.
Ballet dancer Madeline Jones always knew she wanted to be a dancer and grew up in a similar small town community to Queen Anne's County.
"The arts are so important to share," she said.
Dancing, especially ballet, is a connection of mind and body and requires brain power as well as physical performance and coordination, she said.
Jones' favorite part of any performance is the engagement with the audience especially with children and particularly on a small scale stage.
Supporting professional dance and bringing inspiration to the community, the Carole Cascio Fund seeks to introduce students of all ages to developing artistry through choreography and dance, Pucci said.
The Carole Cascio Fund collaborates with the community in Kent and Queen Anne's counties and works closely with local partner Queen Anne's County Public Schools. Community support has been phenomenal in ensuring the mission, Pucci said.
"Everyone deserves to understand the value of the arts. It is a great experience for all ages," he said.
The mission of the nonprofit continues through dedication and relies strongly on community support and donations to continue.
"We want to keep doing what we're doing," Pucci said.
Information and donations to the Carole Cascio Fund can be found at: https://www.carolecasciofund.org.

title: Country Cooking: The recipe box
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: The recipe box

 March 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: News 
 
 877
 Words 

 Read News Document

 I decided to do some spring cleaning a few days ago — I should have known better.It never fails. I always come across something that three hours later I am still involved with. This time it was the recipe box with my collection of Mom's recipes that she wrote down for me.
These old simple cooking recipes from the '30s, '40s, '50s and '60s never fail to consume the rest of the day, just remembering her love of the kitchen and cooking. Some of the recipes are beginning to fade, but they are still precious to me.Mom had beautiful handwriting.
Let's explore some of these recipes.
QUICK & EASY BREAD PUDDING
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Break up 6 slices of bread and place in a mixing bowl. Add 2 tbsps of melted butter, 4 beaten eggs, 2 cups milk, 3/4 cup sugar, 1 tsp cinnamon, 1 tsp vanilla and 1/2 cup raisins. Mix well and pour into a greased baking pan. Bake for 45 minutes or until the top springs up when touched. Serve warm.
LAURA'S CRAB CAKES
In a large mixing bowl, place 2 to 3 pounds of fresh lump crabmeat and add 1/3 cup mayonnaise, 1 1/2 tbsps mustard, 2 to 3 large eggs, 1 1/2 tsp Old Bay seasoning, 1/2 cup soft breadcrumbs, 1 pinch cayenne pepper, salt and pepper to taste. Mix into crab cakes and fry in hot oil or broil. Make sure they are golden brown on top, but watch closely so they do not burn.
GREEN LIMA BEAN SOUP WITH DUMPLINGS
To a big soup pot, add either a big piece of salt pork or a ham bone with about 6 to 7 cups cold water and proceeded to let it cook until boiling began. At this point, add a quart of canned tomatoes from last year's canning or a size 10 can of store-bought tomatoes. Cover and let simmer for about an hour. Add about 4 to 5 cups of fresh green lima beans, one medium can of white or yellow corn, about a tbsp of sugar, 3 to 4 small peeled white potatoes (cut into chunks), salt and pepper to taste, cover and let cook while you make the dumplings.
DUMPLINGS — combine 2 cups flour, 1 tsp salt, 2 tsps baking powder, 2 tsps oil or lard, and water to moisten, Mix well adding enough water to make a stiff dough. Roll out on floured surface and cut into 2-inch squares and when bean soup is almost cooked add dumplings.
MOM'S BAKING POWDER BISCUITS
Heat oven to 450 degrees. Sift 2 cups of all-purpose flour, 3 tsps baking powder, and 1 tsp salt into a mixing bowl. Cut in 1/4 cup lard or shortening. Make a well in the center and add 3/4 cup milk. Stir quickly and lightly with a fork just until dough clings together in a ball. Do not over-handle. Turn dough out on a lightly floured surface. Knead gently 8 to 10 times. Flour your hands and pinch off the balls of dough about 1/2 in size and roll in your palm placing on an ungreased baking sheet or simply cut out with a cutter. Place biscuits on baking sheets about 1 inch apart . Bake for 12 to 15 minutes or until golden brown. Serve warm.
EASY ZUCCHINI BREAD
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. In a large mixing bowl, place 1 1/2 cups peeled and shredded zucchini with 1/4 cup oil, 1 beaten egg, 1/2 cup brown sugar, 1/2 cup white sugar, 1 tsp vanilla, 1 1/2 cups flour, 1 tsp cinnamon, 1 tsp nutmeg, 1 tsp baking soda, and 1 tsp baking powder. Mix well and pour into a greased loaf pan and bake for 50 to 60 minutes or until done. This recipe card had a note that said it was given to Mom by one of her friends and that it was GOOD in capital letters.
MOM'S FRIED GREEN TOMATOES
Combine 2 large eggs with 1 cup buttermilk and set aside. Combine in a shallow bowl or pan two cups of all-purpose flour with 2 cups cornmeal, 1 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp black pepper. Wash the tomatoes and slice into 1/3-inch slices. Pour about 1/4 to 1/2 inch of vegetable oil or olive oil into a fry pan. Dredge the tomato slices through the egg mixture and then into the flour mixture and then place in the hot oil in a frying pan — cook about 2 minutes on each side (until lightly browned). Remove from pan to a flat dish with paper towels to absorb oil. Sprinkle the tops only with light sugar — serve warm.
All these recipes may seem to be so old fashioned to the younger cooks, but they were part of my teenage years and on into my early housewife years. When the more modern gadgets and appliances began to appear, I was right on board for change.
Funny how I still used some of the "old fashioned ways" to cook as I still do today! Right up until her death, Mom still cooked "her way" with her iron fry pans, baking pans, percolator coffee pot on the stove top, the hand beater, and hand washing the dishes.
However, one day a microwave appeared on the countertop, a gift from one of my brothers. Mom loved it.

title: Kent Island Heritage Society marks 50 years of preservation
author: REBECCA PLACEK
content:
Kent Island Heritage Society marks 50 years of preservation

 March 28, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: REBECCA PLACEK | Section: Life

 STEVENSVILLE — The Kent Island Heritage Society celebrated its 50th anniversary on March 25, highlighting five decades of preserving local history and acquiring significant historical sites.Founded in May 1975 by five local women — Marian Stewart, Mary White, Emily Denny, Mildred Schoch and Annie May Price — the society has become a cornerstone of Kent Island's historical preservation efforts. During the anniversary event at Historic Christ Church, four key speakers reviewed the organization's achievements and the island's rich history.
The society's journey began with William Claiborne mapping and claiming Kent Island in 1631. Over the years, KIHS has acquired several important historical properties, including:
- The Cray House (1809), renovated and opened in 1977
- Stevensville Train Station (1902), donated in 1987
- Kirwan House (1879) and Museum Store (1889), willed to the society in the 1990s
- Historic Stevensville Post Office (1877), purchased in 1997
- Historic Stevensville Bank (1809), obtained in 2000 through a $1 annual lease from owner Bill Hufnell
- Kent Island Heritage Center Museum (formerly "School House #2"), acquired in 2023 through a bequest from former treasurer Lynne Riley Coleman
Upcoming events include the Maryland House and Garden Pilgrimage on May 3, featuring tours of the Historic Bank, Train Station/Caboose, Cray House and Historic Christ Church. The society's annual Kent Island Day celebration will take place May 17, featuring a parade, entertainment, food, vendors and exhibitors in Historic Stevensville. The new Kent Island Heritage Center Museum is scheduled to open during this event.
Kent Island Heritage Society historic sites are open to visitors the first Saturday of each month from April through November, on Kent Island Day and during special group tours.
For more information, visit https://kentislandheritagesociety.org/

title: Former Chesapeake Music competitor makes professional concert debut
author: JOHN MALIN
content:
Former Chesapeake Music competitor makes professional concert debut

 April 2, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: JOHN MALIN | Section: Music 
 
 289
