title: Talbot Treasures will showcase county artifacts, memories this Saturday
author: Konner Metz
content:
Talbot Treasures will showcase county artifacts, memories this Saturday

 June 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 504
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Inside the Waterfowl Festival building sit some relics of Talbot County history, such as a penny from 1794, a baton from a beloved St. Michaels High School band director, and a rare whiskey decanter decorated to celebrate America's bicentennial.They are some of the early entries into Talbot Treasures, a joint effort between Talbot250 Commission, Talbot Historical Society and Waterfowl Festival leaders to assemble a display of artifacts.
The Talbot Treasures collection will be open for the public to view on Saturday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. at the Waterfowl Festival building on South Harrison Street. Talbot County communications coordinator Sarah Kilmon beamed with excitement Thursday as she perused through some of the items.
"We'd like to tell as many stories of Talbot County as we can," Kilmon said.
Kilmon, who leads Talbot250 and its efforts to celebrate America's upcoming semiquincentennial in 2026, contributed to the collection herself, adding photos of and items belonging to her grandfather, Louis Scott Kilmon.
He was the St. Michaels High School band director for over 30 years before retiring in 2001. His baton — the same one he's using in old photos of him conducting — and trombone will be shown off Saturday.
"He retired in 2001, but his legacy still echoes in the halls of the school and in the lives of those he inspired," Kilmon wrote on her item description.
A few items down from the trombone and baton is a special edition whiskey decanter, which dates to the nation's bicentennial in 1976. It was found in the basement of the Waterfowl Building by sheer luck and is now cleaned up for show.
Waterfowl Festival Executive Director Deena Kilmon, Sarah's mother, said the building itself — which is nearing its 100th anniversary in a couple years — is jam-packed with history. The number of groups, organizations and people that have used or borrowed the building lends itself to some neat stories, she said, such as when it was an old shooting range or when former President John F. Kennedy made a campaign stop there in 1960.
"The hundreds, and hundreds and hundreds of people that have been in here is mind-blowing," Deena Kilmon said.
On Saturday, even more history will be captured in the building formerly known as the Easton Armory.
Many other items have been brought in already or are expected. Some of the oldest include a 1794 penny from the Talbot County Women's Club and a silver spoon submitted by Talbot County Council Vice President Pete Lesher that dates back to 1810 and the Royal Navy.
During the exhibit Saturday, attendees can vote for the item with the best story and the most unique artifact. Talbot Historical Society board members will host a panel on antique valuation and auctioning.
"Many of these stories still resonate today," said Talbot Historical Society Executive Director Peggy Morey in a press release. "We hope visitors will not only learn from these items and their histories but will also find meaningful connections to our community and the challenges we face now."

title: Atwood's 'A 3 Month Journey' on display at the Foundry
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Atwood's 'A 3 Month Journey' on display at the Foundry

 June 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 320
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Mary Elizabeth Atwood, a Caroline County native, presented "A 3 Month Journey" at the Foundry in Denton on Friday. The show exhibited art that Atwood worked on during a three-month period in the upstairs art room of the Foundry.During that period, Atwood created more than 40 pieces of art. She said when she begins creating, she can't stop.
"Three months of working, and once I start creating, I don't know how to stop," Atwood said. "... I meditate every day. So more like contemplation, so I don't listen to something that's just being still and I think that helps clear my mind and sometimes that's how I paint also… I will look at the canvas, and then I'll just go and pick out the paints, put them on beside the canvas, and then pretty much I know what I'm going to do."
Along with presenting her art pieces, Atwood performed another form of art, presenting multiple poems. Atwood says her writing process is the same as her painting process, except for one major part.
"It's almost the same thing except I can't sit down and just write," Atwood said. "I have to have a pen and paper beside me and pencil and paper, even when we're traveling, because if something hits me, I have to write it down. Just a line."
Atwood finished the paintings within the first month and a half in the art studio of the Foundry, but before that she also starting creating archetype figures to be presented as well. According to Atwood, those figures represent a season in life everyone man or woman may experience.
George Karos II, executive director of the Foundry, says artist like Atwood, who participate in the artist in residence program, bring exposure to the Foundry.
"In terms of visibility, branding, it opens up opportunities for us to not only be known as a little green building with the guitar player out front," Karos said.

 CENTREVILLE — A celebration of freedom, unity and heritage brought the community together June 14 as the Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center hosted its seventh annual Juneteenth festivities.The all-day event featured an expanded parade, live music, dancing, readings by prominent Black authors, a visit from the Mobile Library, a breakfast buffet, free haircuts, basketball clinics, vendors, food trucks and exhibits inviting the public to explore Kennard's museum and resource library.

title: 'Dorchester Dreams' becomes county song
author: Lily Tierney
content:
'Dorchester Dreams' becomes county song

 June 20, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 429
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Singer-songwriter Jayla Elise performed her song "Dorchester Dreams" in front of the Dorchester County Council and attending residents at Tuesday's council meeting after it being adopted as the first ever official county song.Elise's song showcases the pride, unity, hope and resilience that resonates across generations in Dorchester County. In "Dorchester Dreams," Elise honors the legacy of those who have contributed to the county, including Harriet Tubman and current families.
"To everyone who has been a part of Dorchester County or grew up here, I want to thank you for actually being the inspiration for every lyric that I wrote down," Elise said before performing her song. Elise said although she isn't originally from Dorchester County, she wanted to capture the feeling of what it means to call a place home even if you're not from there.
Elise is an independent artist who grew up in Prince George's County, where she found her voice in state choirs and formal performing arts training, according to her website.
"Being an independent artist, there's a sense of liberation behind that," Elise said. She said being independent allows her full creative control over her image, sound and process. Elise is managed by the Barzini Family Music Group, which aims to establish the Eastern Shore as an up and coming music scene.
"It's no doubt in their minds, and mine too, that this is going to be where entertainment is going to find its home very soon," Elise said. The Barzini family and Elise believe this because of Cambridge's famous former resident, Harriet Tubman.
"For the culture, there's the big three: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Malcolm X and Harriet Tubman," Elise said. King was from Georgia, which has a thriving entertainment scene, Malcolm X was from Brooklynn, the birthplace of hip-hop, and now they believe it's Cambridge's time.
The lyrics to "Dorchester Dreams" were inspired by community and hopes to bridge the generational gap by highlighting shared memories among people who can be vastly different yet share the place they call home.
Elise's aspirations do not stop at the county level. She is currently working on a song for Maryland 250, an organization dedicated to preserving Maryland's history ahead of the 250th anniversary of the nation next year.
According to Council Vice President Mike Detmer, Elise's song will be performed at official events, civic ceremonies and educational programs throughout Dorchester County.
Elise wants to use her platform to build community and empower others to shoot for the stars. "Everybody has a gift. How are you going to use it in this world?" she said.
Elise's music can be found at jaylaelise.com.

title: Old Trinity Church celebrates its 350th anniversary
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Old Trinity Church celebrates its 350th anniversary

 June 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 530
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHURCH CREEK — The appropriately named Old Trinity Church is celebrating its 350th anniversary this year. It is the oldest church in the nation still used for regular Sunday service.The Colonial-era church was built sometime between 1675 and 1690 on over four acres and has undergone significant renovations since, but it has not lost its original charm. The Rev. Dan Dunlap said that in the 1850s, the church was remodeled in the Victorian style.
"100 years later, under the oversight of Col. Edgar Garbisch, and his wife Bernice Chrysler Garbisch and the Chrysler family, they restored the church again, but this time they went back to the colonial style," Dunlap said.
Dunlap said the church is roughly 38 feet long and 20 feet wide and was built to hold "100 souls." However these days, he said on an average Sunday worship, the same familiar 25 to 30 faces sit in the pews.
Dunlap has been the rector of Old Trinity for 11 years and was a former professor of historical theology and worship at Houston Graduate School of Theology. He has organized multiple historic services and events to commemorate the 350th anniversary of the Old Trinity Church.
In February, the church held battleground reenactments like one for the "Battle of the Ice Mound," which took place 210 years ago off the nearby James and Taylors islands as one of the final battles of the War of 1812.
The next day, during regular church service, they used the 1662 Book of Common Prayer of the Church of England, which Dunlap said would have been the prayer book early settlers used.
Old Trinity Church hosted its second of three special historical services for the 350th anniversary on June 15 using the 1789 Book of Common Prayer, the first prayer book used by the Episcopalian Church in the United States. Dunlap said the service was very well attended.
"We're having a lot of fun with this," he said. According to Dunlap, the church is planning to have a third historical service sometime this year and will be hosting an event open to the public in September.
The church's graveyard is the final resting place for six veterans of the American Revolution, four from the War of 1812, and several veterans from both sides of the Civil War. Dunlap said they are still selling plots in the graveyard.
Dunlap said the church is open to the public and wants to encourage people to come and check it out regardless of religious affiliation.
Along with the four acres of church property, which houses the cemetery, Old Trinity also owns an additional 85 acres of property right on Church Creek. "It's just a very peaceful slice of Heaven, and it's situated right on the creek," Dunlap said. "It's very scenic."
"A big slice of this area we maintain, and we do so by letting a local farmer, the same family that operates Emily's down the road, farms the property," Dunlap said. He said their recent corn crop has started growing tall.
"There seems to be an intersection between the sacredness of the place as a place of worship, but also a place where nature and faith come together," he said. "It's like an intersection of the two."

title: Juneteenth celebration honors powerful stories
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Juneteenth celebration honors powerful stories

 June 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: Local News 
 
 502
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The Juneteenth Celebration hosted by the Academy Art Museum on Saturday focused on the power of storytelling and using it to honor African American history, culture and resilience, according to Jennifer Chrzanowski, the deputy director at the museum.Chrzanowski said she and the other Juneteenth committee members selected performers who were storytellers to stay on the theme of "Our Freedom! Our Story!" Among them was Jeffrey Boston Weatherford, a children's illustrator and performance poet from High Point, North Carolina.
"Connecting the culture is imperative," Weatherford said. "They call the United States the Melting Pot, but sometimes we act like it's water and oil and not melting together, so it's necessary."
When he wasn't presenting on stage, Weatherford was manning a booth displaying his books alongside his mom, writer Carole Boston Weatherford, and his wife. Later in the event, he stepped into the museum, where his exhibition was on display.
The exhibition featured words and images from Carole and Jeffrey Boston Weatherford's book titled "Kin: Rooted in Hope," which reconstructed the history of the Weatherford family. The exhibition will be on display at the museum until June 29.
Outside of the museum, visitors could visit the vendor booths or enjoy a performance by several musical acts on stage.
St. Michaels High School student Ruby Fisher took to the stage to perform two songs and read two poems. She said her favorite part was seeing everyone's faces and getting to share her voice.
Her third time at the festival, Fisher said she returns each year because of its importance.
"It helps to bring the community together, and it helps support history and how it needs to be remembered," Fisher said.
The Academy Art Museum partnered with Building African American Minds and the Frederick Douglass Honor Society to organize the celebration. Dina Daly, the Executive Director of BAAM, said the Juneteenth event is important because it teaches students to understand and appreciate the day's history.
"I think for many years, only the Black community really knew about Juneteenth, or even some young kids didn't really understand the meaning of Juneteenth," Daly said.
Juneteenth, which became a federal holiday in 2021, marks the emancipation of enslaved African Americans.
To spread awareness of the history of Juneteenth, the Academy Art Museum holds an essay contest for middle and high school students. Leading up to the celebration, students had the opportunity to submit an essay about what Juneteenth means to the youth today, with the opportunity to win a cash prize.
"It gives them the opportunity to research it, to actually understand, and to put their thoughts into words that they can express themselves and then maybe they get an award," Daly said.
This year marked the Academy Art Museum's 14th annual Juneteenth Celebration, and Chrzanowski and Daly both agreed that the event was necessary, serving as an opportunity for locals to gather together and honor their history through a troublesome time.
"There are a lot of places that are now on these budget cuts, and they're cutting Juneteenth as a celebration," Chrzanowski said. "But we continue to go strong."

 CHESTERTOWN — The Kent County chapter of the Delmarva Pride Center is proud to announce that it will host the powerful photo exhibit "Authentic Selves: Celebrating Trans and Nonbinary People and Their Families" at the Garfield Center for the Arts in Chestertown throughout the month of June, in honor of Pride Month.Developed by Family Diversity Projects, "Authentic Selves" is a traveling exhibit that uses photography and personal narratives to amplify the voices and lived experiences of transgender and nonbinary people across the United States. title: ‘Colorful Visions’ opens First Friday at The Artists’ Gallery
author: Staff Writer
content:
‘Colorful Visions’ opens First Friday at The Artists’ Gallery

 June 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 425
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — The Artists' Gallery will feature the work of one of its exhibiting artists, Carol McClees, on First Friday, July 4, in a body of work titled Colorful Visions. McClees' goal is to create a vibrant painting that conveys a sense of life, vibrancy and movement — in her words, "ALIVE WITH COLOR!"A contemporary artist and award-winning painter, McClees' self-directed education has included studying with some of the best national and regional artists. While she has worked in a variety of mediums, she favors painting in oil.
McClees has exhibited her paintings in many juried shows throughout the United States, including but not limited to Coos Art Museum (Oregon), American Society of Marine Artists East Regional Show hosted by Biggs Museum of American Art (Delaware), Washington County Museum of Fine Arts (Maryland), and Buffalo Naval Park Museum (New York), as well as Working Artists Forum's Local Color and the Waterfowl Festival (Easton). Her work is part of many private collections throughout the Mid-Atlantic, Midwest, West Coast and New England. McClees is an active member of many art organizations, including the American Society of Marine Artists, Working Artists' Forum and Mid-Atlantic Plein Air Painters Association. Her degrees include an RN and an MBA in marketing.
Born and raised in New England, McClees is married to a native Marylander and lives in Baltimore. She enjoys sailing on the Chesapeake Bay aboard her 36-foot Skean Dhu, tennis, Nantucket basket weaving, embroidery and reading.
McClees' artistic inspiration comes from a maritime landscape, a beloved animal or an architectural delight, whether painting in plein air or in her home studio. "Striving to achieve a painterly realism one brush stroke at a time, using abundant color, and supporting textural tools is my artistic goal. I love to find and capture the unique moment in time when the subject matter comes to life — that fleeting moment when the magical effects of the sun cause dramatic play between lights and darks. When accomplished, I believe that artistic tension is at its best, revealing a painting Alive with Color, which evokes thoughtful emotion and allows the viewer to complete the story."
The public is invited to attend the Artists' Gallery's opening reception for McClees on First Friday, July 4, from 5 to 7:30 p.m. Her paintings will be featured in the gallery throughout the month of July. The Artists' Gallery is located at 239 High St. in Chestertown, and is open Tuesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Sundays from 12:30 to 4:30 p.m. For more information, visit www.theartistsgalleryctown.com or call 410-778-2425.

title: Fireworks, art and history will collide in Vienna
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Fireworks, art and history will collide in Vienna

 June 30, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 150
 Words 

 Read News Document

 VIENNA — Instead of fireworks in July, the Vienna Heritage Society will host fireworks in September as part of the Music on the Nanticoke Free Summer Concert Series.The Heritage Society is currently accepting donations to make the dream a reality. The goal is to raise $12,000 for the firework display, but the town has not yet reached its goal, said Vienna Town Clerk Toni Alexander.
Dorchester County's Golden Touch Band will be playing, and Alexander said there will be local food trucks, snow cones and will be a family friendly event.
"Celebrate our history, support the arts, and bring joy to locals and visitors alike," reads the PayPal donation page. Donations can be made via cash, check or credit card at the town office or through a QR code that can be found on Vienna Maryland's official Facebook page.
"We are excited to bring this event back for another year," Alexander said.

title: A marriage of inconvenience at the library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
A marriage of inconvenience at the library

 July 3, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life 
 
 995
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Not too long ago, I was trying to decide what to give my nephew's fiancée for her birthday.A professional singer-songwriter, Sophia is brilliant, beautiful and, for one so young, uncommonly comfortable in her bones. She once seriously considered becoming a Buddhist nun.
What do you give a woman who doesn't seem to need anything at all?
Sometimes my brain reminds me of those magic 8 balls we played with as children. You would ask the thing a question, shake it, and à la the oracle at Delphi, a tiny black placard with an enigmatic answer on it would float up into a small window on the 8 ball's surface.
À la the 8 ball, a tiny black placard now floated up into my mind with the phrase "Black Dogs" inscribed on it.
I first read Ian McEwan's novel "Black Dogs" when it came out in 1992. In those days I was rather protective of Mr. McEwan. I'd discovered him a few years earlier when his 1987 novel "The Child in Time" came out, and though the literati were doubtless already celebrating him, no one I knew was as yet reading the man. I thought of him as my discovery.
And, so far as I was concerned, "Black Dogs" confirmed my prescience.
So I bought a copy of the thing, wrapped it in gift wrapping as best I could (picture a spider's untidily bundled prey), and shipped it off to Sophia. And, of course, as soon as I pulled out of the post office parking lot, I began to fear I'd screwed up.
It had been 30 years since I read "Black Dogs." What if the book wasn't as good as I recalled?
Depending on how you define "library," Melissa and I have three. There are the formal shelves in our living room, full of first editions, art books and field guides; there is the library in my study — poetry, languages, a set of Britannica and Melissa's history texts; and there's the paperback library in the attic — fiction, more textbooks and a bookcase devoted to histories of early monasticism and Anglo-Saxon England.
I found my old copy of "Black Dogs" in the attic, picked it up, and soon discovered that, once again, I couldn't put it down.
McEwan's novel is presented as a memoir of a couple's on-again, off-again marriage. Bernard and June meet while working for British Intelligence during World War II, marry at the conclusion of that conflict, and, for their honeymoon, go on a long walking tour through northern Italy and the south of France.
As was fairly common among intellectuals in the '30s and '40s, the two of them have seen the rise of Hitler's fascism as the natural enemy of mankind and, consequently, become attracted to what seems fascism's equally natural opposite, communism. Before setting out for war-torn Europe, the young idealists have taken what they think of as both a daring and exciting leap into the future: they have officially joined the Party.
But in Languedoc, toward the end of their walking tour, June has an encounter with a pair of feral hounds that utterly upends her faith in communism, to say nothing of any other –ism. It is an event that, for the rest of their lives, will haunt, trouble and blight their marriage.
Curiously, "Black Dogs" is told from the point of view of the couple's son-in-law who, orphaned at an early age, comes to think of his wife's parents as his own. The book recounts the role he plays in trying to reconcile them to each other and to each other's divergent views of reality: Bernard's materialistic and socialist, June's entirely metaphysical.
As it happens, the son-in-law proves to be the perfect foil for both. While in Bernard's company, he finds himself drawn to the man's optimism, his belief that the world's problems are caused by perfectly rational forces and, therefore, are susceptible to perfectly rational solutions. While in June's, he is equally affected by her spirituality, the notion that he is in the presence of someone who has achieved an uncommon and otherworldly wisdom.
But he also finds their ironclad certainties maddening, the fact that neither will admit the other might not be entirely wrong.
Again and again, though, we come back to the dogs. Bernard sees the animals as representing a minor episode in his life, one that, due to his wife's improbable obsession with the things, has driven her from him and the life they had once hoped to share. June sees them as the proof of Hamlet's declaration that "There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy…" — though she would substitute Bernard's name for Horatio's.
Better than I have here, McEwan piques his readers' interest by referring repeatedly in the book to June's encounter with the dogs without ever actually explaining what that encounter entailed. It is only in the last 40 pages of the novel that he returns us to that arid plateau in Languedoc in the spring of 1946 to witness the event itself in a rush of writing that is as fine and evocative as any I have ever read.
It has been one of the great privileges of my life to hike in the south of France — cicadas droning in the heat, air scented with rosemary and thyme — to round a promontory and find myself looking out over a vast gorge, a gap in the mountains opposite revealing a sparkling sliver of Mediterranean Sea.
If that sounds like something you'd like to do, I recommend you take a walking tour through Ian McEwan's "Black Dogs." You'll find it in the fiction section of the Talbot County Free Library under the call letters MCEW. Later, at the end of your day, as you sit in the shade in front of the local auberge, a glass of rosé resting on the table before you, I'd ask that you send a little book lover's request heavenward that Sophia will enjoy the experience as much as you have.

title: Two new shows opening at Easton's Zebra Gallery
author: Staff Writer
content:
Two new shows opening at Easton's Zebra Gallery

 July 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Arts

 On Friday, July 18, from 5 to 7 p.m., the Zebra Gallery will open two new shows featuring artists Gabriel Lehman and Evan Fitzgerald.Gabriel Lehman's show, "A Bird's Eye View," will feature his fanciful, dreamlike landscapes with a particular emphasis on clouds, imbuing a sense of joy and wonder into his art. Lehman is a self-taught artist who started painting in 2009 after a career in construction with a focus on flooring for 14 years. Despite not having any formal training, Lehman's unique perspective and whimsical style quickly gained him a following.
Lehman is also offering painting classes from July 14 to 19 to learn his secrets to gorgeous clouds and fantastic creatures. Classes offered include "Three-Color Clouds," where students will learn the secrets of capturing the softness, depth and movement of clouds while transforming three simple colors into breathtaking skyscapes.
The "Sunset Skies" class offers students an enchanting journey through the colors of dusk as they learn to paint breathtaking sunsets on 16-by-20-inch canvases. In this immersive class, students learn how to capture the delicate gradients, vibrant hues and ethereal beauty of the sky at its most magical moments.
The "Rays of Light" class guides students through techniques to achieve the perfect balance of light and shadow, subtle color blending and atmospheric perspective, making the clouds look like they could float right off the canvas. This class invites participants to explore the endless possibilities of acrylic paint while creating stunning skyscapes that will brighten any space. All skill levels are welcome to all of these classes.
Evan Fitzgerald's current work explores the ideas of persona. The word persona is rooted in the Latin word for a theatrical mask. Carl Jung described persona as a social mask that we all put on — something to embody, a different mask for a different setting. By obscuring the subject's face, their headdresses are the focal point. The individual is merely a pedestal for displaying these objects.
"Both of these artists bring such creative and whimsical works to the gallery. I hope visitors will be mesmerized by the details these painters bring to their paintings. We are thrilled to have them exhibiting here," said Susan Schauer John, owner of the Zebra Gallery.
For more information or to sign up for Gabriel Lehman's class, call 410-253-9131 or email thezebragallery@gmail.com. The Zebra Gallery is located at 5 North Harrison Street in Easton (across the street from the Historic Tidewater Inn). The gallery hours are Thursday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. or by appointment. For further information, visit sfsfiber.art or thezebragallery.com.

title: Big bands, big booms: Big Band Night and fireworks cap St. Michaels Fourth of July
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Big bands, big booms: Big Band Night and fireworks cap St. Michaels Fourth of July

 July 8, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 421
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ST. MICHAELS — More than 1,700 people from around the Eastern Shore and beyond showed up to the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum on Saturday night to celebrate the July 4 weekend, enjoy the 18-piece big band and watch St. Michaels fireworks display.The Shades of Blue Orchestra provided entertainment for the whole family, spanning genres and generations through their tunes. The father-daughter duo Tony and Gia Liberto joined the band for multiple songs, belting out ballads alongside the instrumentalists.
"The talent must run in the family," said Michael Walker, conductor of the Shades of Blue Orchestra.
According to Shannon Mitchell, vice president of engagement for the Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum, the Shades of Blue Orchestra has been playing at Big Band Night for at least the past decade.
Between songs, Walker thanked and honored the veterans who attended, gushed over how honored he was to be a part of this and spoke about the importance of music education.
"It has real value to the human brain," he said.
Walker guided the band into "Fly Me To The Moon" by Frank Sinatra, which Tony Liberto sang with grace and ease. The dance floor filled with couples of all ages and a sister duo wearing matching American flag dresses who maybe stopped dancing one time throughout the night.
Delawareans Renee Goolday and Mitch Greene said they always wanted to visit St. Michaels and saw Big Band Night as the perfect opportunity.
"I saw the fireworks were going to happen tonight, and I thought this was perfect weather so we drove the Jeep down," Goolday said.
Mitchell said Big Band Night is unique compared to other festivals and events in the area with the focus being on music and fireworks, having a bring-your-own beverage model, there being few food vendors and cheaper tickets making it more accessible.
This year, the space next to the museum's welcome center was used for inflatables like slides and a bouncy house with a speaker playing the big band, so parents didn't miss out. According to Mitchell, in previous years this area was extra viewing space for the fireworks.
The Chesapeake Bay Maritime Museum is situated in front of where the firework display is set, making it a premier destination for the show. As the sun began setting, the museum's lighthouse and gazebo glimmered in red, white and blue.
By 9:30 p.m. all eyes were fixed on the show in the sky. Bursts of colors reflected on the Bay as the Star Wars theme song played in the background.
"Wow, Mommy!" a little boy said emphatically after each firework went off.

author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Fourth free gospel concert in Denton marks the halfway point for series

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: Caroline

 DENTON — The fourth free gospel concert of the eight-concert series is set to take place at Calvary Baptist Church in Denton on Friday, July 11, at 6:30 p.m. Russ Yates, vice president of Holiday Park, hopes the series can reach people and teach them about Jesus."Well, hopefully it reaches a lot of people that need to know about Jesus," Yates said. It certainly gives the Christian community an outlet to do something, that's basically free."
The free concert will feature groups Port City Quartet, from North Carolina, and The Hyssongs from Rockport, Maine.
Holiday Park campground hosted concerts and events before COVID-19, after COVID, Yates closed the park, but recently with the direction from God, he was led to continue events but at a different venue.
"We did 30 years from 1989 to 2019 here at the campground. And then when COVID hit we had to shut down everything," Yates said. "Then we lost all of our people that volunteered to help because we needed about 50 people to put on the concerts. I really thought that was the end of it. Then last year during the winter, I started getting the feeling the Lord wanted us to start this up again, and I called the church and asked them what about us doing it there.
"Pastor Don Reynold said 'Russ, I've been praying you would start this up again,' and I was like, 'Well, looks like that's what we're going to try to do.' So the church was all behind it and have been real supportive."
Yates said events like this are good for the community because it's free, and it gives believers fun activities to enjoy.
"We just hope the outreach reaches a number of people that need it," Yates said. "I hear all the time from Christian people there's nothing for Christians to do. We certainly are trying to do our best."

title: QACHS art students partner with Haven Ministries to share 'hope for homes'
author: SUBMITTED NEWS
content:
QACHS art students partner with Haven Ministries to share 'hope for homes'

 July 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SUBMITTED NEWS | Section: Arts 
 
 426

 CENTREVILLE — The Queen Anne's County High School Chapter of the National Art Honor Society continues to shine a light in the community through their ongoing partnership with Haven Ministries and their Art for Your Home project. In 2025, students donated 13 framed original soft block prints to support individuals and families in transition — offering not just artwork, but a sense of hope and dignity for those facing financial hardship or transitioning into permanent housing.The Hope for the Home extension of the project was established in 2018 through a collaborative effort between Queen Anne's County Public Schools Visual Arts Supervisor Michael Bell, Haven Ministries, the Hope Warehouse, and Rick Strittmater, executive director for the Queen Anne's County Centre for the Arts. It has since become a valued tradition in the school's arts programming, one that allows student artists to earn Service-Learning credit while making a meaningful contribution to their community.
"It's been incredible to see this meaningful project grow year after year," said Bell. "I'm proud to see our students still partnering with Haven Ministries, and using their talents to bring light and beauty into the homes of those who need it most."
This year, students learned soft block printing techniques to produce unique, framed works of art for the Haven Ministries Art for Your Home program. These pieces are displayed on the walls of the Hope Warehouse, where clients can select one to take home — free of charge.
"One of my core beliefs as an artist and a teacher is that we can each use our talents and efforts to lift people up and give back to the communities we live in," said Stephanie Zeiler, Queen Anne's County High Art Department Chair and district Lead Visual Arts Teacher. "It is my hope to instill community stewardship in my students and show them they can make a positive difference in this world, even at their young age."
Sophomore artist Lilly Askew shared, "I feel very fortunate to have had the opportunity to create art for someone that may not have access to it because of whatever barriers they face. I hope our art makes their space feel a little more like home and helps brighten their walls."
Peter Grim, executive director of Haven Ministries, praised the initiative: "This personalization of space helps to create a feeling of home and develop a sense of worth and value. Without you and so many other wonderful supporters, this important opportunity would not exist."
Through compassion and creativity, Queen Anne's students continue to leave a lasting impact — one artwork at a time.

title: James Beard Finalists: Cultural collaboration of cuisine, character
author: Lily Tierney
content:
James Beard Finalists: Cultural collaboration of cuisine, character

 July 10, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 781
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Fusions of flavor, cuisine and culture came together Wednesday evening at Easton's Bas Rouge for a five-course inaugural "cultural collaboration dinner" series.The event showcases Bas Rouge and 2024 James Beard award winning Chef Harley Peet's commitment to honor fellow James Beard finalists through dynamic culinary partnerships that highlight the rich diversity shaping Mid-Atlantic food culture.
Peet and Bas Rouge welcomed five-time semi-finalist and 2024 Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic Finalist Kevin Tien alongside 2024/2025 James Beard Finalist, Pastry Chef Susan Bae of Washington, D.C.'s Moon Rabbit to Easton to kick off the dinner series.
Although the five-course meal did not have a theme per se, every dish honored the Mid-Atlantic seasonal produce through Peet and Tien's unique and distinct cooking styles. For each chef, seasonal cooking and sustainable sourcing are baseline practices at their restaurants.
Peet and Tien met at the James Beard Awards in Chicago and hit it off from the jump. After a little over two decades in the industry, Peet said he now has an eye for picking out chefs who have something special.
"There's Michelin Stars handed out all the time, but there's special ones," Peet said. "And Kevin and his team and his concept and everything he's doing, it just struck a chord in Chicago. We struck a chord."
Peet describes his culinary style as "all over the board" meshing Japanese, classic French, "redneck s--- from Tilghman Island," and Americanized dishes with Italian twists. Tien described his style as "Cajun Asian."
Tien's Vietnamese background and Louisiana upbringing have shaped his approach to cooking. However, he said he didn't truly embrace Vietnamese cuisine until the pandemic when he had a pivotal mindset shift. He said he stayed away from Vietnamese food because it was seldom regarded in fine dining, but when he changed his mindset and opened Moon Rabbit, the possibilities were endless.
"People come to our restaurant and they expect traditional Vietnamese food, and there's none of that on the menu. So either they, like, really love what we're doing or they hate what we're doing," Tien said. "And I'll be honest, the people that hate what we're doing are actually our own people, which can be a little frustrating."
Tien said these days, he tries not to take it too personally and is focused on his and his team's happiness and the ability to continue to foster relationships with other chefs and restaurants outside of D.C.
Peet and Tien said that historically, chefs were siloed and collaboration efforts like this were not a common occurrence, but this is beginning to change in the industry.
"I think the humanitarian side is super important as well, the chef has been brought out of the kitchen, and the customer's been brought into the kitchen," Peet said.
With the rising popularity of shows like "The Bear," a movie-like version of chef's berating their servers, yelling at kitchen staff and being all around hateful has become the picture of back-of-house life, but Peet said it's not like that anymore.
"I've been in some kitchens with some old-school guys and, you know, it's just not fun," he said. Tien said he thinks this is partially because chefs have less ego and are respecting each other's work more.
Tien and Peet certainly respect each other's work, and it showed through each plate that was delivered to the table.
The Menu
The meal began with canapés by Bas Rouge which included an incredibly refreshing avocado agua fresca in a shot glass and local blue crab Causa, a cold, savory Peruvian-style potato dish.
This was followed by canapés by Moon Rabbit, a blend between French and Vietnamese flavors, which included Ga Ran Pâté, Vietnamese fried chicken, chicken presse and pâté, and Bo Luc Lac, a classic Vietnamese dish with marinated cubed beef and black pepper beef served in a crunchy tartlet.
Then guests were presented with fluffy taro milk bread served with an earthy culantro garlic butter followed by scallop crudo in a light yet acidic coconut sauce. The next plate was a beautiful display of octopus and Viet Cajun blood sausage with crunchy golden raisins and mostarda. Servers then presented guests with a gorgeous crab cake Wellington with a vegetable demi-glace in the middle.
For dessert, pastry chef Susan Bae made a Vietnamese coffee mousse that was almost too beautiful to eat. The stunning dessert tasted as good as it looked bursting with flavors of coffee, chocolate and citrus in every bite.
"It keeps things exciting too," Tien said about the collaboration. "Sometimes I get really lost in the day-to-day grind of our restaurant, and I forget to take the blinders off, so this is also a good way for me to get away, even if it's just for a day or two and reset mentally and go back really inspired."

 Mountains of paperwork and research later, the congregation of West Nottingham Presbyterian Church in Colora celebrated the official designation of their building as part of the National Register of Historic Places.A plaque noting the designation was unveiled Sunday, July 6 after morning worship services. The Maryland church is located in Colora near Rising Sun in the northeast part of the state.
Credit for completing that application went to Emily Kilby and Cindi Lamb-Wiley.
"We worked for over a year," Lamb-Wiley said of the process. "Emily was a better writer. I'm a better form filler."
Kilby said the church building on Firetower Road in Colora was already on the National Register but the information was inaccurate.
"The person who wrote it, their information reads the chapel was built in 1880 but it was built in 1804," Kilby, a noted local historian, said of the decades-old submission.
Kilby and Lamb-Wiley discovered that, what in the past had been a two page, hand-written file, would now be 50 pages of documentation to include a description of the historic attributes of the stone building.
"My brother Rick helped a lot," Kilby said. "He got up in the rafters and took pictures of the chestnut beams."
Rick Kilby said ship-building techniques were used in the construction.
"These beams weigh 3,000 pounds each," he said of the massive support beams in the rafters. Equipment that would have been used to raise the mast of large ships of that era were brought to the site.
"Can you imagine in 1800 trying to raise these heavy beams?" Emily Kilby said.
West Nottingham Presbyterian Church originally was in Rising Sun; the location of which is still not determined, Kilby said. The Colora church replaced that building.
The ladies had to write, re-write and re-submit information, challenged by the online technology of today.
"You have to fill it out just so and the photos have to be the right size," Kilby said.
Her research — which included issues of the Cecil Whig that covered the construction — gave her new insight about West Nottingham Presbyterian Church. Her research included the cemetery.
"The woman who invented the eye chart is buried here. So is the man who was the vice president of US Steel," Kilby said. "It's amazing, the richness of the history here."
"We don't want to have that history forgotten," she added. "This really is an amazing piece of history."

title: Eastern Shore singers perform at D-Day ceremonies in France
author: SUBMITTED NEWS
content:
Eastern Shore singers perform at D-Day ceremonies in France

 July 12, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: SUBMITTED NEWS | Section: Local News 
 
 462
 Words 

 Read News Document

 NORMANDY, FRANCE — Each year on the sixth of June, visitors from all over the world gather in Normandy, France to honor the sacrifices made during the D-Day invasion on that day in 1944 and this year included Queen Anne's Chorale.Many special events and wreath laying ceremonies take place to commemorate D-Day and the landing of Allied Forces on its shores during World War ll.
Each year the premier All-American D-Day Band and Community Chorus is assembled to perform at some of these commemorative events. The band and chorus are comprised of instrumentalists and singers from across the United States. With their music, they are the American musical ambassadors to France.
An invitation to sing in the All-American Community Chorus was sent to a local group, the Queen Anne's Chorale in Centreville. In addition to this honor, their Artistic Director, Robert Huntington, was chosen to conduct the chorus. Fourteen singers, along with family and friends, participated in this memorable trip.
Before leaving, however, they met several times to practice so they were ready to rehearse with the other singers upon arrival in Paris. The concert repertoire with an "Americana" theme included "Down to the River to Pray," "The Yellow Rose of Texas," "Swinging on a Star" and "Let There Be Peace on Earth."
Their itinerary for the nine-day trip began with a special guided tour, stopping at several significant areas dedicated to the D-Day battles of Normandy Campaign. Both the Chorus and Band joined forces for a Wreath Laying Ceremony at the Utah Beach Memorial. The Choir traveled to the American Cemetery at Omaha Beach and were able to tour the solemn place of honor. The Chorus presented concerts in the town square and in the Church in Sainte-Mere-Eglise as part of the Musical Salute to Liberation. They also participated in the annual D-Day Memorial Parade held there.
Before returning home, the Chorus also had an opportunity to explore Paris and perform an afternoon concert at La Madeleine Cathedral.
As Chorale singers began planning their trip to France, they found that their town of Centreville had yet another connection to D-Day, 1944. Sadly, one of its young men, U.S Army Private First-Class William H. Quillen, fought with the 29th Infantry Division and lost his life on the sixteenth of June 1944 during an ensuing battle. He received the Purple Heart and is buried in the Normandy American Cemetery.
Upon learning about Private Quillen, the Chorale, with the assistance of the Queen Anne's County Library in Stevensville, researched and identified his grave site coordinates. On June 5, Chorale members placed a flag on his grave in Normandy honoring his courage and sacrifice for the United States and the Allied Forces. A picture was taken with Chorale singers holding flags from both Queen Anne's County and the town of Centreville.

title: Historic Christ Church bell to be restored
author: REBECCA PLACEK Special to The Star Democrat
content:
Historic Christ Church bell to be restored

 July 14, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: REBECCA PLACEK Special to The Star Democrat | Section: News 
 
 287
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — The Historic Christ Church Bell Tower in Stevensville will be restored with proceeds from the May 3 Maryland House and Garden Tour of Queen Anne's County.On July 7, board members from the Queen Anne's County Historical Society presented a check for $9,010 to Nancy Cook of Friends of Historic Christ Church.
Cook gave a talk on the 1631 founding of Kent Fort on Kent Island, the third-oldest permanent English settlement established by William Claiborne.
He and settlers built the first Christ Church on the south tip of Kent Island. In 1680, a new town and Christ Church were moved to the new town of Broad Creek, where Bay City is now. Then, in 1880, Christ Church was moved to the new town of Stevensville.
The new Christ Church was built in 1880 in Queen Anne style. The bell tower is in the "lancet" chimney style. Wooden pegs and bricks were reused from the earlier Christ Churches. Historic Christ Church recently was designated as the Arts & Cultural Center of Historic Stevensville.
Mike Thomas has researched the church bell. The bell was made in 1880 by the McShane Bell Foundry of Baltimore, America's oldest bell company, established in 1856. The bell is bronze, rings in C sharp, and weighs 400 pounds including the mountings. In 1880, the bell was shipped to the Rev. Thompson, Christ Church, Stevensville. Church bells are rung for religious and ceremonial purposes such as Christmas and for significant events such as weddings.
Donations also are needed for Christ Church upkeep. Checks may be sent to: Nancy M. Cook, 124 Bryce Road, Queenstown, MD 21658. Historic Christ Church is nonprofit organization registered with the state of Maryland. Donations are tax-deductible to the fullest extent of the law.

title: Plein Air Easton artists take on Tilghman Island in paint-out competition
author: Konner Metz
content:
Plein Air Easton artists take on Tilghman Island in paint-out competition

 July 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 501
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TILGHMAN ISLAND — Artists took to Tilghman Island on Monday to paint some of the island's most iconic spots and views for Plein Air Easton's annual Paint Tilghman competition.Many of the 58 juried artists put their talents on display in Tilghman Island as part of Plein Air Easton's 21st annual weeklong outdoor painting competition.
By Monday evening, around 50 paintings hung in the Tilghman Island Inn, many for sale. Some depicted Monday morning's sunrise, while others showed views of Knapps Narrows Bridge. One artist painted the renowned Tilghman Island Country Store.
The artists chose their spots Monday morning and had until 4 p.m. to complete their works before heading to the inn for submissions.
Coakley Brown, of Richmond, Virginia, said she loves the environment around the Chesapeake Bay. The chance to paint around Tilghman wasn't as much competitive as it was fun, she said.
"This is play time," Brown said.
It was Harsh Agrawal's first time at Plein Air Easton. He came all the way from London and gained a deep appreciation for how unique Talbot County's different towns and islands are.
"All the towns, they have a different character," Agrawal said.
Agrawal completed two paintings, both of which were sold Monday. Driving around the island during the day, he happened upon the perfect view: a unique, battered barn house with dark clouds looming over it on an otherwise sunny day. During the hot and humid afternoon full of mosquitoes, Agrawal painted the barn.
He typically does two plein air events in the United States each year. He said the competitions are a great chance to explore new places.
Port Republic artist Freeman Dodsworth has been on the plein air circuit for three years, but 2025 is his first time in Easton. He sat in front of a radar tower in Tilghman Island on Monday overlooking the waters, about seven miles from his house on the western shore.
"The best way for me to meet other plein air painters is to paint outside," Dodsworth said.
Jess Bellis, the Avalon Foundation's chief financial and operating officer, said there's a "higher concentration of new artists" this year than Plein Air Easton has seen in a long time. It gives a "freshness" to the entire week, she said.
Many pieces sold during Monday's exhibit. One piece of note, a 20-by-16-inch canvas of boats and a large cloud passing over, hadn't sold as of around 6:30 p.m.
But that soon changed when the artists' choice award was announced. Baltimore County artist Palden Hamilton and his oil painting, "Passing Giant," was named Paint Tilghman's most outstanding work by the judging artists.
Following the announcement, it was only a matter of minutes before Avalon Foundation volunteers placed a "sold" slip of paper next to the artwork.
"Thank you so much. It means so much to me to be awarded by my peers," Hamilton said, accepting his award. It was his second consecutive year winning an artists' choice award.
While competition-based, many of the artists said the Plein Air Easton event is a week of creativity and camaraderie.
"It's always good energy," Agrawal said.

title: Paint-by-numbers project brings Easton community together
author: BROOKE ENSMINGER
content:
Paint-by-numbers project brings Easton community together

 July 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BROOKE ENSMINGER | Section: Local News 
 
 525
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Downtown Easton visitors paused Friday to help paint a community backdrop at Plein Air Easton.Outside the Tidewater Inn and the Avalon Theatre, a large paint-by-number canvas united community members to participate in Easton's Plein Air event. This is the first time Plein Air Easton has had a community paint event.
The artist behind the creation and organizer of the event is Maggii Sarfarty. A Plein Air Easton alumnus and art director of the Factory Arts Project, Sarfarty partnered with the Avalon Foundation to bring community members together to paint, regardless of skill level.
"Plein Air Easton has just always been about coming and seeing competition artists and other art in our community, but I think the Avalon really wanted to reach out and find something that everybody could participate in," Sarfaty said.
The painting for the project was "Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose" by American artist John Singer Sargent. Sarfaty said the original Plein Air piece was painted in a garden in Worcestershire, England, in 1885.
The painting was divided into three panels that would later combine to form a single backdrop. Participants grabbed paint cups labeled with numbers and followed the design.
The project was created in collaboration with the Factory, a nonprofit performing arts organization in Easton. The finished product served as the backdrop for the Factory's radio show, which began about 30 minutes after the community paint project was finished.
The paint-by-numbers design allowed people of all skill levels and ages to contribute. Both young children and older adults picked up brushes and brought the painting to life.
Sue McWilliams, of Easton, spent the event with her young niece, Sutton Martin, who was visiting. McWilliams said the event was a great opportunity for kids, and Sutton agreed. It was Sutton's first time painting with a large group.
"Everybody helps, and you get to talk a lot, and it's just harmony," Sutton said.
A two-hour event, people came and went, and most of the painting was completed by the end of the first hour. Sarfarty estimated about 70 community members stopped by to paint.
"I love getting creative, but I never like to start things from scratch," Sarah Kilmon, of Easton, said. "So, having a project that is made to help people get creative together is so much fun."
Kilmon, who has modeled and acted in prior years at Plein Air Easton, decided to have a more relaxing experience this year. She said painting alongside the community was peaceful, and the radio show backdrop "is totally the Factory's vibe."
Jessica Bellis, director of finance and operations at the Avalon, led an applause for Sarfarty at the end of the event.
"This is a totally wild and weird idea that we just executed on," Bellis told the crowd. "This paint-by-numbers masterpiece that Maggii made is awe-inspiring."
The finished painting hung behind the performers during the radio show. Instead of seeing it close up, split into sections and flat on a table, the three boards came together on stage to reveal the intricate piece the community had helped create.
With the first-ever community paint event over, there are still plenty of opportunities for community members to participate in the Plein Air Easton festivities. The annual event ends Sunday.

title: Adkins Arboretum plans to add Woodhenge
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Adkins Arboretum plans to add Woodhenge

 July 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 493
 Words 

 Read News Document

 RIDGLEY — Vicco Von Voss is working with Adkins Arboretum to erect "Woodhedge."A local woodworker and artist, Voss said the idea of a Woodhenge, an art installation modeled after Scotland's famous Stonehenge, came from the emotions of his work.
"I'm a woodworker, and part of what we do is we salvage local trees that have been diseased or fallen," Voss said. "We have a mill here, and we cut these trees open. I've noticed that when my sawyer, he's cutting a tree, and the tree is really beautiful, everybody feels really good. Then when we get to a tree where the tree is kind of diseased and rotten, the mood kind of changes.
"I said to my sawyer, I said, 'Isn't that interesting when you have a tree that is all good and healthy and beautiful, your energy is good and positive. When you get a tree that's all diseased and rotten inside, you might be blaming it on something.' Isn't it interesting that you're exposing the energy of the tree and you're really receiving what is happening within the tree."
Voss hopes Woodhenge will make visitors think and feel emotions and energy from the tree.
According to Abby Lorenz, director of public engagement for Adkins Arboretum, conversations with Voss went on a for long time, but the energy shifted on the project after receiving a grant in July.
"More recently the energy and movement around this project is through a Public Arts Planning Grant with Maryland State Arts Council," Lorenz said. "He received a grant funding to focus on the planning of the installation, so right now we have created a survey for people to give feedback on what they think on the project. So I think that's a big part of what we're looking for because this is not just art for artists, it's public art."
The next step for Woodhenge is applying for a second grant for $30,000 in the fall to begin construction, but according to Voss, they will need to do some fundraising to complete the $75,000 project.
Lorenz said the focus right now is informing the community about the project and getting their thoughts and ideas.
"We just recently had a community meeting where we invited people that had knowledge of Stonehenge and cultural landscapes to come together and give their feedback and ideas, and Vico shared his plan and intention of really opening one tree so that you feel like you're inside of one tree," Lorenz said.
At the feedback meeting, residents shared on how they felt visiting Stonehenge and how that same feeling and cultural significance can be conveyed in a tree landscape.
"I think there's excitement, there's intrigue and in a way that people are interested in really what does it mean," Lorenz said.
While there is no set timeline for the project, Lorenz and Voss believe Woodhenge will be built and open to the public in 2026 or 2027.
Woodhenge would sit on Nancy's Meadow on the north side of the Adkins Arboretum property.

title: Listen to the rhythm at the Chestertown Farmers Market
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Listen to the rhythm at the Chestertown Farmers Market

 July 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Life 
 
 461
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTEROWN — Each Saturday morning at the Chestertown Farmers Market on High Street, customers can find a refreshing variety of items from produce to baked goodies and handwoven crafts.Last weekend, among quilters, painters and wood carvers, author Marianne Laino Sade was selling her children's books, "TAPUM" and her latest "TA DA".
"TA DA" is especially welcome as baby's first book, recommended for ages 0-4 and their caregivers. "Children need their parents, grandparents, caregivers and guardians to read to them. It is so important for fundamental growth," Sade said.
So the books need to be interesting to the babies and those reading to them. And they certainly are.
Sade's offerings Saturday were each signed by the author. The artwork in her book is created in a collage style, using cut outs and concepts gleaned from her experiences as an English major and librarian across Maryland, New York and Pennsylvania.
Her first book published in 2022, "TAPUM" features a colorful drum on the cover and each element within the drum: the sun, the sea, a lion, are all pages in the book.
Done in that unique collage style, using patterns and dark and light contrasts, there is great attention to detail on each page.
You can hear the song playing along as you read.
"TAPUM!" is the sound of the drum in the world all around. Can you hear its rhythm? "TaPUM, Tapum, TaPUM!"," the back panel reads.
Sade said "TAPUM" came to her while awaiting a bus in New York in the 80's and just hearing that sound repeated. She was again inspired from attending a drum event featuring many world drummers including Babatunde Olatunji, hailed as the father of African drumming in the United States.
"TA DA" came about a little differently. Sade combined animals and music, visualizing frogs, dogs, birds and other colorful critters wanting to be a music band. With a nod to the Chester River Packet, the animal band perform at the end of High Street by the water.
The book talks about the universal appeal of music: "TA DA" celebrates the joy of making music together" and is a companion book to "TAPUM" following a musical theme.
Both books have thick, durable board pages and were appealing to families passing through the market such as Joseph and Amanda Carchi and their baby daughter Marie and son Owen. Little Marie smiled widely pointing at the pictures while Joseph read to her.
"These are very cool," Amanda noted.
So far, "TA DA" is doing well in sales too, selling at least 100 out of the 500 they ordered, Sade's husband Chris pointed out.
And perhaps as many authors tend to do, she is toying with a trilogy.
Sade said she has been reflecting about her childhood but would say nothing further, not wanting to spoil the big surprise.
Check out her books at msadeart.com.

title: Plein Air Easton inducts 2nd Hall of Fame class
author: Konner Metz
content:
Plein Air Easton inducts 2nd Hall of Fame class

 July 18, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 593
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — As Plein Air Easton wraps up its 21st year, the largest juried outdoor painting competition in the country is adding to its Hall of Fame roster.This year, Plein Air Easton inducted eight new members to its Hall of Fame, which began in 2024 with 11 inductees. This year's class is made up of Mary and Hall Kellogg, Hali and Scott Asplundh, David Grafton, Diane Dubois Mullaly, the Troika Gallery and the Working Artists Forum.
All inductees were nominated and then selected by a five-person committee.
Some are artists, while others are dedicated supporters of the plein air event over the years. But all of them have been integral to the competition's growth, said Avalon Foundation Executive Director Al Bond.
On Monday, Tilghman Island residents Mary and Hall Kellogg were recognized at the Paint Tilghman exhibit, a venture they helped begin over a decade ago.
Bond told the crowd that the Kelloggs — also the founders of the Tilghman Watermen's Museum — are to thank for the Paint Tilghman tradition.
"They saw the potential for plein air painting to tell those stories to new audiences," Bond said. "Thanks to them, an entire island has become a part of Plein Air Easton's history."
"Their generosity, their warmth, their belief in the value of preservation have left a lasting legacy for Plein Air Easton," he added.
Bond discussed the impacts of the other Hall of Famers in an interview Friday.
The Alspundhs, regular patrons of the festival's art every year, were some of the first people to make Plein Air Easton a fun, family tradition, Bond said. Thanks to Hali and Scott, he said, families and groups of friends began to see Plein Air Easton as a social outing for those that love art.
"The Asplundhs sort of showed the way," Bond said.
Grafton and Mullaly were two artists inducted into the Hall of Fame this year. Both have been involved since the jump, Bond noted.
Grafton died before the pandemic, but his impact on the festival has been lasting.
"David was a very well-known artist, so I think that his early involvement, it lent some legitimacy to what was a brand new thing at the time," Bond said.
Meanwhile, the executive director said that Mullaly was one of the original organizers of quick draw, a painting competition open to the public every year during the festival. Bond called Mullaly a "very accomplished artist."
Located on South Harrison Street, the Troika Gallery has been around for nearly three decades. Leaders at the art gallery helped get Plein Air Easton off its feet 21 years ago.
"They've been there the whole time in a very roll-up-your-sleeves and solve-the-problem kind of way," Bond said.
Bond credits the involvement of local artwork to the Working Artists Forum, an Easton-based nonprofit group of artists. The forum hosts a Local Color exhibit during Plein Air Easton, showcasing and selling art from Delmarva-based artists.
On Monday in Tilghman Island, Mary Kellogg thanked the Avalon Foundation and Bond for the recognition, but was quick to point out the volunteers that have made Plein Air Easton's 21 years possible.
"This has been a huge, huge honor. It's not just us," she said. "It's all those people out there, many of them wearing green aprons. The volunteers at the museum who are tireless workers on weekends and throughout the year."
Kellogg shouted out the Avalon Foundation's leadership, including Bond, chief financial and operating officer Jess Bellis, art director Suzy Moore and Plein Air Easton coordinator Marie Nuthall.
"They should have their own Hall of Fame," Kellogg said.
Plein Air Easton continues through Sunday. For a schedule of events and more information, visit pleinaireaston.com.

title: Kent County finds music that moves them at fair
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Kent County finds music that moves them at fair

 July 22, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: Headlines 
 
 504
 Words 

 Read News Document

 TOLCHESTER — Wednesday night, at the Kent County Fair, beneath the stars, local line dancing instructor Minnie Maloney guided folks on how to shift their weight, stepping to the beat to country, rock and hip-hop songs.After a sweltering afternoon judging chickens, canines and hogs, from 7 to 9 p.m., at the main pavilion, 4-H'ers let their hair down to line dance, something Maloney has been doing for over 20 years.
Everyone had something to dance to from music like "Barsong" by Shaboozey, "I was on a Boat" by Old Dominion, "Boots on the Ground" by 803Fresh, and "Jacked Up" by Colt Ford.
"It was an honor to bring some line dancing joy to the Kent County Fair," she said. "Even through the heat and sweat there were smiles and comments about how much fun it was."
At age 40, with fiery red hair and cowboy boots, she ain't stopping any time soon.
"I'm back dancing, it feels great," she said, recently recovering from plantar fasciitis, an inflammation along the bottom of the foot resulting in heel pain.
Yoga and proper stretching is getting her back to full strength, teaching Monterrey turns, (like 180 dance turns) rock steps and rock forwards.
Whether at the 4-H fair, teaching at the local VFW, or conducting classes in private parties, she loves seeing people having fun, memorizing the routines and producing all the positive results from line dancing.
For Maloney it is more than a hobby, it is a life choice that affects her on many levels and shares that joy she found early in life.
At age 12, she fondly remembers dancing with her father at the VFW in Fairlee learning her first line dance: "Baby Likes to Rock It" by the Tractors. The steps just made sense to her, clicking, connecting to her skill when dancing with her friends making up their own routines.
Past her teen years and 20s, dancing was not only fun but therapy for her. Maloney struggles with anxiety and depression, she acknowledges, and there is no better healing than scooting and scuttling past that.
"Dancing forces you to stay in the moment. You forget everything going on in your life."
While bartending for extra money at the American Legion in 2015, there was a push to draw more people. Maloney told them about her line dancing, and they gave her a shot instructing once a week, bringing joy to patrons.
Then she participated as a line dance instructor in the Wild Wild West fundraiser event for St. Martin's Ministry to help generate funds for those battling poverty.
Since then she has been teaching Mondays at the YMCA in Centreville under "Dancingontheshore," at the VFW, as well as private lessons, going off what she has seen from other instructors.
"It's a community builder. We're right beside you helping you. There is no race, age, no discrimination. We're here together."
She watches her students gain self esteem and confidence, relaxing and having fun.
"Some people come in having never danced in their life. They can be real self conscious at first, but I get them to lighten up."

title: Hip-Hop meets High Street
author: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com
content:
Hip-Hop meets High Street

 July 23, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WILL BONTRAGER wbontrager@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 764
 Words 

 Read News Document

 When headed down High Street in Chestertown toward the water, you may notice the building near Dixon Drive has gotten a little more colorful.Across the field, the side of 800 High Street is covered in graffiti-style art — checkered patterns, winding vines, sun rays and messages such as "Labor of Love," alongside odes to the former Dixon Valve building and Vita Foods.
These were two former businesses located on the property — historic places with plenty of stories still to tell and a new generation beginning to learn about them.
The art is part of a two-week summer course called the Hip Hop Time Capsule. High school students from Cecil, Queen Anne's and Kent counties, along with Washington College student interns, were taught local history while exercising creativity in a way that merges both.
The project is spearheaded by Washington College's Starr Center for the Study of the American Experience, Chesapeake Heartland: An African American Humanities Project, and the Kohl Gallery, in partnership with Minary's Dream Alliance.
Organizers selected and supervised the students.
For two weeks, they worked with musicians, college professors and museum professionals to research, explore, document and interpret the rich history of African American music in Kent County.
In past years, students composed original tracks using digitized audio clips to build beats. They wrote lyrics or performed spoken word pieces and layered them over music, producing original songs complete with cover art.
Pat Nugent, director of civic engagement at Washington College, has led the innovative class for the past five years.
And innovation is the name of the game. Since an innovation plant is being established at 800 High Street, organizers moved the Hip Hop Time Capsule program into the building — a natural fit, said Darius Johnson, director of the Starr Center's Chesapeake Heartland Project.
"We really wanted the students to feel like they have a stake in what we're doing here," Johnson said. "So having it at the innovation plant just made sense. And the music is a great hook."
"Our student interns have come together to learn a number of skills and trades, to reflect on our community's past and future, and to make their mark on this evolving property at the heart of Chestertown," Nugent said.
"The tables, benches, murals, posters and music they designed and brought into being have enriched the site and will ensure the innovation plant becomes a vibrant crossroads for both campus and community."
Organizers pared down the original pool of 60 students to just under 40. Selected participants received an introduction to hip hop, explored local art, learned about the historic uptown area and studied the histories of Vita Foods and Dixon Valve.
Based on survey responses, students were assigned to one of four tracks: music, murals, metalwork or screen printing, Johnson said.
They spent a two-hour workshop with an instructor from their chosen track. For example, Eastern Shore native Shelton Hawkins oversaw the murals and shared his experience beautifying basketball courts — a skill that has taken him across the globe, including painting the Golden State Warriors court.
In each workshop, students learned about the origins of hip hop, explored how to make their mark and practiced self-expression using modern technologies, Johnson added.
They also had access to 5,600 digitized materials of Black history — including photo albums, home movies, oral histories, interviews and documents dating back as early as the 1700s.
The class began July 14 and concluded Friday, July 25, when close to 100 children from the Horizons of Kent and Queen Anne's program attended a special event, broadening the program's reach and impact.
Participants were also paid for their involvement: high school students received $1,200 each and the 11 college interns received $1,422.
Johnson said the students gained confidence from the experience.
"It has been a really beautiful process," he said. "Students built trust, overcame fears, developed employable skills and analyzed their community with critical eyes."
For those who voiced concerns about the art on the building in historic Chestertown, Johnson offered reassurance.
The artwork is only temporary.
It served as a way for interns to express creativity and passion, engage in community outreach and strengthen local ties.
"We know that the foundation of a successful innovation plant has to be built on relationships and be responsive to community interests," said Sara Clarke-De Reza, chair of the education department at Washington College. "Programs like Hip Hop Time Capsule help us imagine how this space might be best developed to meet the needs of the next generation of makers, innovators and entrepreneurs."
The program encourages students to become both civic leaders and innovative designers.
Follow along with the continuing work of the innovation plant on Instagram: @wc_innovation_plant. Learn more about Chesapeake Heartland at chesapeakeheartland.org.
