title: Country Cooking: Memories of crabbing and clamming
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Memories of crabbing and clamming

 July 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking | Section: News 
 
 1366
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Pulling away from the local seafood store yesterday with a basket of fresh caught and fresh steamed crabs surely brings back memories of the 1950s and 1960s.Mom would set aside the designated weekday for crabbing. The other chores would be done. Mom would back the pickup out, and we would load the supplies, which included the baskets with inner tubes attached to help the baskets to float, the chicken necks for bait, the heavy string to tie the hook and sinker to, crab nets, towels, a picnic basket with sandwiches and a big jug of water with chunks of ice inside.
We loaded up and rode in the back of the truck so we could hoot and holler at our friends as we rode through town. Our friends would holler, "Take me" as we passed because they knew the fun we would have along with the work involved.
Our destination would be one of two country landings with docks for crabbing and areas for swimming. The first one was Mumford's Landing off St. Martin's Neck Road (now a development off the Route 90 bridge outside of Ocean City) and the second one was a little dock called Little Georgetown, just down the road from our farm on the Delaware side.
Upon arriving at the landing, Mom picked a spot to tie our strings on the dock poles. We took the lines and hung the nuts, bolts and sinkers on the bottom so the weight held the line down. Then we tied on the bait.
You had a choice — go swimming now or later, but you had to move down a good distance to stay away from the baited lines. Mom would get two baskets ready, grab a crab net and walk along the shoreline and crab. Someone stayed back with another net and basket to gradually pull up the lines, placing the net under the line to catch the falling crabs. Sitting on the dock would be one- or two-bushel baskets with lids to place the freshly caught crabs in.
If it was a slow catching day, the bushel basket would be set at the shoreline to partially filled with water to keep the crabs alive. Meanwhile, back on the farm, whoever stayed behind was pulling out one of the largest iron pots, used for winter hog killing and summer beet cooking. They placed stick-seasoned pieces of wood to start the fire to steam the crabs.
Upon arriving at home, the still kicking crabs were unloaded, the fire started and the Old Bay seasoning was put in. Once the crabs were bright orange/red in color, the fire was pulled away and the crabs pulled and placed on the picnic tables to be picked.
Of course, we ate the delicious meat until we were full, and then we put it in containers to be carried to the kitchen to be made into dishes such as crab cakes, crab soup and much more.
So let's explore what to make with our crabmeat.
CRAB CAKES
1 large egg, 1/4 cup mayonnaise, 1 tbsp chopped fresh parsley (or 2 tsps dried), 2 tsps Dijon mustard, 2 tsps Worcestershire sauce, 1 tsp Old Bay or J.O seasoning, 1 tsp fresh lemon juice (plus more for serving), 1/8 tsp salt, 1 lb fresh lump crab meat, 2/3 cup saltine cracker crumbs (about 17 two-inch crackers).
Whisk the egg, mayonnaise, parsley, Dijon mustard, Worcestershire sauce, Old Bay, lemon juice and salt together in a large bowl. Place the crab meat on top, followed by the cracker crumbs. With a silicone spatula or large spoon, very gently and carefully fold together. You don't want to break up that crab meat. Cover tightly and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 1 day. Preheat oven to 450 degrees. Generously grease a rimmed baking sheet with butter or nonstick spray, or line with parchment paper or a silicone baking mat. Using a 1/2 cup measuring cup, portion the crab cake mixture into 6 mounds on the baking sheet. Don't flatten. Use your hands or a spoon to compact each individual mound so there aren't any lumps sticking out or falling apart. Bake for 12–14 minutes or until lightly browned around the edges and on top. Drizzle each with fresh lemon juice and serve warm. Cover leftover crab cakes tightly and refrigerate for up to 5 days or freeze for up to 3 months.
MARYLAND CRAB SOUP
1 28-oz can whole tomatoes (cut into small pieces), 3 cups water, 2 cups beef broth, 1 cup frozen lima beans, 1 cup frozen baby carrots, 1 cup frozen yellow sweet corn, 2 tbsps chopped onions, 1 tbsp Old Bay or JO seasoning, 1 lb lump crabmeat.
Place all ingredients, except crabmeat, in 4-quart saucepan, Bring to boil on medium heat. Reduce heat to low; cover and simmer for 5 minutes. Stir in crabmeat; cover and simmer for 10 minutes.
CLAMS WITH GARLIC SAUCE
Clamming was also something we enjoyed doing. This meant a trip out into the water knee to waist deep with the clam rakes and innertubes. While we were there crabbing at the Isle of Wight Bay, my brothers would walk the edge of the marsh back towards Ocean City and clam near the rocks. It had to be low tide to get the best clams. Otherwise we'd buy them from the waterman who'd clam near Assateague.
3 dozen clams (scrubbed), ½ cup cornmeal, 1 tbsp salt, ¼ cup olive oil, 1 small onion (minced), 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 small dried red chili, 2 bay leaves, ¼ tsp hot paprika, pepper.
In bowl, cover the clams and cornmeal with water; add the salt and soak 45 minutes; drain and rinse. Heat the oil in a large non-reactive skillet. Add the onion; cook until soft. Add the clams, lemon juice, chili, bay leaves, paprika and pepper. Cover and cook over high heat, stirring constantly, removing the clams as they open. Garlic Sauce:4 garlic cloves minced,¼ cup parsley minced,½ cup fish stock or ¼ cup bottled clam juice diluted with ¼ cup water, In blender, puree garlic with 5 tbsps of the parsley, add the fish stock and garlic mixture to a skillet; cook until sauce is slightly thickened. Divide the clams among four soup plates. Spoon the garlic sauce on top and garnish with remaining parsley.
CLAMS LINGUINE
Kosher salt, 1 lb linguine, 6 tbsps extra-virgin olive oil, ½ cup finely chopped shallots, 6 cloves garlic (coarsely chopped), ½ tsp red pepper flakes, 2 lbs Littleneck clams (scrubbed), ¼ cup plus 2 tbsps fresh flat-leaf parsley (finely chopped), 3 tbsps unsalted butter, 1 tsp lemon zest, 1 tbsp lemon juice.
In large pot over high heat, bring 4 quarts of water and 2 tbspss of kosher salt to a boil. Add the linguine and cook according to the package directions until just shy of al dente (the pasta should still be firm to the bite since it will cook another minute or two in the sauce). Drain in a colander (do not rinse), reserving ½ cup of the cooking water for the sauce. Meanwhile, in a very large sauté pan over medium-high heat, heat the olive oil until hot but not smoking. Add the shallots and garlic and sauté until just golden, about 30 seconds. Add the wine, red pepper flakes, ¾ tsp kosher salt, clams, and ¼ cup of the parsley; bring to a simmer and cook, covered, until the clams open, 6 to 8 minutes. Discard any unopened clams. Add the pasta to the sauté pan with the clams. (If you don't have room for everything in one pan, transfer the clams to a plate and cover to keep warm. When ready to serve, add them back to the pasta on a serving platter). Increase the heat to medium and cook the linguini with the clams, tossing occasionally, until the pasta absorbs most of the sauce and is just tender, 1 to 2 minutes. If necessary, add some of reserved cooking water to keep moist. Remove the pan from the heat. Add the butter, lemon zest, lemon juice, and the remaining 2 tbsps of parsley; toss to coat. Taste and adjust the seasoning with more salt, lemon zest and/or lemon juice, if necessary. Transfer to a serving dish or bowls and serve.

title: 'Dorchester Dreams' provides fresh role models
author: Lily Tierney
content:
'Dorchester Dreams' provides fresh role models

 July 29, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Dorchester 
 
 383
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Dorchester County Council members giggled and pointed at the cartoon depictions of themselves as they passed around the first iteration of the "Dorchester Dreams" children's book.The children's book depicts comic-like versions of residents and tells the story of the Barzini Family Music Group coming to Dorchester and joining the community.
The Barzini Family Music Group was created in 2023 and moved to the Eastern Shore from the DMV area last year. Founder and CEO, Derrick "AB" Taylor said the group has plans to create a book series along with their music projects to provide children in the community with contemporary, relatable role models.
"I've always been a big advocate of education. And, like I said, everybody in the Barzini Family are all under 32," Taylor said.
Though the members of the music group are young, they are determined to make a lasting impact on the Eastern Shore. Taylor, originally from Philadelphia, said he sees the Shore as the next premier music destination and the children are paving the way.
"The children kind of dictate the market in a way," said Taylor.
For Taylor, seeing the music industry as a well rounded machine rather than a single engine is critical. He puts an emphasis on alternative career paths within the industry, highlighting that success can be achieved through education in fields such as finance, writing, and business rather than solely through traditional routes.
The book gets its name from a song written by one of the music group's young members. Jayla Elise wrote "Dorchester Dreams," which became the official song of Dorchester County in June.
In the team's book series, they also plan to have one on "The Heart of Maryland," which ties into the team's efforts to accomplish a state song.
Elise will be performing "The Heart of Maryland" at minor league baseball games across the state beginning on August 8, 22 and 28.
The Barzini Family team is planning to read their children's books at the Girls and Boys Club in Cambridge. They have even purchased a blue crab and muskrat costume for the occasion.
"It's kind of like the Batman effect. We don't really have superpowers, but our power is that we keep going," said Taylor. "I wanted them to see themselves as like, 'I probably don't think I can do it, but at least I can try.'"

title: Find your personal landmarks at the library
author: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library
content:
Find your personal landmarks at the library

 August 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: BILL PEAK Talbot County Free Library | Section: Life 
 
 1027
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Do they still teach "the classics" these days? They certainly did in my time. And they were presented as faits accomplis, no questions asked."These are the classics, you will read and remember them: 'Tess of the D'Urbervilles,' 'Moby Dick,' 'A Tale of Two Cities,' 'Huckleberry Finn,' 'Wuthering Heights,' 'The Scarlet Letter.'" — the titles apparently handed down from on high.
Occasionally a teacher would pitch "1984" or "The Grapes of Wrath" into the mix, as if to prove he or she had indeed survived into the 20th century, but for the most part, classical literature seemed to have thrived in the 19th century and promptly expired at its conclusion.
But nothing is permanent in life, not even "the classics," and from what little I know of current pedagogical fashion, most of the titles listed above probably figure in few syllabi these days (though I pray "The Grapes of Wrath" and "1984" still make the cut). Which is probably for the best.
I'm sure the advent of "World Literature" has introduced any number of worthy novels to the canon that my little mid-20th century Kentucky school would never have heard of.
I will probably miss out on most of these new discoveries. I just don't have the time or the inclination anymore to keep up with literature's latest wunderkind. Which is not to say I don't have my own personal list of classics, works that have opened my eyes not just to new ways of seeing, but, just as important, to the way life is actually lived.
Graham Swift won the Man Booker Prize in 1996 for "Last Orders," but to my way of thinking, "Wish You Were Here" and "Waterland," are his best books. These past few weeks, my wife recovering from surgery, I've found myself rereading "Wish You Were Here." It is, in my opinion, a powerful, disquieting "classic."
The story is told in the third-person singular, primarily from the point of view of its main character, Jack Luxton.
The book opens with Jack sitting upstairs in his bedroom, awaiting the return of his wife Ellie. It is raining hard, a scattershot drumbeat on roof and windows. As Jack waits, he recalls important passages from his life. From time to time, he glances at the shotgun lying on the bed beside him.
Jack was raised in southwest England, on a farm that generations of Luxtons had called home. It was all he knew. There were his father and mother, his little brother Tom, and the dairy cows they milked twice daily. Life was simple, local. Everything had its time and place. Life had always been like this. Life, so far as he was concerned, would always be like this.
But then Jack's mother died, and Jack had to become a sort of mother to his little brother, whom he loved — though love was a word no longer spoken in that now motherless house.
But Jack, a large man, unsure of himself, a bit of a fumbler, still felt love, and some of it he felt for the little girl growing up on the farm next door, Ellie. And Ellie returned that love. In their teens, they began to meet secretly whenever Ellie's father was away.
I have to admit, I have only a vague memory of the mad cow disease that struck England's beef and dairy industries in 1996. I read about the outbreak in the papers, felt, I'm sure, a passing sympathy for the farmers affected, and then moved on. We learn of catastrophes every day now; spending too much time on each would leave us paralyzed.
But when the catastrophe strikes you … Well, that's another story altogether. And that's what happens to Jack.
Jack, his father and his little brother must watch as their livelihood, the cows they have known and cared for all their lives, cows that to all outward appearances remain perfectly healthy, are rounded up by government edict and "culled," their carcasses set alight.
First his mother dies — his mother who held the family together, his mother who was the keeper of the family history and traditions — and then the cows that gave that history, those traditions, their meaning, are destroyed in a single seemingly senseless act of butchery. Well, it would take something out of you.
And, as it turns out, those deaths are just the first in a series of deaths Jack must face and try to bear. We all have our tragedies to contend with, no one escapes life unscarred, but for most of us, if we're lucky, providence punctuates the bad times with long spells of the good. But that is not true for everyone.
And as we learn of the multiple sorrows and paltry joys of Jack Luxton's life, that shotgun remains on the bed beside him.
Reading back over this column, reading the previous line, I find myself wondering why anyone would want to read this book. Why do I want to read, and reread, this book?
Would it help if I told you Swift's writing is masterful? Would it help if I told you Jack and Ellie's relationship — with all its human flaws and human tenderness — is as true to life as any I have ever read?
What do we want from classics? What makes a classic a classic? Do we want fairy tales, pie in the sky, or do we want life as it is actually lived, life as we have lived it?
I don't know. I'm not sure. Certainly there are times when I want escape, when I want Jack Reacher to step into a scene and save the day; but when it comes down to real life, I find Jack Luxton's clumsiness and uncertainty, his feelings of incompetence, closer to my own experience of life as it must be suffered — and as it must be enjoyed — every day.
So let's leave it at that, like Jack Luxton, I'm uncertain why Swift's novel moves me so. All I know for sure is that reading "Wish You Were Here" always gives me, oddly enough, a sense of strength, the feeling that, if I have fears and loves in common with a man as basically good as Jack Luxton, then maybe there's hope for me yet.

title: 'Keeping history alive': Eastern Shore threshing and steam show marks 65 years
author: Konner Metz
content:
'Keeping history alive': Eastern Shore threshing and steam show marks 65 years

 August 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Caroline 
 
 481
 Words 

 Read News Document

 FEDERALSBURG — In 1961, Jim Layton and some neighbors gathered off of Route 313 to thresh wheat using one steam engine. That modest demonstration of farm work quickly gained popularity. It's taken a life of its own for the last 65 years.The Eastern Shore Threshermen & Collectors Association hosted the 65th annual Wheat Threshing, Steam & Gas Engine Show over the weekend, drawing hundreds to the showgrounds outside Federalsburg.
Trish Layton Todd, Jim Layton's daughter and the association's president, reflected on the original gathering in 1961. Farming technology has modernized the process in the decades since, but every year, the Threshermen Association puts on the threshing show for locals and visitors.
"Keeping history alive," Layton Todd said of the event's purpose. "We try to do it with working demonstrations, to show the wheat threshing. Now we have the modern combine. Before you had that, it was labor-intensive work because you had to do a lot of it by hand. And then of course the threshing, you had threshing days, where that's all you did.
" ... (We are) hoping to teach people about it because it's good to know where you come from."
Classic steam engines, tractors and other farm equipment were on display Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Misty conditions halted the wheat threshing demonstrations Friday, but not the rest of the weekend.
Attendees enjoyed live music, food, a flea market, lawn and tractor games and more. Layton Todd pointed out how vendors and tent operators were more than happy to show event-goers the history of different traditional techniques, such as blacksmithing.
"Most of the people, if they're here and they have something they're exhibiting and showing, they like for you to show interest and stop and talk," she said.
Mark Williams, a blacksmith from Snow Hill, has been coming to the steam show since the mid-1990s. He first did it as a favor to a friend, but it's since become tradition.
As he finished up his blacksmithing on Friday and packed up, Williams said some of his creations take hours or days.
"Things that are a challenge for me to design and make are the ones I like the most," Williams said.
"I make hearts out of horseshoes," he added.
Elsewhere, some attendees took to miniature tractors to race in a friendly competition.
Each day, the association hosted a parade in the evening, showcasing classic steam engines from around the country, as well as tractors and other farm equipment. Many kids and teenagers rode on the tractors during the parade.
Layton Todd said a key aspect of the event is getting the youth involved and understanding the history and evolution of farming.
She noted that the Eastern Shore Thresherman & Collectors Association is 100% volunteer-based. The group has forged ahead to organize the annual show — this year's shirts for volunteers proclaimed, "65 years ... and still steaming."
The 66th annual Wheat Threshing, Steam & Gas Engine Show is slated for Aug. 7-9, 2026.

title: 'Made with love': Delaware film festival will feature 58 short films
author: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com
content:
'Made with love': Delaware film festival will feature 58 short films

 August 7, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Josh Shannon jshannon@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 564
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The Newark Independent Film Festival is returning for its second year next week.The Delaware event is set for Aug. 14, 15 and 16 at Chapel Street Players on Creek View Road.
"We're offering audiences something completely different, something that was made with love," organizer Kazy Tauginas said. "Regardless of genre, the filmmakers that made these films, they put their souls into them, and you can feel it on the screen. I think that people will be very pleasantly surprised at the quality of the films that they're going to be watching."
The festival will feature 58 short films spanning many genres, including horror, drama, comedy, documentaries and art-house films. Filmmakers are coming from all over the United States and from as far away as Germany.
"Just hearing the stories and what people went through just to tell something that they felt was really important to them at that time, that separates us from what studio films are all made for," Tauginas said. "They're all profit-driven. Indies are a lot of times just driven by the heart."
There are also a number of films that were shot right here in Delaware, including "Return to Hockessin No. 107C," which is about the history of the Hockessin Colored School, and "Unseen American Dream," a documentary about a blind couple from Wilmington raising sighted children.
"Delaware locals have their own category at my festival," Tauginas said. "And then, of course, we have filmmakers from Los Angeles and New York and everywhere in between."
Tauginas is an actor, director and writer who has written and starred in more than 20 independent films. His acting career also has included guest spots in major television shows, and he has appeared in several movies, including "The Equalizer 2," starring Denzel Washington.
He lives in Newark and also works as a real estate agent and serves on the Newark Planning Commission.
The film festival will include the premier of the feature film "Mirror Life," which Tauginas wrote, directed and starred in. The movie is about a woman who's searching for her cousin who disappeared after entering an illegal human clinical trial.
Tauginas said that major film studios are moving more and more of their productions overseas, leading to fewer opportunities for actors here. That's part of what inspired him to start the film festival, to provide an opportunity to showcase more independent films.
"Filmmakers are going to be able to see their film on screen, in front of an audience, on the big screen with a dynamic sound system in a proper venue, so that it can get the attention that it deserves," he said. "I think it's a really important thing, especially for independent artists."
He added that he hopes the festival is an economic boost for Newark as the filmmakers from out of town arrive in Newark, stay at the Hyatt Place hotel on Main Street and patronize local restaurants and shops.
Tauginas, who used to own the Korner Diner on Main Street, said he knows that the summer is a slow time for Newark businesses. With a location right off Interstate 95 and a walkable downtown, Newark is a great place for the festival, he said.
"I can't think of a better place that you would want a film festival," he said.
The Newark Independent Film Festival will show 58 films in seven blocks spread over three days. Tickets for each block are $15. For more information and to buy tickets, visit newarkindependentfilmfestival.com.

author: Lily Tierney

 CAMBRIDGE — The walls of the Harriet Tubman Freedom Center look a bit different these days.Currently, they are covered by a "one of a kind" art exhibit depicting Tubman in various artistic mediums through the lens of 40 artists from all over the globe.
"Harriet: A Taste of Freedom" was curated by Maryland-based artist Larry Poncho Brown and will be featured at the center through Sept. 30. The exhibit is free and open to the public.
"It gives a different twist here in Dorchester County with Harriet Tubman and people to engage in a modern view in some type of atmosphere with art expression," Harriet Tubman Freedom Center President Alex Green said. "It's a really cool exhibit."
The walls emphasize Tubman's strength through her serious and intentional facial expressions, show her softness through depictions of her as a child, and allow her humanity by representing her in such a multifaceted way.
For Green, inspiring people to learn and understand history, particularly Tubman's character of unselfishness and community support, and adopt community-minded values can help prevent communities from repeating past wrongs. It is particularly important for the younger generations, which is why the center provides youth programming, Green said.
"We want to understand how history pretty much played out, with information, not partisanship. We just want to understand," Green said.
Green said the exhibit is a great opportunity to inspire youth to learn the history of Tubman and Dorchester County.
"The younger generation can carry the torch further with understanding. The lack of it is going to cause us to repeat the things that have happened," Green said. "So I think it's very important that children get a chance to engage. Get Harriet introduced, let them make a decision on how they want to process it," he said.
There is an emphasis that everyone is welcome at the freedom center, as long as they believe freedom is the ultimate goal. That is why the door says, "Turn into freedom," Green said.
"In here, we want you to feel free with your opinions as long as it's in the context of freedom," Green said.
The different styles of the gorgeous depictions of Tubman are true representations of freedom. Green said it was difficult for some of the artists to give them away because they've grown so attached.
The Harriet Tubman Freedom Center is located at 3030 Center Drive in Cambridge, and "Harriet: A Taste of Freedom" is open from Tuesday to Friday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. and Saturday from 9 a.m to 3 p.m. It will run until Sept. 30, with the potential of the exhibit being extended through Dec.
"That way we give people more of a chance to be engaged with it, because you come out, look, walk around, you can leave a donation, or you don't have to. You can sign your name, or you don't have to. It's not a requirement. It's not like $5 at the door. But you just can come and take in this amazing exhibit," Green said.

title: 'Brings back memories': Local artists take stab at famous art
author: Konner Metz
content:
'Brings back memories': Local artists take stab at famous art

 August 9, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 558
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Inside the Troika Gallery, an exhibit gives local artists the chance to display their own takes on some of the most well-renowned pieces of art.Twenty-two works make up the "Fabulous Forgeries," an annual tradition where artists choose a historic work to model on their own canvases.
The artists of the original works must be dead for at least 100 years, and the recreations have to be two inches smaller or larger to avoid copyright issues, said Troika Gallery owner Laura Era.
"It brings back memories because most of them are beloved pieces," Era said.
Era and gallery manager Peg Fitzgerald say Fabulous Forgeries is Troika's most popular exhibit. Fitzgerald notes that it's educational for adults and kids interested in art history. Plus, it's an artist favorite.
"The artists that do it, love it," Fitzgerald said. "They're probably even thinking right now for next year."
Some like John Eiseman have a personal connection to their works.
As a kid, one of Eiseman's favorite paintings was an 1872 work by French painter Claude Monet titled "Argenteuil." It is kept in the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C.
Eiseman, 66, spent his childhood years between St. Michaels and the nation's capital. Monet's depiction of a town and river near Paris reminded Eiseman of the Miles River.
"It reminded me of a placid day somewhere on the Miles," Eiseman said.
But something was always missing. More than 40 years after falling in love with the painting, Eiseman got to add that missing piece: his granddaughter's late American retriever. He placed the dog on a long, empty road that leads toward a castle in the background of the painting.
Era herself has four works in the forgeries collection.
Her favorite is a recreation of an 1873 self-portrait by German painter Anselm Feuerbach. She saw it online and couldn't miss the opportunity to recreate it.
"I just kept coming back to it because he was doggone handsome," Era said.
Era says Fabulous Forgeries is all about studying the history of art. Modern artists can learn from the technique, brushwork and color combinations used by the original painters, she said.
"It's a nice exercise, and it's certainly a learning exercise for any artist," Era said. "And many times, if you go to museums nowadays, you'll see people, there'll be artists that will be copying the old masters with their easel."
The exhibit was judged by Dan Weiss, former president and CEO of The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Palden Hamilton was awarded judge's choice award for his work, "Roses," after Abbott Handerson Thayer.
Other awards and honorable mentions were handed out to Era, Eiseman, John Davis Held, Christine Drewyer and Lynne Lockhart. The exhibit is open through Aug. 30. Voting for the people's choice award remains open.
Some of the works model the originals as closely as possible. Others add their own twists.
Drewyer drew inspiration from an 1888 flower pot painting by Vincent van Gogh. She added a cat, which tore up some of the flowers, and titled it, "Vincent's Bad, Bad Kitty."
The unique flair of each artist has cemented Fabulous Forgeries as a fan favorite each year, Fitzgerald said.
"They just love it," she said of gallery's viewers. "They just love to see how it's interpreted, how the artist decides to do their painting."
The Troika Gallery, located at 9 S. Harrison St., is open on Mondays and Thursdays to Saturdays from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.

 GREENSBORO — The Greensboro Historical Society has found its new location just blocks away from its current location, where the town said in June that the historical society could not longer keep its offices and artifacts.After months of discussion, the Greensboro Town Council voted on June 5 to give the historical society 120 days to vacate the Weaver Building.
Longtime Caroline County resident William Satterfield will allow the historical society to rent his building on Sunset Avenue, which in the 1960s was a bar and a hardware store.
The historical society was first told about a potential move out of the Weaver Building in March, when officials raised the need for more space to house town agencies. The town determined the building could be used to house either the police department or the town employees' office, but the council has leaned toward moving the police department.
With the move on the horizon, historical society Acting President Robert Moser talked to society staff and members about what is needed to ensure a safe relocation.
While no official move date is set because of new location repairs, the historical society will create a packing committee; a new location cleaning and repair committee; a moving committee; and a building, management and security committee.
The committees will be made of historical society members and community members. The historical society is asking community members to donate boxes, bubble wrap and their time to help.
"We're going to reach out to people within the community, and hopefully word of mouth from friend, to friend to friend gets people out there an opportunity to come and help," Moser said.
"We've had quite a few people reach out to us in regards to letting us know when the move is going to happen or what they can do and how they can help us facilitate the move," he said.
In addition to the move, the historical society is set to hold its biggest fundraiser of the year on Sept. 19.
The 22nd annual Greater Greensboro Open golf tournament is low on sign-ups right now, Moser said, but the historical society hopes for good participation to help with costs at the new location.
"It is our largest fundraiser in the year, which is going to be very important for us now since we have different utilities, internet and all that stuff that was provided to us through the town for the past seven years is now going to be our responsibility to pay," Moser said.
If you are interested in helping the Historical Society with moving, contact Rdmoser60@gmail.com.

title: Elitist label betrays character
author: Staff Writer
content:
Elitist label betrays character

 August 16, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: Editors Inbox 
 
 227
 Words 

 Read News Document

 On today's social media, I've read no less than six citations of Newt Gingrich's 1995 citation of NPR: "As far as I am concerned, there's nothing public about it; it's an elitist enterprise."That statement is, of course, primarily about his own ego, being cited first. But to call NPR "elitist" betrays the network's character.
Recall the weekly series over four decades ago, "IBM's Your Heart of Music: The Program About Life and the Classics that Help You to Live It," of which I was writer, producer and host. It was the program in which you heard common topics from life — the death of a parent, the birth of a child, being in love, trouble with your boss — and what the great composers thought of such themes in their works.
Listeners wrote and called, some in tears, grateful for a broadcast that spoke to their common lives. Elitist? No way. And personally, the show taught me so much about becoming a priest.
Truth is, listeners stumbled onto Your Heart of Music because they were already tuned in for our trustworthiness of NPR's news and human interest reporting. Listener research has long proven NPR has the broadest appeal of all things on the air.
But let us pray for the lonely Mr. Gingrich and his old citations, who has lost so many friends.
THE RT. REV. JOEL MARCUS JOHNSON
Retired Anglican Bishop
Easton

title: Singing Captains to lead Buffett celebration at The Mainstay
author: BOB FORD Special to the Star Democrat
content:
Singing Captains to lead Buffett celebration at The Mainstay

 Author/Byline: BOB FORD Special to the Star Democrat | Section: News 
 
 552
 Words 

 Read News Document

 ROCK HALL — Jimmy Buffett was a musical legend with a phenomenal career and a unique following, but on the Chesapeake Bay, he was just another boater looking for good fishing, good food and good times.Well, maybe not just another boater. When Last Mango, his 42-foot custom sportfisher, made its way north to Sag Harbor in the spring, or south in the fall to the tropical climes that inspired many of his songs, Buffett delighted in exploring the bay from the ocean to the C&D Canal. He even filmed a music video at Thomas Point Light on one of the trips.
Boaters, beach bums and backyard pool drifters all lost a friend when Buffett died at 76 on Sept. 1, 2023, due to complications from a rare form of skin cancer.
To honor the Labor Day weekend anniversary of his passing, and to celebrate his musical legacy, the Singing Captains are performing a Buffett-only concert of his hits on Sunday, Aug. 31, from 4 to 6 p.m. at the outdoor amphitheater of Rock Hall's iconic music venue, The Mainstay.
It will be a "family-friendly celebration of music, memories and Margaritaville vibes, with special musical guests and good company," according to Mark Einstein, a member of the Singing Captains and a day-job charter boat captain in his own right.
The event is ticketless and free to the public, with a suggested donation of $10 to help The Mainstay continue its mission of providing a wide variety of musical offerings for the community. The Mainstay cash bar will be operating, with margaritas and more. Ice cream will be available for purchase from Get the Scoop, and That Place on Main will have Cheeseburgers in Paradise on the menu at the show.
Opening for the Singing Captains, and joining them on a number of Buffett songs that follow, will be steel pan virtuoso Trevor Stubbs. He is a native of Trinidad, where the instrument was first fashioned out of industrial steel drums. Stubbs, who is one half of the duo Island Vibes, has played at The Mainstay previously. Beginning with the song "One Particular Harbor," a 1983 release from the album of the same name, Buffett often used steel pannists on his Caribbean-flavored songs.
"What connects Rock Hall to the Jimmy Buffett thing is that this is a premier sailing and boating town. We've all got Hawaiian shirts, and we like to emulate that laid-back lifestyle that his music captured," Einstein said. "His music, when it burst on the scene, influenced the whole boating world. You would hear it walking down literally any dock."
Buffett, originally from Pascagoula, Mississippi, made his way to New Orleans and Nashville before discovering that Key West was just the right latitude for his attitude, and the tropical-tinged hits followed quickly. Over the course of his career, Buffett sold more than 20 million records, and 17 of his albums were either gold or platinum in sales. He was posthumously inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2024.
Those attending the Buffett celebration at The Mainstay will find plenty of seating at the open-air amphitheater, but if so inclined, there is room on the lawn for beach chairs, too. Visitors can bring those, wiggle their toes in the grass and pretend it is sand.
"Wear your loudest shirt and come help us toast Jimmy," Einstein said.

title: Country Cooking: Memories and recipes from grandparents
author: MARIE SAVAGE Country Cooking
content:
Country Cooking: Memories and recipes from grandparents

 Grandparents Day is Sept. 7 this year. In 1978, the late Jimmy Carter, who was the president, designated the first Sunday after Labor Day each year to honor grandparents.What a wonderful day to honor those important people in our lives. My grandparents died many years ago, but the memories live on. Generations have changed; grandparents are younger (it seems), lifestyles are somewhat different, but we still have Mom-Mom and Pop-Pop.
My mother and I would sit and talk about days I spent with my paternal grandparents. They too had a large farm, and my older siblings and I would help with farm work.
I recall thinking that the grandparents' farm duties were out-of-date compared to the "modern" equipment my dad used. Then my older brother's fourth generation farm down on the river was ultra-modern.
My grandparents were an important part of my life. My maternal grandmother died at age 18 when my mom was 2 years old, so I never had the pleasure of knowing this person who gave me the best mother ever. My paternal grandparents were dear to me as they were all I had.
I have lots of stories to share with you all in the coming months. Stories of mischief and fun growing up with large families on large farms.
Food seemed to be a very popular activity for grandparents when the grandchildren came. I have many great memories of special dishes such as fresh made biscuits, pies, dumplings, soups, stews, beans and fried chicken.
Cooking is a tradition that still happens today with my own grandsons.
A few times a month, one of my grandchildren has spent the day with me. A few years ago, when we ran out of things to do, we started baking. This has been so much fun.
Not only have we developed math skills, reading skills, and the ability to follow directions, but we have also developed an awesome relationship between generations.
Our first bread to be made was banana bread.
BANANA BREAD
1/2 cup shortening, 2 eggs, 1 cup sugar, 2 cups flour, 1 tbsp sour milk, 1 tsp baking soda, 2 ripe crushed bananas, 1/2 cup crushed nuts (optional).
Cream shortening with eggs and sugar. Add flour, sour milk, baking soda, crushed bananas and nuts. Mix well and bake in a preheated 350-degree oven for one hour. For best results, use a medium size baking pan.
PUMPKIN BREAD
2 2/3 cups sugar, 2/3 cup shortening, 4 beaten eggs, 2/3 cup water, 1 can pumpkin puree (1 lb), 3 1/3 cups flour, 1/2 tsp baking powder, 2 tsps baking soda, 1 1/2 tsp salt, 1 tsp cinnamon, 1/2 tsp ground cloves, 2/3 cup chopped walnuts, 2/3 cup chopped dates.
Cream together sugar and shortening. Stir in eggs, water and pumpkin. Sift together flour, baking powder, baking soda, salt, cinnamon and cloves. Mix well with the wet ingredients. Add walnuts and dates. Pour into two greased 9-by-5-inch pans. Bake at 350 degrees for one hour and 15 minutes.
GRANDMA'S ROSEMARY DINNER ROLLS
1 package (1/4 ounce) active dry yeast, 1/4 cup warm water (110° to 115°), 3 cups bread flour, 2 tbsps sugar, 1 tbsp minced fresh rosemary, 3/4 tsp salt, 2/3 cup warm 2% milk (110° to 115°), 1 large egg (room temperature), 1/4 to 1/3 cup canola oil, 1 large egg yolk, 2 tbsps 2% milk.
In a small bowl, dissolve yeast in warm water. Place the flour, sugar, rosemary and salt in a food processor: pulse until blended. Add the warm milk, egg and yeast mixture; cover and pulse 10 times or until almost blended. While processing, gradually add oil just until dough pulls away from sides and begins to form a ball. Process 2 minutes longer to knead dough (dough will be very soft). Transfer dough to a greased bowl, turning once to grease the top. Cover and let rise in a warm place until doubled, about 1 hour. Punch down dough. Turn onto a lightly floured surface; divide and shape into 12 balls. Roll each into a 15-inch rope. Starting at one end, loosely wrap dough around itself to form a coil. Tuck end under; pinch to seal. Place 2 inches apart on greased baking sheets. Cover and let rise until doubled, about 30 minutes. For egg wash, in a small bowl, whisk egg yolk and milk; brush over rolls. Sprinkle it with remaining rosemary. Bake at 350 degrees until golden brown, 18-22 minutes. Remove from pans to wire racks; serve warm.
EASTERN SHORE SWEET POTATO BISCUITS
2 cups mashed sweet potatoes, 3/4 cup sugar, 2 1/4 cups flour, 1 1/4 tsp salt, 2 tsps baking powder, 5 tbsps shortening.
Mix sweet potatoes with sugar, flour, salt and baking powder. Add 5 tablespoons shortening last and mix dough. Roll dough and cut with biscuit cutter or roll into small balls 3/4 inch thick. Bake at 450 degrees for 20 to 25 minutes.
FRIED CHICKEN
1 frying chicken, salt, 1 1/2 cups flour, pepper, paprika, 1 1/2 cups shortening.
Wash chicken in cold water and cut into pieces. Soak in cold water for a few minutes with 1 tsp of salt. Drain chicken. Season flour with salt, pepper and paprika to taste. Heat shortening in a fry pan. Dredge the chicken in the flour mixture and place in the oil. Cook until golden brown on both sides, about 20 minutes on each side. Drain on paper towels. I usually mix my flour mixture in a brown paper bag and shake to coat. I also save the flour mixture to make a gravy in the grease when chicken is cooked.
GRANDMOTHER'S SOUTHERN COLLARD GREENS
2 tbsps lard or shortening (divided), 1 large onion (chopped), 6 garlic cloves (minced), 1 1/2 pounds smoked ham hocks, 6 cups water, wine, 2 tsps seasoned salt, 1 to 3 tsps crushed red pepper flakes, 1/4 tsp sugar, 1 large bunch collard greens (coarsely chopped).
In a six-quart stockpot, heat 1 tbsp lard over medium heat. Add onion and garlic; cook and stir until tender. Add ham hocks, water, seasoned salt, pepper flakes and sugar. Bring to a boil. Reduce heat; simmer, uncovered, until meat is tender, 55 to 60 minutes. Add collard greens, wine, and remaining 1 tbsp lard. Return to a boil. Reduce heat; simmer, uncovered, until greens are very tender, 55 to 60 minutes. Remove meat from bones; finely chop and return to pan. Discard bones. Serve with a slotted spoon.
GRANDMOTHERS CORN PUDDING
4 large eggs, 1 cup whole milk, 1 can (15 ounces) cream-style corn, 1/2 cup sugar, 5 slices day-old bread (crusts removed), 1 tbsp softened butter. In a bowl, beat eggs and milk. Add corn and sugar; mix well. Cut bread into half-inch cubes and place in a greased 9-inch square baking dish. Pour egg mixture over bread. Dot with butter. Bake, uncovered, at 350 degrees until a knife inserted in the center comes out clean, 50 to 60 minutes.
GRANDMOTHER'S TANDY CAKE
4 large eggs (room temperature), 2 cups sugar, 1 cup 2% milk, 1 tsp vanilla extract, 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 tsp baking powder, 1/4 tsp salt, 1 3/4 cups creamy peanut butter, 5 milk or dark chocolate candy bars (1.55 ounces each) chopped, 2 tbsps butter.
Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. In a large bowl, beat eggs and sugar until thick and lemon colored. Beat in milk and vanilla. In another bowl, combine flour, baking powder and salt; gradually add to egg mixture and mix well. Spread into a greased 15-by-10-inch baking pan. Bake for 20 to 25 minutes or until lightly browned. Cool for 15 minutes on a wire rack. Spread peanut butter over top; cool completely. In a double boiler or metal bowl over simmering water, melt chocolate and butter; stir until smooth. Gently spread over peanut butter. Refrigerate for 30 minutes or until firm.

title: Art exhibit in Easton uses small items to explore larger themes such as war, homelessness
author: Konner Metz
content:
Art exhibit in Easton uses small items to explore larger themes such as war, homelessness

 September 4, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Konner Metz | Section: Local News 
 
 416
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — A new art exhibit in Easton uses small-scale items like twigs to tell large-scale stories involving war, poverty and conflict.Inside the Academy Art Museum, "To the Edge of Your World" by Dutch-Irish artist Anita Groener welcomes viewers into a peaceful setting of grid-like drawings and bird-chirping sounds.
Two main displays — Cradle and Shrapnel — are sculpture works by Groener. They include materials like twigs gathered from walks with her dog that she started collecting more than 10 years ago.
Groener hopes the sculptures help people understand some of "their own baggage" and history.
"Everything's very small, which creates a psychological distance," said Groener, who lives in Dublin, while inside the Easton exhibit space last month. "And that's important because we witness all these world events."
For her, the exhibit is largely motivated by time she spent in the southern United States visiting civil rights monuments, as well as Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Its meaning continues to evolve today, Groener said.
"Like we in Ireland watch what's going on in America," she said. "But it's such a distance, and I'm not taking part in that. Yet it affects us all. Everything that happens in the world, in our lives, affects us and is connected."
The Ireland-based artist doesn't want people to walk in thinking the art will yield certain takeaways. Rather, Groener hopes her art is open to interpretation.
"I like ambiguous readings, because as an artist, you can't be prescriptive," she said.
Groener's exhibit is the Academy Art Museum's first ever international exhibit. Charlotte Potter Kasic, the museum's executive director, said it took "many hoops to jump through" to make happen, but she's happy it panned out.
The opening weekend for the exhibit and a sister documentary film last month drew more than 250 people, Kasic said. They watched "Shelter," a 30-minute short film addressing homelessness on the Mid-Shore. Groener, the Talbot Interfaith Shelter and filmmaker Matt Kresling collaborated on the project.
At the front of Groener's exhibit is the main shelter structure, which is shown at the end of the film. She took around 10,000 pictures of the structure to make the stop-motion scene possible.
Groener said the scene is a "coming together of people" and all about community. Kasic said the audience on opening weekend was captivated by the film.
"No one moved," Kasic said. "They were all very engaged."
The film is slated to show at the Chesapeake Film Festival on Oct. 10 at the Ebenezer Theater in Easton. Groener's exhibit is open at the Academy Art Museum through Oct. 27.

title: Black watermen’s monument proposed for Wells Cove
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Black watermen’s monument proposed for Wells Cove

 September 5, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 653
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — The Queen Anne's County Commissioners approved Wells Cove as the site for a proposed Black watermen's monument Aug. 26, further representing the history and legacy of the county's iconic industry.Tilghman Hemsley, a Queenstown artist and director of American Patriotic Monuments Inc., who created the original Kent Narrows watermen's monument 20 years ago, said he had been approached about the lack of Black representation in that project.
Seeking commissioner approval to establish the new monument on county property at Wells Cove, Hemsley presented mock-ups of the detailed sculptures.
Symbolizing the rich heritage of Black watermen, the monument will depict life-size bronze sculptures featuring a conversation between a head boat captain and an oyster boat worker, according to Hemsley. The piece will also feature other important aspects of the industry, including a man working with clams, a woman picking crabs, another cleaning fish, as well as a young boy with a fishing pole along for the experience.
"It's a sculpture that leans into the whole industry," Hemsley said.
"The piece is designed for the public to be able to come through and be part of the sculpture," he said.
With the history of the Black watermen engraved into the side of the pieces, "it's all about education," he said.
The monument is slated for a location between Bridges Restaurant and the Jetty restaurant. Hemsley emphasized the interactive nature of the work, allowing visitors the opportunity to pass between the pieces and engage with the sculptures as they visit the local area.
The watermen will be life-size bronze sculptures while the boat pieces will be stainless steel and powder-coated, he said.
Hemsley said the design of the pieces should make the monument low maintenance.
The project has already received approval from the Queen Anne's County Parks and Recreation Department and a letter of recommendation from the Kent Narrows Foundation, he said.
The commissioners unanimously approved Wells Cove as the site for the proposed monument. Commissioner Jim Moran noted he would have preferred a competition among artists to design a tribute to Black watermen but supported the plan.
Hemsley noted time is of the essence if the statue is to be ready by July 4, 2026, in celebration of the country's 250th anniversary.
Serving as director of the project, Hemsley said various other artists will be involved in the sculpture work. The proposed monument has an advisory committee that includes watermen, he said.
With commissioner approval, the next steps include seeking funding grants, according to Hemsley.
Although highly appreciated, just like the original watermen's monument, the project would not be solely dependent on county support, he said.
The total cost for the project is estimated at about $475,000. The previous watermen's monument cost about $300,000, he said.
Statues typically take about three years to complete, but Hemsley was confident as long as funding came through.
"It's aggressive, but we can do it," he said.
A fundraising event with auctions, games and music will be held at the Kent Island American Legion Nov. 8 starting at 7 p.m., he said.
Hemsley is also working with the Centreville Veterans Information Committee to create a life-size statue honoring the more than 400 Black soldiers of Queen Anne's County who fought for the Union during the Civil War.
Working with Chesapeake Charities, the veteran statue committee has been hard at work establishing itself as a nonprofit, according to John Wright, statue committee chair.
Wright credited the enthusiasm of the committee in working to establish a historic monument.
"I'm glad I am in a position to help," he said.
With the sculpture to be completed in stages, the committee foresees about a year and a half before a statue stands in front of the Kennard African American Cultural Heritage Center.
Donations can be sent to United States Colored Troops Memorial Fund, P.O. Box 42, Centreville, MD 21617.
As a Maryland nonprofit, American Patriotic Monuments Inc. seeks to lead public arts projects and monuments that celebrate American legacies.
More information, including sponsorship opportunities, can be found at apmiart.org.
Information about Hemsley's work can be found at tilghmanhemsleyfinearts.com.

title: Southern gothic author Wiley Cash named WC Patrick Henry History Fellow
author: Staff Writer
content:
Southern gothic author Wiley Cash named WC Patrick Henry History Fellow

 September 13, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News 
 
 442
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CHESTERTOWN — Washington College's Starr Center for the Study of the American Experience announces the 2025-2026 Patrick Henry History Fellow — Wiley Cash, a best-selling author versed in southern history, mystery and family drama.Cash will be joining the Washington College community for the academic year and teaching an English class while also working on his sixth novel — in his words, "a retelling of the Lost Colony [of Roanoke Island, NC] that braids three storylines while interrogating the tendrils of white supremacy that sprouted from the American colonial experiment."
The Patrick Henry History Fellowship supports outstanding writing on American history and culture by scholars and authors; it offers a $45,000 stipend for the academic year and an opportunity to work with and teach Washington College students and faculty, as well as a book allowance and a nine-month residency in a historic 18th century house in Chestertown. Past fellowship topics have ranged as broadly as the early history of the slave trade, American religious minorities, and the LGBTQ rights movement. Past Patrick Henry fellows have included National Book Prize winner Edward Ball and Scribe Book Award recipient Wil Haygood.
Cash is an award-winning and New York Times bestselling author of four novels. He often uses a multi-character perspective in his works, deploying a range of character voices to tell a richer, more nuanced story.
His work has won numerous awards, including the Southern Book Prize three times, and the Crime Writers' Association's CWA New Blood Dagger and Gold Dagger. He has published extensively on a range of issues, from the environment to music, and is the host of the Our State Book Club podcast and the founder of "This is Working," an online creative community.
"Wiley's work perfectly embodies the Starr Center's approach to history," said Starr Center Director Adam Goodheart. "He's an elegant writer and accomplished storyteller who reaches broad audiences, while also engaging in complex ways with some of the problems and paradoxes at the root of American identity. We're delighted to have him here with us and excited that our students will have the opportunity to learn from this nationally eminent fiction writer."
In the spring, Cash will teach "Signifying on the South" for the College's English department, exploring popular literary portrayals of the American South.
"I'm thrilled to serve as the 2025-2026 Patrick Henry Fellow," Cash said. "My family and I spent a week in Chestertown this summer, and we can't wait to return to such a historic, kind, welcoming community."
On Tuesday, Sept. 23, at 6 p.m. at the Rose O'Neill Literary House at Washington College, Cash will read from his novel, "The Last Ballad." The event is free and open to the public.

title: Nause-Waiwash Band's festival showcases Indigenous heritage in Dorchester County
author: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com
content:
Nause-Waiwash Band's festival showcases Indigenous heritage in Dorchester County

 September 15, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: WENDY WEITZEL wweitzel@chespub.com | Section: Dorchester 
 
 424
 Words 

 Read News Document

 VIENNA — The Nause-Waiwash Band of Indians' annual Native American Festival has had many locations in its 33-year history.It began on Elliott Island, then moved to Andrews, then Cambridge before settling at its current location on the baseball fields in Vienna 21 years ago.
"We've been all over the county," Chief Donna Abbott said. "But the entire county is our ancestral homelands, so it's worked out well for us."
That history was at the forefront of the event Saturday, Abbott said. As she surveyed the field shortly before the Grand Entry, she reflected on how the festival has helped support one of the Nause-Waiwash's most important goals — education.
The festival was designed to celebrate Nause-Waiwash history, culture and traditions and share these with the public.
"And definitely, after 33 years, it has become a tradition," Abbott said.
Since its beginnings, the festival has evolved, incorporating more Indigenous heritages.
At the event Saturday, Abbott highlighted performers from throughout the Americas, including Aztec fire dancers from near Mexico City and hula dancers from Hawaii.
"We also celebrate other nations," Abbott said. "We celebrate the South Americans, we celebrate the Mexicans, the Canadians, the Alaskans. We're all about all Native Americans."
The festival features vendors, demonstrations, food and dancing that aim to educate attendees.
In a shady spot near the back of the baseball field, Leigh Hunteman and her pack of dogs provided information about dog sledding, which finds its origins in Indigenous communities from what is now Canada and Alaska, according to an encyclopedia of Indigenous culture and history produced by the University of Saskatchewan.
Hunteman, a longtime Eastern Shore resident, said she has been coming to the festival since it was located in Cambridge and has been bringing her dogs to Vienna for several years.
The event is a good opportunity for Hunteman to teach people about competitive dog sled racing, which isn't commonly practiced in Maryland, she said. And the dogs are always excited to meet new people, she added.
Abbott said that longtime vendors like Hunteman, along with newer sponsors and vendors, have helped shape the festival into an evolving event that showcases more aspects of Indigenous cultures with each year.
Growing the event is important, she said, because of a shared goal between the festival's participants.
"We're all striving for the same thing," Abbott said. "We're all striving for the same goal, and that is to keep our history alive. There's so much of it that's been lost, and not just ours, but all the Indigenous history."
Abbott said preparations are already underway for next year's festival, which will be held Sept. 19 in Vienna.

title: Denton redesignated as Arts and Entertainment District by state
author: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com
content:
Denton redesignated as Arts and Entertainment District by state

 September 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: AHMAD GARNETT agarnett@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 354
 Words 

 Read News Document

 DENTON — Denton has received a redesignation from the state as an Arts and Entertainment District.The redesignation is followed a 10-year process that must be completed to continue to be named as one of these districts. It allows the town to keep tax incentives that encourage economic development through arts and tourism.
For the tax incentives, Denton is still working on a program or credit that will be given to businesses within the district for promoting arts and entertainment within the town.
The art and entertainment distract program was created in 2001 by the MSAC to provide local governments interested in encouraging arts activity with tools to incentivize artists to live, create and sell work in their towns.
According to a press release from the Maryland State Art Council, in fiscal year 2024, visitor spending in Denton and the 28 other designated districts generated $136 million.
"Small business development in our rural towns and cities is vital to winning the decade," said Gov. Wes Moore in the press release. "The A&E Districts program has a proven track record, showing that state and local investments in the arts not only improve the quality of life for Marylanders, but also lay a foundation for entrepreneurship to thrive."
To earn redesignation, the town of Denton has to apply every decade, demonstrating progress toward economic development goals and continued commitment to attracting and retaining arts activity.
"Essentially, it's a wonderful opportunity to work with our local leaders and create tax incentives for businesses, expand economic opportunities, but also to add to our already established arts and entertainment district designation," said George Karos, executive director for Caroline County Council of Arts.
Karos and town administrator's aide Lisa Orendorf and town council members helped throughout the redesignation application process.
"It's one more amenity, and it's a diverse amenity which is nice for our town," Town Administrator Scott Getchell said. "Just like we have business districts at our shopping centers and so forth, that's an amenity for people to come to… So this is one more thing that makes our town special that we have this Arts and Entertainment District that is managed by the Caroline County Arts."

title: Local artists celebrate 20 years of creativity together in Cambridge
author: Lily Tierney
content:
Local artists celebrate 20 years of creativity together in Cambridge

 September 17, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Lily Tierney | Section: Local News 
 
 383
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Every Wednesday, a group of local artists from a diverse set of mediums and backgrounds comes together to share their latest creations. This segment of their meetings is called "brings and brags."Twenty years ago, the group began meeting at the Dorchester Center for the Arts when it was still in the historic home on High Street. They then relocated to a deli inside of a strip mall, which didn't survive the pandemic. The loyal members began meeting at a park until finding their spot at Peach Blossom Place.
"It's a beautiful building," the group's leader Susan Lester said. "We've had a wonderful experience being here."
The Wednesday Morning Artists are an eclectic group, who bring their unique skillsets together in mixed-media collaborative pieces, one of a kind oil paintings and an array of other media. On the fourth Wednesday of the month, there is a live art demonstration that often includes hands-on participation.
The group is led Lester with support from Robert Gladney and Nancy Hoffman. The members also showcase their work outside of "brings and brags" at the Hyatt Regency on Saturdays during the summer, at community events like Taste of Cambridge and at pop-up art events around town.
Lester said her favorite part about the Wednesday Morning Artists is learning and collaborating with the members. "The fact that we're so diverse, we have such a range of artists, I never even heard of some of the stuff they do," she said.
The wide range of art forms include weaving, pine needle coiling, jewelry designing, photography, sculpting, music, woodcarving and the more traditional forms of art like oil painting and pottery.
"We have pine needle weavers, who knew? I never heard of that," Lester said. "You know, when you think of art, you think of acrylics or oils or watercolors, and it's way beyond that."
The group has also created fellowship outside of Wednesday morning, enjoying monthly dinners and an annual fall picnic at Gerry Boyle Park.
Lester said they are always accepting new members. "And trust me, we don't judge based on level of experience," she said. "Pros, beginners, we want you all, and we'll help you learn how to do it or you can help us learn."
For more information on the artists, future events, and how to join, visit the Wednesday Morning Artists Facebook page.

title: Colonial remains reburied during ceremony at Historic St. Mary's City
author: Madison Bateman Special to Southern Maryland News
content:
Colonial remains reburied during ceremony at Historic St. Mary's City

 September 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Madison Bateman Special to Southern Maryland News | Section: News 
 
 758
 Words 

 Read News Document

 In a powerful moment of remembrance and reconciliation, Historic St. Mary's City hosted a Ceremony of Return on Sept. 20, reuniting the remains of some of Maryland's earliest settlers, including colonial leader Philip Calvert, with the sacred ground where they were first laid to rest nearly four centuries ago.In 1990, archaeologists at Historic St. Mary's City were preparing to reconstruct the 1667 Brick Chapel on its original foundation. In the process, they uncovered three lead coffins buried beneath the chancel of the building. Lead coffin burials were rare in colonial America and typically reserved for individuals of high status.
The remains in the chapel coffins were identified as members of Maryland's founding Calvert family, including Philip Calvert (chancellor, fifth governor of Maryland and son of George Calvert, the first Lord Baltimore), Anne Wosley Calvert and the infant son of Philip.
Archaeologists also dug up the remains of 56 other individuals buried in and around the Brick Chapel. Not much is known about them beyond that they were laid to rest sometime between 1634 and 1730.
Over the past 30 years, a team of archaeologists, historians and scientists from the Smithsonian Institution studied the coffins and their contents to gain insight into early Maryland life, health, diet and funerary practices.
Over the weekend, Historic St. Mary's City hosted a reinterment ceremony, marking the final step in this long-term research effort and returning the individuals to their original resting place in the reconstructed Brick Chapel.
"The Ceremony of Return marks a moment of great significance to Historic St. Mary's City and to our shared understanding of Maryland's past," Travis Parno, the museum's acting executive director and director of research and collections, said. "For the past three decades, nearly 60 of Maryland's founders have shared their stories with us and now they have returned to rest. Their contributions to the establishment of Maryland and the United States cannot be overstated."
About 275 guests gathered to take part in the solemn and symbolic ceremony honoring Maryland's early settlers.
The event began with the thunder of cannon fire from the Maryland Dove, the museum's reconstructed 17th-century tall ship that recently returned from Washington, D.C. The ship, which represents one of the original vessels that brought settlers to Maryland in 1634, also carried back a Maryland flag used during the event.
Next, a formal procession led by a horse-drawn hearse moved from the reconstructed State House to the Brick Chapel.
Among the participants were descendants of the Calvert family, members of the Ark and Dove Society, the St. Maries Cittie Militia, and historical interpreters dressed in authentic 17th-century attire. They were joined by museum visitors and invited guests, all walking together in tribute to the lives, struggles and enduring legacies of Maryland's founding colonists.
At the Brick Chapel, guests heard remarks by historians, archaeologists and other key figures, including Douglas Owsley, curator of biological anthropology at the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History. Following the speakers, a rite of reinterment honored the individuals being laid to rest.
In the Town Center area, costumed museum staff distributed bundles of rosemary, all grown on-site, as a symbolic gesture of remembrance. In the 17th century, rosemary was commonly used in funeral rituals, a tradition closely tied to Anne Wosley Calvert, one of the individuals recently reinterred.
When her lead coffin was excavated in the early 1990s, archaeologists found her remains carefully wrapped in a burial shroud with silk ribbons at her wrists and traces of rosemary scattered across her remains, according to the Maryland State Archive.
"These people have been completely forgotten but this investigation is changing that," Henry Miller, senior research fellow and an archaeologist who worked on the project, said during the ceremony. "They built the foundation on which we stand … they deserve to no longer be forgotten."
DeAnna Poling and her sister, Debora Hanson, recently discovered they were descendants of early Marylanders when they found a document in their grandmother's desk which implied a relation to Gov. Thomas Greene and his wife Anne Cox. The pair were on the initial voyage of the Ark and the Dove that sailed from England to Maryland in 1634.
"I am honored to be here and serve as a pallbearer at this event," Poling said. "I am especially excited we are not just descended from one person but two from the ship. They had the first Christian marriage in provincial Maryland."
"We are finally able to bring these individuals home," Kelsey Bush, descendant of Eleanor Butler, said. "It took over 30 years to get to this point. … Who would have thought we would be standing here today with the reconstructed chapel."

title: Maryland map hooks artists together
author: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com
content:
Maryland map hooks artists together

 September 24, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Jane Bellmyer jbellmyer@cecilwhig.com | Section: News 
 
 489
 Words 

 Read News Document

 There's an interesting piece of art on the wall of the Cecil County Arts Council in Elkton that pays homage to each county in Maryland; made by fiber artists from other states.Colleen Tiefenthal connected with artists in Washington, Florida, Connecticut and New Jersey and each turned out a piece that represents one of the 23 counties for the projected entitled "The Maryland Counties Rug Hooking Project."
"It was a really fun project," Tiefenthal said. "It was my concept and design. Then I reached out to my fellow rug hookers."
The North East woman — an Ohio transplant — hasn't met any rug hookers in Cecil County yet so she's the only local connection to the project. Tiefenthal knew all but two of the 16 rug hookers who had a hand in the map.
"I thought, 'how cool would it be ... that we could do one thing together,'" she said.
She got a grant from the Maryland State Arts Council to fund the project. That $4,000 covered the cost of materials and postage. Tiefenthal said the project taught her how to use a new computer program: Canva.
Work began with her cutting all the pieces of linen for the backing and much of the wool that was used to create each county.
"I sent them kits. They did their parts and sent it back," she said. "One person, it was their first attempt at rug hooking but she's a fabric artist." Most received more than one county to complete. They held several virtual meetings before the rug hooking began.
A board Tiefenthal painted to mimic the Maryland flag in grey tones is the base and each piece is wired onto the board. Accompanying the map is a legend with numbers corresponding to each county. Tiefenthal also created a booklet about the project and added a rug hooked segment of the Maryland flag. Each county is represented by something central to its heritage. For Cecil County, it's the Turkey Point Lighthouse.
Admitting she was nervous waiting for the pieces to return, Tiefenthal said the fear dissolved as she opened each package.
"When the first five to six pieces came back and were wonderful, it gave me confidence," she said. She knew the pieces were going to fit together.
Tiefenthal said it was her husband, Jim, who suggested a separate panel on the bottom of the display.
"It was Jim's idea for the "Touch This" panel," she said. This way the curious can feel the texture of the work but not touch the map itself.
The map visited Salisbury, Md. last weekend and has already made a stop at the North East Library. It's on display at the Arts Council, 135 East Main St. in Elkton until Oct. 7 then it moves to the Elkton branch library Oct. 7 through Oct. 28.
In 2027, it travels to a fiber art show in Newport, R.I. held by the International Guild of Handhooking Rugmakers and to Sauder Village for a similar show in Archibald, Ohio.

title: Local author delivers sing-along Christmas magic aboard 18-wheeler

Local author delivers sing-along Christmas magic aboard 18-wheeler

 September 25, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Grab your trucker hats and road maps — and save room for milk and cookies — as local author and musician J. Brandon Boron of Queenstown is bringing Christmas magic with Santa Claus behind the wheel of an 18-wheeler in a new sing-along illustrated children's book this holiday season.When Santa's reindeer come down sick one Christmas, Santa Claus must take the wheel of a magical flying 18-wheeler to deliver presents on time. Readers are invited to climb aboard and join Saint Nick and his pals as they make the most important delivery of the year — all while performing jaunty trucker tunes.
Fun for the whole family, Santa's 18-Wheel Chrome-and-Steel Sleigh is a sing-along storybook highlighting the holiday spirit and how any challenge can be overcome with resilience, humor and friends by your side.
A lifelong musician, Boron has always loved country music, particularly the fun and upbeat tunes of the truck driver genre. The story of Santa driving an 18-wheeler started as a truck song Boron created that practically wrote itself, he said.
With the song's quick rhymes, upbeat tunes and big imagery, Boron soon discovered it could engage children with fun illustrations. He set to work with others to develop a story for the whole family.
Bringing Santa's "wheely" important mission to life has been a fun experience, especially collaborating with illustrator Shaun Ivie to build on each other's ideas and bring colorful imagery to the pages, according to Boron.
Showcasing cheer and the feel of the holiday season, everyday characters are illustrated throughout the story lending a hand to assist Santa, including police officers safely holding traffic.
Boron said he grew up understanding the important role of truck drivers. His father hauled military missiles and his uncle also drove trucks.
Boron has always loved Christmas and is eager to share that love and inspire others.
Santa's 18-Wheel Chrome-and-Steel Sleigh includes a QR code so families can sing and dance along with Santa's "tireless," one-of-a-kind magic journey.
The end of the book features a discussion guide for readers as well as a template for them to pen their own letters to Santa.
Boron was born in Great Falls, Montana, but has spent most of his life traversing the United States and beyond.
After studying art, music and biology at Colorado State University, the University of Massachusetts and the University of Nevada Las Vegas, Boron currently serves as a musician with the U.S. Army, where he has spent the last two decades performing across Europe, the Middle East and the United States.
Living on the Eastern Shore since about 2018, Boron and his wife, Thordis, fell in love with the area. The two regularly perform as local musicians throughout the community.
A release party is scheduled for Oct. 21 at Uno Mas in Centreville, featuring live music by Brandon and Thordis.
Santa's 18-Wheel Chrome-and-Steel Sleigh goes on sale Oct. 21 from Mascot Kids.
For more information and to hear the original song, visit santas18wheelchromeandsteelsleigh.com

title: National Music Festival alumni to perform at benefit concert for Emmanuel Episcopal Church
author: Staff Writer
content:
National Music Festival alumni to perform at benefit concert for Emmanuel Episcopal Church

 September 27, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Staff Writer | Section: News

 CHESTERTOWN — The National Music Festival, a community-driven event in Chestertown that supports young professional musicians through mentorship, lodging, meals and scholarships, will hold a special fundraising concert Sunday, Oct. 5, at 4 p.m.The concert, hosted by Emmanuel Episcopal Church, will celebrate the church's contributions to the Festival each June. Two acclaimed Festival alumni — cellist David Agia and pianist Leili Asanbekova — will return to perform at Emmanuel Episcopal Church, 101 N. Cross St. Tickets will be available at the door for $20, with proceeds supporting the free lunches the church provides to Festival musicians.
Emmanuel Church's role
Emmanuel Episcopal Church plays a pivotal role in the annual Festival, offering spaces for rehearsals and performances and providing weekday lunches to musicians, mentors and staff.
Festival Executive Director Caitlin Patton praised the support, saying: "It's the generosity of the Chestertown community — particularly our host families and Emmanuel Church — that makes our Festival possible and our community special. This fundraising concert will recognize, at least in a small way, all the essential volunteer effort and generous support that Emmanuel Church provides."
Featured musicians
Cellist David Agia has performed as a chamber musician, recitalist and orchestral player at venues including Carnegie Hall, Alte Oper Frankfurt, Palacio de Festivales, Symphony Space in New York and Historische Stadthalle Wuppertal. He has appeared in numerous festivals and master classes. Agia is an adjunct professor of cello at Rowan University.
Pianist Leili Asanbekova began studying music at age 6. She has performed at concerts, government events and festivals, and won several local and international competitions. She has collaborated with conductors including Marek Moś, Vladimir Spivakov and Yuri Simonov. She is pursuing her Doctor of Music degree at the University of Maryland.
Concert program
The concert will feature three works for cello and piano by Italian and Spanish composers.
Alfredo Casella and Mario Castelnuovo-Tedesco were members of Italy's "Generazione dell'80," tasked with creating a "new Italian sound." Both had complicated relationships with the fascist Italian government. Castelnuovo-Tedesco, who was Jewish, emigrated to the United States in 1939, finishing his career in Hollywood.
Early 20th-century Spanish composer and cellist Gaspar Cassadò's music reflects his Catalan roots. A student of Pablo Casals, he dedicated his cello and piano piece Requiebros to his teacher.
About the Festival
The National Music Festival brings together world-class mentors and young professional apprentices for two weeks each June. The 14th season will run May 31–June 13, 2026.
Apprentices receive full scholarships and housing, mostly with local host families. They rehearse and perform alongside mentors in orchestral, chamber and solo recitals, presenting more than 30 concerts and dozens of open rehearsals.
More information on the Festival, tickets and donations is available at https://nationalmusic.us

title: Dove Valley's groovy, wayout Winestock festival draws 1,000 'hippies'
author: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com
content:
Dove Valley's groovy, wayout Winestock festival draws 1,000 'hippies'

 October 1, 2025 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Carl Hamilton cahamilton@chespub.com | Section: News 
 
 447
